text:
VIC, Spain — Carles Puigdemont, the leader spearheading Catalonia's push for independence, has appealed for European Union intervention in negotiations with Spain regarding the territory's future. Yet, for many locals, the aggressive police response to a prohibited independence vote has closed the door on any potential compromise. 

Politicians across the separatist stronghold of Osona county argue that the deployment of batons and rubber bullets against voters has left the pro-independence movement with only one acceptable outcome: complete secession. 

Joan Coma, a councilor representing the anti-capitalist Popular Unity Candidacy (CUP)—a minor party holding significant leverage over Puigdemont's administration—stated that residents have completely severed ties with the Spanish state, adding that independence will happen unilaterally. Coma, a councilor in the regional capital of Vic, was arrested last year and subsequently released in June while facing charges of inciting civil disobedience. 

Prior to the Sunday vote, members of Puigdemont’s PdeCat party indicated an openness to settling for enhanced political and fiscal autonomy rather than total separation for Catalonia, an industrial and tourism hub that generates a fifth of Spain's economic output and possesses its own language. However, widespread outrage over the crackdown by Madrid—which deemed the vote illegal—makes that path politically perilous. Pursuing anything less than independence risks alienating the grassroots base and fracturing Puigdemont's own governing coalition in the regional parliament.

The Catalan National Assembly (ANC), an influential pro-independence organization responsible for mobilizing massive past demonstrations, viewed Puigdemont's call for mediation as a bid to secure EU recognition for a newly established Catalan state. Adria Alsina, an ANC spokesperson, explained that the EU would facilitate discussions culminating in an agreement that necessarily involves Catalan independence. 

During a Tuesday evening address, Puigdemont announced his intention to ask the separatist-dominated Catalan parliament to formally declare independence within 48 hours of the referendum vote tally, potentially happening as early as the weekend. Such a move would give Spanish Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy grounds to trigger constitutional powers suspending the regional government and calling fresh elections. Critics argue this nuclear option risks fueling further unrest in a territory where secessionists compare Rajoy's tactics to the regime of the late dictator Francisco Franco, whose government suppressed the Catalan language prior to his death in 1975.

An EU representative declined to clarify whether the union would step in to mediate, noting that such involvement in an internal affair of a member state would be highly unusual. While expressing confidence in Rajoy's handling of the situation, the EU executive branch urged both sides to engage in dialogue and reminded Madrid of the importance of upholding citizens' fundamental rights.

Tuesday saw tens of thousands demonstrators take to the streets across Catalonia to condemn the previous Sunday's police violence. The vote has triggered Spain's most severe constitutional crisis in decades and presents a major political hurdle for Rajoy, a conservative known for his inflexible approach to the issue. Meanwhile, citizens outside Catalonia largely oppose independence. In an uncommon intervention on Tuesday, Spain's King Felipe VI accused secessionist leaders of breaking democratic rules and fracturing Catalan society.

Conversations with five pro-independence politicians throughout Osona, a region of farming communities, point to a hardened resolve following the clashes, which Catalan authorities report left roughly 900 people injured region-wide. Jordi Casals, a 39-year-old councilor representing the center-left Esquerra Republicana party in Torello, declared that fear has vanished and turning back is no longer an option. Casals recalled that when he entered politics more than ten years ago, separatist rallies drew only a few thousand attendees, whereas Sunday saw 2.26 million people participate out of 5.34 million registered voters, with approximately 90 percent favoring independence according to regional officials. Unionist voters, however, largely stayed away from the ballot boxes.

Puigdemont maintained a degree of ambiguity regarding his objectives for EU-mediated talks. On Monday, he mentioned that mediation must include a commitment to restoring institutional normalcy. Coma argued that the higher turnout compared to a 2014 informal poll rendered the referendum results binding, prompting the CUP to mobilize local committees to initiate the separation from Spain. The CUP remains vital to the survival of the pro-independence regional government, having previously pushed out Artur Mas as leader in favor of Puigdemont due to stalled progress following the 2014 ballot.

The shift toward widespread separatism gained momentum in 2010 after Spain’s Constitutional Court struck down modifications to Catalonia's autonomy statute, which had previously defined the region as a nation and granted priority to the Catalan language. That ruling sparked a massive protest in Barcelona the following week, where one million people marched under the banner, "We are a nation. We decide!"

Jordi Fabrega, the mayor of Sant Pere de Torello—a town that issued a symbolic declaration of independence in 2012—stated that trusting the Spanish state has repeatedly led to betrayal and broken promises. 

In Vic, a banner bearing the message "EUROPE HELP US" hung from an apartment building on Tuesday. Despite international backlash against the police tactics, most EU member states have voiced opposition to secession. 

Although Rajoy mentioned the possibility of a negotiated settlement this week while defending the police intervention, he firmly rejected independence and advocated for all-party talks to resolve the crisis, leaving the door open to expanded autonomy. 

For residents of Osona towns, situated about an hour north of Barcelona and home to over 150,000 people, the Spanish government's primary role is tax collection, while regional authorities handle healthcare, schools, and local policing. Listening to the radio broadcast post-referendum news in her kitchen, 58-year-old Elvira Ramisa remarked that seeing Rajoy on television offers no sense of representation, as he simply does not speak for her.

BERLIN (Reuters) - Even though negotiations to establish a three-way government collapsed, Chancellor Angela Merkel’s conservative allies are firmly backing her leadership. This steadfast support gives her breathing room and places the responsibility squarely on her rivals in the Social Democratic Party to resolve the country's political deadlock. 

This solid backing from her party is particularly important because certain members of the Social Democratic Party (SPD) previously suggested in private that their condition for reviving a "grand coalition" with the conservatives would be the removal of Merkel herself. Following an inconclusive vote on September 24, the failure of the coalition talks late on Sunday has pushed Germany into its most severe political crisis since the conclusion of World War Two. 

President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, actively working to forge an agreement, understands that Germany's international influence stems directly from its economic strength. Consequently, businesses are eager for a stable coalition to be established quickly to eliminate uncertainty and prevent another round of voting. 

After suffering significant losses in September, SPD leader Martin Schulz—whose party stands as Germany's second-largest and served as the junior partner to Merkel's conservatives in the previous parliament—has maintained that the SPD should rebuild from the opposition benches. However, with Merkel's position inside the Christian Democrats (CDU) secure for the moment, the burden falls on the SPD to assist in creating a coalition now that her attempts to partner with the liberal Free Democrats (FDP) and the Greens have fallen through.

Polling indicates that holding new elections would likely yield outcomes very similar to the September vote. Furthermore, an Infratest Dimap survey conducted for the broadcaster ARD this week revealed that 58 percent of voters want Merkel to stay on as chancellor. While the SPD hesitates, Merkel appears reasonable in her attempts to clear the deadlock.

"One thing is clear: Angela Merkel s position in the CDU is very strong. She is our Number One," David McAllister, a member of the CDU executive committee, told Reuters. Her party is convinced she exhausted all possibilities in trying to build a three-way partnership. These efforts also mended relations with the CDU's Bavarian sister party within the conservative bloc, the Christian Social Union (CSU), which had previously experienced friction over migration issues. 

Another high-ranking CDU official emphasized that replacing Merkel was out of the question because the party lacks a viable alternative. Volker Kauder, who leads the conservative parliamentary group in the lower house, stated that he hopes the Social Democrats will reconsider their refusal to enter another grand coalition.

As part of his broader initiative to encourage a coalition government and prevent additional elections, Steinmeier is scheduled to meet with Schulz on Thursday at 1400 GMT. When questioned about the potential for the SPD to back a minority government led by Merkel or join a fresh grand coalition, an SPD representative pointed toward Schulz's upcoming discussion with Steinmeier, noting, "then we will see what comes afterwards." 

Having previously served as an SPD leader, Steinmeier is holding meetings with heads of all parliamentary parties this week and hopes they can reach a consensus on a new government "in the near future." Merkel's authority is unlikely to face serious challenges until a new administration is in place—and even then, not immediately. 

Only Konrad Adenauer, who guided Germany’s post-war recovery, and her mentor Helmut Kohl have served as German chancellors longer than Merkel. At 63 years old, Merkel decided to seek another term only last November following deep deliberation, stating at the time that she intended to continue "if health allows." Back in 1998, she remarked, "I don t want to be a half-dead wreck when I leave politics." 

She currently appears to be in strong health. Nonetheless, having already governed for 12 years, questions regarding her eventual successor are bound to surface before she completes even half of a new four-year term. For now, however, potential successors are holding back. 

"She will have probably a year or so after a government is formed before the question of her succession becomes an overwhelming issue in German domestic politics," remarked Jan Techau of the American Academy in Berlin. "The moment that starts, her power will be greatly diminished."

Yet, Merkel's immediate task is to construct a new administration. Should Steinmeier fail to persuade the SPD to join a renewed grand coalition, alternative pathways include revisiting a three-way coalition, forming a minority government led by Merkel, or holding fresh elections. 

"Since snap elections won t change relative strengths, my prediction is ... another grand coalition between the only two parties that have learned to compromise," noted Josef Joffe, who serves as the publisher and editor of the weekly newspaper Die Zeit. 

Additionally, the Bild newspaper published a report on Wednesday indicating that certain SPD lawmakers are now questioning their party's stance against a revived grand coalition. Reversing course to partner with Merkel once more could necessitate a leadership transition within the SPD, potentially leading to a shake-up during the party conference slated for early December. 

"The pressure needs to build up within the Social Democratic party," Techau observed, adding that Merkel should concentrate on acting as a responsible caretaker chancellor until a new government materializes. "She just needs to play her own game well and then she can survive."

NEW YORK (Reuters) - Legal action targeting U.S. President Donald Trump regarding foreign payments has broadened. On Tuesday, an updated complaint was submitted to the U.S. District Court in Manhattan by a nonprofit watchdog group that alleges the president is breaching the Constitution by permitting foreign governments to patronize his hotels and eateries. 

The revision introduces new plaintiffs: a restaurant industry association featuring prominent culinary figures Tom Colicchio and Alice Waters among its members, along with a Washington, D.C.-based hotel event planner. This update aims to counter questions regarding whether the initial watchdog organization, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, suffered direct harm and consequently possessed the legal standing required to bring the suit. 

Trump’s response to the filing is anticipated by April 21, following his earlier dismissal of the initial Jan. 23 lawsuit as meritless. Representatives for the U.S. Department of Justice did not promptly provide comments when requested on Tuesday. 

According to the modified legal filing, Trump breaches the constitutional “emoluments” provision—which forbids him from receiving assorted foreign government gifts absent congressional consent—by retaining his business empire ownership, even though management duties have been handed over to his sons, Donald Jr. and Eric. 

The document notes that members of the Restaurant Opportunities Centers (ROC) United Inc, encompassing upwards of 200 dining establishments and nearly 25,000 employees, have suffered unfair losses in patronage, tips, and wages to rival Trump enterprises. Meanwhile, the additional plaintiff, Jill Phaneuf, is employed by a hospitality firm organizing events at hotels situated near Washington's foreign diplomat-heavy "Embassy Row," asserting that Trump's ventures are depriving her of commissions. 

Foreign governments attempting to "curry favor" with Trump by patronizing his establishments result in direct harm to these plaintiffs, the lawsuit argues. The filing highlights that this dynamic has manifested since Trump assumed the presidency, pointing to China granting him trademark approvals after he committed to upholding the "One China" stance maintained by previous administrations. 

The complaint references a statement by White House Press Secretary Sean Spicer: "When asked why defendant changed his position on the One China policy, and whether he had gotten something in exchange from China, White House Press Secretary Sean Spicer answered: 'The President always gets something.'"

U.S. District Judge Ronnie Abrams, designated to the bench by former Democratic President Barack Obama, is presiding over the case. 

Erwin Chemerinsky, dean of the University of California at Irvine law school and part of the legal team representing the plaintiffs, emphasized in a released statement that the lawsuit aims to “uphold one of the most basic aspects of the rule of law: no one, including the president, is above the law.” 

The legal matter is officially docketed as Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington et al v. Trump within the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York under No. 17-00458.

TAMPA, Fla. (Reuters) — Delivering what is expected to be his final major address on counterterrorism, President Barack Obama asserted on Tuesday that military force alone will not eradicate terrorism, while broadly defending his national security policies. Speaking at MacDill Air Force Base in Tampa, Florida, Obama maintained that his policies successfully diminished al Qaeda into a mere fraction of its past strength and forced Islamic State onto the defensive, though he cautioned that the threat of terrorism persists for the nation. 

“Rather than offer false promises that we can eliminate terrorism by dropping more bombs or deploying more and more troops or fencing ourselves off from the rest of the world, we have to take a long view of the terrorist threat and we have to pursue a smart strategy that can be sustained,” the president told the audience. 

On Jan. 20, Obama is set to hand over the presidency to Republican President-elect Donald Trump, who frequently attacked the current administration's counterterrorism tactics. Throughout the campaign, Trump labeled Obama and Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton as the "co-founders" of Islamic State, holding them responsible for the militant organization's initial expansion. 

Although the White House maintained that the address had been scheduled well ahead of the Nov. 8 election and was not intended as a direct rebuke to the incoming administration, Obama emphasized the necessity of upholding American laws and democratic principles. He explicitly pushed back against bringing back waterboarding and implementing religious tests for immigrants—both measures previously endorsed by Trump. 

“The whole objective of these terrorists is to scare us into changing who we are and our democracy,” Obama stated. 

Shortly after assuming the presidency in January 2009, Obama issued an executive order prohibiting waterboarding alongside other "enhanced interrogation techniques," commonly referred to as EITs, though future commanders-in-chief retain the authority to overturn such directives. Waterboarding, which mimics the sensation of drowning, has been widely condemned as torture by human rights organizations and numerous members of Congress. 

While Trump has advocated for "extreme vetting" regarding specific refugee groups entering the country, his earlier campaign proposals included a complete ban on foreign-born Muslims entering the United States. 

When he first took office, Obama intended to wind down American military involvement in Afghanistan and Iraq, shifting the focus toward targeting militant threats against the U.S. wherever they arose. Yet, after over 14 and a half years of conflict, he ultimately had to deploy troops back to Iraq and maintain thousands of personnel in Afghanistan. 

According to Obama, the administration’s strategy of backing local allies instead of launching large-scale ground invasions has proven successful, citing ongoing advancements in the effort to recapture Mosul, Iraq, from Islamic State. 

Conversely, certain counterterrorism analysts argue that the emergence of Islamic State highlights a delayed response by Obama to developing dangers. Robin Simcox, a research fellow at the Heritage Foundation, remarked that Obama's "legacy has been tarnished by the way terrorist groups have regenerated and strengthened in the latter parts of his presidency," despite successful U.S. operations to eliminate specific militant leaders.

Known for its rigorous fact-checking, strong moral compass, and historical avoidance of partisanship, the esteemed American publication The Atlantic generally steers clear of endorsing candidates in presidential races. Operating since 1857, the magazine has broken its own rule only on rare occasions. The first instance occurred when they backed Republican Abraham Lincoln due to his stance against slavery. At that time, the magazine explained that the Republican Party and its nominee offered the sole sensible exit from the nation's severe crisis. Backing Lincoln on behalf of the publication, Lowell pointed out that the core strength of the Republicans stemmed from a moral opposition to slavery, further noting that Lincoln possessed sufficient public experience to function as a statesman rather than a mere politician.

Decades later, racism prompted The Atlantic to make its second-ever presidential endorsement, this time throwing its support behind Lyndon B. Johnson. Rather than showering Johnson with effusive praise, the magazine’s stance primarily served as a rejection of Barry Goldwater's overt racism. Editor Edward Weeks highlighted Johnson's commitment to foreign policy continuity dating back to the Marshall Plan, while also praising the president's ability to resolve civil rights issues and prevent the country from following South Africa's path. Conversely, the editors sharply criticized Goldwater, writing that his tendency to view criticism personally and attack outlets like the New York Times, the Washington Post, and Izvestia echoed Joseph McCarthy rather than the Southwest. While questioning Goldwater's judgment and factionalism, the editors stated they did not doubt his honesty.

Faced with what they view as a hazardous and bigoted demagogue, The Atlantic has chosen to endorse Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton. Much like past endorsements, this decision centers more heavily on the perceived perils of a Trump presidency than on Clinton herself. Although the publication acknowledged Clinton's extensive record in public service, their official statement primarily spotlights the clear risks associated with Donald Trump. 

The magazine described Trump as lacking any public service background or qualifications, comparing his demeanor to an infomercial salesman. Their assessment characterized him as secretive, erratic, xenophobic, appallingly sexist, and heavily reliant on conspiracy theories and racist language. They also pointed out his admiration for authoritarian leaders, his own authoritarian tendencies, his susceptibility to being provoked—a dangerous trait for someone handling the nuclear arsenal—along with his disregard for facts, ignorance of the Constitution, and apparent aversion to reading.

This critical perspective extends far beyond the editorial board of The Atlantic. A massive, unprecedented wave of prominent officeholders and policymakers from Trump's own party—levels not seen since Goldwater ran in 1964—have publicly disavowed him. Long before launching his presidential campaign, Trump positioned himself at the center of the birther movement, an effort aimed at demonizing the nation's first African American president and stoking fear among white Americans regarding dark-skinned foreigners. Having achieved tremendous success with this strategy, he now stands on the threshold of the presidency.

Given this context, the editors of The Atlantic are justified in taking this stand. The fact that a historically non-partisan institution, which has only opposed or supported candidates three times since 1857, has issued such severe warnings about one major candidate speaks volumes. A Donald Trump presidency goes beyond mere embarrassment or bigotry, threatening to become a reckless international and national emergency. While voters outside of the Democratic camp might discount the views of a dedicated Clinton supporter, the perspective offered by a publication like The Atlantic is certainly worth pausing to consider.

Following their victory in the 2016 presidential election, fueled significantly by outreach to the white working class throughout Rust Belt communities, the Republican party positioned itself as a champion for middle-class economic struggles. Yet, that alliance appeared to dissolve rapidly, with coal miners—often viewed as a pillar of American manual labor across West Virginia and Kentucky—becoming early casualties. While Democrats like Hillary Clinton struggled in coal regions due to a perceived disconnect, despite proposing alternative programs for a declining sector, Trump and other Republicans capitalized by pledging industrial revival. 

Presently, a potential government shutdown looms over the refusal of Republicans to fund these workers' healthcare and pension programs. Dismissing the proposal as a "bailout," conservative lawmakers are currently blocking an amendment introduced by Democratic Senator Joe Manchin. This legislative addition aims to rescue the United Mine Workers health and pension framework, which collapsed following the 2007-2008 financial crisis. 

Should the GOP persist in blocking the measure—potentially triggering a government shutdown—more than 16,000 retired miners and their dependents risk losing their health and pension benefits. Manchin’s proposed amendment provides temporary relief extending to April 28, ahead of subsequent budget deliberations. He is collaborating with West Virginia Republican Senator Shelley Moore Capito and Ohio Democrat Sherrod Brown. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell has also expressed support for the amendment's inclusion, although he blocked consideration of it previously and has requested that Democrats pass the continuing resolution without holding up the miner provisions. 

Beyond Capito and McConnell, broader Republican support remains absent, with opponents characterizing the initiative as a government bailout that could establish a dangerous precedent for rescuing other distressed pension and healthcare structures. Meanwhile, Democrats argue that while Wall Street institutions historically received massive taxpayer bailouts, coal miners who fuel the nation are being denied similar support and labeled as asking for handouts. With Democratic senators leading the charge to protect these workers, the legislative standoff threatens a government shutdown if an agreement among Manchin, Capito, Brown, and their colleagues is not reached.

As Donald Trump fills his cabinet with ultra-conservative members of Congress, several seats are left vacant and require special elections. Democrats anticipated picking up at least a couple of these seats, particularly in the Georgia District 6 election featuring Jon Ossoff. Yet, the party missed the mark by under four points, even though Tom Price—who departed to head the Department of Health and Human Services under Trump—had won the same district by more than twenty points the previous November. Across all recent special elections, a clear pattern has emerged showing Democrats achieving significant point-wise gains. Still, moral victories fall short of actual wins, leading to a wave of finger-pointing aimed directly at House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi.

Democratic figures like Ohio Representative Tim Ryan are demanding that Pelosi step aside to make room for new leadership. Reflecting on the Ossoff defeat and the state of the party, Ryan stated that members need to take a long, hard look in the mirror to recognize that the party itself is the root of the problem. He commended Ossoff as a stellar candidate who was nonetheless dragged down by the national baggage of the Democratic Party. It is worth noting that Ryan previously mounted an unsuccessful challenge against Pelosi for her leadership post last November, which could leave lingering bitterness. Massachusetts Representative Seth Moulton also voiced opposition to retaining Pelosi, arguing that the party lacks a concrete plan, a clear vision, and a compelling message explaining why Democrats offer a better alternative rather than simply pointing out that Trump is bad. Moulton believes this shortcoming was clearly exposed in the Georgia race.

However, this criticism misses the mark because Ossoff did not run a campaign against Trump; instead, his platform focused on the economy and healthcare. The factors that largely hindered his bid included a thin resume, the district's forty-year history of solid Republican control, and a united GOP front contrasted with internal Democratic divisions. Throughout the race, numerous Democrats criticized Ossoff for not being liberal enough, and he failed to adequately address the controversy surrounding his residency outside the district he sought to represent.

In the author's view, targeting Nancy Pelosi in this manner would lead to catastrophe. The 2016 cycle divided the party between the hard left faction of Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren and the center-left camp of Hillary Clinton and Barack Obama, yielding poor results. When the party lies in ruins, members must unite to confront their shared adversary: the Republicans who are actively dismantling the United States. While Democrats argue among themselves, demand ideological purity, and attack people holding identical values, the opposition is rolling back civil rights, gerrymandering districts to neutralize Democratic ballots, utilizing false claims of voter fraud to suppress participation, threatening to strip away healthcare, dismantling public education, and jeopardizing the future of the planet.

The standard arguments against Pelosi suggest she represents the Old Guard and must step down because Republicans consistently tie every candidate to her image as an out-of-touch San Francisco liberal, intimidating moderates who fear far-left policies. Yet, regardless of who holds leadership roles, opponents will deploy the exact same rhetoric. They routinely characterize all Democrats as carbon copies of Nancy Pelosi, Bernie Sanders, and Elizabeth Warren, ignoring the vast diversity within the party. That very diversity can become a tremendous asset rather than a liability if internal conflicts cease long enough to heal the fractures of 2016.

Fortunately, the Democratic National Committee appears to push back against this hazardous push originating inside the House Democratic Caucus. Deputy Chairman Keith Ellison commented on the situation by pointing out that Republicans have controlled the seat for thirty-seven years, noting that in a standard year Democrats would have no chance at all, yet they managed to narrow the gap dramatically and put the opposition on the defensive. 

Former Republican Congressman and MSNBC Morning Joe host Joe Scarborough offered perspective on the matter, warning that using Pelosi as a scapegoat provides no benefit to Democrats and advising the party to select candidates who fit their specific districts to secure victories. 

This assessment holds true. Running a New York City liberal in Ohio makes little sense; instead, finding figures similar to Tim Ryan would help carry the entire state. While difficult to admit, regions like South Carolina, rural North Carolina, and Georgia call for figures closer to Joe Manchin than Maxine Waters. A conservative Democrat remains preferable to a Republican under any circumstances. When feasible in those regions, running candidates like Claire McCaskill aligns the contender with the local political environment, adjusts their stances accordingly, and paves the way for victory by properly reading the regional landscape. Above all, the party must recruit figures capable of resonating with the working class, such as Wisconsin Democrat Randy Bryce, who released a compelling campaign ad for his challenge against House Speaker Paul Ryan. Pairing a robust economic message for working families with the overarching platform of tolerance and acceptance—while contrasting it against Republican bigotry—creates a winning formula.

Engaging in internal attacks, revisiting the 2016 primaries and general elections, and prolonging infighting only serves to fracture the party further. Undermining the most effective fundraiser in the House Democratic Caucus—who also historicized the nation as the first female House Speaker—certainly does not offer a solution. 

All members belong to the Democratic Party, sharing core values and drawing strength from diversity. Unifying the party will allow members to rebuild and remove the GOP from Congress in 2018 and the White House in 2020.

TEGUCIGALPA (Reuters) - Following a disputed and delayed presidential vote tally that triggered accusations of fraud from the opposition, Honduras saw civil unrest result in at least one protester fatality, more than 20 injuries, and over 100 arrests related to looting. The electoral tribunal announced that the final outcome of the previous Sunday's presidential election was scheduled for release on Friday at 9 p.m. local time (0300 GMT), though opposition objections threatened to stall the release. 

Initially, counted ballots covering more than half the electorate put television personality and opposition candidate Salvador Nasralla ahead by a five-point margin. The momentum shifted toward the U.S.-backed, center-right incumbent President Juan Orlando Hernandez after tabulation stopped on Monday and remained frozen for over a day, which ignited the demonstrations. 

With Hernandez leading by fewer than 50,000 votes—roughly 1.5 percentage points—when counting was paused, the tribunal announced plans to manually tally about 1,031 disputed ballot boxes containing irregularities, accounting for approximately 6 percent of the total. Nevertheless, Nasralla's center-left coalition demanded a recount across three of the nation's 18 departments and rejected the tribunal's specialized count until their broader review conditions were satisfied. 

Marlon Ochoa, campaign manager for Nasralla's coalition, stated that they are prepared to acknowledge a fair victory by Juan Orlando, but asserted their knowledge that Nasralla actually won, which is why transparency requests are being denied.

International worry has intensified surrounding the political crisis in the impoverished Central American nation, which battles severe drug gang violence and maintains some of the highest homicide rates globally. According to police, a man suffered fatal gunshot wounds during a demonstration in La Ceiba, while approximately 12 law enforcement and military personnel sustained injuries during Friday protests that blocked traffic near the country's primary port and in various other locations. The Hospital Escuela in Tegucigalpa reported at least 10 injured demonstrators in the capital. 

Following police accounts of looting in Tegucigalpa and other urban areas, military leaders urged the public to keep demonstrations peaceful. In San Pedro Sula, the nation's second-largest city, demonstrators set fire to tires, filling the sky with thick black smoke while police deployed tear gas to disperse the gatherings. A police representative reported that on Friday, over 100 individuals were detained on suspicion of looting in San Pedro Sula, with local news broadcasts showing footage of ransacked stores.

As angry demonstrators blocked major thoroughfares and supply lines nationwide on Friday, residents rushed to supermarkets to hoard groceries and supplies. Queues formed at gasoline stations and ATMs, while banks filled with customers seeking to manage their funds. 

Carlos Valle, a 61-year-old retiree waiting in a lengthy queue for fuel in Tegucigalpa, remarked that he was filling his tank in anticipation of trouble because the situation appeared concerning and protests were occurring throughout the city.

Both Hernandez and Nasralla, a leftist-aligned game show host, declared themselves winners following the election. The challenger stated he would refuse to acknowledge the tribunal's outcome due to suspicions surrounding the tabulation procedures. The 64-year-old Nasralla, heading a center-left coalition, is among the country's most recognizable figures and enjoys the support of former President Manuel Zelaya, a leftist removed from power via a 2009 coup. Zelaya intervened on Thursday via a written statement, charging the tribunal with committing "electoral crimes" to benefit Hernandez, who sought re-election thanks to a controversial Supreme Court decision in 2015. 

Furthermore, one of the four magistrates on the electoral tribunal expressed "serious doubts" regarding the counting procedure on Thursday.

Although the Organization of American States (OAS) successfully persuaded both contenders on Wednesday to pledge adherence to the final outcome after reviewing contested ballots, Nasralla repudiated the agreement just hours later. Claiming his rivals sought to steal the election from him, he called upon his supporters to demonstrate in the streets.

Trump's protectionist policies top risk to U.S. economy in 2017: Reuters poll

(Reuters) - Economists have largely bypassed the market enthusiasm that followed the unexpected November election, revealing instead through a Reuters survey that Donald Trump's protectionist stances represent the primary danger to U.S. growth this year. Throughout his electoral bid and subsequently, the incoming president-elect pledged major overhauls to immigration and trade frameworks, floated the idea of heavy duties on Chinese merchandise, and introduced plans for substantial tax reductions. 

Despite recent pullbacks in financial markets and a cooling of immediate inflation expectations, stocks continue to reach record levels while U.S. 10-year Treasury yields have climbed over 25 percent since Election Day. Even so, when polled over the past week, more than two-thirds of the 70 participants answering the specific question identified these protectionist measures as the greatest threat facing the world's largest economy in 2017.

Jim O’Sullivan of High Frequency Economics remarked that the possibility of the incoming administration acting on its anti-free trade rhetoric sits near the very peak of downside concerns. O’Sullivan, who earned the top ranking as a forecaster of U.S. economic data in Reuters polls for 2016 for the second consecutive year, noted his assumption that the new administration will approach the matter pragmatically. 

An additional near-term hazard stems from the strong dollar, which gained roughly 6 percent following Trump's victory and touched a 14-year high early this month. These concerns regarding the surging currency and Trump's confrontational approach are expected to dominate discussions among business and political figures gathering in Davos, Switzerland, for the World Economic Forum.

Proposed infrastructure spending and sweeping tax cuts for individuals and corporations have likewise failed to improve growth projections for the U.S. economy, a metric Trump has targeted to push to 3.5 percent. Given that the economy is nearing full employment—with December recording an unemployment rate of 4.7 percent—over 80 percent of survey participants rejected the notion that this is an appropriate moment for such aggressive tax relief.

Recent survey estimates indicate that fourth-quarter growth slowed to 2.2 percent, down from 3.5 percent in the third quarter. Economists project that the economy will expand at an annual pace between 2.1 percent and 2.5 percent across each quarter of 2017, representing just a 0.1 percentage point increase from earlier forecasts, with the full-year median sitting at 2.3 percent. The highest anticipated growth rate for any single period in 2017 reached 4.1 percent, remaining well below the post-financial crisis peak of 5.6 percent recorded in the fourth quarter of 2009.

O’Sullivan, who held the most optimistic growth outlook among top forecasters, suggested that while people may have assumed growth-reducing protectionism would not be enacted, they might have simultaneously overestimated the extent of fiscal stimulus and resulting economic acceleration. 

Fewer than one-third of survey participants—including three individuals ranked among the top 10 U.S. economic forecasters in previous Reuters polls—revised their 2017 growth predictions upward in the latest survey. Many of these analysts shared O’Sullivan’s view, grounding their revisions in the expectation that Trump would bypass his restrictive trade initiatives in favor of fiscal stimulus.

While these projected expansion speeds might appear healthy given the advanced stage of the economic recovery cycle, they are unlikely to drive inflation significantly past the Federal Reserve’s 2 percent goal. Instead, inflationary pressures are more probable to emerge from retaliatory tariffs if the administration's protectionist platform becomes a global reality. Although wage growth is projected to average 3.0 percent throughout the year—an increase from December's 2.8 percent estimate—the Core PCE Price Index, which serves as the Fed's preferred inflation metric, is anticipated to average 1.8 percent in 2017 and 2.0 percent in 2018, keeping pace with prior projections.

Federal Reserve officials recently cautioned that an expansive fiscal policy amid near full employment could accelerate interest rate increases beyond current market pricing, thereby lifting the U.S. dollar further. O’Sullivan noted that additional declines in the unemployment rate would increase upward pressure on wages and inflation, strengthening the argument for monetary tightening by the Fed.

The broader survey, encompassing over 100 economists and 17 major financial institutions that trade directly with the central bank, indicated that interest rates will likely hold steady between 0.50 percent and 0.75 percent until a 25-basis-point increase materializes in the second quarter. A subsequent rate adjustment is anticipated during the fourth quarter, which would bring the federal funds target range to between 1.00 percent and 1.25 percent, though 14 economists projected a hike as early as March.

WASHINGTON — Urging U.S. Senate Republicans to finally make good on nearly a decade of campaign pledges, President Donald Trump delivered a final appeal on Monday to repeal and replace the signature healthcare legislation of former President Barack Obama. 

Ahead of Tuesday’s scheduled Senate vote regarding whether to advance a healthcare overhaul, Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell committed to a thorough and open amendment process. Speaking at the White House on Monday, Trump pressed lawmakers to act. “To every member of the Senate I say this: The American people have waited long enough. There’s been enough talk, and no action. Now is the time for action,” he stated.

Framed by families who claimed they suffered under the 2010 law commonly referred to as Obamacare, the president added, “So far, Senate Republicans have not done their job in ending the Obamacare nightmare.” 

Although the availability of sufficient votes for McConnell to successfully open debate remained uncertain as of Monday, leadership confirmed the vote would proceed as planned. “I know many of us have waited years for this moment to finally arrive. And, at long last, it finally has. I would urge every colleague to join me,” said McConnell. 

According to his office, Senator John McCain is planning to travel back from Arizona, where he has been recovering from brain cancer, in order to participate in the vote. Meanwhile, moderate Republican Senator Susan Collins reaffirmed her opposition on Monday, announcing she will vote against the motion to proceed.

The GOP faces intense political demands to dismantle the 2010 legislation, which conservatives criticize as federal overreach into the healthcare sector. Yet, the party remains severely split. Moderates worry that the proposed Senate legislation would strip coverage from millions of low-income citizens, whereas conservatives argue the cuts do not go far enough. 

With McConnell struggling to build consensus for either a full repeal-and-replace strategy or a clean repeal, the Republican party holds a narrow 52-48 advantage in the Senate. Given unanimous Democratic opposition, McConnell can lose no more than two members of his own party. 

“The question for every senator, Democrat or Republican, is whether they will side with Obamacare’s architects, which have been so destructive to our country, or its forgotten victims?” Trump asked. 

Despite frequently demanding legislative action on the issue, Trump has historically shown limited focus on intricate policy details. After briefly floating the idea of letting the legislation collapse on its own last week, he subsequently pivoted to pressuring senators to reach an agreement. Monday’s address marked some of the president's most extensive public remarks on the subject to date. 

“Obamacare is death. That’s the one that’s death,” remarked Trump. “And besides that, it’s failing so you won’t have it anyway.”

McConnell intends to put forward a procedural vote on the healthcare measure initially passed by the House of Representatives back in May. A successful vote would allow the House legislation to face amendments directly on the Senate floor. 

Projections from the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office indicate that the Senate's alternative measure could result in 22 million individuals losing insurance coverage. Furthermore, a straight repeal of the law without a replacement could strip 32 million people of their health insurance by 2026, according to the CBO. The agency also projected that individual market premiums would jump by 25 percent in the coming year and double by 2026 under a repeal scenario. 

This ongoing legislative ambiguity has left states, insurers, hospitals, and physicians struggling to anticipate future coverage guidelines and financial support. Meanwhile, surveys indicate that the general public remains anxious regarding prospective alterations to the healthcare framework.

WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump threw his support behind embattled Alabama Republican Senate hopeful Roy Moore on Monday ahead of next week's special election, a race upended by accusations of sexual misconduct against the candidate. According to the White House, Trump called Moore to offer his endorsement. The president later posted on Twitter that the GOP requires the former Alabama Supreme Court justice's victory to lock down votes for crucial priorities like immigration and tax reform. 

Pointing out that Democrats refused to back significant tax reductions with a single vote, Trump argued on social media that this makes winning the Alabama seat essential for Republican Roy Moore. 

Expressing gratitude for the presidential endorsement, Moore replied on Twitter using the campaign's signature hashtag, stating he was eager to battle side-by-side with the president to "Make America Great Again!" He also shared a quote where Trump purportedly told him to go get 'em. 

During the September Republican primary, Trump aligned with Senate leadership by backing Luther Strange, Moore's opponent. The president has sharply criticized the Democratic contender, former U.S. Attorney Doug Jones, portraying him as weak on crime and susceptible to control by congressional Democratic leaders. Emphasizing the stakes on Monday, Trump warned that a Democratic victory in the December 12 contest would severely damage the Republican agenda. 

While the White House indicated the president has no plans to campaign directly for Moore, Trump is slated to host a rally on Friday in Pensacola, Florida, which sits right next to Alabama. 

Even though multiple congressional Republicans have kept their distance following the emergence of sexual misconduct claims last month—allegations that Moore has firmly rejected—the Alabama Republican Party continues to stand behind him. 

Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell stated last month that he credited Moore's accusers and joined fellow senators in calling for him to exit the contest, though by Sunday he shifted stance to say the choice belongs to Alabama voters. 

Weighing in on CNN, Republican U.S. Representative Matt Gaetz described the accusations as deeply serious, noting he would struggle significantly to cast a ballot for Moore. At the same time, Gaetz suggested local electors might choose to hold their noses and support Moore over the Democratic alternative. 

Polling released Sunday by CBS News placed Moore ahead of Jones by six percentage points, with a majority of Alabama Republicans dismissing the claims against him as untrue. A prior Washington Post survey from the previous week put Moore up by three percentage points, though that advantage fell within the poll's 4.5-percentage-point margin of error. 

The allegations involve multiple women who state Moore engaged in sexual assault or misconduct decades ago when they were teenagers and he was in his early thirties. These reports have not been independently verified by Reuters. Now seventy years old, Moore resumed campaigning last week, dismissing the accusations as dirty politics.

Senator Ted Cruz is currently working on damage control following sharp public criticism from former House Speaker John Boehner that quickly made major headlines. Boehner, who stepped down from his post last year and therefore operates without political constraints, informed an audience at Stanford University that while he is no fan of Donald Trump, his contempt for Ted Cruz runs even deeper. Explaining the depth of his animosity, the devoutly Catholic ex-politician famously likened Cruz to the devil incarnate, noting that his aversion goes beyond mere political disagreements. Describing him as the most miserable person he has ever collaborated with, Boehner made it clear that their mutual history is strained. 

This sentiment is hardly unique, as numerous individuals seem to arrive at a similar impression upon interacting with him. In reality, familiarity with Cruz often breeds resentment, a phenomenon highlighted by his former college roommate. Recalling his undergraduate days, his roommate noted that people only tolerated Cruz's presence at upperclassman gatherings out of sheer pity, describing his widespread unpopularity as a unique talent, a sentiment echoed by another acquaintance who recalled detesting him shortly after meeting him during their freshman orientation week.

Former legal associates share this widespread antipathy. Interviews conducted with roughly two dozen attorneys who clerked alongside Cruz reveal a picture of a man overly fixated on the death penalty. Several clerks, hailing from both conservative and liberal chambers, characterized his presentation of crimes as resembling cheap pulp fiction, arguing that his dramatic flair belonged in a prosecutor's closing argument rather than before the nation's highest court. 

Elected officials hold a similarly dim view. Former Senator Bob Dole questioned how Cruz plans to manage legislative relationships, bluntly observing that nobody is fond of the junior senator from Texas, suggesting that distance is preferable when it comes to him.

Cruz attempted to brush off Boehner's scathing remarks by claiming unfamiliarity with the former Speaker. Asserting that they are virtually strangers, Cruz maintained that he would be shocked if they had exchanged even fifty words, claiming to have met him on only two or three occasions. This version of events asks the public to believe Cruz never conversed extensively with the very leader he collaborated with during the 2013 government shutdown efforts.

However, the reality is that Cruz is well acquainted with Boehner, having previously served as his legal counsel. During the 1990s, when Boehner sought a conservative attorney to target a Democratic opponent's political standing, Cruz stepped into that role. 

According to reporting from The Washington Post, the legal battle took place in 1998, when Boehner served as the House Republican Conference chairman and filed a lawsuit against Democratic Representative Jim McDermott of Washington over alleged wiretapping violations. The dispute stemmed from a 1996 recorded telephone conference involving Boehner, then-Speaker Newt Gingrich, and others, which had been intercepted via police scanner by a Florida couple. That couple handed the tape to McDermott, who was then the ranking Democrat on the Ethics Committee while Gingrich faced potential sanctions, and McDermott subsequently leaked the recording to The New York Times, sparking Boehner's retaliation.

During this litigation, Cruz was retained and ultimately held public press events backing Boehner. This move coincided with Boehner leveraging the publicity from the legal challenge to raise funds for his own reelection campaign. It stretches credibility to suggest that Cruz and Boehner did not spend significant time collaborating during that era, especially since the partnership offered clear advantages for both parties, helping Boehner secure reelection while allowing Cruz to market himself as a fierce opponent of Democrats, a persona he later utilized to advance his Tea Party platform when pursuing public office.

That approach was reportedly taken by a Texas judge during a naturalization ceremony for immigrants who had completed the process to become U.S. citizens. Federal judge John Primono, who has administered the oath to over 100,000 individuals throughout his career, used the occasion of Donald Trump's election to allegedly breach judicial ethics and basic decency by telling the newly sworn-in citizens that they must accept Trump as their president. Addressing the captive audience, Primono stated that regardless of whether they voted for him, he is their president, and anyone who dislikes that outcome should move to another country, according to video footage from KENS.

Such remarks directed at individuals seeking to become Americans drew significant criticism. Consequently, U.S. District judges removed Primono from presiding over future citizenship ceremonies due to his partisan comments. Meanwhile, conservatives praised him and elevated him to hero status, a reaction critics argue demonstrates his lack of political neutrality and poor judgment. 

When spoken to by KENS, Primono defended his statements, asserting that his comments aimed to deliver a message of unity and were misinterpreted. Denying any intention to speak for or against Donald Trump, he maintained he was simply trying to offer something hopeful and unifying. Critics, however, dismissed this explanation, arguing that instructing new citizens to support Trump under threat of leaving is inherently intimidating rather than unifying, designed to frighten immigrants into compliance. 

In a nation where political dissent is protected, immigrants should not face such threats, particularly given the hostility Donald Trump has directed toward them over the preceding year and a half. Opposition to his presidency is widespread among immigrants, reflecting a broader sentiment shared by millions of Americans who voted against him, despite his victory through the electoral college, and who continue to protest his policies. 

By invoking a divisive figure and instructing a diverse group of new citizens to accept him as their leader, the federal judge overshadowed what should have been a celebratory milestone. The incident raises concerns regarding how many other judges might adopt similar behavior following the transition in January.

MEXICO CITY (Reuters) - Ahead of the 2018 presidential race, Mexico's left-leaning front-runner presented his prospective cabinet on Thursday, featuring an equal number of female and male members alongside a moderate, U.S.-educated economist slated for the finance post. 

Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador, the former mayor of Mexico City who recently held a 12-point advantage in a poll, aims to shift the nation's strategy regarding education, security, and the economy. The 64-year-old candidate has promised increased assistance for impoverished citizens while avoiding the introduction of new taxes or additional debt. 

To lead the finance ministry, Lopez Obrador selected Carlos Manuel Urzua. Urzua is an academic who previously managed finances for the Mexico City government between 2000 and 2003 during Lopez Obrador's tenure as mayor. Having campaigned twice before and finished as runner-up in the previous two elections, the self-proclaimed nationalist is seeking a victory in next July's vote that would swim against a regional tide of conservative Latin American administrations. A potential victory could also heighten tensions with U.S. President Donald Trump, given Trump's anti-immigrant policies and rhetoric.

Frequently referred to as AMLO, Lopez Obrador balanced his proposed team with eight men and eight women. The roster features a former supreme court judge of high regard and a former interior minister who previously served the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party, known as the PRI. 

Selecting Urzua helped reinforce the perspective that AMLO might manage Latin America's second-largest economy with greater pragmatism than his detractors suggest. Marcos Casarin, who directs Latin America macro services at Oxford Economics, noted in an email that an AMLO government appears increasingly moderate macroeconomically, with Urzua's appointment—as a non-extremist economist—supporting that assessment. 

Along with being an author, researcher, and university professor, Urzua holds a Master's degree and a PhD in Economics from the University of Wisconsin, as well as a mathematics undergraduate degree from Mexico's Tecnologico de Monterrey. Additionally, he is a poet who focuses his writing on economic inequality.

For the interior ministry, Lopez Obrador chose Olga Sanchez, who spent twenty years as a Supreme Court justice and contributed to steering the nation's highest court toward more liberal rulings. Esteban Moctezuma, who held the interior portfolio under former President Ernesto Zedillo, was chosen for the education post. Meanwhile, Rocio Nahle—a chemical engineer and the lower house leader for the MORENA party—was designated to head the energy ministry. 

AMLO's competitors in the July 1 ballot are expected to include Ricardo Anaya, leading a right-left coalition, and Jose Antonio Meade, a former finance minister running for the PRI.

A fresh government audit indicates that the "Obamaphone" initiative has accumulated approximately $9 billion in private financial institutions rather than depositing the funds into the federal treasury, according to recent findings that highlight substantial financial windfalls for telecommunications providers. 

The widely discussed Lifeline Program, which supplies cellular devices to low-income individuals, has drawn scrutiny after a Government Accountability Office (GAO) evaluation suggested that over a third of participants might not meet eligibility requirements. Originally established prior to the Obama administration, the cellphone distribution effort became a prominent emblem of governmental inefficiency during that era, earning widespread notoriety alongside viral moments like that of the Cleveland resident who expressed support on camera for the program before later appearing in a follow-up interview to voice disillusionment with the administration.

According to a 90-page analysis requested by Missouri Democratic Senator Claire McCaskill, who serves as the ranking member on the Senate's principal oversight committee and previously worked as a state auditor, the initiative is failing the public due to absent supervision. Describing the current system as reliant on an honor code that permits telecommunications firms to regularly collect government disbursements without adequate checks, McCaskill emphasized that the setup is unsustainable.

Reporting by The Daily Caller noted that the extensive 90-page GAO document points to widespread dishonesty on application forms, with undercover tests revealing that ineligible submissions gained approval in 63 percent of cases. Furthermore, audits indicated that between 36 and 65 percent of recipients across different categories provided easily disprovable false information yet still received benefits. 

This high level of deception occurred largely because the Federal Communications Commission delegated screening duties to telecommunications businesses that stand to gain financially from maximizing their enrollment numbers. During GAO undercover tests, investigators submitted 19 applications using deliberately flawed criteria and successfully secured Lifeline services from 12 out of 19 providers by utilizing fabricated eligibility papers. Applicants merely needed to claim participation in alternative assistance initiatives such as food stamps or supplemental security income.

When legislative changes were previously debated, telecommunications enterprises placed daily full-page advertisements in outlets circulated among Capitol Hill employees. Notably, the spouse of the chief executive officer for TracFone, the primary recipient of the program's funds, served as a major political fundraiser for former President Barack Obama.

The drivers behind these unprecedented fraud levels stemmed from the FCC permitting entities with financial incentives to handle enrollment verification. Providers frequently parked neon-lit vans outside public housing complexes and welfare offices to sign up customers; one woman recounted to The Daily Caller News Foundation Investigative Group that a representative outside an assistance office urged her to register her toddler. 

Investigators discovered that firms neglected to verify qualifications while the FCC failed to enforce compliance or penalize violators. Furthermore, the agency did not supply numerous providers with access to inter-agency databases that could have facilitated basic verification procedures. 

Meanwhile, Michelle Dowry, frequently referred to as the "Obamaphone Lady," subsequently appeared on the program hosted by Alex Jones to state she had become disillusioned, concluding that the administration's promises amounted to a hoax and that the primary tangible offering received by minority communities during the eight-year period was a publicly funded mobile device.

BAGHDAD (Reuters) - Baghdad declared on Thursday that negotiations regarding the reopening of airports and the supply of foreign currency to banks in the Kurdish autonomous zone will remain off the table unless the regional authorities pledge to uphold the unity of Iraq. Following a September 25 independence vote that the central government deemed unlawful, international flights into the territory were grounded. Furthermore, authorities in Baghdad have urged neighboring nations to close off the borders of the landlocked area. Additional isolation tactics included halting dollar sales to four banks owned by Kurds and demanding an end to independent petroleum exports. 

Despite the overwhelming vote in favor of secession, Kurdish leaders have repeatedly pushed for talks. In an official release, the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) urged Prime Minister Haider al-Abadi to engage in dialogue based on the Iraqi Constitution in order to bypass what they termed collective punishment. The KRG expressed readiness for discussions concerning border crossings, commercial trade, public services, banking institutions, and aviation hubs. 

Nonetheless, a spokesperson for the Iraqi administration stated that any dialogue is contingent upon the Kurds renouncing the outcome of the referendum and committing fully to a unified nation. Speaking to Reuters, the official emphasized that the KRG has to recognize federal sovereignty regarding border security, air and land entry points, safety, and petroleum shipments. 

Generations of Kurds have pursued statehood, arguing that the September referendum was merely intended to initiate peaceful negotiations for eventual independence alongside Baghdad. However, the federal government rejected the vote entirely, pointing out that it took place not only within the autonomous zone but also across contested neighboring territories controlled by Kurdish fighters. 

Neighboring Turkey and Iran, both fierce opponents of Kurdish separatism, have backed Baghdad's rigid stance. Even Washington, a long-time ally of the Kurds, had urged them to call off the vote beforehand. On Thursday, an official speaking for Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan announced that Turkey plans to phase out operations at border crossings with the northern region, working alongside the governments in Baghdad and Iran. Additionally, Turkish Prime Minister Binali Yildirim is scheduled to travel to Baghdad on Sunday for discussions with Haidar Abadi.

Friction escalated Wednesday when Kurdish officials alleged that Iraqi troops and Iranian-backed paramilitaries were massing for a significant offensive against Kirkuk—an oil-rich zone—and territory near Mosul. Both areas lie outside the official autonomous region but have been secured by Kurdish forces since the expulsion of Islamic State militants. 

Baghdad rejected claims of an impending military campaign. Prime Minister Abadi assured the public in a written statement that military forces would not be deployed against Kurdish citizens or used to instigate war. A military representative reiterated that no offensive against Kurdish units was underway, explaining instead that government forces were positioning themselves to clear Islamic State fighters from territory near the Syrian border. 

In a related legal development, Iraq's Supreme Judicial Council ordered the arrest on Wednesday of the Kurdish referendum commission's chairman and two assistants for defying an existing court order that had declared the independence vote unconstitutional.

Kirkuk, a ethnically diverse province boasting substantial oil deposits and currently secured by Kurdish fighters, has become a central flashpoint due to competing claims from both the central government and the KRG. Shiite Muslim paramilitaries, known as Popular Mobilisation, alongside federal troops, have taken positions to the south and west of the city in sectors previously held by Islamic State. The Iraqi government spokesperson noted that recognizing federal authority over Kirkuk is yet another prerequisite for any future negotiations.

Meanwhile, Islamic State remnants continue to hold ground near al-Qaim, where the Euphrates river flows from Syria into Iraq. This marks the final pocket of the country still controlled by the militant group, which seized a third of Iraqi territory back in 2014. On Thursday, the military targeted al-Qaim by dropping leaflets instructing insurgents to surrender or face execution. 

While IS still maintains pockets across the border in Syria, it is currently retreating under pressure from multiple opposing forces, including a U.S.-backed and Kurdish-led coalition, as well as Syrian government troops supported by foreign Shiite militias tied to Iran and Russia. The cross-border militant caliphate effectively shattered in July when U.S.-supported Iraqi forces reclaimed Mosul—the group's primary stronghold in Iraq—following a protracted nine-month campaign.

SAN JUAN, PUERTO RICO — Medical infrastructure across Puerto Rico has plunged into a severe crisis following Hurricane Maria. As the most powerful storm to impact the territory in decades, it left healthcare facilities flooded, covered in debris, and heavily reliant on diesel generators to keep vulnerable patients alive. This precarious condition deepens the suffering across the U.S. territory, home to 3.4 million American citizens. 

For certain individuals, evacuation to the United States remains the sole viable path for medical care. Cheira Ruiz and her infant daughter, Gabriellyz—born two weeks ago with a complex heart defect—faced precisely this situation. The newborn was admitted to the Centro Cardiovascular de Puerto Rico in the capital just before Maria struck the previous Wednesday, though operating under such conditions proved impossible for the medical staff. 

Gabriellyz qualified as one of the earliest infants cleared for an emergency medical flight departing the island post-storm. Living two hours south of San Juan in Guanica, her parents received the positive news on Friday when emergency personnel visited their residence to advise them to prepare for a journey to Miami. Because telephone lines were down, physicians had contacted a local radio station to broadcast an appeal for help finding the family. Prior to departure, however, the parents were informed that space permitted only one accompanying passenger, leaving the mother and child to fly to Miami alone. Ruiz expressed her emotional strain on Saturday, noting she was trying to maintain her strength.

Residents across the island awoke to a drastically altered environment after the disaster. Food supplies are running low, and the collapsed electrical grid could take months to repair. Long lines of pedestrians and motorists stretch for blocks as people attempt to secure limited fuel for vehicles and backup generators. With cellular networks, the internet, and email virtually non-existent, the modern infrastructure has been thrust backward in time, leaving radio as a primary lifeline for news.

Hospitals face mounting hurdles everywhere. Backup generators failed rapidly at certain facilities after the power cut out, while others are exhausting their diesel reserves. Fuel has become so scarce that armed escorts now deliver it to prevent theft, according to Dr. Ivan Gonzalez Cancel, who serves as a cardiovascular surgeon and heads the heart transplant program at the Centro Cardiovascular. Gonzalez Cancel mentioned that another facility requested the transfer of two critical patients due to a lack of power, a request they had to decline because they faced identical conditions.

Healthcare workers are similarly struggling with gasoline shortages for their daily commutes, with individuals waiting as long as seven hours at the few operational gas stations. Marilyn Rivera Morales, a nurse at the facility, noted she possessed just enough fuel to drive to work for another two days. Gonzalez Cancel questioned how staff members would manage to arrive if gas supplies ran out entirely.

The fuel shortage represents only the beginning of the center's troubles. Describing the cardiovascular facility as being in shambles, Gonzalez Cancel pointed out that operating room walls dripped with condensation and floors remained slick due to the absence of air conditioning. Although most patients had been discharged or sent elsewhere, a number remained because their relatives could not be reached via telephone. 

Outside the cardiac center on Saturday, Savannah, Georgia residents Jorge Rivera and his wife Dorca spoke with Gonzalez Cancel regarding her father, who was still inside awaiting a triple-bypass operation. The couple had been visiting the island to look after their family member. With operations scaling back and the local infrastructure crippled, Gonzalez Cancel calculated that open-heart procedures would be suspended for a month or longer, advising the couple to leave. Stressing that he spoke not just as a physician but as a human being, he urged them to secure a flight to Miami, noting the trip takes only two and a half hours.

Departure, however, remains complicated. With the main airport still hobbled, Gonzalez Cancel explained that securing a special waiver from officials was necessary to obtain the medical evacuation flight for baby Gabriellyz. On Sunday, airport travelers without existing tickets were informed that outbound flights might not be available until October 4. 

Officials anticipate that conditions within local hospitals could deteriorate further before any recovery begins. At the territory's largest public hospital, Centro Medico, a disaster medical assistance team deployed by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services is currently establishing makeshift medical units. Commander Michael Garner, a regional coordinator for the operation, suggested this might represent a temporary lull prior to a surge of admissions as other facilities exhaust their generators. 

Garner noted that while the destruction matches that seen during hurricanes Katrina, Harvey, and Irma, Puerto Rico's isolation, communication breakdowns, and fragile infrastructure magnify logistical recovery hurdles substantially. U.S. Air Force Colonel Michael Valle, who arrived on Friday to assist, concurred, emphasizing that the situation feels considerably worse because incoming resources must arrive entirely by air or sea rather than by driving across state lines.

Complicating matters further, a dam in Puerto Rico compromised by heavy rains faced a potential failure on Sunday, threatening communities along the rising Guajataca River. The National Weather Service issued a warning that potential flooding would pose a life-threatening hazard, advising individuals to stay away or risk being swept away.

With the humanitarian crisis expanding, the death toll in Puerto Rico has reached at least 10. The Federal Emergency Management Agency has shared social media imagery showing federal personnel deployed locally, including Coast Guard and search-and-rescue units. Nonetheless, public frustration regarding the pace of aid is growing. Gonzalez Cancel called for a massive military response, while Rivera—a 49-year-old Iraq War veteran waiting for news of his father-in-law—remarked that military assistance has operational limits and predicted the island will require months to recover. He stated that divine intervention feels nearly necessary to fix every light bulb. Dr. Juan Carlos Sotomonte, medical director for Centro Medico’s cardiovascular unit, emphasized that prompt action, divine or otherwise, is urgently required to prevent fatalities from escalating.

MOSCOW (Reuters) — In a move that could indicate anticipation of fresh American penalties, Moscow has introduced a legislative proposal to conceal the identities of financial institutions that provide funding to state-owned weapons manufacturers. Should the measure pass, the central bank would be relieved of its current obligation to disclose the roster of lenders involved in the defense sector, a group that stood at eight institutions at the beginning of October. 

Furthermore, the legislation would grant both the presidency and the government the authority to designate any bank of their choosing for these defense transactions while eliminating the requirement to make the selection criteria public. Present rules stipulate that only lenders controlled by the state or the central bank possessing capital of at least 100 billion rubles, equivalent to $1.7 billion, are eligible for such agreements. 

The legislative push comes as Russian President Vladimir Putin convened a session on Tuesday focused on strengthening the nation's armed forces. 

Relations have remained tense following an August sanctions package signed by U.S. President Donald Trump, intended to penalize Moscow following U.S. intelligence findings of interference in the 2016 American presidential election—claims that the Kremlin has consistently rejected. In connection with that legislation, the U.S. State Department released a roster of 39 Russian intelligence and defense entities last month.

The American legislation mandates that the U.S. president penalize any individual determined to have participated in a substantial transaction with entities operating within or on behalf of Russia's defense or intelligence apparatus. Although this step does not instantly enact fresh sanctions, administration officials noted in October that decisions will be evaluated individually.

Institutions currently appearing on the public disclosure list feature major state-run entities such as Sberbank, VTB, and the Russian Agriculture Bank, alongside privately owned Rossiya and Gazprombank, the latter of which counts the gas giant Gazprom among its stakeholders. 

Meanwhile, three insiders familiar with the discussions revealed to Reuters that Sberbank has suggested creating a dedicated financial institution specifically for backing the country's military sector as a strategy to evade restrictions. Sberbank chose not to issue a statement regarding the matter.

LIMA (Reuters) - Wrapping up his final overseas farewell tour in Peru, outgoing U.S. President Barack Obama mirrored the reassurances he previously offered in Europe, urging international audiences to withhold judgment on President-elect Donald Trump. Following Trump's victory over Democratic nominee and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, international communities have felt deeply unsettled, prompting Obama—who previously labeled Trump unfit for the presidency—to calm these global fears. Speaking on Saturday during a youth town hall in Peru, Obama advised the crowd against anticipating the worst-case scenario. He emphasized that people should hold off on evaluating the incoming administration until it officially takes office and formulates its policies, allowing the global community to then determine whether those actions align with mutual peace and prosperity.

Trump secured his presidential win on a platform featuring promises to temporarily ban Muslims from entering the country, construct a border wall with Mexico, and scrap existing trade deals. In response, Obama has committed to facilitating an orderly transfer of power, expressing confidence that Trump will pivot away from his controversial campaign statements once confronted with the practical realities of governing. During the session, Obama reiterated that the global community should avoid snap judgments and instead allow the president-elect adequate time to assemble his staff, review key issues, and establish an agenda, noting that campaign behavior frequently differs from governance.

At the same time, Obama's attempts to provide comfort are largely rooted in the hope that the incoming team will recognize the value of Democratic-led initiatives, such as the Paris climate accord and the Iran nuclear agreement, despite Trump's vows to dismantle them. Furthermore, the president—who campaigned extensively for Clinton and made his disdain for Trump clear prior to the election—has balanced his soothing remarks with veiled criticisms of his successor. By highlighting democratic principles during his stops in Europe and Peru, Obama addressed issues that critics frequently accuse Trump of overlooking. On Saturday, he remarked on observing nations regressing rather than progressing regarding internet freedom, press freedom, and the treatment of civil society and political adversaries. 

During his campaign, Trump occasionally restricted specific news outlets from attending events and suggested in a televised debate that he would imprison Clinton over her private email server usage as secretary of state. While Obama was able to reassure European allies that the United States would maintain its NATO obligations, his other projections—particularly regarding Latin America—appeared to rely more on hopeful speculation than concrete insights into Trump's agenda. Acknowledging trade as a major potential divergence, Obama stated that he did not foresee significant policy shifts toward Latin America under the new administration. Meanwhile, Trump's Friday announcements of hardline selections for national security adviser, attorney general, and CIA director indicate that his administration is preparing to adopt a stringent approach toward illegal immigration and Islamist militancy.
