WASHINGTON (Reuters) — A faction of 20 moderate House Republicans cautioned on Friday that the push to revise the federal tax code faces serious threats if the upcoming fiscal 2018 budget resolution insists on deep spending reductions. 

Representing the moderate Tuesday Group, these lawmakers addressed a June 30 letter to House Speaker Paul Ryan. They argued that mandating hundreds of billions in cuts to mandatory programs would create severe obstacles for tax reform. Consequently, they urged that the budget process be postponed until Senate Republicans conclude their deliberations on healthcare. 

Spearheaded by Pennsylvania Representative Charlie Dent, the group stated that continuing down the current legislative path threatens to derail tax overhaul efforts. Securing a 2018 budget resolution is mandatory for Republicans to utilize reconciliation, a procedural mechanism that allows a tax package to advance without Democratic votes. 

However, hardline conservatives in the House Freedom Caucus are conditioning their support for any fiscal blueprint on substantial rollbacks to mandatory programs, specifically targeting Medicaid and food stamps—reductions that the moderate faction firmly rejects. 

AshLee Strong, a spokeswoman for Ryan, noted in a released statement that the party has advanced considerably regarding budget choices, and these internal discussions will persist among the conference. Both the Freedom Caucus and the Tuesday Group hold enough voting strength individually to block legislation in the House. 

The brewing conflict has also alarmed external entities, particularly influential business lobbies who fear a political impasse might ultimately kill tax reform entirely. 

On Wednesday, a coalition consisting of the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, the Business Roundtable, the National Association of Manufacturers, and the National Federation of Independent Business issued a joint correspondence to congressional leaders from both parties, emphasizing that comprehensive, pro-growth tax reform remains the paramount reform under consideration. 

Furthermore, congressional aides noted that moderate Republicans are concerned that incorporating mandatory spending cuts into a reconciliation bill would produce politically toxic legislation, slashing assistance for low-income populations while simultaneously delivering tax relief to corporations and high-earning individuals. 

Amid these divisions, the House Budget Committee scrapped its schedule to bring the fiscal 2018 resolution to the floor this week. The decision followed pushback from several committee chairmen who resisted directives to extract $250 billion in mandatory spending, an amount that still falls well short of the far deeper cuts demanded by Freedom Caucus members.

WASHINGTON AND NEW YORK — Behind-the-scenes friction between U.S. President Donald Trump’s chief strategist and his national security adviser has intensified to the point of threatening further upheaval within the West Wing, according to three senior officials. The ongoing clash between Stephen Bannon and Lieutenant General H.R. McMaster is creating instability among top-tier presidential advisers just as the administration is working to regain its footing. While moderate Republicans have pressured the president to dismiss Bannon, Trump refrained from offering a public endorsement during a press conference at Trump Tower in New York on Tuesday, though he left the door open regarding the strategist's future, telling reporters that they would see what happens with Mr. Bannon. 

The outcome of this rivalry could heavily influence major policy decisions, including the fate of the Iran nuclear agreement, troop deployment strategies for Afghanistan, and internal staffing arrangements—all areas where Bannon and McMaster have clashed. Although Bannon has weathered previous threats to his position, Trump has retained him thus far, partly due to his instrumental role in the presidential campaign and his strong backing among the president's core supporters. An individual close to the White House suggested to Reuters that the president appears hesitant to remove him entirely, raising the possibility of a demotion instead, particularly given concerns that an ousted Bannon might turn into a vocal opponent of the administration from the outside.

Meanwhile, two other senior officials aligned with McMaster alleged that he holds Bannon responsible for a barrage of criticism directed at him by Breitbart News—the right-wing outlet previously led by Bannon—along with other ultra-conservative organizations. Over recent weeks, Breitbart has run numerous pieces arguing for McMaster's removal, claiming he lacks commitment to Israel and has filled the National Security Council with Obama administration holdovers. One of these officials noted that the president is aware of McMaster's frustration over these attacks, though they did not specify whether the national security adviser raised the issue directly with Trump or via the new chief of staff, General John Kelly. 

Another McMaster supporter noted that while the general does not explicitly claim Bannon orchestrates the attacks, he believes his former colleague possesses the influence to halt them. During a Sunday television appearance, McMaster repeatedly sidestepped questions regarding his ability to collaborate with Bannon. Neither Bannon nor McMaster provided comments when contacted. 

Aside from termination, options available to Trump include reassigning McMaster outside the White House—potentially returning him to an active military command—or enforcing a truce while keeping both officials in their current roles. Bannon has previously navigated internal power struggles, eventually reaching a detente with the president's son-in-law and senior adviser, Jared Kushner, following a reprimand from Trump. 

Sources supporting McMaster indicated that Chief of Staff Kelly is displeased that the anti-McMaster campaign is projecting an image of internal disarray, complicating his efforts to bring order and discipline to the administration just two weeks into his tenure. Ideologically, Bannon views himself as a champion of Trump's nationalist agenda, advocating for the termination or renegotiation of trade agreements and a more isolationist foreign policy compared to McMaster. Bannon has pushed to abandon the 2015 Iran nuclear deal, which McMaster supports maintaining, and has suggested utilizing private contractors for the conflict in Afghanistan rather than increasing U.S. troop levels, a move advocated by the national security adviser. 

McMaster belongs to a more pragmatic faction that Bannon's camp frequently labels as "globalists." Tensions flared when McMaster restructured the National Security Council, removing four staffers considered close to Bannon. 

Mike Cernovich, a conservative commentator and Bannon supporter, has emerged as a vocal critic of McMaster, launching personal attacks against him. While stating he does not communicate directly with Bannon, Cernovich regards him as a vital counterweight to McMaster and cautions that dismissing Bannon would alienate the president's most dedicated base, suggesting supporters would question the value of backing the administration rather than actively fighting it. 

Additionally, the Zionist Organization of America (ZOA), a conservative Jewish-American and pro-Israel organization with ties to Bannon, has emerged as one of McMaster's fiercest detractors, pushing Trump to remove McMaster from portfolios involving Israel and Iran. Trump himself has defended McMaster, describing him as a good man who is strongly pro-Israel. 

An individual connected to the ZOA rejected the notion that Bannon dictates the group's stance, asserting that they would not abandon their campaign against McMaster despite reportedly receiving requests from Bannon to tone it down. The source expressed deep offense at the suggestion that outside figures direct their messaging, adding that it felt unfortunate to see Bannon taking the blame for actions they insisted were entirely independent.

Trump Is So Obsessed He Even Has Obama’s Name Coded Into His Website (IMAGES)

Despite declaring on Christmas day that work would resume the following day, Donald Trump was found golfing for four consecutive days. The former reality TV personality previously criticized Barack Obama for hitting the links, yet Trump is currently on pace to surpass the total number of golf outings his predecessor logged. 

Philip Bump posted on Twitter on December 29, 2017: "Updated my tracker of Trump s appearances at Trump properties. 71 rounds of golf including today s. At this pace, he ll pass Obama s first-term total by July 24 next year." Along with this was the link https://t.co/Fg7VacxRtJ and an image.

Given this backdrop, a discovery made by a Washington Post journalist regarding Trump's official website stands out as particularly strange, though much of this administration's behavior is unusual. Buried within the backend code was a direct mention of Obama and golf: "Unlike Obama, we are working to fix the problem and not on the golf course." 

However, the implementation of this code was flawed. Christopher Ingraham posted on Twitter on December 28, 2017: "The website of Donald Trump, who has spent several days in a row at the golf course, is coded to serve up the following message in the event of an internal server error: https://t.co/zrWpyMXRcz" with an accompanying image.

Ingraham added in subsequent tweets on December 28, 2017: "That snippet of code appears to be on all https://t.co/dkhw0AlHB4 pages, which the footer says is paid for by the RNC?" and "It s also all over https://t.co/ayBlGmk65Z. As others have noted in this thread, this is weird code and it s not clear it would ever actually display, but who knows."

Shortly after the hidden text was exposed publicly, the mention of Obama was purged from the site. Christopher Ingraham provided an update on December 29, 2017: "UPDATE: The golf error message has been removed from the Trump and GOP websites. They also fixed the javascript  =  vs  ==  problem. Still not clear when these messages would actually display, since the actual 404 (and presumably 500) page displays a different message" alongside an image.

Ingraham further noted on December 29, 2017: "That suggests someone at either RNC or the Trump admin is sensitive enough to Trump s golf problem to make this issue go away quickly once people noticed. You have no idea how much I d love to see the email exchange that led us here."

Furthermore, the programming itself was botched. A user going by the handle @tw1trsux pointed out on December 28, 2017: "The code was f-cked up. The best part about this is that they are using the  =  (assignment) operator which means that bit of code will never get run. If you look a few lines up  errorCode  will always be  404". Tim Peterson echoed this sentiment on the same day, tweeting, "trump s coders can t code. Nobody is surprised."

Ultimately, Donald Trump's preoccupation with Obama manifested even within the technical backend of his web presence while he continued his repeated visits to the golf course. Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images.

text:
BERLIN (Reuters) - German Chancellor Angela Merkel struck an optimistic note on Friday regarding the prospects of forming a government with the Greens and the pro-business Free Democrats (FDP), though her prospective allies warned that negotiations could still break down. Following an election last month that saw her bloc lose support to the far right—and with the Social Democrats (SPD), her previous coalition partners, insisting on moving to the opposition—Merkel is forced to unite three very different political factions to achieve a majority. Ahead of a Monday evening meeting between party chiefs and subsequent detailed discussions by larger teams, Merkel acknowledged to reporters that challenging negotiations are ahead, while maintaining that a successful agreement is possible through hard work and effort.

Should the coalition talks collapse, the likely outcome would be fresh elections, which could provide further momentum to the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) after their parliamentary breakthrough last month. Martin Schulz, the leader of the SPD, dismissed any possibility of reviving the outgoing "grand coalition" if Merkel's current efforts fall through. Speaking to the RND newspaper chain for an interview scheduled for Saturday publication, Schulz stated that a failure by Merkel to form a government would necessitate new elections. Similarly, FDP parliamentary group leader and negotiator Marco Buschmann told the Saturday edition of Die Welt that his party was prepared to transition to the opposition if the alliance did not materialize. Buschmann noted that while a new election might bolster the AfD—which entered parliament with 13 percent of the vote—voters might not use the party as a vehicle for protest if the distinctions among the remaining parties were more apparent.

Negotiators reported that Friday's discussions yielded agreement on easing the financial strain on families, expanding child care availability, and fighting child poverty. Furthermore, the potential partners aligned on backing Germany's commitments to NATO and other international organizations, deepening ties with France, and preserving positive relations with Russia. Nevertheless, significant disagreements persist over topics such as immigration limits, timelines for phasing out coal, climate change strategies, and rising defense expenditures. Additionally, the contentious topic of transportation was entirely bypassed on Friday. FDP deputy leader Wolfgang Kubicki shared with reporters that participants resolved to treat one another more kindly, noting his willingness to give it a try provided everyone cooperates.

Over the weekend, the parties are set to refine their core agendas prior to Monday's leadership summit led by Merkel. Michael Kellner, a prominent negotiator for the Greens, remarked that all the necessary components are present and must now be blended into a cohesive outcome. Conversely, fellow Green negotiator Juergen Trittin adopted a harsher stance in an interview with ARD television, pointing out that after 10 days and 12 discussed topics, the participants have not even managed to agree on their points of disagreement. Both FDP chief Christian Lindner and Buschmann estimated the likelihood of a successful coalition at fifty-fifty, while Green foreign policy specialist Omid Nouripour suggested the discussions could break down entirely. 

While Merkel has expressed her anticipation of a stable administration prior to Christmas, top conservative allies suggest the process might extend into the coming year. Horst Seehofer, the embattled leader of the CSU—the Bavarian sister party to Merkel's CDU—expressed encouragement over what he described as constructive and reliable talks among party leaders lately, while calling on negotiators to keep their disputes private. Advocating for a fresh start in the upcoming days, Seehofer faced criticism from his party's youth wing after pulling out of a scheduled speech to the group, which has advocated for a more contemporary appeal ahead of next year's Bavarian regional elections. Hans Reichhart, who leads the CSU youth organization, warned that this cancellation might worsen discussions surrounding Seehofer's political future following the steep losses sustained in the September 24 election. Prior to this, Seehofer had asked members to postpone any leadership discussions until later in the month, claiming that such debate could weaken his standing during the coalition negotiations.

SYDNEY (Reuters) - A friend of a British documentarian who was reported missing during a quest to locate an isolated tribe in Papua New Guinea reported on Thursday that the explorer has been seen near an airstrip and is waiting to be flown out. Benedict Allen set out in the preceding month to find the Yaifo, an untamed community situated in the northern territory of the isolated South Pacific nation. He traveled without any communication devices and failed to establish an itinerary or an extraction strategy, as explained to Reuters by his associate, Frank Gardner. 

Allen had previously indicated on his blog that his return to the UK was scheduled for the middle of November. Prior to his departure, he posted a message on Twitter on October 11 telling people not to attempt a rescue and noting that nobody would be able to locate him in that part of PNG. However, concern grew among his relatives and associates when he failed to board his scheduled flight home the previous weekend. 

Gardner, who works as the security correspondent for the BBC, explained to Reuters that Allen remains in a vulnerable position. He is currently stranded in an isolated region of the country that can solely be accessed via aircraft because local tribal conflicts have resulted in the destruction of all road bridges. Preparations are presently moving quickly to arrange an emergency flight out for him before the violence spreads to his location. 

Before this update, Gardner informed the BBC that a local tribal commission had actively been searching for Allen, leading to his observation near an airstrip, though Reuters could not independently verify this report. On his personal website, Allen identifies as an adventurer and recounts past expeditions, including an earlier journey in PNG where he endured daily beatings for a period of six weeks as part of an initiation ceremony. His previous travels also feature a trek through a secluded area of the Amazon rainforest where, suffering from severe malaria and starvation, he had to consume his dog.

MOSCOW — On Thursday, Moscow advised Washington to independently investigate the email hacking controversy surrounding the Democratic Party, while simultaneously dismissing Donald Trump’s remarks—which he later claimed were sarcastic—urging Russia to locate Hillary Clinton’s unreturned messages.

The Republican presidential nominee provoked outrage from Democrats a day earlier by publicly calling on Russia to track down tens of thousands of messages from Clinton's time leading the State Department. This followed statements from President Barack Obama suggesting Moscow might attempt to sway the upcoming November 8 election following a Democratic National Committee email leak that cybersecurity specialists attributed to Russian actors.

The Kremlin has firmly rejected any notion of Russian involvement, labeling the allegations as baseless and accusing American politicians of exploiting Cold War anxieties and inventing narratives for political gain. While President Vladimir Putin has attempted to maintain neutrality regarding the American candidates, he has also described the populist businessman as exceptionally gifted, and state-run Russian television broadcasts have generally favored Trump over Clinton.

Speaking on Thursday, Kremlin representative Dmitry Peskov characterized the claims of Russian interference in the Democratic email leaks as verging on absolute absurdity driven by Russophobia. He firmly brushed aside Trump’s remark regarding the retrieval of Clinton’s correspondence, stating that handling those document batches is not Moscow's concern, emphasizing a policy of non-interference and a dislike for foreign meddling in Russian domestic matters. Peskov added that Americans must resolve and understand the nature of these emails independently.

Trump, who has consistently stated his intention to improve bilateral ties with Moscow if elected, also drew criticism by suggesting he might weigh recognizing the Crimean peninsula as Russian territory following its 2014 annexation. Peskov noted that the Kremlin remained indifferent to this statement, asserting it would not alter their officially neutral position on the U.S. election. He remarked that politicians campaigning during a heated race frequently make bold statements that typically become more measured once they assume official responsibilities.

Addressing Trump's comments concerning Crimea, Ukraine's ambassador to the United Nations, Volodymyr Yelchenko, remarked on Thursday that Trump is not currently the American president. He added to reporters that established United Nations resolutions exist and expressed confidence that any future U.S. administration will respect those determinations. The 193-member UN General Assembly passed a resolution in March 2014 invalidating the Moscow-supported referendum that led to Crimea's secession from Ukraine.

Political observers note that a Trump victory would likely be well-received by the Kremlin, given the New York billionaire's frequent praise for Putin, his stated desire for peaceful relations with Russia, and his openness to forming a joint front with Moscow against the Islamic State. Furthermore, Trump's suggestion that he might reconsider NATO's collective defense commitment would likely be viewed favorably in Moscow, where the Western alliance is viewed as an obsolete relic of the Cold War.

An official from the RNC, speaking on the condition of anonymity, explained that the agreement represented under 1 percent of the committee's roughly $150 million advertising allocation. Furthermore, the official characterized the arrangement merely as an ad space reservation rather than a binding guarantee to run advertisements on the platform. Hope Hicks, a spokesperson for the Trump campaign, stated she had no additional comments to offer.

The Republican National Committee serves as the governing body for the Republican Party on a national level. Donald Trump is anticipated to formally secure the party's nomination for the November 8 United States presidential election during the upcoming July convention.

SYDNEY (Reuters) - A decisive majority of Australians have cast their ballots in favor of same-sex marriage, setting the stage for lawmakers to enact legislation before 2017 concludes and touching off jubilant, rainbow-hued festivities on Wednesday featuring participants in wedding attire and glittering outfits who proclaimed that their affection is genuine. Should parliament approve the measure—a step anticipated despite resistance from vocal conservative elements on the government's right flank—Australia will join the ranks of 26 countries that legally recognize these unions. 

As the nation's lead statistician broadcasted the outcome live on a large display in a Sydney park, showing that 61.6 percent of surveyed participants supported marriage equality while 38.4 percent opposed it, crowds of thousands erupted into cheers, embraced, and wept. 

Ian Thorpe, an Australian Olympic swimmer who publicly revealed his sexuality three years prior, described the outcome as a massive weight lifted. Speaking to journalists at the Sydney gathering, Thorpe stated that the outcome establishes equality for individual feelings toward another person, regardless of identity. 

Although the postal survey carried no legal obligation, Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull swiftly affirmed his commitment to introducing a parliamentary bill with the objective of securing passage by Christmas. Turnbull minimized fears of a fracture within his governing coalition, even as conservative members pushed for modifications to safeguard religious liberties that would permit discrimination against same-sex partners. 

Addressing journalists in Canberra following the release of the figures, Turnbull characterized the mandate as clear and massive, noting that millions had spoken and delivered an overwhelming endorsement of marriage equality, voting in favor of fairness, dedication, and affection. A formal marriage equality proposal was subsequently presented to parliament on Wednesday afternoon. 

This outcome represents a historic milestone for LGBTQ+ equality in the country, where homosexual acts remained a criminal offense in certain states until 1997. American television personality Ellen DeGeneres, whose spouse is Australian actress Portia de Rossi, posted a message celebrating the news with the phrase, "It's a g day. Way to go Australia." 

Participation reached nearly 80 percent of qualified voters, surpassing turnout levels seen during the UK Brexit vote and the Irish marriage equality referendum. Fifty-nine-year-old Mark Barry shed tears alongside Gerrard Boller, his partner of three decades and five years, remarking to Reuters that he knew a celebrant who would be thrilled by the outcome. 

Alan Joyce, the Irish-born CEO of Qantas Airways and one of Australia's prominent openly gay corporate executives, addressed the Sydney assembly—many shielding themselves beneath rainbow-patterned parasols—calling the outcome phenomenal and pressing Turnbull to expedite the legislative process. 

Having faced strain from a parliamentary citizenship crisis that stripped him of his deputy and his majority in the legislature, Turnbull found himself, according to political analysts, presented with his initial chance in months to demonstrate definitive authority through the resounding affirmative vote. Monash University political scientist Nick Economou noted that Turnbull should draw strength from the outcome, viewing it as the decisive leadership opportunity he had been seeking. 

Throughout the campaign, the opposing side had mobilized major religious institutions, a strategy that proponents of the measure condemned as harsh and polarizing. Sydney's Catholic Archbishop, Anthony Fisher, expressed profound disappointment that the anticipated outcome would lead to laws further dismantling the traditional structure of marriage and the family in Australia. Bolstered by the strength of the affirmative vote, however, conservative politicians abandoned a rival proposal that would have permitted commercial enterprises, such as bakeries, to deny services like wedding cakes to same-sex couples based on religious objections.

According to individuals familiar with the matter, a probe led by Republican Representative Devin Nunes aimed at determining whether the Obama administration improperly utilized classified intelligence to undermine Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign could ultimately harm both the congressman and the sitting president. 

Insiders note that the documents in question lack any proof that aides to former Democratic President Barack Obama engaged in misconduct. Instead, the material suggests that certain individuals associated with Trump may have breached the Logan Act, a little-known 18th-century statute from 1799 that bars private American citizens from engaging in unauthorized negotiations with foreign governments involved in disputes with the U.S. 

Furthermore, these intelligence reports intersect with the ongoing probe led by special counsel Robert Mueller regarding U.S. intelligence conclusions that Moscow interfered in the November election to support Trump, according to sources who requested anonymity. Mueller's office chose not to issue a statement. The Russian government, which faces American sanctions over human rights violations and the 2014 annexation of Crimea, has consistently rejected accusations of electoral interference. Meanwhile, Trump has repeatedly denied any collusion between his campaign team and Moscow, a controversy that has cast a shadow over his administration.

Nunes, who heads the House Intelligence Committee and maintains a close alignment with Trump, held a clandestine meeting earlier in the year with a White House intelligence staffer before alleging that Obama's team had requested the identities of American citizens appearing in intercepted communications involving Russians and other foreign nationals. The White House declined to provide comments when approached. 

While such names are typically redacted from intelligence intercepts, Nunes claimed that Obama's staff leaked the identities to sabotage Trump's presidential run. A representative for Samantha Power, the former U.N. ambassador whom Republicans and Nunes targeted over allegations of seeking political ammunition, stated that her review of intelligence reports was strictly limited to her official responsibilities. Conversely, a spokesperson for former national security adviser Susan Rice—another official accused by Republicans of mishandling intelligence—did not reply to inquiries.

Special counsel Mueller is actively probing encounters and discussions involving foreign officials, foreign business figures, and Trump associates. Those figures include the president's son-in-law and adviser Jared Kushner, eldest son Donald Trump Jr., former campaign chairman Paul Manafort, and former national security adviser Michael Flynn. 

“An obvious question is how all these meetings and conversations were set up,” one source remarked. “Who set them up? What was their purpose? What were the agendas? Who approved them? Who was briefed on them afterward? Signals intelligence might shed some light on that.” Representatives for the various Trump associates did not respond to requests for comment.

Meanwhile, Democrats argue that the claims regarding leaks brought forward by Nunes and other Republicans are a strategic effort to divert attention away from the multiple congressional inquiries and Mueller's investigation into Russia. 

While the National Security Agency routinely conceals the names of American citizens within intercepted communications, individuals holding the appropriate security clearances have the authority to request unmasked identities for legitimate intelligence reasons. 

“Unmasking Americans is extremely sensitive, and unmasking political opponents is really problematic,” a congressional official noted on condition of anonymity, adding that any requests by Obama administration personnel that lacked proper justification would merit an investigation. However, when pressed for concrete proof that Power or other former aides leveraged intelligence for political gain or leaked it to the press, the official declined to comment.

SOFIA (Reuters) — According to the interior ministry, a tragic collision on a central Bulgarian highway on Friday left nine individuals dead and 19 more hurt after a minibus plowed into a truck. The fatalities included the driver of the bus, which was transporting visually impaired passengers home following a trip to Dryanovo. Several of the survivors sustained critical injuries. 

Taking place shortly after midday (1000 GMT), the crash happened near the village of Mikre—situated roughly 130 kilometers (81 miles) west of Sofia—along the highway linking the nation's capital to the Black Sea port of Varna. Hospitalization was provided to the wounded, though the ministry did not specify the exact count of those listed in critical condition. 

While the precise triggers of the crash remain undetermined, the interior ministry noted that Prime Minister Boyko Borissov directed the transport ministry to conduct a thorough examination of the minibus. Meanwhile, reports from domestic media outlets indicated that the specific segment of roadway near Mikre has been the site of at least eight major automobile accidents resulting in 10 fatalities since 2014. 

Bulgaria, home to 7.1 million residents, maintains the highest rate of traffic fatalities within the European Union. Figures released by the interior ministry indicate that 535 people lost their lives in roadway accidents across the country during the first ten months of 2017.

text:
BRUSSELS/MADRID — Carles Puigdemont, the removed leader of Catalonia, announced on Tuesday that he would participate in the upcoming regional snap vote called by Madrid after the central authorities seized control of the area to halt its secession bid. Nevertheless, he insisted that the campaign for independence would persist. 

Meanwhile, Spain's High Court summoned Puigdemont alongside thirteen members of his dismissed cabinet to appear in Madrid for hearings on Thursday and Friday. During these proceedings, the court will advance allegations of breach of trust, sedition, and rebellion against the group. Following the Spanish legal framework, a magistrate will determine whether the politicians ought to be detained while a thorough probe and potential trial are prepared. 

Puigdemont relocated to Brussels following the regional parliament's unilateral declaration of secession on Friday, leaving uncertainty over whether he would comply with the Madrid tribunal's order. Belga news agency reported that the Belgian crisis unit was reviewing whether local authorities needed to provide security for Puigdemont during his stay. Earlier on Tuesday, he stated that he would only travel back to Spain if the government offered unspecified assurances. 

The agreement by Puigdemont to contest the December 21 regional ballot indicated that, for the moment, the administration in Madrid has secured the upper hand in the prolonged confrontation regarding the prosperous northeastern region, which previously held substantial autonomy. Resistance to the central government's enforcement of direct rule failed to materialize at the beginning of the week, leaving the separatist leadership disorganized. However, a survey published on Tuesday revealed that backing for a separate Catalan state reached its highest point in nearly three years during October. 

Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy had moved to dismiss the regional assembly less than an hour after the declaration was issued on Tuesday, while Spain’s Constitutional Court simultaneously blocked the measure in a largely symbolic action that gained no traction. 

Addressing a press conference in Brussels after dropping out of public view over the weekend, Puigdemont urged the Catalan populace to brace for a lengthy endeavor, asserting that democracy would form the basis of their triumph. He also clarified that he was not seeking asylum in Belgium. 

Rajoy, who has maintained an inflexible position throughout the standoff, is wagering that anti-secession factions will capture the regional legislature and halt the independence movement. Conversely, Puigdemont banks on robust support for the pro-independence faction to revitalize the secessionist movement following several turbulent weeks. 

The Spanish administration reiterated over the weekend that Puigdemont was welcome to run in the election, though it maintained that the judicial proceedings were an entirely separate concern. On Tuesday, the Supreme Court likewise initiated the processing of rebellion and sedition charges targeting regional parliament speaker Carme Forcadell and other prominent leaders. 

Triggered by an October 1 independence referendum, the political crisis stands as Spain's most severe since the restoration of democracy in the late 1970s. Although Spanish courts deemed the vote illegal and less than half of eligible citizens participated, the pro-secession regional government argued the outcome granted a mandate for statehood. Governments in the United States, France, Germany, and Britain have all thrown their weight behind Rajoy while dismissing the prospect of an independent Catalan nation, though certain capitals have urged both sides to engage in dialogue. 

Previously, Puigdemont, Vice President Oriol Junqueras, and other regional figures maintained they would refuse their removal from office. Yet their respective political organizations, Esquerra Republicana de Catalunya and PdeCat, announced on Monday that they would enter the vote, signaling tacit compliance with direct administration from Madrid. 

While separatist sentiment endures in the Basque Country and other regions, the current struggle has fractured Catalonia internally and provoked deep resentment across the rest of Spain. Although two recent surveys hinted that pro-independence momentum might be declining, an official regional poll released Tuesday indicated that roughly 48.7 percent of Catalans favor independence, climbing from 41.1 percent in June and marking the peak since December 2014. The Centre d'Estudis d'Opinio survey, based on 1,338 interviews conducted mostly between October 16 and October 29, represented the initial poll published following the independence declaration. 

Despite his journey to the heart of the European Union, Puigdemont's aspirations to draw the bloc into his dispute appear unlikely to succeed. Member nations have reaffirmed their commitment to Spanish unity, while EU officials in Brussels emphasize that they will interact solely with Madrid, treating the conflict as a strictly internal matter. Mina Andreeva, a European Commission spokesperson, stated in Brussels on Tuesday that their stance remains unchanged. 

Even so, certain analysts argue that the conflict will not dissipate swiftly. Raj Badiani, an economist with IHS Markit in London, noted that Spain faces an era of disruption, with its policy focus consumed by a single political debate while other major challenges are sidelined, drawing parallels to the UK and Brexit. Badiani added that more tangible economic fallout could emerge by early 2018 as uncertainty mounts with Catalans pressing harder for a legally binding referendum. 

Prominent Catalan business associations have endorsed direct rule and urged corporations to maintain their operations locally. Nevertheless, the crisis has already driven over 1,000 companies to relocate their legal bases away from Catalonia, a territory generating roughly a fifth of the economy in Spain, which ranks as the fourth-largest in the euro zone. Spain's IBEX index dipped slightly as Puigdemont began his Brussels address before recovering. 

For some residents in Barcelona, exhaustion appears to be the dominant sentiment. Ernesto Hernandez Busto, a 42-year-old editor, described the situation as farcical and entirely ridiculous, stating that extreme nationalism and separatism have plunged Catalonia into the most absurd predicament and worst inconvenience experienced over the past forty years.

text:
WASHINGTON (Reuters) — Speaking in Columbus, Ohio, on Tuesday, Democratic candidate Hillary Clinton warned that a victory by her Republican opponent, Donald Trump, would trigger what she termed a "Trump recession" and spell ruin for the American economy. Clinton emphasized that her warning transcended standard partisan disputes, pointing out that economists across the political spectrum—left, right, and center—share the view that Trump's economic policies would trigger a new downturn.

This address in Ohio, a crucial battleground state for the November 8 election, marked Clinton's second major speech arguing that the wealthy real estate developer lacks the temperament required for the presidency. Her previous address focused on national security and foreign policy. 

Focusing on Trump's core argument for his candidacy, Clinton remarked, “Donald Trump has said he is qualified to be president because of his business record. So let’s take a look at what he did for his businesses: He’s written a lot of books about business. They all seem to end at Chapter 11; go figure.” The remark was a pointed reference to corporate bankruptcy filings under the U.S. Bankruptcy Code.

The former secretary of state went on to characterize Trump as a self-described "king of debt," accusing him of running up massive liabilities that ultimately forced his enterprises into bankruptcy, costing numerous employees their jobs and destroying value for shareholders. She cautioned that applying such an approach to the federal government would terrify investors and potentially spark an economic disaster.

Simultaneously, Trump took to Twitter during the speech to respond: “I am ‘the king of debt.’ That has been great for me as a businessman, but is bad for the country. I made a fortune off of debt, will fix U.S.”

TEGUCIGALPA (Reuters) — Citizens in Honduras headed to the polls Sunday for a presidential race widely anticipated to secure another term for the incumbent, a leader favored by the United States. This vote comes nearly a decade after he backed the ouster of a predecessor who had similarly raised the possibility of seeking re-election. 

According to polling data leading up to the vote, Juan Orlando Hernandez representing the center-right National Party is poised to benefit directly from a Supreme Court ruling from 2015 that struck down the nation's constitutional limits on presidential terms. His primary challenger is television personality Salvador Nasralla, who leads the Opposition Alliance Against the Dictatorship, an ideological broad-based coalition spanning the left and right. 

Here is a look at the contenders and their primary platforms:

Juan Orlando Hernandez
* At 49 years old, the former leader of Congress attended the Honduras military academy as well as the State University of New York. Hernandez maintains a strong relationship with White House Chief of Staff John Kelly and is regarded by Washington as a dependable partner in Central America.
* Over his tenure, Hernandez has succeeded in boosting economic growth and reducing homicide numbers, while simultaneously extending his political reach deep into the apparatus of the Honduran state.
* Detractors argue that Hernandez—who grew up as one of 18 children in a modest rural household—has suppressed political opposition and aims to entrench his authority. Meanwhile, American officials have expressed a desire for him to revive stalled measures that would legally cap presidential terms, helping to alleviate concerns that he might refuse to step down eventually.
* Operating under the campaign banner "Change has begun and should continue," Hernandez pledges to maintain his aggressive, militarized campaign against criminal gangs that have transformed the Central American country into one of the globe's most dangerous places.
* Under his "Honduras 20/20" initiative, Hernandez aims to attract foreign investment into manufacturing, call centers, and textiles to stimulate the economy. He also intends to advance special economic zones, an initiative that has produced limited tangible outcomes thus far, with the ultimate goal of generating 600,000 jobs over the course of four years.

Salvador Nasralla
* A vibrant 64-year-old television personality known for hosting sports and variety programs, Nasralla of Lebanese heritage has pledged to eradicate rampant violence, systemic poverty, and official corruption.
* His coalition, the Opposition Alliance Against the Dictatorship, incorporates the Liberty and Refoundation Party (LIBRE), which is steered by former President Manuel Zelaya—the leader removed in the past coup—whom many analysts view as the actual power behind Nasralla's movement.
* Tapping into his celebrity status to rally voters frustrated with traditional Honduran politics, the political outsider lagged behind Hernandez by a 15-point margin in the final permitted poll conducted in September.
* Nasralla proposes appealing to the United Nations to establish an independent anti-corruption commission modeled after the one functioning in neighboring Guatemala to investigate and prosecute graft. While he would preserve the Military Police established by his opponent, he aims to introduce a community-focused police force for dangerous neighborhoods, persist in purging dishonest national police personnel, and recruit up to 25,000 fresh officers.
* Economic details from the coalition remain scarce, though the group has floated reductions to the sales tax alongside cuts to a corporate tax implemented by Hernandez that has angered local business leaders.
* Additionally, the Alliance advocates for a public vote regarding the rewriting of the current Constitution, suggesting the task be handled either by a newly formed national assembly or the legislature. They also call for a referendum aimed at curtailing the authority of the Supreme Court, which they contend is overly compliant with Hernandez.

CHICAGO (Reuters) — Among the crowd of hopefuls aiming for the White House is Michael Petyo, a 66-year-old Indiana resident who works as a carpenter, serves as a Russian Orthodox church cantor, and is both a U.S. Navy veteran and a grandfather known for his pride in his homemade nut rolls. While Petyo lacks major financial backers, boasts minimal political experience aside from a pair of unsuccessful congressional bids, and faces virtually nonexistent odds of victory, he remains convinced he belongs in the seat of President Barack Obama. Psychology professionals point to escalating narcissism, a deepening skepticism toward political figures, and social media's capacity for public outreach as key drivers behind this growing wave of ordinary citizens aiming for the presidency.

Federal Election Commission records show that Petyo has joined a pool of over 1,500 contenders, a total that has more than tripled since 2012 when only 417 people ran. This diverse group features participants who have submitted potentially made-up monikers like “Darth Vader” and “Disco Daddy.” Among the official hopefuls are John McAfee, the creator of anti-virus software; Terry Jones, a Florida pastor infamous for orchestrating Koran burnings; and Susan Young, a California social studies educator who entered the race to provide a practical democracy lesson for her pupils. Another contender, Edie Bukewihge, shared her grandmother's chili recipe on her campaign website, vote4edie.org, alongside a pledge that the final two years of her presidency would feel uneventful because she would have already fixed the nation's problems. 

These long-shot candidates are entirely absent from polling data, which instead highlights the battles between businessman Donald Trump and Texas U.S. Senator Ted Cruz for the Republican nomination, alongside U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton leading the Democratic contenders ahead of upcoming contests in Iowa and New Hampshire. 

Yet, Petyo's zeal remains unaffected by the lack of mainstream notice. He frequently draws parallels between himself and the biblical shepherd David, chosen by God to become king, remarking that, like David, words pour from his mouth "like honey from a hive." 

Having satisfied the basic constitutional criteria of being a natural-born U.S. citizen and at least 35 years old, Petyo—who runs a construction business and distributes his business cards at political gatherings throughout the Midwest—believes ordinary connection is vital. "I don’t see how anybody can represent the people unless they’re one with the people," he stated. His policy platform can be found on his campaign site, petyoforpresident.com. During a conversation, Petyo shared various conspiracy theories, asserting that the Internal Revenue Service is actually headquartered in Puerto Rico, that the Federal Emergency Management Agency is preparing detention facilities nationwide, and that domestic government insiders assisted the al Qaeda operatives behind the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

Political psychologist Bart Rossi explained that for individuals like Petyo, the primary goal is simply discovering an audience willing to hear them out. "They want to get their thoughts and ideas out there," Rossi noted. "They want to be on the playing field even if they’re not going to win the game." Meanwhile, leadership expert and psychoanalyst Michael Maccoby noted that society is experiencing profound transformations, leaving many citizens with a deep mistrust of current leadership. "It’s understandable that you have a lot of people thinking they’ve got the answer," Maccoby observed.

Although Petyo identifies as a Republican, he rejects strict party lines, holding pro-union views typically associated with Democrats while simultaneously arguing that American corporations should face little to no taxation. Regardless of his prospects, he is guaranteed at least one ballot cast in his favor. Jim Wright, a 65-year-old retired engineer and longtime friend who distributes leaflets for the campaign, acknowledged that Petyo does not have a "snowball’s chance in hell," but confirmed he intends to vote for him anyway.

WOODBRIDGE, Va. — For Jennifer Carroll Foy, Donald Trump’s presidential win served as the ultimate tipping point, inspiring the 35-year-old public defender to launch her maiden political campaign. Now, her race places her right at the forefront of a Virginia election cycle that political observers are closely monitoring to gauge early public sentiment toward the commander-in-chief. Foy represents just one of 49 Democratic candidates challenging incumbents in Republican-held House of Delegates districts—a notable jump from the 29 candidates who ran two years prior. These upcoming contests will determine whether the Democratic party can successfully channel widespread poll disapproval of the Republican administration into actual ballots, potentially beginning to reverse the staggering loss of nearly 1,000 legislative seats nationwide that occurred during the presidency of Barack Obama.

Having harbored long-standing frustrations regarding the state legislature's stance on women’s rights, Foy is targeting a Washington suburban district situated within one of the 17 Republican-led areas that backed Democrat Hillary Clinton in the previous election. Speaking to Reuters, Foy remarked that Trump simply confirmed fears of societal regression rather than progress, adding that she felt compelled to act because she believed the time and person for the job were right now and herself. 

Currently, the Republican party maintains a comfortable 66-34 majority within the lower chamber of the state legislature. While Stephen Farnsworth, a political science expert at the University of Mary Washington located in Fredericksburg, anticipates that Democrats will capture notable ground—particularly by zeroing in on suburban territories—he noted to Reuters that a complete chamber flip would demand a dramatic erosion of the president's base. According to Farnsworth, achieving a Democratic majority in the House of Delegates would necessitate a massive political tidal wave.

A shift in the broader national atmosphere has certainly lifted the spirits of Virginia Democrats. Since the January inauguration of the New York-based real estate developer, grassroots opposition to Trump has energized countless citizens and sparked massive turnouts for street demonstrations. Furthermore, a survey released on May 22 by the Washington Post alongside George Mason University’s Schar School indicated that 59 percent of state voters expressed dissatisfaction with Trump's job performance, while only 36 percent offered their approval. 

David Toscano, who serves as the Democratic leader in the state House, emphasized that enthusiasm remains robust due to a dual dynamic. He stated that voters are motivated both by supporting a candidate and by casting a ballot in opposition to another. Conversely, Mark Walter, who leads the national Republican State Leadership Committee, noted that his organization is keeping a close watch on Virginia, though he pointed out the challenge in predicting how public opinion regarding Trump will ultimately shape the outcomes. New Jersey remains the sole other state hosting statewide legislative races this autumn, though Democrats already hold majorities in both of its chambers. 

Despite the influx of Democratic challengers, the Virginia Republican Party remains unperturbed. State elections department figures from the end of March show that Republicans amassed $6.5 million for House campaigns, significantly outpacing the $2.8 million raised by Democrats. John Whitbeck, the party’s chairman, maintained a confident stance in a Reuters interview, emphasizing that they are sticking to their proven playbook of raising substantial funds, knocking on doors across communities, and securing victories in numerous races.

Toscano pointed out that Democratic contenders plan to center their platforms on several key friction points, including congressional Republican efforts to dismantle the Affordable Care Act—Barack Obama’s defining domestic achievement—alongside Trump’s temporary hiring freeze affecting the majority of federal workforce positions. Additionally, candidates intend to highlight the economic record of Democratic Governor Terry McAuliffe, pointing to his administration's creation of thousands of jobs and billions in capital investment as a major asset, according to Toscano. 

Although term limits prevent McAuliffe from seeking another term, the advantage held by his fellow Democrats in the gubernatorial race is anticipated to provide downstream momentum for the party's House hopefuls. Among their most promising pickup opportunities is the 2nd District, a region characterized by sprawling residential developments, strip malls, and the Quantico Marine base. Clinton carried this area by a margin of 21 points last November, reflecting the broader political shift in a state that historically leaned Republican in presidential contests.

Before reaching the general election, Foy and fellow Democratic contender Josh King will square off in a primary on June 13. The victor will advance to the November ballot to meet Republican Laquan Austion for the seat being vacated by a retiring Republican incumbent who opted against running again. Interestingly, all three contenders report that everyday constituents express greater worry over everyday local concerns—such as traffic congestion, educational systems, and environmental pollution stemming from power plant coal ash—than national politics involving Trump. King, a 36-year-old deputy sheriff who faced a narrow defeat in his 2015 bid for the same seat, acknowledged the ambient presence of the Trump effect while stressing that their campaign channels its energy directly into localized priorities.

DAKAR (Reuters) - According to a publication released on Monday by Human Rights Watch, security personnel in Congo enlisted upwards of 200 former rebel combatants living in exile to help quell demonstrations opposing President Joseph Kabila twelve months prior, instructing these fighters to employ deadly force. Throughout the December 2016 civil unrest—which erupted after the presidential ballot was postponed and Kabila declined to relinquish power—authorities shot and killed scores of individuals. 

Although the nation's constitution dictated that Kabila must vacate office following a 2016 succession vote, the election has since been pushed back to December 2018. In response, activist networks and opposition figures have promised new demonstrations this month in an effort to compel his departure. Human Rights Watch compiled its findings by speaking with nine Congolese intelligence and security operatives (largely referenced without naming them), M23 commanders, and 13 combatants belonging to the M23 insurgent faction who were reportedly gathered from Uganda and Rwanda, both bordering nations.

When reached for comment, the administration's official spokesman chose to remain silent. Meanwhile, Delphin Kahimbi—identified in the documentation as a coordinator for the initiative and the director of military intelligence for the nation—refuted claims that he enlisted M23 personnel, labeling the conclusions "ridiculous and absurd." A public statement was also issued on Monday by M23 president Bertrand Bisimwa, who maintained that while Kinshasa had signed up deserters and former members who had previously been expelled, the group's central leadership had no part in the matter.

Decades of conflict rooted in disagreements over territory, ethnicity, and the control of resources have claimed millions of lives in eastern Congo, where the M23 originally launched an uprising in 2012. United Nations forces and the Congolese military ultimately crushed the M23 near the end of 2013. Following the defeat, authorities pledged amnesty to the vast majority of the hundreds of insurgents who escaped into Uganda and Rwanda, though that initiative has remained deadlocked.

The documentation indicates that Congolese security agencies sought out the M23 last year due to a lack of confidence in their own regular forces by Kabila. Dispatched to Goma in the east, the capital of Kinshasa, and Lubumbashi (the country's second-largest city), these combatants were blended into units of the presidential guard, army, and police force. The document notes that they received directives to shoot to kill during the demonstrations. In exchange for their participation, individual M23 participants were paid hundreds of dollars, while those leading the recruitment cautioned them that a departure of Kabila from office would strip them of all safety guarantees. 

Ugandan military representative Richard Karemire rejected assertions that insurgents had been enlisted on Ugandan territory, while officials in Rwanda were unavailable for immediate comment.

Frustrated by widespread indifference—including from the mainstream media—regarding a foreign government's alleged interference in the U.S. presidential election and Donald Trump's numerous international business connections that pose potential national security risks, the grassroots collective known as the Pantsuit Action Network is taking matters into its own hands. 

Commonly referred to as Pantsuit Nation, this community, which grew out of staunch support for Hillary Clinton, is positioning itself as a force for fairness and honesty in the country. To compel lawmakers to look into Trump's extensive overseas financial entanglements, the organization has launched a new initiative. With just a few simple steps, supporters can reach out to their congressional representatives and demand that inquiries be opened through the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform as well as the Senate Ethics Committee.

The group's messaging states that Trump's financial and business conflicts are not only unethical, but also run contrary to the law and the constitution. They are pressing citizens to urge both the House Oversight Committee and the Senate Ethics Committee to wrap up their respective investigations before the inauguration, ensuring that any disqualifying conflicts are addressed prior to taking office, with the overarching goal of keeping foreign influence out of the Oval Office. 

Individuals looking to get in touch with their senators and local U.S. representatives can do so by visiting their official websites. Additionally, supporters are being encouraged to text the word INVESTIGATE to 528-86. 

The organization stresses that it is vital to prevent a foreign power from successfully dictating a U.S. election. Failing to investigate these CIA findings risks establishing a dangerous precedent that the nation is vulnerable to external manipulation—a prospect that should alarm everyone, regardless of nationality. Citizens are being strongly urged to contact their elected officials immediately.

NEW YORK (Reuters) - According to individuals familiar with the situation, former federal prosecutor and white-collar defense attorney David Miller has surfaced as a potential successor to Preet Bharara for the role of Manhattan U.S. attorney. The sources, who requested anonymity because these conversations are private, stated that Miller—currently a partner at the New York firm Morgan, Lewis & Bockius—has recently engaged in discussions regarding the position with members of Congress, as well as officials at the White House and the U.S. Department of Justice. Previously, the administration's consideration of Miller for this prominent position had not been made public. 

Media reports and sources had previously identified Edward McNally, a partner at Kasowitz Benson Torres, as the frontrunner among at least four candidates under evaluation. It remains uncertain who currently holds the advantage for the job, which necessitates a presidential nomination and subsequent Senate confirmation. Representatives for the Justice Department, Morgan Lewis, and Kasowitz all chose not to provide comments, while the White House did not reply to inquiries concerning Miller's candidacy. 

Regarded as one of the most vital positions within the American legal apparatus, the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York oversees over 200 prosecutors managing high-profile matters that span from financial crimes on Wall Street and cyber threats to corruption and terrorism. Alongside financial sector investigations, the incoming appointee will take charge of an ongoing probe into Fox News Channel concerning hush money payments tied to sexual harassment allegations, as well as the prosecution of a Turkish gold trader in a politically sensitive case that has drawn ire from Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

At age 43, Miller previously served as an assistant U.S. attorney under Bharara from 2009 through 2014. During that timeframe, he participated in the office's aggressive push against insider trading and acted as lead counsel for prosecutions involving narcotics, mail fraud, and embezzlement schemes. At present, Bharara’s former deputy, Joon Kim, functions as the acting Manhattan U.S. Attorney. Bharara was dismissed in March after declining to tender his resignation alongside 45 other Obama-administration U.S. attorneys, an ouster that came as a surprise given that President Trump had asked him to remain in his role back in November. Bharara had cultivated a formidable reputation as a relentless pursuer of political corruption—regardless of political affiliation—and as Wall Street's chief prosecutor.

Both Miller and McNally maintain affiliations with law firms that have connections to President Donald Trump. Sheri Dillon, a Morgan Lewis partner, participated in Trump's January press conference detailing his strategy for avoiding conflicts of interest. Meanwhile, Kasowitz has represented Trump in various legal matters for over a decade, and David Friedman, a former name partner at the firm, secured confirmation in March to serve as the U.S. ambassador to Israel. Both candidates are registered Republicans.

Prior to his tenure under Bharara, Miller worked as a trial attorney within the Justice Department's counterterrorism division and held the position of assistant general counsel for the Central Intelligence Agency. During his time at the CIA, he aided in the prosecution of Lewis “Scooter” Libby, who was convicted of obstruction and lying during an investigation into the disclosure of a covert CIA officer's identity—a case that intensified debates surrounding the Iraq war. 

Current and former colleagues characterize Miller as a talented, strictly procedural attorney who, if appointed, would likely safeguard the office's traditional independence. Carrie Cohen, a Morrison Foerster partner whose tenure as a Manhattan prosecutor overlapped with Miller's, remarked that he would be an excellent selection, noting that choosing someone with prior experience in the office bodes well for maintaining its historical tradition of bringing cases without fear or favor.

McNally, who is 61, boasts a diverse background across government and law. He functioned as the interim U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Illinois spanning late 2005 and 2006, and worked as a Manhattan prosecutor under Rudolph Giuliani during the 1980s. Additionally, his resume includes a stint as a White House speechwriter under President George H.W. Bush, service as general counsel for terrorism and homeland security, and three years operating as senior counsel in the Justice Department’s criminal division.

Additional individuals mentioned in media coverage as potential candidates include Edward O’Callaghan, a partner at Clifford Chance, and defense attorney Marc Mukasey, whose father held the attorney general position under Republican President George W. Bush. Neither Mukasey nor O’Callaghan replied to emailed requests for comment. 

Historically, the office of the Manhattan U.S. Attorney has been held by notable figures such as Giuliani—who later became New York City Mayor and a Trump adviser—alongside James Comey, currently the FBI director, and Robert Morgenthau, who served as the real-life inspiration for the initial district attorney character on the television show “Law & Order.” Furthermore, according to his LinkedIn page, Miller previously ventured into television by consulting for "Showtime’s" drama series “Billions,” which was reportedly inspired in part by Bharara's probe into hedge fund manager Steven Cohen.

WASHINGTON — A wealthy businessman stepping into the political arena for the very first time, advocating for an end to international trade pacts and demanding stronger security on the southern border. Sound familiar? It is the exact blueprint of Donald Trump, but the candidate is Paul Nehlen, who is mounting a primary challenge against House Speaker Paul Ryan in his home state of Wisconsin. Ryan represents the absolute pinnacle of the Washington Republican establishment—something both Trump and Nehlen are eager to disrupt.

While numerous GOP strategists worry that Donald Trump’s polarizing presidential campaign could drag down congressional candidates in November, a select group of contenders are adopting his platform, even if they keep the man himself at arm's length. An upset defeat suffered by Ryan or another prominent incumbent would send massive shockwaves through the political landscape, potentially forcing establishment figures to reconsider their stances on immigration policy and free trade agreements. 

Take New Hampshire, where Trump carried the primary by a twenty-point margin. Former Republican state senator Jim Rubens, an open supporter of the billionaire businessman, is now trying to unseat incumbent Senator Kelly Ayotte. Down in Arizona—another territory won by Trump—state senator Kelli Ward is actively campaigning against veteran Senator John McCain. Ward has been courting voters right outside Trump rallies and echoing his border security rhetoric, though she has stopped short of formally endorsing his presidential run.

This friction between grassroots outsiders and entrenched establishment figures is not entirely new, having simmered across the party for several election cycles. However, Donald Trump has provided the insurgency with a much more visible and popular champion. This trend has appeared in various states. In Alabama, Jonathan McConnell campaigned outside a Huntsville Trump rally while trying to unseat veteran Senator Richard Shelby. Meanwhile, in North Carolina, Representative Renee Elmers acknowledged voting for Trump in her state's primary as she fought off a primary challenger of her own.

Even so, unlike the massive anti-establishment wave that swept Tea Party candidates into office back in 2010, these current challengers do not appear to signal a sweeping national groundswell against Washington. This points to clear boundaries for Trump's unique brand of politics, which frequently clashes with traditional Republican orthodoxy on taxation and trade. Nathan Gonzales, an independent congressional analyst based in Washington, noted his surprise that no House or Senate incumbents have actually fallen in primaries driven purely by enthusiasm for Donald Trump or Ted Cruz. Shelby, for instance, decisively defeated McConnell in the Alabama Republican primary. Gonzales pointed out that while other politicians can attempt to mimic Trump's rhetoric, nobody else can replicate Trump himself.

At the same time, many political operatives and analysts warn that conservative voters deeply unhappy with Trump as the nominee might simply stay home in the general election, inadvertently handing congressional seats over to Democrats. 

On paper, challenging Paul Ryan looks like a fool's errand. The speaker commands a massive campaign warchest and enjoys broad popularity both nationally and locally. A Marquette University Law School poll conducted the previous month showed Ryan holding an approval rating above 80 percent among Wisconsin Republicans. Yet, memories are short in politics. Less than two years prior, Eric Cantor, then the second-ranking Republican in the House, was widely viewed as a rising star in the party. Yet Cantor suffered a stunning defeat in Virginia during the 2014 primaries at the hands of an obscure conservative college professor, David Brat, despite looking utterly untouchable beforehand. Nehlen noted in an interview that this specific race proved to him that such an upset was entirely possible.

Ryan has repeatedly faced sharp criticism from Trump over the $1.1 billion federal budget agreement brokered with Democratic President Barack Obama. Furthermore, Ryan’s backing of comprehensive immigration reform and major trade deals like the Trans-Pacific Partnership stands in direct opposition to Trump's platform. Nehlen pointed to those exact two policy areas as his primary motivation for taking on the speaker, though he stopped short of officially backing Trump's White House bid.

Jim Rubens, running against Ayotte in New Hampshire, harbors no such hesitation, telling Reuters that he truly admires Trump's independence. Like the presidential candidate, Rubens advocates for constructing a physical barrier along the southern border and eliminating birthright citizenship, the legal principle granting automatic citizenship to anyone born on U.S. territory. 

Ayotte, currently serving her first term, was once a darling of conservatives when she first won in 2010 with the backing of Sarah Palin during the height of the former Alaska governor's influence. However, her support for immigration reform alienated those same conservative base voters. She also angered moderates by voting against legislation designed to prevent individuals suspected of terrorism from purchasing firearms. Gonzales observed that Ayotte finds herself in a position where she cannot launch fierce attacks against Donald Trump because she desperately needs every single Republican vote she can get in the state.

Out in Arizona, Ward is taking on McCain—the moderate 2008 Republican presidential nominee—within a state where tensions surrounding immigration remain exceptionally high. Ward has publicly voiced support for Trump's assertion that Mexico has been intentionally dispatching criminals into the United States, a claim that the Mexican government has strongly dismissed. 

Nevertheless, Ward smells opportunity. A poll published the previous month by Public Policy Polling revealed that McCain's approval rating among Arizona Republicans sat at just 33 percent.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — On Thursday, House Speaker Paul Ryan rolled out a national security strategy centered on robust defense, marking the latest phase of a conservative legislative platform designed to bring Republicans together following a contentious primary season. 

The strategy takes direct aim at President Barack Obama, accusing the Democratic administration of presiding over nearly a decade of unfulfilled commitments, compromises, and withdrawals regarding the conflict in Syria, the international accord with Iran, strained diplomatic ties with Russia, and interactions with an aggressive North Korea. 

Under the proposal, several key foreign policy milestones of the Obama presidency—such as the Iran nuclear agreement and the diplomatic opening toward Cuba—would be reversed. The document also pushes back against initiatives aimed at shutting down the detention facility at Guantanamo Bay. 

Without specifying exact figures, the agenda demands a halt to defense spending cuts and insists on stable, sufficient funding levels. 

Certain aspects of the blueprint diverge from the foreign policy positions held by presumptive GOP presidential nominee Donald Trump, whom Ryan has backed. Notably, the document omits any call for a massive wall along the southern border, which remains a central theme of Trump’s campaign. Instead, Ryan advocates for border protections utilizing elevated fencing, airborne surveillance, and radar systems. 

At the same time, the strategy aligns with specific worries raised by Trump regarding Muslim immigration, advocating for stricter vetting procedures for refugees and exploring methods to prevent the radicalization of young people, a topic that drew heavy criticism after Trump proposed a temporary ban on Muslims entering the country. 

“We must constantly reassess our defenses in order to find and close security gaps so that Islamist militants cannot slip into our country undetected,” the document states. 

Rejecting an isolationist approach, the platform adopts an aggressive stance against extremists overseas, asserting that Washington must keep all potential measures available and dismantle terrorist safe havens. 

While Trump has frequently questioned traditional U.S. alliances, Ryan’s proposal reinforces the significance of NATO, defines the relationship with Israel as foundational for regional stability in the Middle East, pushes for harsh penalties against Iran, and urges a firm stance against Russian actions alongside support for Ukraine. Furthermore, it encourages the expansion of trade pacts and suggests that foreign assistance should be geared toward fostering self-reliance in recipient nations. 

Increased protection for diplomatic personnel and overseas installations is also emphasized, referencing the 2012 incident in Benghazi—an event frequently invoked by Republicans to target former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, who is running against Trump. 

As the nation’s top-ranking elected Republican, Ryan has framed this series of policy proposals as a method to present a unified legislative vision to the electorate for the upcoming year. This follows the release of his poverty-reduction platform earlier in the week, with subsequent proposals focusing on federal regulations, constitutional limits, healthcare, and tax code overhauls anticipated in the near future.

LITTLE HOCKING, Ohio (Reuters) — The controversy in Washington surrounding Donald Trump Jr.’s acceptance of Russian assistance during the previous presidential campaign draws little more than perplexed expressions along the Appalachian Highway in southern Ohio. Across this predominantly rural, heavily Baptist region where support for Trump remains strong, local reactions span from total unawareness of the ongoing Russia probes and complete apathy to a conviction that certain media outlets are actively trying to bring down the Republican president and his relatives. 

Interviews conducted with twenty individuals across various Ohio communities revealed widespread dismissal of the continuous news cycle concerning the June 2016 meeting between the president's eldest son and an individual he understood to be a Russian government attorney offering potentially damaging details about Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton. These details came to light when Trump Jr. published email correspondence on a Tuesday during ongoing inquiries into U.S. intelligence findings that Moscow attempted to assist Trump's electoral victory. While Moscow has rejected accusations of election meddling, the president has likewise rejected claims of campaign collusion with Russian officials, occasionally characterizing the idea as "fake news."

Lisa Walker, a 54-year-old thrift shop owner in Little Hocking, sported an American flag t-shirt and mentioned that her husband worries someone might attempt to assassinate the president. Having both cast ballots for Trump, she has kept up with the media coverage regarding the president's son, interpreting the Russia probe as evidence that adversaries are actively trying to target the administration. Expressing her frustration, she stated she wishes critics had more productive pursuits than playing games and attacking the president. 

Across Jackson and Piketon, the difficulties faced by Donald Trump Jr. seemingly reinforced backing for the president and his family, whom residents frequently view as besieged underdogs. Gary Abernathy, editor of the Hillsboro Times Gazette in the Highland County seat of Hillsboro, noted that a prevailing local sentiment is that the press is bent on ruining Trump. Pointing out that his publication was among just six nationwide to back Trump during the election, Abernathy observed that the continuous focus on Russia simply validates local suspicions. He added that while critical or aggressive coverage of Donald Trump is acceptable to him, the current approach feels like an intentional effort to pull him down, noting the disproportionate, wall-to-wall coverage given to a single twenty-minute meeting between Trump Jr. and a Russian lawyer.

Trump secured Highland County with over 76 percent of the vote, exceeding the performance of the 2012 GOP nominee, Mitt Romney, by 12 points. This rural Midwestern voting surge proved crucial to Trump's overall electoral triumph. 

The meeting involving Trump Jr. generated further inquiries and news coverage regarding potential collusion and possible violations of U.S. law. Federal Election Campaign Act regulations prohibit foreign nationals from making contributions to domestic political campaigns. 

Nationwide public opinion regarding Trump and Russia was sharply polarized even prior to these newest revelations. A June Reuters/Ipsos survey indicated that half of all Americans believed the president or his campaign staff collaborated with Russia to sway the 2016 election, whereas 33 percent rejected this notion and the remaining respondents expressed uncertainty. Conversely, among Republicans, two-thirds rejected the idea of campaign collusion with Russia, while one-fifth believed it occurred and others remained unsure.

Meanwhile, at a Jackson Bob Evans restaurant, three Walmart employees taking a lunch break—all of them Trump voters—offered blank stares when questioned about the investigations into Russia. Chastity Banks stated that she had never heard of the matter, a sentiment shared by her two coworkers.
