During an appearance on the Fox Sports 1 program Undisputed back in September, rapper Lil Wayne—legally named Dwayne Michael Carter Jr—asserted that he has "never dealt with racism." The New Orleans native pointed out to host Skip Bayless that his concert audiences are filled with numerous white fans, which led him to believe racism isn't real. 

These remarks sparked significant backlash across social media platforms. In response, Carter clarified his perspective by recounting a pivotal childhood incident involving the person who saved his life. When he was 12 years old, Carter accidentally shot himself in the chest. As he lay on the floor, responding police officers forced their way into the residence, initially stepping right over his body while conducting a search for narcotics and firearms. 

Carter noted that the officers who first rushed inside were "blacker than me," yet the singular cop who paused to assist him was described as "white as snow." This officer, affectionately referred to as "Uncle Bob," scolded his colleagues for ignoring the wounded boy and personally transported Carter to the medical facility. The rapper recalled that the officer remained at the hospital, waiting until medical personnel confirmed, "He's gonna make it." Emphasizing this memory, Carter stated, "Yeah, he was a cop, and my life was saved by a white man. I don't know what racism is."

Even though he made those statements to Bayless, Carter subsequently acknowledged that racism does indeed exist. Nonetheless, he maintained that when performing on stage, his crowds consist of diverse individuals rather than any single demographic or culture. "It's people—those people out there in that crowd," Carter explained, adding that because he is fortunate to experience that kind of environment, he must remain honest about never having witnessed racism personally, according to the Daily Mail.

Previously, Lil Wayne sat down for an interview with Nightline, a conversation where the hosts reportedly grew frustrated when the rapper refused to provide the responses they anticipated. When Nightline presenter Lindsey Davis tried to characterize him as sexist and misogynistic, Carter brushed the labels off as unimportant. He also caught the host off guard regarding his perspective on marijuana, stating his priorities in order were God, family, his children, music, and lastly weed. The interview ultimately concluded in frustration after Davis appeared displeased by his reluctance to endorse the Black Lives Matter movement associated with Barack Obama.

LONDON (Reuters) — An individual convicted of leaking details to Israel to assist in the assassinations of high-ranking nuclear researchers has received a death sentence in Iran, according to statements made Tuesday by Tehran's prosecutor. While Abbas Jafari Dolatabadi refrained from naming the accused individual, human rights organization Amnesty International noted a day prior that Ahmadreza Djalali—an Iranian physician who lived and studied in Sweden—had faced a death ruling in the country on accusations of spying. 

Between 2010 and 2012, at least four researchers lost their lives in what authorities in Tehran described as a targeted campaign designed to undermine the nation's nuclear energy initiatives. Previously, Iran executed an individual in 2012 in connection with these deaths, alleging connections to Israel. 

Addressing the most recent ruling, Dolatabadi informed the judiciary's official news outlet that the accused held multiple encounters with the Israeli intelligence service, Mossad, handing over classified data regarding Iranian military and atomic facilities in exchange for financial compensation and residency status in Sweden. The official publication's headline referred to the condemned individual as a Mossad agent. 

Meanwhile, Amnesty indicated that the judicial ruling specified the defendant collaborated with the Israeli government, which subsequently assisted in securing his Swedish residency. Neither the Iranian authorities nor Amnesty specified the exact date when the judgment was handed down. 

In Sweden, the government spoke out against the ruling, confirming that officials had addressed the issue with Iranian diplomats in both Stockholm and Tehran. Swedish Foreign Minister Margot Wallstrom expressed opposition in an email, stating that capital punishment is rejected in all situations, calling it an irreversible, cruel, and inhumane practice that lacks justification within modern jurisprudence. 

Djalali, who practiced medicine and taught at the Karolinska Institute—a medical university based in Stockholm—was detained in April 2016. According to the London-based human rights group, he was denied legal counsel for seven months, which included a three-month period spent in solitary confinement. 

Philip Luther, who directs Amnesty’s advocacy efforts for the Middle East, asserted that Djalali received his death sentence following a profoundly flawed trial, demonstrating both Tehran's continued reliance on capital punishment and a blatant disregard for legal standards. 

While Washington rejected Tehran's claims suggesting American involvement in the scientists' deaths, Israeli officials maintained a stance of silence, declining to address the accusations. 

According to Dolatabadi, the convicted person supplied Mossad with details concerning 30 military and atomic experts, a group that included Massoud Ali Mohammadi, who died when a remote-controlled explosive device fastened to a motorcycle detonated near his Tehran residence. The judiciary further stated the defendant had connections to the targeted killing of nuclear engineer Majid Shahriari, who perished in a November 2010 bombing. 

The wife of the accused, Vida Mehrannia, currently resides in Sweden alongside their two children and shared with Amnesty that her husband's psychological and physical well-being has experienced a severe decline during his imprisonment. Amnesty shared her plea demanding his freedom due to an absence of any actual offenses. 

At the Karolinska Institute—where Djalali earned a PhD in disaster medicine back in 2012—the vice-chancellor voiced serious apprehension. Ole Petter Ottersen noted in a published university statement that Djalali spent years collaborating with international scientists to enhance hospital capabilities in regions grappling with severe poverty, war, and crisis situations, while urging that he be granted a fair trial adhering to proper legal procedures.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) - On Tuesday, U.S. President Donald Trump launched criticisms against the probe into purported Russian interference during the previous year's American election, while simultaneously alleging—though providing no proof—that Ukraine aided his Democratic opponent, Hillary Clinton. Through a couple of morning posts on Twitter, the Republican leader additionally asserted that U.S. Attorney General Jeff Sessions had adopted a “very weak position” concerning the Democratic candidate. He pointed to what he termed “Ukrainian efforts to sabotage Trump campaign - quietly working to boost Clinton’,” though he provided no further details or evidence regarding any Ukrainian involvement in the 2016 race. 

These ongoing investigations into potential Russian meddling and possible connections between Moscow and his campaign have cast a shadow over the president's initial half-year in office. A request for comment sent to the Ukrainian president’s spokesman did not receive an immediate reply. However, the Ukrainian Embassy located in Washington rejected assertions that Kiev attempted to sway the U.S. vote. 

“We stand by our words that the government of Ukraine didn’t help any candidate in (the) election. Ukraine is proud of bipartisan support in the U.S.,” the embassy stated via Twitter. 

Additionally, Dmytro Kuleba, who serves as Ukraine’s permanent representative to the Council of Europe, wrote on Twitter: “Trump writes that we interfered in the elections in the USA, while Putin says that we threaten Russia. There was a time when we were peaceful buckwheat sowers who kept themselves to themselves.” 

While American intelligence agencies concluded that Moscow tried to influence the presidential contest, the Russian government has rejected these findings, and Trump has maintained that his campaign had no collusion with Russia. Federal congressional committees and a special counsel are currently looking into the claims. Prior to the voting in November, the FBI investigated how Clinton managed her emails during her tenure as secretary of state under Democratic President Barack Obama, though the bureau ultimately concluded that criminal charges were unjustified.

Patriots who care about the nation are being urged to abandon Macy’s and prioritize American citizens instead. The retailer's customer service line—1 (800) 289-6229—is being highlighted for citizens to voice their frustration over progressive pressure tactics, express support for Donald Trump's stance on lawful immigration, and announce the cancellation of store credit cards, bringing an end to their business with the company.

Republican presidential contender and real estate developer Donald Trump urged a boycott of the department store chain on a Wednesday, following the company's decision to pull his merchandise from their shelves. Earlier that day, Macy's announced it was severing ties due to what it termed derogatory remarks regarding Mexican immigrants made by Trump during his campaign kickoff event, where he alleged that Mexico was dispatching criminals and drug traffickers across the border.

Alongside a formal press release condemning the corporation, Trump took to Twitter to criticize Macy's for having a lax stance on border protection. He posted that supporters of strong borders, halted illegal immigration, and intelligent international trade agreements should avoid shopping at the retailer, echoing similar sentiments in multiple tweets on July 1, 2015.

This development follows a wave of corporate distancing from Trump over the preceding week. Organizations including NBC, Univision, and Mexican broadcaster Televisa previously stated they would drop broadcasts of the Miss Universe Organization pageants due to his remarks regarding immigrants. During his campaign announcement speech in June, transcripts show Trump remarking that the individuals coming from Mexico often bring drugs, crime, and sexual assault, though he added that some are presumably good people.

Insisting his target was the Mexican government rather than its population, Trump pushed back fiercely against the corporate entities severing ties. He announced a $500 million lawsuit against Univision, labeled NBC as weak, and maintained that he was the one who terminated the relationship with Macy's rather than the reverse.

Furthermore, he contended that the retailer's rejection demonstrated the hurdles faced by wealthy individuals entering the political arena. In his Wednesday announcement, he noted that achieving success makes seeking the presidency exceptionally difficult, while reiterating his independence from corporate influences like NBC and Macy's, which he claimed demonstrated support for illegal immigration through their actions. The affected merchandise sold at the stores included priced items such as $70 dress shirts, $65 neckties, and a cologne named Success, as reported by Business Insider.

MOSCOW (Reuters) — During his court appearance on Monday, former Russian economy minister Alexei Ulyukayev claimed he was under the impression that a bag containing $2 million in cash, handed to him by Rosneft chief executive Igor Sechin, was actually a present of high-end alcohol. 

Ulyukayev stands trial on charges of extorting a bribe and could receive a maximum prison sentence of 15 years if convicted. Sechin, who is a trusted confidant of President Vladimir Putin, allegedly provided the $2 million last year on Nov. 14. According to the prosecution, the money served as a payoff for Ulyukayev's approval of Rosneft's acquisition of another state-controlled petroleum firm, Bashneft. Law enforcement officers took Ulyukayev into custody at the Rosneft offices shortly after Sechin transferred the locked brown bag—alongside a small basket containing sausage—which prosecutors described as part of the gift. Putin dismissed Ulyukayev from his ministerial post the following day.

Addressing the judiciary, Ulyukayev maintained that he genuinely believed the items were meant as a present, arguing instead that he had walked into a trap. He told the courtroom that the entire incident was a premeditated operation and a set-up directed against him. 

The defense team has been working to justify why their client took the bag from Sechin, particularly since court transcripts show neither man spoke about the contents. Ulyukayev explained to the court that during his tenure as economy minister, Sechin had visited his workplace on a couple of occasions typically carrying a large bag filled with various presents. He noted that Sechin had previously gifted him a watch and an oil-derrick model in person, besides sending food hampers for birthdays and similar occasions. A prosecutor acknowledged that Ulyukayev had also been given alcoholic beverages by Sechin previously. In Ulyukayev's view, these exchanges were simply a matter of standard etiquette.

The former official recounted that the heavy bag—weighing approximately 15 kg or 33 lbs, given to him during the law enforcement sting at Rosneft's headquarters—led him to believe it held costly wine or spirits. He added that a month prior, Sechin had pledged to reward the successful conclusion of the Bashneft privatization by giving him a wine he had never tasted before. Because of this promise, Ulyukayev testified, finding money inside the bag came as a complete surprise.

Despite being a principal witness, Sechin has not appeared in court despite receiving four separate summonses. A letter submitted by his legal counsel explained that his absence was due to ongoing business travel.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — Obstacles emerged on Tuesday in the Trump administration's quest for a replacement FBI director as a prominent moderate judge and a conservative lawmaker both indicated they were passing on the opportunity. Sources close to U.S. Senator John Cornyn of Texas and Judge Merrick Garland informed Reuters that they advised both men against pursuing the top law enforcement post, warning them that they would be walking away from stable, impactful positions to step into an environment defined by intense political friction and controversy. 

According to these advisers, who spoke anonymously, anyone taking on the role of FBI director would face minimal job security and intense political spotlight following Donald Trump's sudden dismissal of James Comey on May 9. The hesitation from Garland and Cornyn—surfacing just three days prior to Trump's stated timeline for a potential appointment—highlights the administration's struggle to secure a candidate amid ongoing internal turbulence. 

Comey's removal, which targeted the official overseeing the inquiry into potential ties between the 2016 campaign and Russia, sparked widespread anger among legislators on both sides of the aisle, including members of the president's own party. An individual close to Garland, the top jurist on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, noted that the judge is deeply devoted to his current work and has no desire to exit the court system. Meanwhile, Cornyn released a public statement confirming he had let the White House know his highest impact lies in pushing forward a conservative agenda from his seat in the Senate. 

White House Press Secretary Sean Spicer informed the press on Tuesday that an appointment could still be made before the president departs on his inaugural overseas journey on Friday, adding that the Department of Justice continues to vet potential choices. 

A number of Republican senators had previously championed Garland, a surprising shift given that they previously blocked confirmation hearings when Democratic President Barack Obama put him forward for a Supreme Court vacancy the prior year. Their logic appeared rooted in the idea that Garland's appointment could appease Democrats and help rebuild public trust in the bureau's political neutrality. During an appearance on Bloomberg Television, Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, a Republican, described Garland—a former federal prosecutor—as an objective professional. 

A second anonymous source familiar with Garland explained that he consulted confidants who pointed out that accepting the FBI job meant abandoning a secure, permanent judgeship for a position where he could be fired by the president at a moment's notice. Additionally, a Republican Senate staffer mentioned that Cornyn’s team feared transitioning to the bureau might prematurely derail the political future of the third-term Texan and his staff. 

Concurrently, a representative for another contender on the administration's radar, former New York City Police Commissioner Ray Kelly, age 75, revealed that Kelly is likewise facing pressure to withdraw from consideration. While Kelly has not outright rejected the possibility, he has yet to undergo a formal interview. Another individual whose name had circulated, Republican Representative and former federal prosecutor Trey Gowdy, stated on Monday that he holds no interest in the directorship. 

The challenges in recruiting for key government positions extend well beyond the bureau. Three individuals who turned down discussions about joining the administration noted that the president's tendencies to publicly contradict advisers, demand unwavering personal loyalty, and sideline officials who disagree with him have deterred numerous seasoned professionals. A senior official remarked that drawing capable candidates to serve in the current administration is growing steadily harder, adding that many experienced veterans with deep expertise are either departing entirely or seeking roles abroad to distance themselves from the White House.

Casts Of Broadway’s ‘Hamilton’ And ‘Color Purple’ Give Stunning Musical Tribute To Fallen Icon Prince (VIDEO)

Following the unexpected and devastating passing of legendary musician Prince on Thursday, the global community has been left in a state of shock, leading to a massive wave of mourning and incredible homages to an artist who profoundly defined modern music and pop culture. Two standout tributes came directly from Broadway, where the performers of both Hamilton and The Color Purple dedicated the conclusion of their Thursday evening performances to honoring the late star through music. 

For their tribute, the actors in Hamilton treated the audience to a choreographed dance routine set to an instrumental version of "Let's Go Crazy," widely recognized as one of the musician's most enduring and famous tracks, with footage of the moment shared via Raw Story. Meanwhile, the ensemble cast of The Color Purple opted for a vocal rendition of the timeless anthem "Purple Rain," the very track that launched Prince to massive chart-topping success following the debut of his 1984 album sharing the same title, featuring a moving homage led by production star Jennifer Hudson. 

These fitting and breathtaking tributes reflect the monumental impact of Prince, whose status as a defining figure in contemporary music and whose legendary influence will leave a lasting void felt deeply by everyday fans, prominent celebrities, and listeners everywhere. Gratitude is owed to Broadway for offering such touching homages during a period of collective grief.Featured image via Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images

TALLAHASSEE — Prominent trial attorney and major Democratic fundraiser John Morgan delivered a major blow to the party ahead of the 2018 elections by announcing in a post-Thanksgiving statement that he is cutting ties with the Democrats. In the same message, he suggested that Democratic Sen. Bill Nelson ought to skip a re-election bid and instead run for governor to secure a meaningful legacy.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — A group consisting of 40 former national security officials and retired U.S. diplomats has sent a letter to Secretary of State Rex Tillerson, appealing to him to preserve the State Department's refugee bureau, according to a document reviewed by Reuters on Monday. The signatories warned that moving the functions of the Bureau of Population, Refugees and Migration (PRM) to different departments, as currently proposed by the Trump administration, would weaken the nation's diplomatic influence when dealing with overseas crises. Signers of the appeal included high-ranking former figures such as former Deputy Secretary of State William Burns, former Under Secretaries of State for Political Affairs Nicholas Burns and Wendy Sherman, along with former Middle East peace envoy Dennis Ross. 

The communication, which additionally carried the signatures of 18 leaders from non-governmental humanitarian organizations, emphasized that whether dealing with situations in Afghanistan, Iraq, Kenya, South Sudan, or Turkey, the State Department must closely align its diplomatic outreach with emergency aid efforts. The letter stated that abolishing the assistance operations currently handled by the PRM would severely harm the Secretary of State's ability to sway policy matters critical to the United States. 

In response, State Department spokeswoman Heather Nauert noted that Tillerson approaches the ongoing restructuring of the agency without any fixed ideas about the final results. She mentioned that Tillerson considers the functions carried out by both the PRM and the Bureau of Consular Affairs to be vital for achieving the agency's goals of safeguarding citizens and securing national borders. 

Previously, a budget document reviewed by Reuters outlined a plan to shift the management of the U.S. Refugee Admission Program—which aids in resettling refugees domestically—over to the Department of Homeland Security. Initially broken by CNN on June 30, the memo was described by a former official as having been drafted by the White House domestic policy council, and it suggests both dissolving the bureau entirely and reassigning its remaining duties to other entities. 

Both the memorandum and the outreach from former diplomats highlight an ongoing broader conflict concerning immigration and refugee strategies. This broader context features executive orders from President Donald Trump that temporarily barred most refugees and travelers from several Muslim-majority nations—orders that faced legal challenges—alongside internal discussions regarding the financial aspects of refugee resettlement and increased enforcement against illegal immigration. 

The topic was anticipated to surface during a Monday evening hearing before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, scheduled for 5 p.m. (2100 GMT), where Deputy Secretary of State John Sullivan was set to speak regarding the department's restructuring initiatives.

WASHINGTON — Congressional Republicans are considering reaching across the aisle to strike a bipartisan budget pact with Democrats, mirroring an agreement from nearly four years ago, as internal divisions persist over appropriations for the upcoming fiscal year that begins October 1. 

With a lengthy August recess approaching and only 20 working days left on the calendar, a number of GOP lawmakers point out that joining forces with Democrats could help clear a packed legislative agenda. That agenda currently features a separate budget resolution, an infrastructure package, tax reform, and a raise for the federal debt ceiling. 

Back in December 2013, current House Speaker Paul Ryan—then a Republican representative—and Democratic Senator Patty Murray successfully negotiated a two-year compromise. That accord rolled back certain spending reductions for the 2014 and 2015 fiscal years in exchange for long-term spending cuts, and it was signed into law shortly thereafter. 

Reaching a similar bipartisan accord now could prevent a government shutdown threatened by President Donald Trump, while also avoiding a restrictive funding cap for federal agencies. 

"I think what we need is another Ryan-Murray sort of proposal," remarked Republican Representative Mike Simpson, a high-ranking member of the House Appropriations Committee, which oversees the drafting of yearly spending legislation. Following a meeting of House Republicans, Simpson noted that discussions surrounding the concept remain preliminary.

Although Republicans hold majorities in both chambers, they have pushed back against the severe spending reductions put forward by President Trump. At the same time, internal disagreements persist regarding overall spending allocations for the following year, particularly concerning the military expansion requested by the president.

A bipartisan accord represents merely one path forward. An alternative approach involves fast-tracking a single, massive fiscal 2018 spending bill through the House during July, bypassing the traditional process of drafting twelve separate appropriations measures. Pushing through such a package would give Republicans a concrete legislative win to present to voters during the August recess, following months with relatively few accomplishments. 

Because time is short for such an undertaking, Speaker Ryan could potentially find himself limited to passing a national security-focused spending measure dedicated to funding the military and related security operations. Certain GOP members are pushing to elevate defense spending to $640 billion, a move that would necessitate severe reductions to non-defense initiatives favored by moderate Republicans. 

Additionally, lawmakers face the task of approving a budget resolution to lay the groundwork for tax reform. Members of the House Budget Committee indicated that they aim to mark up that specific measure prior to June 30.

Without pressure, South Carolina is unlikely to change its stance, leaving the flag flying over a campus that includes African American students, a situation Smith argued requires external force to correct.

Opposing Smith's measure, Armed Services Committee Chairman U.S. Rep. Mac Thornberry, R-Texas, introduced an amendment to the amendment. His addition exempted universities that had already voted to remove the flag from losing ROTC funds, effectively neutralizing the original proposal. Thornberry expressed that it would be unfair to penalize individuals attempting to do the right thing when the obstacle lies with the state legislature. 

U.S. Rep. Joe Wilson, the sole South Carolina representative on the committee, shared a letter he received that day from The Citadel's president, Lt. Gen. John Rosa, which opposed Smith's amendment. Rosa wrote to the Republican congressman that relocating the flag aligns with the college's core values of duty, honor, and respect, but emphasized that these values also mandate adherence to the law.

WASHINGTON/NEW YORK (Reuters) - According to individuals close to the inquiry, legal representatives for former national security advisor Michael Flynn have broken off talks with the legal team representing U.S. President Donald Trump, marking a potentially pivotal development in the ongoing investigation into alleged ties between the Trump presidential campaign and Russia. On Wednesday, Flynn's defense attorney, Robert Kelner, reached out to Trump's personal lawyer, John Dowd, to inform him that the situation had evolved to a stage where sharing information was no longer feasible, according to two individuals with knowledge of the conversation who spoke to Reuters on Friday. The cessation of communication between the two legal camps was initially broken by The New York Times. 

As a retired Army general, Flynn occupies a pivotal position in the federal inquiry headed by Special Counsel Robert Mueller, which aims to determine whether members of Trump's team coordinated with reported Russian attempts to influence the 2016 election. Insiders noted it remains uncertain whether Kelner initiated the contact because a cooperation deal had been struck with Mueller's office, or simply because Flynn opted to engage directly with the special counsel. 

Addressing the situation on Thursday, Trump's counsel Jay Sekulow stated, “No one should draw the conclusion that this means anything about General Flynn cooperating against the president.” Meanwhile, both Dowd and Peter Carr, a representative for Mueller, opted not to provide comments on Friday, a stance shared by Kelner and officials at the White House.

Having served as a senior campaign advisor prior to stepping into the role of national security advisor within the Trump administration, Flynn's testimony or cooperation would serve as a significant tool for Mueller's probe. Earlier in March, while unsuccessfully pursuing immunity so his client could speak before House and Senate panels probing the matter, Kelner remarked, “Mr. Flynn certainly has a story to tell, and he certainly wants to tell it, should the circumstances permit.”

Insiders close to Mueller's inquiry indicated that Flynn could offer valuable perspective across three primary focal points: potential coordination between Moscow and the 2016 Trump campaign; prospective financial misconduct, such as money laundering, by campaign associates; and whether President Trump attempted to obstruct justice by dismissing former FBI Director James Comey in May while the bureau looked into campaign ties with Russia. 

Moscow has consistently refuted allegations of election meddling. Concurrently, Trump has repeatedly rejected claims of campaign collusion with Russia, dismissing the investigation as a witch hunt. 

Two congressional insiders participating in separate investigations concerning Trump campaign interactions with Russia noted that a major line of inquiry centers on whether Flynn or other associates ever dangled the prospect of lifting U.S. economic sanctions against Russia in exchange for advantageous commercial agreements. Informants familiar with the matter told Reuters that these prospective arrangements included a nuclear power venture backed by Russian entities that Flynn had previously advocated for among prospective Middle Eastern clients. 

“At this point, there is no evidence of an effort to negotiate that kind of deal, but Flynn is near the top of the list of people who probably would know if there was any such effort,” observed one congressional source, who spoke anonymously.

Trump dismissed Flynn on Feb. 13 following revelations that Flynn had conversed regarding U.S. sanctions with Sergei Kislyak, the Russian ambassador at the time, during December—just prior to Trump's inauguration—and subsequently provided misleading accounts of those discussions to Vice President Mike Pence. While Flynn has admitted to interacting with Kislyak as far back as 2013, he has refrained from detailing the specifics of his talks with the diplomat during and following the presidential campaign, though he acknowledged the discussions touched on multiple topics.

Sources close to the investigation have pointed out that Flynn faces examination from the special counsel across several fronts. Mueller's team has looked into whether Flynn provided false information to federal authorities regarding his foreign trips, earnings, and interactions listed on security clearance documentation. Additionally, investigators have scrutinized his employment for Russian clients, alongside the legality of work performed for a businessman connected to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

Furthermore, sources stated that Mueller has been reviewing the involvement of Flynn’s son, Michael Flynn Jr., in various business operations conducted by his father spanning Russia, Turkey, and other locations, a factor that could create substantial leverage for Flynn to collaborate with investigators. Barry Coburn, who represents Flynn's son, chose not to issue a statement.

Voters in California have voted in favor of a ballot initiative legalizing adult recreational cannabis use, establishing the country's most heavily populated state as a major hub for the expanding commercial weed industry and marking a significant triumph for advocates of drug law reform. Wednesday morning updates covering over 90 percent of precincts indicated that Proposition 64 secured a comfortable victory, with approximately 56 percent of the electorate supporting it and 44 percent voting against. 

As the most substantial among five states considering similar measures to permit recreational cannabis, California's green light brings legalization across the entire American Pacific Coast. Washington and Colorado initially legalized recreational cannabis back in 2012, followed subsequently by Oregon, Alaska, and the District of Columbia. Additionally, advocates celebrated a win on Tuesday for a comparable initiative in Massachusetts, marking the initial foothold for legal recreational cannabis in the New England region. Nevada residents also voted in favor of recreational legalization, whereas neighboring Arizona turned down a similar ballot question. Meanwhile, the outcome in Maine remained undecided as of Wednesday morning. 

The Marijuana Policy Project, which stands as the country's premier advocacy group for reforming cannabis laws, similarly anticipated the success of initiatives allowing medical marijuana in Florida, Arkansas, North Dakota, and Montana. Prior to Tuesday's elections, cannabis had already been legalized in some capacity—either recreationally, medically, or both—across 25 states. Based on data from the U.S. Census, the green light in California alone—housing a population of 39 million—results in nearly 20 percent of all Americans residing in jurisdictions where recreational marijuana is permitted. Notably, California previously pioneered medical marijuana legalization nationwide by passing its initial measure back in 1996.

Backed by an alliance of advocates that featured tech billionaire Sean Parker alongside Democratic Lieutenant Governor Gavin Newsom, the newly approved initiative grants adults the right to carry and consume up to an ounce of cannabis for personal enjoyment. The legislation additionally authorizes individuals to grow up to six marijuana plants at home. Beyond personal use, the measure sets up a framework for licensing, overseeing, and taxing cannabis sales, while granting municipal authorities the power to regulate commercial distribution locally. Although California residents previously rejected a similar proposition back in 2010, surveys demonstrate that public sentiment has evolved considerably since that time. 

Critics of drug law reform contended that such policies present serious public safety hazards and would increase youth accessibility to marijuana. Conversely, specialists noted that these recent ballot questions feature advanced oversight frameworks designed to prevent minors from obtaining cannabis and to exclude criminal organizations and cartels from the supply chain. Observers also highlighted projections pointing to hundreds of millions of dollars in fresh state tax income generated by cannabis commerce, alongside billions in broader economic output. 

Fresh market investors expressed enthusiasm about entering a recreational cannabis industry that certain projections suggest could attain a value of $50 billion within the coming ten years. John Matsusaka, a political science professor at the University of Southern California, noted that public perception among these voters has shifted away from viewing the substance like cocaine and toward viewing it more like beer. Furthermore, civil rights organizations supported the legalization push, contending that existing marijuana regulations have historically resulted in the disproportionate imprisonment of minority populations for minor drug infractions.

text: BELFAST (Reuters) - A well-placed source has indicated that former U.S. President Bill Clinton—instrumental in the region's historic peace agreements—could make a trip to Belfast this week in an effort to resolve the ongoing political stalemate that has persisted for months. Previously, Clinton visited Belfast back in March for the funeral services of Martin McGuinness, where he pressed local leaders to complete the mission initiated by the former IRA commander who turned into a pillar of the peace initiatives. Central to the ongoing negotiations between the pro-British Democratic Unionist Party and Irish nationalists Sinn Fein is a sharp dispute regarding protections and rights for speakers of the Irish language. While the facilitating British and Irish administrations remain hopeful that the power-sharing administration might get back on track this month, the involved political groups emphasize that significant hurdles still remain.

BRUSSELS (Reuters) — On Tuesday, members of the NATO alliance expressed support for President Donald Trump’s choice to deploy additional military personnel to Afghanistan, a move tied to a revised American strategy that calls for increased contributions of both soldiers and financial resources from U.S. allies. Although Trump campaigned for the presidency advocating a rapid exit from the country, he shifted his position on Monday by committing to an intensified military offensive against the Taliban, declaring that American forces would fight to achieve victory. According to government officials, the president approved authorizations to dispatch roughly 4,000 additional American soldiers to join the approximately 8,400 troops currently stationed in Afghanistan. Nevertheless, his address omitted specific performance metrics for concluding the conflict, which originated with the 2001 U.S.-led invasion and which he noted had demanded a massive cost in lives and financial resources. 

Trump stated that Washington would request that international partners and NATO allies back the updated strategy through proportional increases in funding and troop levels, expressing certainty that they would oblige. This remark indicated that the administration intends to maintain pressure on foreign partners, who have previously faced demands from Trump to increase defense contributions alongside his earlier characterization of the alliance as outdated—though he has since walked back the "obsolete" label since entering office. 

In an official statement, NATO Secretary General Jens Stoltenberg noted that the alliance stays entirely dedicated to the mission in Afghanistan and expressed eagerness to review the path forward alongside international partners, allies, and Defense Secretary James Mattis. Stoltenberg pointed out that NATO currently maintains 12,000 personnel in the region, with 15 nations having already promised further reinforcements. 

A prominent NATO participant, the United Kingdom, described the American pledge as highly positive. British Defence Secretary Michael Fallon noted that during a conversation with Mattis the previous day, they concurred that despite existing difficulties, maintaining involvement is essential to support the fragile democratic system and mitigate terrorist risks directed at Western nations. 

Germany, which has frequently been targeted by Trump regarding its level of military expenditures, similarly voiced approval for the fresh U.S. blueprint. A representative for the German administration stated that sustained involvement remains vital on the road toward regional stability. European partners had previously committed additional personnel back in June without specifying exact figures, preferring to hold off until the administration clarified its regional approach. 

Nearly sixteen years following the initial American-led intervention—which followed the September 11 attacks orchestrated from Afghanistan by al Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden—the nation continues to grapple with an ongoing Taliban insurgency and a fragile central authority. Trump remarked that he understood the sentiments of citizens exhausted by endless conflicts without clear triumphs, yet warned that a sudden departure would leave a dangerous void that extremist organizations like al Qaeda and Islamic State could exploit.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — U.S. Interior Secretary Ryan Zinke is set to deliver his recommendation to the White House on Saturday regarding whether the Bears Ears monument in Utah should be reduced in size or revoked entirely. This upcoming decision will establish a precedent for the Trump administration's wider examination of protected public lands that could potentially be opened up for commercial development. The exact timing for when this choice will be publicly disclosed remains uncertain. 

Although the 1.35 million acres making up the Bears Ears designation are not thought to hold vast quantities of petroleum, natural gas, or coal, several other protected sites under Zinke's review do harbor such resources, elevating the significance of the Bears Ears verdict for corporate energy interests. Below is an overview of those locations:

BASIN AND RANGE: Established as a 704,000-acre national monument in southeastern Nevada by Barack Obama in 2015, this territory lies within the Chainman Shale formation, viewed by certain sectors of the drilling sector as a high-potential deposit.

BEARS EARS: Formed in late 2016 by Barack Obama just prior to the end of his presidency, this 1.35 million-acre southeastern Utah monument encompasses two well-known buttes and possesses moderate oil and gas prospects. Prior to its protection status, EOG Resources had already secured drilling leases inside the area.

CANYON OF THE ANCIENTS: Set aside by Bill Clinton as a 178,000-acre national monument in southwestern Colorado in the year 2000, this location was already utilized by the petroleum industry. Consequently, the former president permitted existing energy operations to persist under specific restrictions.

CARRIZO PLAIN: Designated by Bill Clinton in 2001, this 204,000-acre site in California sits in a region with a history of petroleum prospecting and holds moderate prospects for commercial extraction. Pre-existing extraction rights belong to the California Resources Corporation within a section of the monument, though a major discovery has not yet been achieved.

GRAND STAIRCASE-ESCALANTE: Established by Bill Clinton in 1996 as a 1.9 million-acre expanse in southern Utah, the Utah Geological Survey indicates that this monument contains an estimated 62 billion tons of coal, alongside coal bed methane and potential commercial reserves of petroleum.

UPPER MISSOURI RIVER BREAKS: Created by Bill Clinton in 2001, this 495,000-acre region in central Montana was evaluated by the U.S. Geological Survey in 1995, which estimated the presence of 58.2 to 719.9 billion cubic feet of natural gas and 14 million to 180 million barrels of oil.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — Secretary of State Rex Tillerson announced on Friday that the United States has designated a special representative to spearhead diplomatic efforts concerning the conflict in Ukraine. Tillerson noted that the decision to fill this role came following a prompt from the Russian president. 

Kurt Volker, a veteran diplomat and former U.S. ambassador to NATO, will take charge of pushing forward American objectives outlined in the 2015 Minsk accord, which aims to de-escalate fighting in the Donbass area of Ukraine. According to the State Department, Volker is scheduled to travel alongside Tillerson to Kiev on Sunday. 

The crisis began when Russia took over Crimea in 2014, and the government in Kiev continues to claim that Moscow supports eastern separatist fighters, a charge the Kremlin rejects. The Minsk pact mandates a truce in the east, pulling back heavy weaponry from the combat zones, and institutional changes granting greater self-rule to eastern regions. 

Speaking to journalists in Hamburg, Germany, following a discussion between Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump during the G20 summit, Tillerson stated, “At the request of President Putin, the United States has appointed a special representative for Ukraine, Ambassador Kurt Volker.” 

In Kiev, President Petro Poroshenko expressed approval of the appointment via Twitter, asserting it would aid in stopping what he termed Russian aggression and bringing Crimea back under Ukrainian control. Poroshenko's post called the decision an essential and well-timed step toward safeguarding the country's borders and sovereignty. 

Volker brings a background as a career diplomat, having held the post of permanent representative to NATO through both the George W. Bush and Barack Obama administrations. At present, he works as a national security and foreign policy specialist at the McCain Institute for International Leadership, which is part of Arizona State University. 

In an official statement, Tillerson praised the selection, expressing total faith in Volker's capability to guide the peace process forward while reaffirming Washington's dedication to the goals of the Minsk accords. 

Meanwhile, Julie Smith, an ex-Pentagon official focused on NATO and European affairs during the Obama presidency, voiced support for Volker specifically, though she expressed confusion over Tillerson's remark that Putin had initiated the appointment. Smith, currently a senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security, questioned whether Ukraine had previously been a low priority for the current administration, calling the framing of the announcement a strange choice of words.

Oklahoma House Bill 3098 was passed on Thursday by the state House of Representatives, advancing legislation that permits the open carrying of firearms without requiring a permit or training. Authored by state Representative Jeff Coody, the measure is grounded in the belief that the right to bear arms is granted by both the Constitution and God, intended for the self-defense of Bible-believing Christians. Coody described the legislation as the ultimate freedom bill regarding open carry, while co-author Representative Jeff Bennett emphasized that self-defense is a God-given right.

During the debate, Democratic Representative Emily Virgin questioned the wisdom of allowing individuals to carry weapons without knowing how to operate them or locate the safety mechanism. Coody dismissed the concern, stating that government does not grant permission to exercise freedoms. While the bill bars convicted felons from openly carrying firearms, it does not apply the same restriction to individuals subject to domestic violence protective orders. Furthermore, the legislation contains no mandate for safety courses or training. 

When questioned about the absence of training requirements, Coody contrasted gun ownership with driving, noting that driving is a privilege whereas the Second Amendment is a constitutional right. Another lawmaker, Representative Mike Brown, questioned whether the government held a responsibility to protect citizens, to which Coody responded in the negative, maintaining that a greater prevalence of firearms enhances overall safety. Conversely, critics pointed out that rape rates in Oklahoma reached a ten-year high following the enactment of the state's concealed carry law, and drew comparisons to automobile regulations from 1950 to 2014 that successfully reduced traffic fatalities through reasonable safety standards without infringing on the ability to drive with proper licensing and training.

Prior to passing in a 73-15 vote with 13 abstentions, the legislation had originally proposed eliminating licensing and training requirements for concealed carry as well. The measure now advances to the state Senate for consideration. Representative Virgin issued a warning regarding the potential consequences, stating that the combination of domestic violence and increased firearm access without training or background checks would lead to fatalities.

An outspoken critic of the Affordable Care Act's repeal is blasting conservatives, with a former evangelical pointing out the hypocrisy in supporting such a move. Bruce Horst is intimately familiar with the struggle of securing medical coverage while managing pre-existing conditions. Before the implementation of Obamacare, insurance providers consistently turned him away, leaving his household exposed to the financial devastation of a potential medical emergency. The health law ultimately protected Horst and his relatives from potential medical bankruptcy. 

Despite the legislation providing coverage to upwards of 30 million people, lawmakers in the House and Senate recently pushed through a late-night vote to dismantle it, an action that drew cheers from conservatives. 

This celebration drew sharp criticism from Horst. Now an atheist, he utilized Facebook to heavily chastise these self-described evangelical Christians for celebrating what he characterized as a death sentence for countless individuals. Expressing his views online, Horst stated his belief that determining medical assistance based strictly on an individual's financial capability is immoral, adding that his perspective is informed by biblical teachings. He noted that as of 2010, he had spent his entire adult life as a Conservative Evangelical Christian, eventually observing that fellow believers opposed affordable health insurance for individuals like him. According to Horst, these churchgoers had been misled into believing that extending coverage to others would negatively impact their own access to care.

Reflecting on his past faith, Horst explained that he once felt he would be judged on the Final Judgment Day based on how he treated the "least of these," referencing the twenty-fifth chapter of the book of Matthew. Upon realizing that his fellow Christians lacked similar convictions and seemingly disregarded the words of Jesus, he ultimately lost his belief entirely. 

Observers have noted a decline in church attendance among conservatives, and critics argue that such callousness and hypocrisy help explain why individuals like Horst walk away from the faith. The effort to strip millions of necessary medical care only reinforced his decision to leave the church.

Furthermore, Horst targeted congressional Republicans and criticized the contradiction of conservatives who claim to be "pro-life" while supporting policies that he claims will strip coverage from roughly 18 million Americans at the urging of Conservative Evangelical Christians. Pointing out that friends of his owe their survival to Obamacare, he argued that his former Christian peers are not genuinely pro-life, but are instead manipulated—likely to maintain tithes and secure votes for preferred candidates. 

While uncertain of the immediate legislative future regarding healthcare, Horst expressed that he would be pleasantly surprised if the president persuaded Congress to broaden coverage for everyone. However, he maintained that if his Christian acquaintances continue to insist that medical care should depend on personal wealth, they would face the condemnation attributed to Jesus in Matthew 25. Concluding his thoughts, Horst suggested that conservatives backing these measures are contradicting the teachings of Jesus and merely pretending to follow the faith.

BERLIN (Reuters) — On Friday, members of the digital activism network Avaaz dismantled a temporary barrier close to the historic Berlin Wall. The demonstration was organized to encourage American citizens residing in Germany to cast ballots opposing Donald Trump, the Republican candidate, in the upcoming November 8 U.S. presidential election. Participants drew a parallel to Trump's campaign pledge to construct a massive barrier along the U.S.-Mexico border to block migrants. Furthermore, the protest took place right by the Brandenburg Gate, echoing the historic 1987 moment when U.S. President Ronald Reagan challenged Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev to "tear down this wall."

A crowd of cheering campaigners, numbering in the dozens, used their bare hands and rubber mallets to flatten the 2.5-meter (8.2-foot) barrier, which featured a printed likeness of Trump and red and blue signs that read "Stop Trump" and "Tear Down Trump’s Wall." Spectators, numbering around 150, watched the event and shouted slogans such as "The wall must come down!" as the structure collapsed. 

According to information released by Avaaz, roughly 8 million U.S. citizens reside outside the country, though a mere 12 percent participated in the 2012 presidential contest. Emma Ruby-Sachs, who serves as the deputy director for Avaaz, noted that expatriate Americans represent a hidden swing state capable of swinging the current election, with a significant population based in Germany. Meanwhile, a Reuters/Ipsos survey released the previous week indicated that 42 percent of likely voters favored former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, while 38 percent threw their support behind the Republican candidate and businessman.

Representative Luis Gutierrez, a staunch advocate for granting amnesty to undocumented immigrants, has dismissed the tragic death of Kate Steinle as "a little thing," arguing that critics routinely weaponize isolated incidents to push for the complete termination of sanctuary city policies. During a broadcast addressing a Rasmussen Reports survey revealing that sixty-two percent of the American public rejects sanctuary city protocols, Spanish-language broadcaster Telemundo shaped its reporting to support the continuation of these controversial municipal rules. 

Reporting live from Chicago—itself a sanctuary city—Telemundo journalist Janet Rodríguez featured an undocumented individual defending the policy alongside statements from Congressman Gutierrez, who downplayed the killing of Steinle by a repeat offender and five-time deportee in San Francisco. Although Rodríguez did mention the survey data showing widespread public opposition and support for penalizing sanctuary cities by withholding federal dollars, she offered only a single dissenting perspective, highlighting presidential candidate Donald Trump's characterization of sanctuary cities as "a disgrace." 

Furthermore, the broadcast misinformed viewers regarding the broad, cross-party opposition to these measures. Rodríguez claimed during the segment that the poll predominantly reflects Republican viewpoints on eliminating sanctuary cities or cutting their federal funding. In contrast, the actual survey results demonstrate that federal funding cuts are backed by seventy-nine percent of Republicans, sixty-six percent of unaffiliated voters, and forty-six percent of Democrats, while Department of Justice legal actions against sanctuary jurisdictions are supported by seventy-nine percent of Republicans, sixty-five percent of independents, and forty-three percent of Democrats.

United States Attorney General Jeff Sessions appears to have experienced a sudden recollection regarding Russian contacts during the 2016 race, after previously testifying under oath that he had no knowledge of such communications. 

Back in January during his confirmation proceedings, Sessions assured Senator Al Franken (D-MN) that he was unaware of any campaign associates interacting with Moscow officials. Now, however, that stance is shifting following the Monday unsealing of court records. These documents show that former Trump campaign adviser George Papadopoulos proposed organizing a summit between Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin in March 2016, boasting of helpful contacts to make it happen.

Adding to the scrutiny, an archived Instagram post from Trump's official profile places Sessions in the room when Papadopoulos pitched the idea. This development is drawing intense focus from Special Counsel Robert Mueller's ongoing investigation into the Russia scandal. According to an NBC insider, Sessions actually shot down the proposed meeting, although sources indicate it remains ambiguous whether the Attorney General presently remembers turning it down. NBC reporter Ken Dilanian noted on social media that while the proposal was indeed rejected by Sessions, his personal recollection of doing so remains uncertain.

Senator Franken expressed sharp frustration over what he characterized as a recurring trend of misleading statements given under oath regarding interactions with a foreign adversary that meddled in the election. In a formal statement, Franken accused Sessions of repeatedly obscuring the truth about both his own encounters with Russian operatives and his knowledge of similar outreach by fellow campaign staffers. Stressing the need for accountability to safeguard future elections, Franken declared that these latest findings severely undermine public and congressional trust in the Attorney General's testimony. 

This follows previous assertions by Sessions in June, where he maintained he was completely uninformed about any discussions involving potential Russian election interference by anyone associated with the campaign.

DHAKA (Reuters) — Khaleda Zia, the former prime minister and leader of the opposition in Bangladesh, flew back to the country on Wednesday following a medical trip to Britain that lasted over three quarters of a year—more than three months. Ecstatic crowds of supporters greeted her arrival. For years, the political landscape of Bangladesh has been defined by the bitter feud between Khaleda and Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, meaning her reappearance could spark a surge in political engagement ahead of the general election slated to take place before the end of next year. Both political figures share ties to past national leaders and have taken turns holding the office of prime minister over the years. 

During the time she was away, a minimum of two arrest warrants were handed down against her regarding political unrest, though she already held bail status concerning various legal matters. While her legal counsel has brushed off these charges as politically motivated harassment, Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) spokesperson Mohammad Shamsuddin indicated that she could potentially present herself in court on Thursday to address the matters. Meanwhile, the inspector general of police, Mohammad Shahidul Huq, mentioned to the press that orders for her apprehension had not been given to him. 

A massive crowd of party members carrying banners and placards assembled near the international airport located in the capital city of Dhaka to greet her return. At the same time, Bangladesh faces the monumental challenge of managing the arrival of more than half a million Rohingya Muslim refugees fleeing Myanmar starting in late August, a humanitarian crisis that threatens to turn into a contentious point of division as the election approaches.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Following a dominant string of victories on Super Tuesday that propelled her further ahead in the race for the Democratic presidential nomination, Hillary Clinton quickly turned her attention to the Republican front-runner, Donald Trump. Claiming victory in seven out of eleven contested states—most notably the populous state of Texas—the former first lady solidified her lead over challenger Bernie Sanders as both vie to head the Democratic ticket in the upcoming November 8 presidential election. These wins, which included sweeping the South, also set the stage for a prospective matchup against the billionaire real estate mogul and reality television personality, who similarly triumphed in multiple Republican contests on Tuesday. 

Amidst these electoral successes, campaign fundraisers reported that financial backers are increasingly eager to support her bid through the general election. Dane Strother, a Democratic strategist based in Washington D.C. who is unaligned with any campaign, remarked that Clinton is effectively the nominee and must now pivot toward confronting Trump. 

During a Miami rally following her multi-state wins on Tuesday evening, Clinton directly addressed Trump, criticizing his tendency to insult opponents while reiterating her opposition to his proposed 1,000-mile wall along the Mexican border. Emphasizing that the stakes in the election have never been higher, she argued that the rhetoric from the opposing side has reached unprecedented lows, adding that attempts to divide America into "us and them" are fundamentally wrong.

According to delegate tallies compiled by the New York Times early Wednesday morning, Clinton secured 527 delegates for the upcoming Democratic nominating convention compared to 325 for Sanders, out of the 2,383 required to clinch the nomination. Jim Manley, a Washington-based Democratic strategist backing Clinton, noted that shifting her focus to Trump was a necessary yet hazardous maneuver. Pointing out that Trump is likely to retaliate aggressively—noting that "he'll go right in the gutter"—Manley warned of the inherent risks. Trump has frequently targeted Clinton over her handling of crises in Iraq and Syria during her four-year tenure as secretary of state, and has hinted at reviving past controversies surrounding former President Bill Clinton.

Members of Clinton’s national finance committee indicated that the campaign is observing renewed enthusiasm from contributors looking past the primary season. Tom Sacks-Wilner, a committee member, noted a clear transition toward the general election, observing that the finance department is no longer raising objections to it. Federal rules permit donors to contribute $2,700 for the primary phase and an additional $2,700 for the general election, allowing a combined total of $5,400 per individual. Furthermore, a Los Angeles-based fundraiser reported an uptick in local inquiries regarding contributions for post-California campaigning, alongside a surge in willingness among volunteers to offer their time following the recent victories.

This optimistic outlook represents a notable contrast to conditions from three weeks prior, when the campaign was reeling from Sanders’ decisive victory in New Hampshire and a narrow second-place finish in Iowa, where the Vermont senator captured a substantial share of younger voters. That momentum began to shift following Clinton's win in South Carolina, bolstered by robust backing from African-American voters—a demographic where Sanders has faced challenges connecting through his democratic socialist platform. National figures from a Reuters/Ipsos tracking poll conducted between February 26 and March 1 showed nearly 53 percent of Democrats favoring Clinton versus 43 percent for Sanders, recovering from a dead heat earlier in the month and improving significantly since just before the South Carolina primary on February 27.

Meanwhile, Sanders has also sought to frame himself as a viable general election opponent against Trump. Jeff Weaver, Sanders’ campaign manager, released a statement on Tuesday highlighting the campaign's $42.7 million fundraising total for February. Stressing that Trump will command substantial financial resources for November, Weaver emphasized the necessity for the Democratic nominee to secure hundreds of millions of dollars to successfully challenge the Republicans.

Additionally, progressive groups connected to the party cautioned against dismissing Sanders prematurely despite the Super Tuesday outcomes, pointing out his stronger polling prospects in upcoming northern states with predominantly white electorates. Charles Chamberlain, executive director of Democracy for America, issued a statement arguing that political pundits in Washington were mistaken when they initially claimed the nomination contest was settled before Sanders entered the race, and remain wrong in declaring it over now. 

(Editing by Richard Valdmanis and Alistair Bell) This article was funded in part by SAP. It was independently created by the Reuters editorial staff. SAP had no editorial involvement in its creation or production.

French leader Emmanuel Macron urged Baghdad over the weekend to dissolve all armed groups in the country, specifically pointing to the state-approved, Tehran-supported Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF). This public demand from a prominent Western figure is unusual. The statement, delivered after talks in the French capital with Kurdish officials from Iraq, highlights the delicate diplomatic tightrope Baghdad must walk between Tehran and Western nations—countries that remain at odds—following their joint efforts against Islamic State.

During a press briefing alongside Iraqi Kurdish representatives in Paris, the French president emphasized the necessity of a step-by-step demilitarization, particularly targeting the Popular Mobilisation groups that have taken root in the country recently, alongside the gradual disbanding of all other militias. 

Leadership under the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) contends that the predominantly Arab Shiite PMF has committed numerous violations against Kurdish populations residing in regions of Iraq shared by multiple ethnic groups. Meanwhile, the administration of Iraqi Prime Minister Haider al-Abadi rejects claims that these forces engage in widespread or organized abuses, promising legal consequences for any personnel found culpable of infractions. As government troops come closer to proclaiming a final defeat of Islamic State, stripping the PMF of its weapons is widely viewed as Abadi's greatest political hurdle.

A subsequent statement issued by Abadi's office in Baghdad noted a telephone conversation with Macron, reporting that the French leader reiterated support for maintaining a united Iraqi state. However, the official readout omitted any reference to Macron's push for dissolving the militias.

A sharper rebuke came from Iraqi Vice President Nuri al-Maliki. The former premier, who had previously faced pressure from both Washington and Tehran to step down due to his inability to halt Islamic State, characterized Macron's remarks as an intolerable meddling in domestic matters. In a published statement, Maliki asserted that France's stance is completely unacceptable and damages the sovereignty and official bodies of Iraq.

The gathering in Paris between Macron, KRG Prime Minister Nechirvan Barzani, and Deputy Prime Minister Qubad Talabani marked the initial high-level international engagement for Kurdish authorities following the independence vote held on September 25. While foreign ministers like U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson and British Prime Minister Theresa May traveled to the country subsequent to the vote, their visits were restricted to Baghdad, omitting any stops in the Kurdish regional capital of Erbil. Prior to the vote, Western governments had urged the Kurds to abstain from the referendum and pursue talks with the central authorities instead.

Reiterating his backing for talks, Macron stressed the importance of negotiations between the central authorities in Baghdad and the semi-autonomous Kurdish administration based on the Iraqi charter. He expressed confidence that meaningful discussions could result in Baghdad lifting its measures against the Kurdish territory.

The vote for secession defied the central government and sparked concern in neighboring Turkey and Iran, both of which deal with their own Kurdish populations. In response, government forces in Iraq took control of Kirkuk and other contested zones. The fallout led to the resignation of longtime Kurdish president Masoud Barzani, prompting the regional administration—now headed by his nephew Nechirvan—to seek a negotiated resolution to the standoff.

Speaking on Saturday, the Kurdish premier expressed hope that Paris could assist in mediating the conflict with Baghdad, adding that the regional administration acknowledges the ruling by Iraq's Supreme Federal Court which declared the independence vote unconstitutional and its outcomes invalid. According to the Erbil-based media outlet Rudaw, Barzani stated that they have entered a different phase, the matter of the referendum is concluded, and the regional government's stance is well-established.

Additionally, Macron advocated for the long-overdue application of Article 140 of the Iraqi charter to resolve ownership of regions contested by Baghdad and Kurdish authorities. The provision originally mandated a vote by the conclusion of 2007 in Kirkuk and other oil-rich zones claimed by both sides to decide whether local inhabitants preferred integration into the Kurdish territory. Because that vote never materialized, the KRG frequently pointed to it as justification for proceeding with its own unilateral independence referendum.

NEW YORK/FORT LAUDERDALE, Fla. — For a significant portion of Donald Trump’s base, his choice to launch missile strikes against a Syrian airfield in response to a chemical weapons attack demonstrated decisive leadership and strength, aligning with their expectations from the November election. Speaking with reporters, more than a dozen individuals who voted for Trump acknowledged that direct military engagement in Syria seemingly contradicted the isolationist, “America First” platform he championed during his run for the White House. Yet, unlike prominent far-right figures who openly condemned the military action in Syria, the majority of Trump supporters surveyed across Texas, New York, and Florida argued that the strike did not violate his pledge to prioritize American interests above all else. 

Anthony Calvanese, a 28-year-old construction foreman interviewed on a sidewalk in Staten Island, New York, expressed enthusiastic approval, stating he loved the decision and that the president had made it clear from day one that he would not tolerate nonsense and needed to project global superiority. 

This military order marked a departure from Trump's 2016 campaign promises to steer clear of Middle East entanglements, as well as his past criticism four years prior of then-President Barack Obama for not retaliating against the Syrian government after a previous chemical attack on its citizens. These apparent contradictions drew sharp criticism from his most dedicated supporters on the far right. Paul Joseph Watson, a London-based editor for the U.S. conspiracy-promoting outlet Infowars—which Trump has previously praised—posted on Twitter that he was completely off the Trump train, while prominent white nationalist leader Richard Spencer labeled the move a betrayal and the death of the “America First” agenda.

Conversely, several voters maintained their faith in the president's ability to fulfill his commitments. Todd Recknagel, managing partner at a private equity firm in Panama City Beach, Florida, explained via phone that the action deepened his backing by proving Trump is capable of adapting his perspective based on unfolding events, adding that he values a leader who stands up for principles and compares the stance to former President Ronald Reagan. 

Other supporters felt the sheer brutality of the poison gas attack left the administration with no alternative. Tom Harney, a 64-year-old yacht broker from Lauderhill, Florida, remarked outside a local diner that failing to respond would have made the nation as culpable as those who ignored Adolf Hitler's march across Europe during World War II. 

This perspective was shared by Brooklyn attorney Joseph Mure Jr., who told a reporter outside a Staten Island courthouse that innocent victims, including women and infants, were murdered, adding that he wished the military had deployed twice the volume of ordnance. The assault involved U.S. naval warships in the Mediterranean firing a barrage of Tomahawk missiles at the targeted airfield. 

Additional supporters pointed out that the move reinforced Trump’s tough persona and campaign vows to rebuild the armed forces, signaling that the United States retains its global leadership role. Art Tillberg, 67, of Coral Springs, Florida, noted that the country was no longer leading from behind, invoking a frequent Republican critique of Obama’s 2011 campaign against Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi.

At the same time, dissent remained among certain Trump voters who shared the far-right's view that the operation violated campaign pledges. Anthony Sage, a 42-year-old retired Army staff sergeant with service tours in Iraq and Afghanistan, argued outside the Fort Hood Army base in Killeen, Texas, that the operation ran counter to the “America First” doctrine, dismissing the engagement as a misuse of American resources and time while domestic needs should take precedence. 

Similarly, Abdi Mohamed, a 23-year-old Somali immigrant and Trump voter residing in St. Paul, Minnesota, voiced concern during a phone interview that the president was reversing his outsider stance and yielding to the influence of the political establishment and standard system. 

Meanwhile, a small group of voters experienced internal conflict, feeling uneasy about entangling the nation in the prolonged civil war in Syria while remaining reluctant to turn away from the president. Melanie Groves, a 39-year-old small business owner from Louisville, Illinois, who had recently organized a pro-Trump rally, admitted she was undecided, hoping the action served strictly as a firm warning regarding crossed red lines while acknowledging fears from critics that it could spiral toward a major global conflict.

While Senator Ted Cruz has been enjoying momentum in the Republican primary race, this trend likely persists only because the electorate has not yet gotten to know him well. Finding a more profoundly unlikable presidential contender would prove nearly impossible, according to practically every individual who has ever crossed paths with him personally. 

Although opposition from Democrats who view his conservative platform as morally and intellectually objectionable comes as no shock, alarms are now ringing within his own political ranks. Former presidential hopeful Bob Dole stepped forward this week to publicly challenge Cruz, delivering some blunt assessments. Voicing doubts regarding his party loyalty, Dole remarked that hearing Cruz utter the word "Republican" is a rarity. Instead, Dole noted, Cruz consistently relies on the term "conservative," before offering his own label for the senator: an "extremist." Dole also questioned how Cruz plans to manage relations in Congress, bluntly stating that nobody likes him.

Yet, Dole's critique may actually understate the reality. Cruz's ultimate loyalty belongs neither to the Republican Party nor to conservatism, but rather to himself. This is the exact politician who nearly single-handedly forced a federal government shutdown simply to make a point regarding Obamacare. The maneuver cost the nation billions of dollars, damaged the international financial credibility of the United States, and ultimately achieved nothing—though it certainly elevated Cruz's public profile. When considering whether Cruz would repeat such actions, the answer is that he has already attempted to do so.

Dislike for Cruz extends far beyond political figures across the aisle, however. His past is populated by acquaintances eager to share accounts of how socially awkward, eccentric, and misanthropic he was during earlier years. Craig Mazin, his former college roommate at Princeton and now a well-known figure, has spent recent years continuously ridiculing Cruz online while painting an unsettling portrait of their time together. 

Mazin has noted on social media that gaining thousands of followers was hardly worth the experience of rooming with Cruz for a year. He has explicitly stated that Cruz is not a friend, and that he loathes both the man and everything he stands for, even labeling him a "huge asshole" around the time of his Senate election.

Any suspicion that Mazin held a petty or isolated grudge—perhaps over messy living habits—is dispelled by other college contemporaries who echo the exact same sentiments. Another former classmate corroborated Mazin's portrayal, noting that anyone who suspects Mazin is exaggerating is mistaken, as he personally loathed Cruz within an hour of meeting him during freshman week. 

When The Daily Beast sought out additional college peers to verify these accounts, they uncovered a widespread consensus characterizing Cruz as a creepy and politically extreme jerk. Alongside Mazin and another individual named Leitch, several anonymous classmates described the young Cruz using terms like abrasive, intense, strident, crank, and arrogant. Specifically, four different people independently used the word creepy, pointing out Cruz's peculiar habit of wearing a paisley bathrobe while walking to the far end of the dorm hallway where female students resided. Mazin recalled frequently fielding complaints from the women asking him to keep his roommate out of their hallway.

The unsettling impressions left by Cruz are so pervasive that they surface even in contexts entirely unrelated to his personal popularity. A recent report in The New York Times detailing his stint as a law clerk for Chief Justice William Rehnquist quickly shifted focus toward former colleagues expressing discomfort over what they described as a morbid fascination with murder that unsettled everyone in the office. 

Interviews with roughly two dozen former Supreme Court clerks—spanning both liberal and conservative chambers—portrayed Cruz as obsessively fixated on capital punishment. Several felt that his delivery when recounting crimes resembled a dime-store novel, appearing better suited for a prosecutor addressing a jury than a clerk advising the nation's highest court.

Unpopularity is not restricted to coworkers, roommates, lawmakers, and commentators, as ordinary citizens share similar views. An ABC News analysis from 2014 evaluated political popularity by examining Facebook discourse and discovered that 61 percent of all mentions of Ted Cruz on the platform were decidedly negative.

Despite universal animosity from those who encounter him, Cruz manages to sustain his political career through backing from a compact yet influential faction of millionaires supportive of his anti-government agenda. Furthermore, his relentless, opportunistic drive for the spotlight ensures his survival; in the realm of politics, the adage that any publicity is good publicity holds true. As Cruz continually appears on Fox News, conservative audiences gradually acclimate to his inherent creepiness.

Translating this particular behavioral pattern into an effective presidency remains difficult to envision. At a critical juncture in international diplomacy, placing an overwhelmingly unlikable figure in the Oval Office could prove disastrous. Furthermore, Cruz's history demonstrates a willingness to prioritize self-aggrandizement over the national interest, as evidenced by the government shutdown. 

The widespread aversion toward Cruz—which intensifies the closer one gets to him—should serve as a major red flag regarding his character, raising serious questions about whether such an individual is fit to lead the most powerful country in the world.
