During the upcoming regional visit by United States Vice President Mike Pence, Palestinian President Mahmoud Altman will refuse to hold discussions with him, according to a statement made on Saturday by the Palestinian foreign minister. This decision serves as a direct rebuff to the recent declaration by President Donald Trump acknowledging Jerusalem as the capital of Israel, a policy shift that reverses decades of established American foreign relations. 

Following the announcement made on Wednesday, protests in Gaza turned violent for the third consecutive day. The unrest was fueled further after Palestinian factions designated Friday as a "day of rage," leading militants to launch rockets into Israel. In response, Israeli air strikes on Saturday resulted in the deaths of two Palestinian gunmen.

The Trump administration's decision regarding Jerusalem has sparked widespread anger throughout the Arab world and caused concern among Western partners, who view the step as a setback for peace efforts that could potentially ignite additional regional conflict. Following an emergency gathering in Cairo late Saturday, Arab foreign ministers formally requested that Washington reverse its choice, characterizing the action as a catalyst for widespread regional hostility. The Arab League issued a declaration labeling the announcement a severe breach of international law that carries no legal weight and is considered null.

Ahead of discussions in Paris on Sunday with French President Emmanuel Macron—followed by meetings with European foreign ministers in Brussels—Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addressed his critics publicly. He noted that while he has encountered European disapproval over the U.S. decision, he has not heard any corresponding condemnation regarding the subsequent rocket attacks directed at Israel or the harsh incitement faced by the country. 

While Israel views the entirety of Jerusalem as its capital, Palestinians claim East Jerusalem as the seat of government for an independent nation they hope to establish in the future. The majority of the international community regards East Jerusalem—annexed by Israel following its capture during the 1967 conflict—as occupied territory, maintaining that the ultimate status of the municipality ought to be determined through upcoming bilateral negotiations. Meanwhile, the current U.S. administration asserts its ongoing dedication to the peace process, arguing that any credible peace framework would place Israel's capital in Jerusalem while declining to specify the city's boundaries. Furthermore, American officials contend that previous approaches are obsolete and must be discarded to restart stalled talks.

Speaking to reporters in Cairo prior to the Arab League assembly, Palestinian Foreign Minister Riyad al-Maliki announced that the Palestinian leadership will seek a replacement for the United States as a mediator in peace negotiations and intends to pursue a resolution through the United Nations Security Council. He stated that they will look to Arab allies and the broader international community for a new facilitator. Additionally, a Turkish presidential source revealed that leaders Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Emmanuel Macron will collaborate in an attempt to convince Washington to alter its stance. 

State news agency MENA also reported that Egypt’s Coptic Church has declined a potential meeting with Pence. Representatives for the White House and the State Department did not provide comments when asked. Palestinian officials confirmed that Pence had originally scheduled a meeting with Abbas for December 19. Efforts to revive the stalled peace talks are currently being spearheaded by Trump's advisor and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, though these initiatives have yielded limited visible progress so far.

In the aftermath of Friday night's rocket fire from Gaza toward Israeli communities, Israel reported that its retaliatory air strikes successfully hit two weapons manufacturing sites, a military compound, and a weapons depot. Hamas, the group governing Gaza, verified that the two individuals killed in the early morning strikes were its members, and the organization has continued to encourage Palestinians to maintain their confrontation against Israeli forces.

Saturday's demonstrations were somewhat calmer compared to the previous two days. Approximately 60 Palestinian youths engaged in stone-throwing directed at Israeli soldiers along the Gaza-Israel border, resulting in at least 10 injuries from Israeli gunfire, according to the health ministry. Concurrently, in the occupied West Bank, demonstrators burned tires and hurled stones and firebombs at Israeli troops, who utilized tear gas, water cannons, rubber bullets, and occasionally live ammunition to disperse the crowds. The Israeli military reported a single arrest among the protesters.

In East Jerusalem, roughly 60 individuals gathered near the walled Old City for a demonstration. Mounted police and paramilitary border officers deployed tear gas to break up the assembly. Police spokesman Micky Rosenfeld stated that 13 participants were detained, and four officers sustained minor injuries from thrown stones.

These events follow widespread demonstrations on Friday, which drew thousands of protesters into the streets and left two Palestinians dead during clashes with Israeli troops along the Gaza border. Numerous others sustained injuries in both Gaza and the West Bank, while crowds gathered across Muslim and Arab nations to show their support. 

According to the Turkish presidential source, Erdogan and Macron reached a consensus during a telephone conversation that the U.S. policy change poses regional concerns, prompting Turkey and France to mount a joint diplomatic initiative aimed at overturning the decision. Erdogan also engaged in telephone conversations on Saturday with the leaders of Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, and Lebanon, and previously scheduled an emergency session of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation to take place in Turkey the following week.

Addressing the Manama Dialogue security conference in Bahrain on Saturday, a high-ranking official from the United Arab Emirates described the U.S. policy change as a present handed to radical elements. Anwar Gargash, the UAE Minister of State for Foreign Affairs, remarked that extremists and radicals will exploit the decision to amplify hate speech.

As the destructive Hurricane Irma tracked closer to Florida and the wider southeastern region of the U.S., Georgia Governor Nathan Deal directed residents on the state's coastline—encompassing the historic city of Savannah—to evacuate immediately on Thursday. According to the governor's official announcement, the mandatory directive goes into effect at 8 a.m. on Saturday, applying to locations east of Interstate 95 alongside select areas west of the highway. 

Alongside the evacuation order, Deal authorized the mobilization of as many as 5,000 personnel from the Georgia National Guard for storm response duties and broadened the existing state of emergency to cover 30 counties in the southeastern part of the state. This directive impacts urban centers such as Brunswick and Savannah. Data from WSB-TV notes that Georgia has not experienced a hurricane of Category 3 strength or greater since 1898. Urging residents to take action, Deal stated that everyone in potentially affected coastal zones should leave promptly.

Having already left a trail of destruction and at least 10 fatalities across multiple Caribbean islands, Irma moved past the Dominican Republic and toward Haiti on Thursday, standing out as one of the strongest Atlantic hurricanes seen in a hundred years. Projections from the National Hurricane Center indicate that Irma is poised to strike Florida on Sunday as a severe Category 4 hurricane, with dangerous flooding and storm surges expected to begin within the next two days. Meanwhile, the Miami-Fort Lauderdale region faced intensifying fuel shortages on Thursday as purchasing volumes soared to five times typical levels. Although the hurricane's precise trajectory remains unpredictable, it poses a potential threat to Georgia and the Carolinas by early the following week.

MOSCOW — A draft agreement released by the Russian government on Thursday indicates that Moscow and Cairo are working toward a pact that would permit military aircraft from both nations to utilize each other's airfields and airspace. 

The proposed accord was detailed in an official decree bearing the signature of Prime Minister Dmitry Medvedev, dated Nov. 28. Within the document, the Russian Defence Ministry is instructed to engage in discussions with Egyptian counterparts and to execute the agreement upon reaching a mutual consensus. 

Prior to the decree's release, Russian Defence Minister Sergei Shoigu traveled to Cairo for discussions with the nation's political and military leaders on Wednesday. The document noted that the text had already undergone preliminary review with Egyptian authorities and received Medvedev's backing. 

Since initiating a military campaign in September 2015 to back Syrian President Bashar al-Assad, Russia has shown indications of a desire to broaden its footprint in the area. American officials asserted in March that Moscow had stationed special operations forces in Egypt close to the Libyan frontier, though the Kremlin disputed the claim. 

Furthermore, Moscow has built strong relations with prominent Libyan commander Khalifa Haftar. Haftar spoke with Shoigu through a video link originating from a Russian aircraft carrier in the Mediterranean earlier in the year and has also traveled to Moscow. 

Under the terms of the draft text, Russian and Egyptian military jets would gain mutual access to airbases and airspace by providing a five-day notification in advance. The agreement is anticipated to remain in force for a duration of five years, with the possibility of a renewal.

NEW YORK/WASHINGTON (Reuters) — Prominent figures within religious conservative movements largely maintained their backing for Donald Trump over the weekend, following the publication of a 2005 video in which the Republican presidential nominee used crude sexual language about women. While most avoided issuing outright condemnations of Trump, some did voice anxieties that the leaked footage—which captured the former reality television personality bragging on an open mic about attempting to seduce a married woman and grabbing women—might dampen voter turnout among evangelicals on November 8. Rather than breaking with the candidate, these leaders emphasized the critical necessity of blocking Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton from capturing the White House, influencing the composition of the Supreme Court, and advancing progressive policies. 

Even though his running mate, Vice presidential nominee Mike Pence, stated he could not defend the remarks, key conservative figures stood firm. Gary Bauer, who leads the Campaign for Working Families, affirmed his continued backing for the ticket. While acknowledging Trump's remarks were deeply improper, Bauer argued that the core dilemma of the election remained unchanged, warning that Clinton would champion measures that undermine religious freedom, foster abortion, compromise national security, and leave borders vulnerable.

White evangelicals account for roughly a fifth of the American populace, per data from the Public Religion Research Institute, serving as a vital demographic required for a Trump victory. Serving historically as a bedrock for the GOP, this constituency powered George W. Bush’s 2004 reelection and maintained high turnout levels in 2008 and 2012 for Mitt Romney, despite concerns among some believers that the candidate was overly moderate, as noted by Pew Research Center findings. Throughout the race, evangelicals have backed Trump enthusiastically despite the New York billionaire embracing their platform relatively late in life, often favoring him over more overtly devout primary rivals like Ted Cruz.

Steve Scheffler, leading the Iowa Faith and Freedom Coalition, admitted disappointment while leaning on his faith, noting that scripture teaches everyone is a sinner and that personal past mistakes are universal. He added that Clinton carried her own baggage, pointing specifically to her husband's historical marital scandals. Describing Trump's actions as disgusting without attempting an excuse, Scheffler confirmed he would still cast a ballot for the Republican nominee.

Nevertheless, politically engaged Christian conservative organizers across the nation expressed concern that the controversy could discourage their base from voting. Religious activist David Lane pointed out that while these voters would not back Clinton, the scandal might keep them away from the polls entirely, describing it as a potentially significant issue. Lane suggested that much depended on Trump's showing in the upcoming Sunday evening presidential debate and his capacity to demonstrate personal growth to Christian voters. During the Las Vegas showdown, Trump doubled down on his demands for enhanced enforcement at the southern border, asserting that stopping drug inflows is vital. He pledged to target major traffickers operating domestically, leading into his controversial statement about removing "bad hombres."

Throughout his campaign, Trump has faced substantial criticism for provocative statements regarding unauthorized Mexican immigrants. When launching his bid in June 2015, he alleged that Mexico was dispatching criminals and rapists across the border. Furthermore, Mexican President Enrique Pena Nieto stated after an August meeting with the GOP nominee that Trump's proposed policies could pose a severe danger to Mexico.

Later in the evening, as Clinton argued that raising taxes on affluent individuals would help sustain Social Security—and suggested Trump would similarly owe more unless he found a way to avoid it—Trump interrupted with the remark, “Such a nasty woman.”

WASHINGTON (Reuters) - According to a high-ranking member of the transition team on Wednesday, President-elect Donald Trump plans to select former Georgia Governor Sonny Perdue for the position of agriculture secretary on Thursday. At 70 years of age, Perdue previously worked on the agricultural advisory panel for Trump's campaign. The Senate, which is controlled by Republicans, will need to confirm the choice, which finalizes the proposed cabinet selections for Trump right before his inauguration ceremony on Friday. 

By selecting a past governor originating from the South, Trump bypassed potential candidates originating from core Midwestern Farm Belt regions, which account for the majority of the nation's wheat, corn, and soybean production—staples of agricultural exports. In contrast, Georgia stands out as a major producer of peanuts and cotton. During his tenure leading Georgia, Perdue faced a major drought in 2007, implementing water conservation measures and even organizing a prayer gathering for rain outside the statehouse. 

A Republican, Perdue won two gubernatorial terms and held office from 2003 through 2011. Prior to that role, he served as a state senator for a rural district situated approximately 100 miles, or 160 kilometers, south of Atlanta. In 1998, he changed his political affiliation from the Democratic Party to the Republican Party amidst changing demographics and local redistricting efforts. 

Amidst a declining farm economy marked by dropping commodity prices, the agricultural sector backed Trump strongly. American Soybean Association (ASA) President Ron Moore expressed his belief that Perdue would advocate for agricultural exports during a phone interview, stating that he expects the nominee to heavily support trade. Earlier this month, the ASA joined forces with 16 other agricultural organizations to call upon the incoming administration to safeguard and improve trade in agriculture and its benefits for rural communities. 

Because Trump frequently targeted China during his campaign for unfair trade practices, trade remained a central theme, which is vital to the farming sector. In 2015, American food and agricultural exports shipped to China exceeded $20.2 billion. Driven by robust demand from China—which purchases nearly 30% of the domestic harvest—soybean prices climbed 16.2 percent throughout 2016. Furthermore, these soybean shipments contributed to an increase in the U.S. gross domestic product during the third quarter. 

Nevertheless, certain agricultural producers worry that Trump’s rhetoric regarding China might sour trade dynamics and jeopardize exports. Earlier in the week, a prominent state-operated newspaper in China cautioned that American plane manufacturer Boeing Co and U.S. agricultural goods could become targets of retaliation should a trade war begin under Trump. 

American Farm Bureau President Zippy Duvall voiced support for Perdue, describing him as a powerful advocate. Conversely, environmental organizations criticized the selection. Kari Hamerschlag, who serves as the deputy director of food and technology at Friends of the Earth, argued in an official statement that farmers require a leader within the USDA dedicated to defending conservation initiatives that build resilience against severe weather, rather than someone who relies on praying for rain. 

Following the conclusion of his tenure as governor, Perdue established a global trading company named Perdue Partners, which offers consulting and services to businesses seeking international export opportunities. His cousin, David Perdue, holds a seat in the U.S. Senate representing Georgia. The nominee does not share any family relation with the poultry executive Frank Perdue.

PARIS — French President Emmanuel Macron laid out a grand blueprint for European renewal on Tuesday, advocating for tighter integration on defense and immigration alongside a dedicated budget for the euro zone—though translating these proposals into reality could prove difficult. 

Taking the stage at the Sorbonne just two days after Germany's federal election, where Chancellor Angela Merkel's CDU/CSU conservative alliance suffered its worst showing since 1949 and saw its room to maneuver on European policy constrained, the 39-year-old French leader delivered a nearly two-hour address marked by immense self-assurance and ambition. Yet, with the European Union currently strained by east-west tensions and struggling to move past nearly a decade of debilitating economic turbulence, Macron's earnest and occasionally lofty discourse ran the distinct risk of being ignored.

Framing Europe as an institution in urgent need of a relaunch, the former philosophy student and investment banker, framed by French and European Union flags, argued that deep cooperation is vital across a wide array of areas, including asylum policy, border security, corporate taxation, intelligence sharing, defense, and financial stability. 

"The only path that assures our future is the rebuilding of a Europe that is sovereign, united and democratic," he stated, adding that by the start of the next decade, the continent ought to establish a joint intervention force, a common defense budget, and a unified action doctrine.

Overhaul of the European Union was a cornerstone of Macron's centrist presidential campaign. Both he and Merkel have frequently emphasized their desire for France and Germany—the two largest economies in the bloc and its traditional engines of change—to spearhead integration. However, only five months into his five-year term, Macron confronts the reality that the 63-year-old Merkel, who is seeking a fourth term, has less political capital to expend than either leader might have wished. While her conservative alliance remains the largest force in the Bundestag, forming a workable majority will likely require a coalition with the Greens and the pro-business Free Democrats (FDP), both of which are hostile to many of Macron's core proposals.

German Foreign Minister Sigmar Gabriel, a high-ranking member of the Social Democrats (SPD)—whose party has ruled out joining another grand coalition—praised the address as "a passionate plea against nationalism and for Europe." 

"He can count on us," Gabriel affirmed.

Rather than moderating his message to align with the preferences of Merkel, the Greens, or the FDP, Macron kept his vision sweeping and expansive, while also putting forward concrete suggestions for bolstering the euro zone. Highlighting the necessity of democratic accountability, he argued that a budget must be paired with robust political leadership headed by a shared finance minister, alongside rigorous parliamentary oversight at the European level.

The fiscally conservative FDP strongly opposes the creation of a euro zone budget or any mechanism that could facilitate financial transfers from wealthier member states to poorer ones, as well as the potential pooling of national debt. Furthermore, the party has advocated for phasing out Europe's ESM bailout fund—which Macron wants to transform into a European Monetary Fund—and supports amending EU treaties to permit member countries to exit the euro zone.

"You don't strengthen Europe with new pots of money," Alexander Lambsdorff, an FDP member of the European Parliament, posted on Twitter following the address. In an official statement released by the FDP in Berlin, Lambsdorff added, "The problem in Europe is not a lack of public funds, but the lack of reform. A euro zone budget would set exactly the wrong incentives."

Without shying away from addressing Germany directly, even as Berlin navigates the political fallout from Sunday's vote, Macron challenged the two nations to completely integrate their markets and corporate regulations by the year 2024. 

"We share the same European ambitions and I know her commitment to Europe," Macron said of Merkel. "I'm proposing to Germany a new partnership. We will not agree on everything, not immediately, but we will discuss everything."

Speaking in Berlin on Monday, Merkel stressed the importance of moving beyond empty catchphrases and offering specific details on how to improve Europe. It remained uncertain whether Macron's speech satisfied that criterion from her perspective. 

Nonetheless, Martin Selmayr, chief of staff to European Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker, noted that the French proposals for strengthening the euro zone would be evaluated alongside Juncker's own ideas during a euro zone summit scheduled for December. Meanwhile, Italian EU Affairs Minister Sandro Gozi predicted the address would spur European leaders into action.

"An excellent speech by Emmanuel Macron on reviving the European Union. Let's work on this together, starting tomorrow at the Lyon Summit," Gozi remarked, referencing an upcoming meeting between French and Italian leaders focused on industrial policy.

Macron noted that he hoped his recommendations would influence Germany's coalition negotiations, which are not anticipated to kick off until mid-October and could drag on for months. 

"Some had said I should wait for the coalition talks to be concluded," Macron observed, noting that had he waited, the reaction in Berlin likely would have been: "Your proposals are great but it's too late, the coalition deal already lays out what will we do on Europe for the next four years."

WASHINGTON (Reuters) - According to a Reuters/Ipsos survey published on Monday, fifty percent of America’s likely voters are counting on the presidential debates to assist them in choosing between Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton and Republican contender Donald Trump for the November 8 election. 

This data highlights the immense pressure facing the two White House contenders as they get ready for their initial face-to-face encounter at Hofstra University in Long Island, New York. This upcoming prime-time television event is projected to attract a massive viewership of 100 million citizens, comparable to the Super Bowl. 

The survey indicates that roughly half of likely voters believe the showdowns will assist in clarifying their vote, a figure that includes 10 percent who are currently undecided. Conversely, 39 percent stated the debates would offer no assistance, while 11 percent remained uncertain about the impact. 

Demonstrating a strong desire for clarity from the broadcasts, 72 percent of those surveyed indicated they expect moderators to fact-check the candidates and correct false statements. The poll showed this sentiment was shared by 73 percent of Trump backers and 82 percent of individuals supporting Clinton. 

“It helps the audience, particularly me, to recognize what’s bull crap and what’s real,” remarked 63-year-old teacher Harvey Leven from Farmington Hills, Michigan, adding, “It’s easy for the candidates to quote a statistic and people accept it.”

At present, Clinton maintains a narrow national lead in the majority of national polls and holds vital edges in essential battleground states such as North Carolina and Ohio. The most recent Reuters/Ipsos data puts her 4 percentage points ahead of Trump nationwide. Her support had experienced a decline over the preceding weeks following renewed scrutiny regarding her private email server usage as secretary of state, alongside questions concerning her family's foundation.

NO TO NAME-CALLING

Following several months of aggressive campaigning and reciprocal insults, numerous voters anticipate a more restrained and civil encounter. Trump has previously suggested that Clinton belongs in prison over her email practices during her tenure as America's chief diplomat, whereas Clinton has characterized Trump as racially biased and temperamentally unsuited for the presidency. 

The survey revealed that 61 percent of participants have no desire to witness such mudslinging. 

“Quit picking on each other,” expressed 48-year-old Lisa Miller from St. Louis, Missouri. “This isn’t a playground. Grow up and talk about your plan.”

The survey additionally indicated that the largest share of likely voters hopes the contenders will focus their discussions on employment and economic matters. 

“I’ll tell you with Donald Trump I want to see that he has rational answers to questions without name calling,” Leven stated. “I want to try to get beyond the political hocus pocus that both of them are doing and try to see who they really are.”

Carried out in English across all 50 states via the internet, the Reuters/Ipsos poll gathered responses from 2,124 American adults. This group included 1,337 individuals classified as likely voters based on their registration status, voting background, and declared commitment to participate on Election Day. The survey's measure of accuracy, known as a credibility interval, stands at 2 percentage points for the entire pool of respondents and 3 percentage points for the likely voters.

The U.S. Department of Justice advised Judicial Watch that the FBI has found 30 pages of records concerning the June 27, 2016, airport tarmac encounter involving former President Bill Clinton and former Attorney General Loretta Lynch. The Justice Department suggested that any non-exempt portions should be turned over by November 30, 2017, according to the lawsuit Judicial Watch v. U.S. Department of Justice, docketed as No. 1:16-cv-02046. 

These upcoming records are being provided due to a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit. The legal action was initiated after the Justice Department failed to answer a July 7, 2016, FOIA submission that asked for multiple items: all FD-302 forms from the FBI's probe into former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton's private email server use while in office; all communication records among FBI personnel concerning that same investigation, which covers exchanges with the Department of Justice, the White House, the Democratic National Committee, and the Hillary Clinton presidential campaign; and all documents tied to the June 27, 2016, interaction between Bill Clinton and Loretta Lynch.

Initially, the FBI told Judicial Watch that no records existed regarding the tarmac gathering. Yet, through a separate legal matter, the Justice Department uncovered emails showing Justice Department personnel corresponding with the bureau about the meeting. Consequently, an August 10, 2017, letter from the FBI explained that a deeper review suggested relevant records might exist, prompting the reopening of the FOIA request. Meanwhile, the Trump Justice Department has declined to release the talking points formulated by the Obama Justice Department to handle media questions regarding the disputed June 27 encounter at Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport between Bill Clinton and Loretta Lynch.

The private meeting took place on a parked private aircraft at Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport in Arizona on June 27, 2016, unfolding while the investigation into Mrs. Clinton's email server was active and shortly before the public release of the Benghazi report involving the Obama administration and Mrs. Clinton. On June 30, Judicial Watch petitioned the U.S. Department of Justice Office of the Inspector General to launch an inquiry into the rendezvous. 

Tom Fitton of Judicial Watch expressed sharp criticism, stating that the FBI is out of control and that it is remarkable these records were only discovered after the agency was caught concealing them in a separate legal proceeding. He added that Judicial Watch will keep fighting in court for clarity regarding the FBI's document handling, and demanded that the bureau end its obstruction and immediately make the new files public. This litigation has already compelled the FBI to make part of its Clinton investigative file public, though over half of those files remain withheld, and the bureau indicated it expects to finish processing those materials by July 2018.

Questions have long persisted over whether the Obama Justice Department and the FBI afforded special treatment to Clinton and other potential targets or witnesses. The Obama administration granted several immunity deals, encompassing Cheryl Mills, former Chief of Staff to Clinton; John Bentel, former head of the State Department’s Office of Information Resources Management; Heather Samuelson, executive assistant to Clinton; Brian Pagliano, a State Department IT worker who managed Clinton's private server; and a staff member at Platt River Networks, the firm that serviced the server. It remains uncertain if Hillary Clinton herself was granted any form of immunity.

Additionally, a political action committee directed by McAulilffe—a longtime ally and political backer of Bill and Hillary Clinton—contributed nearly $500,000 in 2015 to Jill McCabe during her run for the Virginia State Senate. The Virginia Democratic Party, heavily influenced by McAuliffe, provided an extra $207,788 to Jill McCabe's campaign. At that time, in July 2015, Andrew McCabe led the FBI’s Washington, D.C., field office, which supplied personnel to the Clinton email investigation, prompting multiple lawsuits from Judicial Watch concerning the McCabe, FBI, and Clinton controversy.

A federal appeals court decided on Friday to freeze a controversial Arizona voting statute backed by Republicans, blocking its implementation until the conclusion of Tuesday's election. This ruling provides a win for Democrats amid a broader, nationwide web of lawsuits concerning voter access. Earlier in the legislative session, Arizona lawmakers approved the measure to ban advocacy organizations from gathering completed early ballots from citizens and dropping them off at election centers as part of voter mobilization campaigns. 

The legal challengers, which featured the Democratic National Committee, contended that the legislation was unconstitutional due to its disproportionate negative effect on minority voting access. Within the state's presidential contest, recent polling has indicated a narrow advantage for Republican Donald Trump over his Democratic rival, Hillary Clinton. 

Earlier in the week, the San Francisco-based 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals agreed to reconsider a prior decision that had declined to halt the statute, opting for a hearing before an expanded panel of 11 judges. According to court documentation, that panel delivered a 6-5 vote on Friday to bar the state of Arizona from implementing the rule immediately. Subsequently, Arizona submitted an emergency request to the U.S. Supreme Court on Friday afternoon, seeking an overturn of the 9th Circuit decision. 

Democrats have maintained that Republican-led states pursue such regulations to suppress turnout among minorities and other demographic groups that typically support Democratic contenders. Conversely, Republicans argue that these rules are essential safeguards against electoral fraud. 

In his opinion, 9th Circuit Chief Judge Sidney Thomas noted that the ruling would not interfere with the administration of the presidential election in Arizona. He stated that the order merely blocks the enforcement of legislation that would otherwise turn the collection of validly cast ballots by third parties into a criminal offense. Thomas and five other judges, all of whom were appointed by Democratic presidents, formed the majority. Meanwhile, five dissenting judges—every one of whom was appointed by a Republican president—maintained that the judiciary ought not to intervene in state statutes so close to Election Day while early voting is actively taking place. The jurisdiction of the 9th Circuit encompasses nine Western states, which includes Arizona. 

Arizona Secretary of State Michele Reagan expressed dissatisfaction with the outcome in a public statement, warning that the ruling would create voter confusion and lower participation rates. Meanwhile, a spokesperson for the Democratic National Committee was not immediately available for remarks. 

In a separate legal development on Friday involving a key battleground state, a federal judge in Ohio issued an order prohibiting Donald Trump’s campaign from verbally harassing voters or taking photographs of them near polling locations.

Winding about 60 miles westward from the Brownsville area, the structure is punctuated by numerous large gaps that allow vehicles and pedestrians to pass freely. Even where the barrier is standing, it frequently fails to deter unauthorized crossings. Farmer Ray Loop pointed out muddy footprints scaling multiple sections on his land, remarking that climbers can clear the height in about a minute and a half.

Authorized back in 2006, this imperfect South Texas barrier highlights the myriad obstacles—including difficult terrain, international treaties, expensive legal battles, and massive costs—that could hinder President-elect Donald Trump’s signature campaign promise of erecting an unbreakable wall across the entire 2,000-mile frontier. Denise Gilman, a law professor and director of the Immigration Clinic at the University of Texas at Austin, described the barrier as consisting of “more holes than it is fence.” Internal government emails secured by Gilman via a court order and reviewed by Reuters indicate that these gaps were the result of local political pushback, property rights litigation, and cost-efficiency calculations.

Jason Miller, a spokesperson for the Trump transition team, declined to address these potential hurdles, stating that the incoming president will have ample opportunity to delve into policy specifics following his January inauguration. However, during an interview on CBS’ “60 minutes” the previous month, Trump acknowledged for the first time that fencing could be utilized in certain sections. “There could be some fencing,” he remarked, adding, “I’m very good at this. It’s called construction. There could be some fencing, but some areas, a wall is more appropriate.”

Fifty-one-year-old Ray Loop backs tougher immigration measures and voted for Trump, yet he remains skeptical about physical barriers. Speaking from his pickup truck while driving past border patrol vehicles on his property, Loop dismissed the concept: “That is not going to work. There are places where it makes sense logistically, but all the way from Texas to California? No.”

Acting as a primary artery for unauthorized crossings, the Rio Grande Valley has emerged as a central hub for immigration enforcement. U.S. Customs and Border Protection defended the infrastructure in a statement, emphasizing that fencing forms part of a broader strategy that incorporates ground agents, cameras, motion sensors, and aerial surveillance. Meanwhile, Jon Feere, a legal policy analyst at the Washington-based Center for Immigration Studies, which advocates for robust border security, suggested that a comprehensive approach must extend beyond a single wall. He noted that while fencing can significantly complicate clandestine crossings, it cannot serve as a standalone solution.

The Secure Fence Act, enacted in 2006 under Republican President George W. Bush, severely miscalculated the expenses required to build roughly 670 miles of planned barriers spanning from California to Texas. By the time Democratic President Barack Obama declared the project largely finished in 2011, the allocated $2.4 billion had only funded about half of that intended distance, figures from a U.S. Government Accounting Office report show. Both Obama and Democratic presidential contender Hillary Clinton had voted in favor of the legislation during their time as U.S. senators.

In the South Texas region, original blueprints calling for a double layer of reinforced fencing spanning roughly 200 miles between Brownsville and Laredo were eventually reduced to a single-layered, interrupted barrier covering only about a third of that span. Challenging border geography sparked numerous land rights disputes that drove up expenses and prolonged construction timelines. With roughly 1,200 miles of the frontier situated along the winding Rio Grande in Texas, constructing a barrier directly on the actual border is physically impossible. 

Furthermore, the International Boundary and Water Commission, established jointly by the two nations in 1889, prohibits any obstruction to the river’s natural flow, meaning any wall must be positioned on flood plain levees. In South Texas, this requirement pushed the fence as far as two miles north into U.S. territory. As a result, properties ended up stranded on the Mexico-facing side in a sort of no man’s land, forcing the government to reimburse owners for diminished land value. 

Loop’s residence and the vast majority of his farmland sit on the southern, Mexico-facing side of the barrier inside U.S. territory, though he resolved his eminent domain litigation with the government under confidential terms. Another prolonged legal battle dragged on for seven years across 140 court filings as Eloisa Tamez challenged government efforts to strand a portion of her family's historic acreage—originally granted by the King of Spain in 1767—behind the wall. The federal government ultimately settled for an undisclosed amount and agreed to install several access gates through the fence on her property. 

Economic fallout is also evident elsewhere; the Fort Brown Memorial Golf Course in Brownsville was trapped behind the barrier and ultimately shut down in 2015 after suffering steep losses from patrons who mistakenly believed entering the facility meant leaving the United States. 

Legal authorities note that while Trump would likely face little difficulty acquiring land via eminent domain for national security projects, property owners may now demand higher payouts since earlier construction phases established clear precedents of falling property values. Legal experts indicate that several compensation and property disputes initiated during the Bush administration could bleed into the Trump era, potentially triggering a fresh wave of litigation. Efren Olivares, regional legal director for the Texas Civil Rights Project’s South Texas office—which has represented landowners in barrier disputes—warned that court battles will inevitably stall any construction efforts for months or even years.

Economic and local political factors also present significant hurdles. A major gap persists just west of Brownsville, where residents in an affluent community successfully fended off construction. Internal correspondence from U.S. Customs and Border Protection reveals that authorities deliberately steered clear of high-value real estate. In a March 2007 operational report, divisional bureau chief Jeffrey Self wrote that the agency would avoid building fences in urban zones where real estate prices proved too prohibitive.

Apprehensions along the southwestern border have surged recently as border security took center stage during the political campaign. According to data from Customs and Border Protection, U.S. authorities detained 408,870 individuals attempting to cross over the twelve-month period ending in September, marking a 23 percent increase compared to the previous year. 

In McAllen, situated about 55 miles west of Brownsville, Mayor Jim Darling reported that human smugglers are actively boosting their trade by urging migrants to cross before a Trump wall materializes. Darling, who holds a nonpartisan seat but backed Republican Texas Governor Greg Abbott during his 2014 bid, stated that the community now faces an escalated immigration challenge. Should the existing South Texas fencing be extended westward, it is expected to terminate near Rio Grande City. There, independent Mayor Joel Villarreal views the project as a misallocation of taxpayer funds that could inadvertently enrich Mexican criminal cartels controlling the smuggling routes. He warned that traffickers will retain the means to guide people across, forcing migrants to pay the cartels their cut.

As transgender visibility increases, conservative lawmakers have ramped up efforts to introduce restrictive measures dictating restroom usage. 

In an attempt to decode this political fixation, Williams interviewed multiple transgender individuals alongside one of their primary critics, Colorado Republican State Representative and Chaplain Gordon Klingenschmitt. Williams challenged the lawmaker regarding his assertion that transgender individuals are merely "confused," effectively dismantling his argument. Expounding on his religious views, Klingenschmitt explained to Williams why he views transgender people as a danger to the nation, stating that they desire to confuse not only their own identities but everyone else's as well, and questioning why the government should participate in this pretense and force others to be dishonest.

Klingenschmitt attempted to pivot the conversation toward religion, though he insisted on a wardrobe change beforehand, stating he would discuss religious freedom once he changed into his "alter ego." Williams waited for him to complete his transition so he would feel at ease during the discussion, while Klingenschmitt remained oblivious to the irony of the moment.

When pressed by Williams on his intense dedication to advancing anti-transgender measures, Klingenschmitt characterized the situation as perversion, claiming individuals adopt transgender identities simply to gain access to violate others' rights. Addressing his background as a chaplain, Williams then posed the question of whether it would be fair to assume all priests are pedophiles. Klingenschmitt answered in the negative, and when asked why, he responded that some individuals engage in criminal behavior while others do not. However, Klingenschmitt claimed he could not apply that identical reasoning to transgender people, dismissing the comparison as "apples and oranges." Williams ultimately gathered that Klingenschmitt’s core worry was that permitting transgender women to use restrooms corresponding to their gender identity would lead to sexual assault, despite the total absence of any documented instances of sexual assault occurring as a result of such policies.

text: Court filings released on Wednesday show that a federal judge in Alabama has finalized a permanent injunction that prohibits state authorities from refusing marriage rights to same-sex couples. U.S. District Judge Callie Granade submitted the order on Tuesday, resolving a legal challenge against Alabama's prohibition on gay marriage that began in 2014 and reaffirming her early 2015 ruling that found the state statute unconstitutional. The question of gay marriage stood at the forefront of a nationwide controversy until the Supreme Court of the United States determined in June 2015 that the U.S. Constitution guarantees marriage rights to same-sex couples. Even after that nationwide ruling, authorities in Alabama persisted in fighting the legal shift. Roy Moore, the chief justice of the Alabama Supreme Court, faced suspension last month after directing state probate judges through an administrative directive to withhold marriage licenses from gay couples. Meanwhile, in March, the state's highest court threw out requests from opponents of same-sex marriage aimed at reviving the state-level ban, though it declined to rescind or nullify its own March 2015 decision supporting the restriction, which had been issued shortly before the high court's nationwide ruling. Susan Watson, who serves as the executive director for the American Civil Liberties Union of Alabama, remarked that the measure establishes closure by permanently barring the state from applying marriage regulations that discriminate against gay relationships, adding that this permanent protection was essential given the intense opposition from the state. Representatives representing Alabama Attorney General Luther Strange, who is listed as a defendant in the case, were unavailable for statements on Wednesday. Legal counsel for Strange had previously requested the dismissal of the lawsuit on the grounds that the state was already adhering to federal regulations. Nonetheless, Judge Granade argued in her decision that a commitment to stop the behavior does not make a permanent injunction obsolete. She pointed out that the behavior of the suspended chief justice and other authorities implied that further efforts might arise to challenge the constitutional marriage rights of gay couples, noting in the text that there is no absolute certainty that the unconstitutional marriage statutes of Alabama will not be implemented again in the future.

MADRID/BARCELONA (Reuters) - Amid an escalating political standoff that has already impacted the economy and sparked concerns about ongoing instability, regional officials in Catalonia stated on Saturday that they refuse to submit to direct governance from Madrid. Spanish Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy had announced earlier in the day that he would utilize special constitutional authorities to dismiss the local administration and trigger fresh elections, responding to the region's push for a break from Spain.

Catalan President Carles Puigdemont characterized Rajoy's actions as the most severe assault on the Catalan populace since the era of Spain's military dictatorship. Puigdemont made this assertion following his October 10 symbolic independence declaration, which came in the wake of a secession referendum. This marks the initial instance of the central administration seizing control of a regional body since the country transitioned back to democracy. 

Justifying the measures, Rajoy argued they are vital for resolving a division within the nation that has already forced a downward revision of economic growth projections for the euro zone's fourth-largest economy. Following participation in a peaceful protest, Puigdemont rejected the central government's intervention, though he held back from confirming whether he would actualize threats to press forward with independence before the intervention is officially enforced. 

In a televised broadcast, Puigdemont stated he is asking the Catalan parliament to convene a plenary session so that citizen representatives can evaluate this attempt to dismantle their government and democracy, allowing them to determine an appropriate response. 

To enact direct rule, Rajoy requires the approval of the Spanish upper house, having secured support from King Felipe and the primary opposition faction in Madrid. The objective, according to Rajoy, is to reinstate legal order and societal harmony—both of which have suffered significantly—safeguard the economic recovery currently facing risks in Catalonia, and hold elections under normal conditions.

The Senate vote, slated for next Friday, would grant Madrid complete authority over Catalan public media, police, and finances, while limiting regional parliamentary powers for a duration of up to half a year. This timeline could potentially provide the secessionist camp with strategic flexibility. 

Carme Forcadell, the speaker of the regional parliament, rejected Madrid's actions and labeled Rajoy's move a coup. During a televised address, Forcadell asserted that Prime Minister Rajoy aims to strip the Catalan parliament of its democratic status, a development she vowed would be resisted. 

The regional assembly is anticipated to convene on Monday to consider scheduling a session that could formally declare a Catalan republic. Furthermore, local media outlets have suggested Puigdemont might opt to dissolve the assembly and schedule his own elections prior to next Friday, which, under regional regulations, would occur within a two-month span. Such a step would allow Puigdemont to bypass the six-month schedule outlined by Rajoy and capitalize on strong anti-Madrid sentiments currently prevalent in the area.

Pro-independence organizations have historically mobilized crowds exceeding one million individuals to protest Madrid's reluctance to negotiate an arrangement. Alongside his cabinet, Puigdemont participated in a Barcelona rally, displaying yellow ribbons to back two prominent pro-independence figures currently imprisoned on sedition allegations. Tens of thousands chanted for freedom while waving secession flags and holding placards with slogans such as "Defending our land is not a crime" and "Let's proclaim the republic."

Abel Fernandez, a 38-year-old builder wearing an independence flag at the protest, expressed his view that Rajoy's activation of the constitutional article would accomplish nothing, adding that authorities cannot silence the portion of Catalonia supporting independence or the right to self-determination.

According to Catalan officials, roughly 90 percent of participants in the October 1 referendum voted in favor of breaking away. However, turnout stood at 43 percent of the electorate, with most unionist voters boycotting the ballot. The secession drive has encountered fierce resistance throughout the rest of Spain, caused deep internal divisions within Catalonia, and resulted in hundreds of businesses relocating their legal headquarters outside the region, though Rajoy appealed to them on Saturday to remain.

Rajoy’s center-right People's Party administration maintains that Puigdemont repeatedly violated the law while advancing the independence agenda, and the government has secured solid backing from the opposition Socialist Party. Pedro Sanchez, the Socialist leader, emphasized that there are no differences between his party and the PP regarding territorial unity. 

The secessionist movement has decried the detention of leaders as political prisoners, while human rights organizations have criticized the aggressive police methods deployed to block the referendum.

BRUSSELS (Reuters) - Amid rising euroscepticism and with the UK's 2019 departure on the horizon, the European Commission put forward a series of concepts on Wednesday to strengthen euro zone integration as a way to help unify the wider European Union. The executive branch of the EU unveiled these measures to offer the 19 nations using the single currency stronger safeguards against future economic downturns. Nevertheless, initiatives to reinforce solidarity among these 19 countries have triggered anxiety among the eight member states outside the currency union, who fear marginalization as second-tier members with diminished influence and reduced funding going forward. In an effort to calm these anxieties, the Commission emphasized that every initiative remains accessible to all EU participants, despite this approach contradicting the vision of certain currency bloc leaders like French President Emmanuel Macron. Macron has advocated for establishing a separate euro zone parliament, a dedicated finance minister, and a currency bloc budget totaling hundreds of billions of euros. The Commission's blueprint includes financial incentives rewarding nations for structural overhauls, alongside dedicated funds to help non-euro states prepare for eventual currency adoption, a requirement for all members except Denmark. However, Germany, a dominant political force, promptly dampened expectations regarding a central element of the strategy, casting uncertainty over its prospects. 

The Commission expressed support for establishing a designated "stabilisation function" for the currency bloc, arguing that the European Central Bank's monetary policy cannot adequately address downturns affecting only isolated members of the euro area. According to the Commission, this mechanism would function as a financial pool utilizing loans and a comparatively "limited grant component" to safeguard investments. To remain credible and impactful, officials stated it should possess the capacity to disburse a minimum of 1 percent of GDP while retaining borrowing privileges. Oversight of this "stabilisation function" would rest with the Commission, and participation would be restricted to countries that comply with EU regulations. Financing would be generated through EU budget loans, voluntary state contributions, and borrowings from the currency bloc's rescue fund backed by guarantees from the broader EU budget. The Commission noted that achieving this requires establishing "a limited borrowing capacity" within the upcoming EU financial framework. 

Germany voiced skepticism, however. Acting German Finance Minister Peter Altmaier remarked that it is unhelpful to anticipate outcomes, noting that the departing administration remained unconvinced regarding the necessity of establishing additional safety nets at the European level. Rather than creating a euro zone finance minister, the Commission suggested appointing a pan-European Minister of Economy and Finance. This individual would simultaneously serve as a senior official within the European Commission and lead the gatherings of currency area finance ministers. Additionally, this official would direct the operations of the bailout fund as head of its governing board, a role presently filled by the president of the Eurogroup representing euro zone finance ministers. The Commission indicated that this position could be established upon the inauguration of the subsequent European Commission in November 2019, with the appointee answering directly to the European Parliament. Presently, the leader of the euro zone finance ministers—the closest equivalent to a unified financial chief—frequently appears before the parliamentary economic committee, though that body holds no authority to hold them accountable. Furthermore, currency bloc finance ministers show little eagerness to permit the Commission, which currently holds merely observer status at their regular sessions, to direct their deliberations.

Additional proposals for currency bloc integration, originally advanced by Berlin, involve converting the government-controlled bailout mechanism into a European Monetary Fund. The Commission endorsed this concept while insisting that the EMF operate as an official EU entity subject to oversight by the European Parliament—a condition officials suggest national governments will reject. The Commission aims to secure consensus on the EMF from national governments and the European Parliament by the middle of 2019, intending for the fund to supply a 60 billion-euro backstop to support the bank-financed Single Resolution Fund. At the same time, the Commission omitted any mention of the initiative—championed by Germany, Slovakia, and the Netherlands—to institute a sovereign insolvency framework designed to compel governments into maintaining disciplined fiscal habits. Market analysts remained underwhelmed by the Commission's announcements. ING economist Carsten Brzeski remarked in a client briefing that an initial review of the paperwork suggests virtually nothing will transform, describing the day's initiatives as positive in intent yet derivative and far from revolutionary.

ANKARA (Reuters) - Legal authorities in Turkey announced on Thursday that they have opened a probe into accusations that relatives of President Tayyip Erdogan transferred millions of dollars overseas for tax evasion purposes, though they noted questions remain regarding the validity of the paperwork supporting the assertions. 

The leader of the primary opposition faction, the Republican People's Party (CHP) headed by Kemal Kilicdaroglu, stated earlier in the week that Erdogan's relatives funneled $14 million to an enterprise located in the Isle of Man, displaying paperwork he claimed substantiated the financial movements. 

Erdogan rejected the claims as fabrications, asserting on Thursday that Kilicdaroglu would face consequences. Having led the nation's political landscape for roughly a decade and a half, Erdogan continues to stand as Turkey's most widely supported political figure by a large margin. Critics contend that his governance has grown progressively authoritarian, particularly following an unsuccessful coup attempt in the previous year; nonetheless, the CHP faces difficulties in mobilizing backing to contest the President. 

The opposition party has stopped short of alleging that Erdogan, his kin, or any of the firms reportedly tied to the financial transfers engaged in illegal behavior. 

The chief prosecutor's office in Ankara stated it was initiating an inquiry into the claims and mentioned that a representative for Bellway LTD—the entity identified by Kilicdaroglu as the recipient of the Erdogan family's capital—had labeled the records as fraudulent. Furthermore, authorities requested that the CHP surrender all related files. 

Ozgur Ozel, who serves as the deputy chairman of the CHP, indicated that the political organization would cooperate with the prosecutor's directive. 

In addition to these developments, the CHP submitted a formal parliamentary request calling for a probe into the accusations, though the legislative body, where Erdogan's governing AK party holds a majority, voted down the motion on Thursday.

Following the sudden dismissal of the official heading the probe into the administration's connections to Russia, White House press secretary Sean Spicer reacted in a peculiar fashion. Late Tuesday evening, following a short interview with Fox Business on the White House grounds, Spicer sought shelter in the bushes to dodge inquiries, as reported by The Washington Post. Along with his staff, Spicer crouched behind a high hedge. Returning to his office required navigating a crowd of journalists eager for answers regarding Donald Trump's abrupt termination of FBI Director James Comey.

To make it back inside, the press secretary had to get past that horde of reporters. For hours, Spicer and his team twisted themselves into knots trying to justify the unexpected firing. According to The Washington Post, Spicer initially intended to release the major news via an email statement, but the transmission was too slow, leading him to stand in the press office doorway around 5:40 p.m. and yell the statement to nearby reporters. He promptly disappeared while his staff locked the office door. Although the press team initially hinted at a possible briefing, they soon announced there would be no further comments that evening.

However, as both Democratic and Republican lawmakers raised alarms and voiced heavy criticism over the firing, Spicer and two top spokeswomen were soon briskly walking up the White House drive to defend the president across CNN, Fox News, and Fox Business. In the intervals between these television appearances, Spicer spent several minutes concealed within the foliage. Janet Montesi, a press office executive assistant, eventually stepped out from the bushes to inform journalists that Spicer would address questions on the condition that they did not film him. 

That was when Spicer emerged from his hiding spot to engage with the press corps. "Just turn the lights off. Turn the lights off," Spicer insisted. "We'll take care of this. Can you just turn that light off?" His request was accommodated, leaving him positioned in near total darkness between a pair of tall hedges, surrounded by more than a dozen journalists. For the next ten minutes, he addressed a barrage of inquiries, often hemming, hawing, and stammering. When asked when Trump and Comey last spoke, Spicer responded, "Uh, I don't know. I don't know. There's some—I don't know. I don't know."

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — The White House pushed back on Friday against a media report suggesting the Trump administration weighed a plan to deploy the National Guard for gathering up undocumented immigrants, insisting no such strategy exists. While addressing the press, White House spokesman Sean Spicer stopped short of completely ruling out that the concept might have been brought up informally within some corner of the administration. 

The initial story came from the Associated Press, which detailed a draft memo from the Department of Homeland Security outlining a potential mobilization of as many as 100,000 National Guard members. Spicer strongly condemned the reporting during his briefing, calling the claim entirely false and emphasizing that there is zero initiative underway to employ the National Guard for rounding up undocumented individuals. 

Echoing those denials, Department of Homeland Security spokesperson David Lapan stated clearly that the agency is not looking into calling up the National Guard to enforce immigration laws. 

According to the Associated Press, the Jan. 25 draft document had reportedly circulated among DHS personnel for roughly a fortnight, directed at the acting leaders of both U.S. Customs and Border Protection and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The 11-page paper allegedly proposed a historic level of military involvement in immigration control spanning the four states sharing a border with Mexico—Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and California—along with seven neighboring states: Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Colorado, Oklahoma, Arkansas, and Louisiana. Furthermore, the news outlet noted the text was intended to guide the execution of President Donald Trump's sweeping Jan. 25 executive orders concerning border security and immigration.

A Homeland Security official, who spoke anonymously, characterized the paperwork secured by the news organization as a very preliminary draft assembled by staffers for Homeland Security Secretary John Kelly. The anonymous source explained that any mention of the National Guard was removed prior to reaching Kelly's attention. Although the final memo intended for Kelly remains incomplete, the official indicated it is anticipated to wrap up shortly.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — Donald Trump, a leader typically recognized for a stern and abrasive public persona, faces a chance this Saturday in Houston to display a softer, more compassionate demeanor, potentially reaching citizens who have voiced opposition to his administration. Previous president Barack Obama earned the title of "comforter-in-chief" for his frequent participation in comforting those affected by mass violence and terrorism. However, the severe flooding resulting from Hurricane Harvey represents the initial major national crisis during Trump's tenure. According to White House announcements, Trump's itinerary includes meetings with flood victims and rescue volunteers in Houston, followed by a trip to Lake Charles, Louisiana, another location severely impacted by the weather event.

During his initial journey to the region on Tuesday, Trump deliberately avoided the actual disaster area to prevent interfering with ongoing rescue operations. Instead, his schedule consisted of briefings with cabinet officials, local and state authorities, and emergency responders. Nevertheless, he faced backlash for failing to interact with those suffering from the most destructive storm to strike Texas in half a century, with critics arguing his focus was placed too heavily on governmental logistics rather than human hardship.

Matt Mackowiak, the Travis County Republican Party chairman in Texas, acknowledged that the criticism was fair, despite commending the administration's overall management of the crisis. 

With more than one million individuals forced from their homes by Harvey and an estimated death toll reaching up to 50 amid record-breaking river levels and gridlock in Houston, Saturday's excursion presents Trump with an opportunity that Mackowiak urges him to maximize. Establishing an emotional bond with the nation remains beneficial for a U.S. president, Mackowiak noted, suggesting it could prove particularly advantageous regarding the portion of the population currently critical of his administration. Data from the Reuters/Ipsos tracking poll indicates that roughly 59 percent of Americans express disapproval of Trump's presidential job performance.

While Obama became well-known for crying following the 2012 elementary school shooting in Newtown, Connecticut, that claimed the lives of 20 children, Trump's public expressions of emotion have historically been limited mostly to frustration directed at journalists and detractors. A notable departure occurred following the April chemical weapons assault by the Syrian government that resulted in the deaths of over 70 people, a significant portion of whom were children. During a press conference after the event, Trump remarked on the lethal nature of the chemical gas used against innocent babies and children, stating that such actions cross numerous boundaries. 

Earlier, during his presidential campaign, families who lost relatives to undocumented immigrants praised him for personally conveying condolences regarding their tragedies. 

Conversely, he drew heavy criticism for his handling of the civil unrest in Charlottesville, Virginia, the previous month, where critics felt he prioritized assigning blame and arguing with opponents over calming a shaken country. 

Trump initially built his public reputation as a Manhattan real estate developer known for aggressive negotiation tactics, an image he further reinforced through a hit reality television program where he routinely dismissed underperforming participants without sentiment. Throughout his campaign for the presidency, he frequently emphasized the importance of being "tough" and lauded business leaders described as "killers." Mackowiak observed that, judging by his background and professional history, public displays of sympathy or empathy do not appear to come naturally to him.

On the other hand, Family Research Council president and pastor Tony Perkins argues that a warmer disposition exists beneath the surface. Perkins accompanied Trump during a campaign stop to visit flood victims in rural Louisiana the previous year, where Trump and current Vice President Mike Pence traveled through the disaster zone distributing diapers and bottled water. 

According to Perkins, Trump instructed his motorcade to pull over repeatedly so he could converse directly with affected residents, revealing a compassionate demeanor and a visible emotional reaction to the devastation. 

Gerard Landry, mayor of Denham Springs—a Louisiana municipality of 10,000 residents where nearly 80 percent of structures suffered flood damage—spoke with Trump at a local high school. Landry recalled that the president shook his hand, placed a hand on his shoulder, and expressed confidence in the city's recovery and the mayor's leadership. Anticipating the loud persona seen at campaign rallies, Landry instead encountered someone entirely unexpected, describing him as grounded and very different in person. 

Perkins believes the Saturday journey gives Trump an opportunity to demonstrate that specific aspect of his character to the broader public, describing it as entirely genuine and authentic.

WASHINGTON, 2016 — A leading adviser to Donald Trump pushed back Sunday against an audio recording from the 1991 archives, expressing doubt that the Republican presidential front-runner ever pretended to be his own publicist to boast about his dating life. This media storm unfolded right as the Democratic camp intensified its scrutiny of the billionaire businessman's personal integrity. 

The Washington Post published the audio file on Friday, featuring an individual calling himself "John Miller," a representative for Trump, discussing the real estate mogul's relationships with a journalist from People magazine. During an appearance on CNN's "State of the Union," top campaign aide Paul Manafort stated that the voice on the tape did not sound like Trump, despite the candidate's history of acknowledging the past use of fake names. 

Manafort remarked that the audio was barely intelligible, adding that he could not identify the speaker and ultimately chose to believe Trump's denial. Trump himself asserted on NBC’s “Today” program on Friday that the voice did not belong to him, even though he previously admitted to adopting at least one pseudonym when talking to the press years ago.

The original 1991 feature in People playfully referred to Miller as an enigmatic public relations agent who bore a striking vocal resemblance to Trump. Just days after publication, the reporter behind the tape, Sue Carswell, stated that Trump had confessed to pulling a prank by acting as Miller and offered an apology. 

Having essentially secured the GOP nomination earlier in the month for the upcoming November 8 election, Trump has focused on bridging divisions within the party following resistance from several prominent figures. Meanwhile, supporters of front-runner Hillary Clinton have characterized Trump as untrustworthy, placing particular emphasis on his past remarks about women. 

Since locking down the nomination, Clinton has stepped up her attacks on Trump's character, recently pointing to his withheld tax returns as a sign that he is concealing information. In response to accusations that he frequently judges women based on physical appearance, Trump reacted with frustration and retaliated by questioning how Clinton and her spouse, former President Bill Clinton, handled women who came forward with allegations of sexual misconduct against the former president. Bill Clinton previously acknowledged engaging in extramarital relationships with White House intern Monica Lewinsky and Arkansas performer Gennifer Flowers.

On Sunday, Trump took to Twitter to mock a New York Times piece featuring accounts from multiple women who claimed his remarks regarding their physical appearance and unwanted advances made them uncomfortable over the years. The same article also noted his history of elevating women to high-ranking roles, an uncommon practice within the real estate sector at the time. In a Sunday post, Trump wrote that everyone was mocking the newspaper over what he termed a weak hit piece concerning him and women.

Also on Sunday, Democratic President Barack Obama used a university commencement address to take aim at Trump's platform, specifically targeting his call for a temporary prohibition on foreign Muslims entering the United States. Speaking to graduates at Rutgers University in New Jersey, Obama argued that isolating or looking down upon Muslims and proposing differential treatment at the border violates American values and goes against national identity.

While news reports from the early 1990s frequently mentioned that Trump occasionally adopted fake PR personas to influence press coverage, the actual recording of such an instance only surfaced recently and rapidly gained traction across the American media landscape. The NBC sketch comedy series "Saturday Night Live" even featured a parody involving an actor playing Trump who phoned journalists under the alias "John Pepperoni." 

Trump's history of using fictitious representatives first came to light in 1990 during a legal deposition, where he testified to communicating with reporters via telephone under the alias John Baron, which appeared in some media accounts as John Barron. Newsday quoted him following the testimony as saying that numerous individuals employ pen names, citing Ernest Hemingway as an example.

text:
STRASBOURG, France — According to the president of the European Commission, the bloc ought to establish a unified economy and finance ministerial post, though he argued against setting up an independent budget or legislative assembly exclusively for the currency union. During his address on the state of the union delivered Wednesday to the European Parliament, Jean-Claude Juncker proposed that this official should oversee economic matters across the entire bloc rather than just the countries sharing the single currency, while also presiding over the group of currency-zone financial chiefs and answering directly to European lawmakers. 

Officials within the bloc explained that opting for a single finance chief spanning all member states instead of strictly the currency block is a deliberate strategy to ward off a split among the 27 nations remaining after the UK departs in 2019. The concept of a dedicated financial lead for the euro area has previously been championed by Emmanuel Macron, the French leader. A French diplomatic insider disclosed on Wednesday that Macron plans to present comprehensive reform plans regarding the currency area on the 26th of September, arriving just days after the German federal elections. Additionally, during discussions last month, German Chancellor Angela Merkel informed Macron that she could envision a merged European economic and financial portfolio.

Stressing the need for reform, Juncker told the parliament that the bloc requires a dedicated economy and finance leader who can encourage and back structural changes throughout member nations. He added that this official ought to synchronize all available financial tools designed to assist any member country suffering through an economic downturn or severe crisis. 

Rather than establishing a completely brand-new office, Juncker suggested that the responsibilities should be assigned to an existing vice president of the European Commission—a proposition certain to draw fierce opposition from currency-zone administrations, particularly in Berlin. 

His remarks form part of a broader conversation concerning the long-term structure of the 19-member currency area. Juncker asserted that this group should eventually grow to encompass all remaining member states that currently operate outside the single currency and lack a formal exemption from adopting it. 

To facilitate this, Juncker announced plans for a new accession mechanism to provide technical and monetary support for countries seeking to transition to the euro, though he omitted specific details. He maintained that by the time of Britain's exit in March 2019, participation in both the single currency and the bloc’s banking union—featuring unified supervision, a resolution authority, and a joint deposit guarantee framework—ought to be standard for every member. 

Despite this vision, while nearly all EU nations outside the currency union are legally bound to adopt the euro once specific conditions are satisfied, certain major economies like Poland and Sweden currently have zero intentions of doing so anytime soon, arguing that maintaining their national currencies provides greater economic adaptability.

Regarding proposals from Paris and Berlin to institute an independent currency-zone budget alongside the broader long-term EU spending plan, as well as a distinct parliament for the single-currency nations, Juncker dismissed both concepts outright. He argued that instead of a standalone budget, the currency area requires a robust budgetary line embedded directly within the overarching EU budget, and he expressed opposition to a separate legislative body, emphasizing that the European Parliament already serves as the parliament for the currency zone.

Furthermore, Juncker proposed converting the currency-zone's rescue mechanism, known as the European Stability Mechanism (ESM), into a fully integrated European Monetary Fund operating as an official institution of the bloc, transitioning away from its current intergovernmental structure. He indicated that the anticipated European finance minister would likewise oversee this new fund. While withholding specifics regarding potential new responsibilities for the proposed fund, he noted that the Commission intends to unveil formal proposals outlining both the fund's new duties and the powers of the European finance minister in December. 

Meanwhile, financial ministers from the single-currency area are scheduled to kick off discussions regarding the future of the monetary union on Friday during an informal gathering situated in Tallinn, the capital of Estonia.
