President Trump Fires Acting Attorney General, Sally Yates

21st Century Wire reports that an official statement released today by the Office of the Press Secretary announced the dismissal of acting Attorney General Sally Yates. This decision came after Yates directed attorneys within the Department of Justice to avoid defending the administration's executive order concerning travel restrictions. According to the Press Secretary's announcement, Yates let down the Department of Justice by declining to uphold a lawful directive intended to safeguard American citizens. Meanwhile, President Trump utilized Twitter to voice his frustration, posting a critical message stating that Democrats were intentionally stalling his cabinet nominees solely for political motives, noting they are focusing entirely on obstruction. 

To fill the vacancy, Dana Boente, serving as the United States Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia, was appointed as the new acting attorney general. Within the official release, Boente provided a statement expressing his privilege to assist President Trump in this capacity while awaiting the confirmation of Senator Sessions, adding that he intends to uphold and apply national laws to safeguard the public and the country. Coverage from RT further elaborates on the unfolding situation, noting that Yates was removed from her position on a Monday, shortly after reports emerged regarding her instructions to Justice Department lawyers. 

In a social media post, Press Secretary Sean Spicer confirmed that President Trump designated Dana Boente from the Eastern District of Virginia to step in as Acting Attorney General, following the dismissal of Sally Yates. The official statement from the Office of the Press Secretary reiterated that Yates had turned her back on the Department of Justice by failing to execute a legal order crafted to defend the population of the United States. 

Boente, originally appointed during the Obama administration, had previously won confirmation through the Senate for his former role as U.S. Attorney. Representatives from the Trump administration informed journalists on Monday evening that this prior confirmation sufficed to permit him to sign Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act warrants, which authorize surveillance targeting perceived foreign dangers inside the United States. Observers noted this situation is highly unusual, given that Boente's previous Senate approval did not explicitly include authorization for FISA approvals—a power traditionally limited to the attorney general and deputy attorney general, both of whom have historically received direct Senate confirmation for those specific offices. Questions remain regarding whether this administrative step will encounter legal challenges. 

Addressing his new assignment, the newly appointed Acting Attorney General stated in the press release that he felt deeply privileged to aid President Trump until Senator Sessions receives confirmation, emphasizing a commitment to defending and enforcing domestic laws to guarantee the protection of the nation and its people. 

Before her dismissal, Yates authored a letter—highlighted by the New York Times—explaining her stance, in which she stated her responsibility to ensure that legal positions maintained in court align with the institution's fundamental duty to pursue justice and uphold righteousness. She added that she was currently unpersuaded that defending the executive order aligned with those duties, nor was she convinced of the order's legality. 

In reaction to Yates's actions, the President turned to Twitter to denounce the move, attributing it to broader Democratic obstructionism driven by political agendas, and remarked on the involvement of an Obama-appointed attorney general. Following her firing, former Attorney General Eric Holder, who held office under President Obama, took to social media to back Yates, praising her as a skilled attorney and individual of integrity who has devotedly served the country with distinction and whose judgment deserves trust.

Right as the Department of Justice got ready to launch an investigation into the toxic water crisis in Flint, Michigan, an unoccupied office holding the municipality's water documentation was reportedly broken into. For upwards of a year and a half, local citizens had been raising alarms regarding the smell, appearance, and taste of their tap water. Back in January 2014, reports noted that the water tasted foul, smelled bad, and resembled "chocolate milk on tap." Nonetheless, representatives within the administration of Republican Governor Rick Snyder insisted to the citizens for months that the water posed no danger. These claims persisted despite independent analyses revealing elevated lead concentrations within the municipal water supply.

Public anger and intense media scrutiny grew as subsequent testing verified a steep rise in lead levels found in the blood of Flint children. Investigative journalist Curt Guyette, working with the ACLU, subsequently brought to light significant compromising evidence demonstrating that Snyder's staff was aware the municipal water was unsafe for consumption. This ACLU inquiry revealed that officials manipulated tests and fabricated paperwork, violating the law repeatedly to conceal the reality that the water was essentially toxic. 

On January 6, the U.S. Department of Justice formally declared it was getting ready to initiate an official probe into the lead-poisoning crisis in Flint. Amidst these developments, an alleged break-in occurred at Flint City Hall. City representatives verified on January 11 that the incident specifically targeted the empty room housing the local water documents. 

Police Chief James Tolbert and Mayor Kevin Weaver have declined to clarify whether any documents were taken from the space. Regarding security footage of the incident, Chief Tolbert stated that the video fails to display anything. It appears remarkably convenient that an intruder targeted the precise empty room containing the municipal water files right as those documents were about to face heavy legal and public examination. The circumstance that the intruders entered and exited a municipal facility completely unseen by witnesses and undetected by security cameras also appears extremely convenient. 

Throughout Michigan, residents have demanded the apprehension of Governor Snyder as mounting evidence indicates he and his staff knowingly permitted the population of Flint to consume lead-poisoned water for upwards of twelve months while maintaining that it was secure. Considering current knowledge regarding Snyder, the probability that this break-in was unconnected to the contaminated water crisis remains virtually nonexistent. This water crisis tied to Rick Snyder increasingly resembles the Watergate scandal associated with Richard Nixon.

text:
An episode of the Disney-owned ABC program "Scandal" featured a character undergoing an abortion accompanied by the holiday song "Silent Night," while a narrator stated that family destroys rather than completes a person. This broadcast drew immediate criticism for functioning as an extended promotional segment for Planned Parenthood, courtesy of a media conglomerate that largely built its success on content for children. Critics questioned how supporters of the company could market theme parks as destinations for families while simultaneously broadcasting the termination of pregnancies. 

The connection between the program and the organization became clearer upon examining the background of the show's creator. Following the broadcast, the abortion provider publicly commended the episode, and cast members defended the decision to portray the procedure against the backdrop of a Christmas hymn. This alignment was unsurprising, given that "Scandal" creator and producer Shonda Rhimes serves on the board of directors for Planned Parenthood Los Angeles. 

Commentators noted that the theme was not new for Rhimes, who had previously incorporated abortion storylines into her earlier series, "Grey's Anatomy." Observers suggested her history with Catholic schooling contributed to a rebellious approach, and pointed to past personal interviews where Rhimes discussed raising children without being married and expressing no desire to have a husband in her home. Beyond "Grey's Anatomy" and its spin-off "Private Practice," ABC picked up her pilot script for "Scandal" in 2011. In a previous interview with Time magazine, Rhimes defended the inclusion of the topic on television, arguing that polarizing and debated issues ought to be discussed on screen.

The fifth-season episode, titled "Baby, It's Cold Outside," featured the lead character, presidential partner Olivia Pope—played by Kerry Washington—obtaining an abortion during the broadcast. At the same time, a fictional Republican senator, Mellie Grant, portrayed by Bellamy Young, sustained a successful Senate filibuster to prevent the defunding of Planned Parenthood. 

Immediately following the broadcast, Planned Parenthood released a statement praising the production and the creator for demonstrating that audiences will watch when women share their stories. The organization emphasized that the storyline highlighted threats to reproductive health care and the consequences of defunding services such as contraception counseling, STI testing, cancer screenings, and abortions. The statement also referenced statistics regarding the prevalence of the procedure among women and commended the network and creator, while expressing hope that members of Congress would take notice.

After the procedure, the main character is shown back at the White House drinking red wine while classical music plays. Meanwhile, the Media Research Center issued a sharp critique, condemning the broadcast as a prolonged commercial for the organization and labeling the scene featuring the Christmas hymn alongside an abortion as an exhibition of moral decay. Cast member Kerry Washington voiced her backing for the organization on social media by utilizing specific hashtags associated with the episode's plotlines.

text:
Countless surveys concerning the presidential race are currently circulating, with the vast majority pointing to either a tight tie or a lead for Hillary nationwide and in battleground states. According to the logic that this implies manipulation or bias, Breitbart opted to hire Gravis to run its very own survey. The outcome placed Hillary ahead of Trump with 42 percent to 37 percent in a four-way contest. The survey contacted 2,832 individuals on August 9 and features a 1.8 percent margin of error, meaning Hillary's advantage extends past that threshold.

Alex Marlow, the editor-in-chief at Breitbart, commented on the survey by stating that it is an open secret that surveys are routinely spun and manipulated to manufacture momentum for specific candidates or issues. He added that the initial national survey from the Breitbart News Network launches a significant effort to provide readers with an accurate evaluation of where Americans stand on important subjects and figures, free from the filter of the mainstream media. 

It is quite revealing when a survey executed with the goal of neutrality yields identical outcomes to those deemed biased. This particular effort shows Hillary ahead of Trump by five percentage points. In a four-way matchup, the latest Reuters/Ipsos survey also shows a five-point advantage for Hillary, while Economist/YouGov places her up by six points, and Rasmussen Reports has her leading by three points.

Despite large crowds for Trump and smaller ones for Hillary leading critics to call the surveys flawed, Breitbart and Gravis attempted a positive spin, arguing the data highlights opportunities for Trump to expand his voter reach. Doug Kaplan, the managing partner at Gravis, suggested that an 11 percent backing for Trump among the Black community poses an issue for Hillary, apparently basing this on the premise that her support from this demographic falls short of Obama's 2012 numbers.

Additionally, Hillary secured strong results on a question asking whether respondents agreed or disagreed that Donald Trump or Hillary Clinton would fight for people like them. In total, 39 percent believed Hillary would fight for them, compared to 38 percent for Trump. Among Muslim respondents, an impressive 84 percent expressed confidence that she would fight for them. Naturally, Trump lacks that level of backing from the Muslim community, largely due to his Islamophobic statements directed at them.

Ultimately, Breitbart ended up embarrassed, having tried to demonstrate one reality and failing completely. Their findings merely suggested that either Gravis shares the same bias or that surveys happen to be far more accurate than conservatives care to admit.

text:
Four additional women have stepped forward to level sexual assault accusations against former President Bill Clinton. These developments unfold just as Hillary Clinton recently delivered a public address about defending women, raising questions about whether she will continue to support her husband. 

Information regarding these claims comes via Edward Klein—former editor-in-chief of the New York Times Magazine and author of multiple books concerning the Clintons, including *Guilty as Sin* from 2016 and his more recent release, *All Out War: The Plot to Destroy Trump*, which came out on October 30, 2017. According to well-positioned Democratic Party sources alongside an official who worked in both the Clinton and Obama administrations, the 71-year-old former president is facing these serious new allegations.

The sources indicate that the current claims pertain to incidents occurring after Clinton's departure from the White House in 2001, adding to a history previously marked by other allegations of sexual misconduct. Lawyers acting on behalf of these women are working in coordination and have alerted Clinton of their intent to initiate four distinct lawsuits against him.

During ongoing discussions, legal counsel for the claimants is seeking significant financial settlements in exchange for keeping the matter quiet. A representative from Clinton's legal defense has acknowledged that these new allegations exist. 

Historically, Clinton provided an $850,000 settlement in the late 1990s to resolve a sexual harassment claim brought by Paula Jones, a former Arkansas state employee—a legal battle that ultimately triggered Clinton's impeachment by the House of Representatives and subsequent acquittal by the Senate in 1999. 

Sources close to Clinton's inner circle report that current settlement talks have reached a pivotal phase. Should these negotiations break down, the four anonymous women reportedly plan to publicize their sexual assault claims through a press conference. This would place Clinton among the most prominent names on a growing roster of public figures, ranging from Harvey Weinstein to Kevin Spacey, facing recent accusations of sexual assault.

The fresh claims involve events that occurred over a decade ago during the early 2000s. At that time, billionaire investor Ron Burkle employed Clinton to work within his Yucaipa companies. Clinton aided Burkle in drumming up business, traveling globally aboard Burkle's private aircraft—a plane informally dubbed "Air F**k One"—accompanied by numerous attractive young women. The four accusers, whose identities remain undisclosed, worked in junior roles at Burkle's organization during their late teenage years and allege they were sexually assaulted by the former president.

Following a series of tweets last week in which the sitting president claimed his predecessor had monitored his phones prior to the election—an assertion made entirely without supporting documentation—his administration has begun attempting to backtrack. Following the social media posts, administration officials scrambled to support the unprecedented claims directed at the former president. Concurrently, former President Barack Obama reportedly reacted to the unsupported allegations with visible disbelief.

The unfounded conspiracy theory also prompted a response from House Intelligence Committee Chairman Devin Nunes (R-CA) and Ranking Member Adam Schiff (D-CA), who established a Monday deadline for the administration to supply evidence supporting the assertion. Observers noted that Nunes, typically a firm supporter of the president who had previously attempted to downplay the administration's controversy regarding Russia, apparently found the situation unsustainable.

During Monday's press briefing, White House press secretary Sean Spicer attempted to soften the impact of the unsubstantiated allegations—specifically the claim that the predecessor had ordered an unauthorized wiretap on Trump Tower—by stating that the president "doesn't really think" Barack Obama "tapped his phone personally," as noted by Politico. Spicer told the press corps that the president did not believe the former leader physically performed the wiretapping himself.

In an effort to defend his superior, Spicer argued that the tweets referred broadly to "surveillance" rather than a literal wiretap, despite the fact that the president used the specific phrase "wire tapping" in one of his March 4 posts without providing evidence. Spicer suggested that the presence of quotation marks around the term in a single tweet indicated the statement was not meant literally. Spicer remarked to reporters that numerous media outlets had previously covered surveillance and related activities during the 2016 election, pointing to the quotation marks as evidence of a broader meaning. He further questioned the whereabouts of proof while referencing reporting from outlets present in the room.

The basis for Spicer's references remained ambiguous. While news organizations have covered investigations by intelligence officials into potential connections between the campaign and the Russian government—including intercepted communications involving campaign aides and Russian officials as part of probes into election interference and monitoring of the Russian ambassador—no credible source or evidence has emerged indicating that Obama wiretapped or surveilled Donald Trump during the campaign.

The president's original March 4 statements included quotation marks in only one of three relevant posts. One tweet asked if it was legal for a sitting president to engage in wiretapping during a presidential race before mentioning a court rejection. A second tweet expressed confidence that an attorney could build a case regarding phones being tapped in October ahead of the election. A third post criticized the process as reminiscent of Nixon and Watergate, using an alternative spelling for the word "tap" and labeling the individual a "bad (or sick) guy."

Consequently, the Department of Justice has requested additional time from the leaders of the House Intelligence Committee to gather documentation substantiating the claims, indicating an ongoing lack of verified evidence.

During a midnight vote, a trio of Republican senators brought down the party's healthcare legislation, revealing that certain members of the GOP were never truly invested in dismantling Obamacare. Susan Collins representing Maine, Lisa Murkowski hailing from Alaska, and John McCain of Arizona struck down the "skinny" Republican bill resulting in a final tally of 49 to 51. Observers watched as McCain entered the chamber and delivered a thumbs-down gesture to register his vote, which was met with audible astonishment from those in the room.

Explaining his decision to reject the skinny repeal measure in the early hours of Friday morning, John McCain stated through a formal release that the proposal failed to achieve the necessary objective of properly replacing Obamacare, and he felt it wrong to push through such modifications without bipartisan backing.

The complete text of John McCain's explanation regarding his vote against Donald Trump's skinny healthcare repeal reads as follows:

Ever since the start, it has been my conviction that Obamacare needed to be done away with and substituted with an alternative that boosts market competition, reduces expenses, and enhances treatment quality for citizens. The skinny repeal measure considered by the Senate today fell short of those objectives. Although the proposal would have eliminated several of the heaviest regulations imposed by Obamacare, it provided no substitute to genuinely overhaul our medical system and provide reasonably priced, high-grade healthcare to the population. The assertion by the Speaker that the House might agree to a conference committee fails to alleviate my worry that this empty legislative shell could be revived and enacted at any moment.

I have repeatedly pointed out that a primary flaw of Obamacare was its enactment by Democrats through strict party-line votes without drawing a single Republican vote. Repeating past errors that caused the breakdown of Obamacare—which has manifested in my home state of Arizona through soaring insurance premiums and insurers abandoning the market—is something we must avoid. 

We are obligated to go back to proper legislative procedures by returning the measure to committee, conducting public hearings, gathering contributions from both political parties, listening to the advice of governors across the country, and drafting legislation that ultimately brings affordable medical care to the public. The difficult labor expected and deserved by our citizens must be carried out by us.

The failure of these medical reforms delivered a major setback to the legislative agenda of Donald Trump. The inability of Senate Republicans to clear even the minimal version of the repeal measure demonstrated that broader healthcare changes might be unachievable. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky expressed his disappointment, calling it a letdown and stating his regret that their endeavors fell short on this occasion, before declaring that it was time to move forward and placing the healthcare measure on hold while the Senate pivots to different bills in the upcoming week.

On Twitter, Mr. Trump shared his reaction by stating that three Republicans along with 48 Democrats failed the citizens of the nation, reiterating his initial stance to let Obamacare collapse on its own and address it subsequently.

SEOUL (Reuters) - North Korean cyber actors likely managed to infiltrate the database of Daewoo Shipbuilding & Marine Engineering Co Ltd in April of last year, making off with designs for South Korean naval vessels, according to a South Korean opposition politician. 

While Pyongyang routinely faces accusations from South Korea and other nations regarding digital assaults, it typically responds by either ignoring the claims or issuing outright denials. 

Speaking with Reuters via phone, Kyung Dae-soo, a member of the primary opposition Liberty Korea Party, stated there is near-total certainty that hackers from the North executed the breach and accessed confidential files belonging to the firm. 

Because Daewoo Shipbuilding has constructed various naval craft for South Korea—including submarines and Aegis-equipped ships—there is a strong probability those specific blueprints were compromised, according to the lawmaker. 

Kyung, who was briefed on the matter, explained that the cyber intrusion was uncovered by a specialized cybercrime investigation unit operating under the South Korean Ministry of Defence. 

He noted that the probe's investigators did not reveal the exact level of sensitivity or classification attached to the stolen files. 

Meanwhile, a representative for Daewoo Shipbuilding stated that officials at the company were unaware of the situation prior to Tuesday morning and were currently verifying the information shared by Kyung. 

The determination that North Korea was responsible stems from similarities between this breach and past digital incursions attributed to Pyongyang, Kyung mentioned. 

Intelligence points to North Korean hackers as the culprits behind a recent digital bank robbery in Taiwan, which adds to a growing pattern of attacks aimed at the global SWIFT financial messaging network. 

Just earlier this month, a different South Korean parliamentarian reported that North Korean actors had pilfered a vast quantity of classified defense records, featuring joint wartime strategies formulated by South Korea and the United States. 

Furthermore, officials in Britain announced last week their assessment that North Korea orchestrated the WannaCry ransomware incident in May, an episode that paralyzed corporate operations and public sector functions globally, such as the public healthcare system in England.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — While much of the political world has fixated on whether he might launch a presidential bid, Republican Paul Ryan has effectively quieted questions regarding his fundraising prowess for fellow members of Congress. Federal Election Commission records examined by Reuters reveal that Ryan pulled in in excess of $9 million via his "Team Ryan" apparatus, spanning his inauguration as U.S. House Speaker on October 30, 2015, up through January’s close in 2016. This financial collection aids House Republicans along with party organizations, outpacing the roughly $6 million that former Speaker John Boehner brought in during the identical three-month span for the 2014 cycle, as well as the approximately $7 million he gathered during the 2012 presidential race. 

Based on FEC records submitted through February 29, Ryan has channeled a minimum of $8 million directly to the National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC), an organization supporting GOP congressional bids, once again surpassing Boehner's totals from both 2012 and 2014. Consequently, the NRCC heads into an election year boasting its largest cash reserves to date, holding a $2 million advantage over its Democratic counterpart, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee. 

Representative Ann Wagner, who serves as the NRCC finance chairman, described Ryan's appeal, stating that he represents an ideal asset for any finance chair when it comes to collecting donations. She added that the unpredictability surrounding the presidential nominees for both political parties this cycle has likewise boosted contributions for congressional contenders. 

These figures show Ryan overcoming critics who questioned last year whether he could keep pace with Boehner's fundraising totals while simultaneously maintaining his promise to spend weekends at home with his relatives. Within the American political landscape, fundraising capability serves as a major indicator for higher political ambitions; however, Ryan—who was the party's vice presidential nominee in 2012—has repeatedly rejected notions that he seeks a 2016 White House campaign. 

During an interview with talk radio host Hugh Hewitt while on a congressional trip to Israel, Ryan reiterated his stance, asking to be left out of the discussion and stating he is not that individual. Even so, Ryan remains the focus of rumors suggesting he could surface as a compromise choice if the party convention ends in disarray this coming July. He firmly dismissed the idea, stating he is not running for president and that the matter is settled. 

Even with his strong financial track record, Ryan faces potential hurdles on the horizon. At a recent event within Ryan's home district, backers of Republican front-runner Donald Trump responded with boos simply at the sound of his name. Furthermore, a conservative from Wisconsin has formally declared a primary challenge against Ryan for the upcoming August Republican congressional primary. Back in Washington, Ryan is also tasked with sustaining a fragile truce established among competing factions of congressional Republicans. Passing a federal budget serves as his initial hurdle, and he runs the risk of angering conservatives should compromises with Democrats become necessary to avert a government shutdown—a criticism previously leveled against Boehner. 

Kyle Kondik, a political analyst at the University of Virginia Center for Politics, noted that Ryan faces difficulties comparable to those encountered by Boehner, explaining that the current Republican base harbors strong skepticism toward its own leadership. Kondik observed that merely holding the speakership position could eventually diminish Ryan's standing among the Republican faithful.

text: Legal scholar Jonathan Turley thoroughly dismantled the argument for obstruction brought forward by Joe Scarborough against President Trump, offering a sharp and well-reasoned breakdown explaining why such charges would be unwarranted. Though identified as a Democrat, Turley is widely viewed as a balanced legal analyst who strictly follows the letter of the law. While political figures on the left react intensely, legitimately qualified legal minds like Turley are dismissing the matter entirely. Despite a complete lack of evidence pointing to any wrongdoing, discussions surrounding impeachment continue to circulate. Professor Jonathan Turley laid out his perspective: There was fully sufficient justification to dismiss Sally Yates when she, serving as the acting Attorney General, directed the Department of Justice to decline enforcement of the President's immigration executive order. Furthermore, establishing obstruction of justice generally demands proof of an action taken to interfere with either a congressional or judicial proceeding, and crucially, neither of those proceedings was underway at that moment. Additionally, it is typically necessary to demonstrate that the action was carried out with corrupt intent as defined by the statute, and this situation simply fails to satisfy that standard.

As Congress dives deeper into leak-related inquiries, FBI Director James Comey faced intense questioning during a House Intelligence Committee session. Committee Chairman Devin Nunes attempted to corner Comey, seemingly hoping to elicit remarks that would implicate non-Republicans entangled in the ongoing Russia controversy. 

Instead of uncovering the truth behind potential treason, Nunes managed to highlight how the GOP prioritizes party defense over genuine investigation. The turning point came with a specific inquiry: whether the FBI would incorporate information regarding the Hillary Clinton campaign, its associates, or the Clinton Foundation into their probe if brought forward by the committee or the public. 

Despite the widespread agreement that Russian interference favored Trump, the line of questioning shifted back toward Clinton. Nunes underscored this direction with a follow-up asking if connections to Russian intelligence services or agents would generate investigative interest. 

Refusing to take the bait, Comey responded that the bureau evaluates any information brought to them regarding suspected unlawful or improper behavior, noting this applies broadly and that the public constantly submits tips which they are encouraged to continue doing. 

Nunes' approach appeared aligned with Donald Trump's pattern of using social media outbursts to deflect blame. Frustrated by Comey's confirmation that the Russia investigation is active, Trump has utilized Twitter to shift focus toward leaks and accusations against Clinton rather than addressing the mounting evidence against his own administration. 

Trump's social media activity included posts questioning contacts between the Clinton campaign and Russia, alongside claims regarding the DNC denying FBI access. 

The focus on Clinton by Nunes appears far from coincidental, leading critics to suggest the GOP leadership needs to refocus on the job at hand.

Republicans reportedly advised Donald Trump to stay off Twitter while former FBI Director James Comey appeared before Congress, leaving his eldest son to handle the social media outburst instead. 

During the hearing on Thursday, Comey's released Wednesday opening statement detailed a January dinner where Donald Trump requested his allegiance, quoting the president as saying, "I need loyalty, I expect loyalty." Comey also recounted a February meeting following the dismissal of Mike Flynn over discussions with Russian officials. 

According to Comey, the president brought up Flynn again, stating, "He is a good guy and has been through a lot." While maintaining that Flynn did nothing wrong in his communications with Russia aside from misleading the vice president, Trump added, "I hope you can see your way clear to letting this go, to letting Flynn go. He is a good guy. I hope you can let this go." These statements strongly suggest that Trump attempted to obstruct justice and dismissed Comey to derail the Russia probe.

As the Senate proceedings unfolded, Donald Trump Jr. launched into a series of posts on Twitter. "1/3 Flynn stuff is BS in context 2 guys talking about a guy they both know well. I hear 'I hope nothing happens but you have to do your job,'" he wrote. He followed up with, "2/3 very far from any kind of coercion or influence and certainly not obstruction!" and concluded with, "3/3 Knowing my father for 39 years when he 'orders or tells' you to do something there is no ambiguity, you will know exactly what he means." He added the hashtag #givemeabreak, remarking that hoping and telling are entirely different concepts that someone like Comey should understand.

Social media users immediately pushed back against his commentary. 

Ciaran Jenkins responded on Twitter, writing, "So that's how it works. Donald Trump's son hears different words to the ones actually coming out of his mouth." 

Another user, Crenshaw, posted, "Your dad has conditioned you to hear what you want to hear." 

David J. Maloney chimed in with, "Uday chimes in." 

AugieBunker wrote, "Your dad was just called a liar by the head of the FBI, multiple times." 

Paul L. noted, "This would hold up if you ignore the fact that your father then fired Comey for doing his job. Maybe time to let the adults talk, Donnie." 

Adam questioned, "So why did your pops fire Comey if all Trump was doing was 'hoping' Comey would drop the Flynn investigation?" 

Lee P. added, "Grow up boy, he is not a CEO but the President, different standards." 

AvaHarlow stated, "Are you kidding me! You need to educate yourself. It IS obstruction!" 

Using the hashtag #beginningoftheend and #fakepresident, gaeagirltalks asked, "@realDonaldTrump so you think the POTUS should be 'suggesting' that someone obstruct justice." 

Chris Floyd joked, "Yes, when he says, 'Eric, use your charity to take money from cancer patients and put it in MY pocket,' he means it!"

The author of the original commentary concludes that Donald Trump committed obstruction of justice and argues that he, along with all his associates and his children, should face impeachment, prosecution, and prison time rather than remaining in the White House, pointing to Trump's demands for loyalty from Comey and the subsequent firing over the Flynn investigation.

text: WASHINGTON (Reuters) — A senior Democratic lawmaker in the House of Representatives criticized Valeant Pharmaceuticals International Inc on Tuesday, demanding further information regarding its ties to Philidor RX Services while rebuking the drugmaker for failing to hand over any requested materials or documents to Congress. text:
Due to a lack of willing performers for Donald Trump's upcoming inauguration, attention has turned to those who have no choice in the matter: the famous Radio City Rockettes, who find themselves bound by their contracts. A boycott of the ceremony has been declared invalid by the performers' union. 

BroadwayWorld successfully verified and published the contents of a message sent by the American Guild of Variety Artists addressed to its members who dance as Rockettes, following backlash over the news that certain members objected to taking part in the presidential swearing-in.

The message explained that an inquiry had come in from a dancer worried about stepping into a volatile political environment, but went on to emphasize employment obligations. It noted that the company leadership, represented by Mr. Dolan, naturally wanted the troupe featured at the national event just as they had been previously in 2001 and 2005, making any talk of a boycott out of the question. While acknowledging personal political freedom, the correspondence stated that such matters do not belong on the job.

Emphasizing the point with bold and underlined text, the communication clarified that part-time staff members are free to pass on the assignment, whereas full-time performers are required to participate. Delivering top-tier performances to represent a decades-old American institution is described as the core responsibility, aiming to bring clarity to the employment reality.

Members of the troupe are pushing back against the situation. Rockette Phoebe Pearl shared her feelings on Instagram, explaining that while she typically avoids political statements online, the emotional weight of the decision forced her hand. Learning that the performance had been predetermined brought feelings of embarrassment and disappointment. She described her colleagues as smart and compassionate women, calling it appalling to perform for someone whose values contradict their own. Speaking strictly for herself, she revealed that the cast has been performing with heavy hearts and tears since learning the news, concluding with a declaration that they refuse to be coerced, accompanied by a hashtag labeling him not her president.

Despite these protests, the requirement remains in place. Donald Trump previously appeared on tape admitting to sexual assault by forcing himself onto women and suggesting his celebrity status excused it. In a grim parallel, these women now face the threat of job loss if they refuse to perform for him against their will.

Support for the dancers can be shown by reaching out to their union to express that they should not be compelled into uncomfortable situations. 

A post on Twitter by Kevin Clamato on December 23, 2016, highlighted the situation, stating that the Rockettes were being contractually forced to appear at the inauguration while facing threats of termination or legal action from the AGVA.

The dancers bear no responsibility for the lack of voluntary performers willing to take the stage for Trump, which led to the reliance on bound contracts, and they ought not to live in fear of unemployment for refusing to take part for someone they view this way.

MOSCOW (Reuters) - Russian leader Vladimir Putin expressed his expectation on Friday that communication with U.S. President Donald Trump will persist, following their initial encounter on the sidelines of the G20 summit in Hamburg earlier in the month. 

Addressing employees at the Lebedinsky mining facility in the Belgorod region, Putin remarked, "If the dialogue were to go on, as you’ve said in this sense, in a humanitarian sense, there is the chance to hope that the dialogue develops further." The broadcast of this gathering was handled by Russia 24 television. 

Putin reiterated his positive assessment of Trump's listening skills, noting, "He reacts to the interlocutor, at the reasons, he is involved in the discussion even if he doesn’t like something and he doesn’t agree with something, he asks some questions, reacts to the interlocutor’s reasoning." 

During their time in Hamburg, Putin previously stated his view that a personal rapport had already been formed with Trump, observing at the time that the real-life president differs significantly from his television persona. 

Additionally, addressing the ongoing situation in Ukraine during his Friday remarks, Putin indicated his anticipation that the crisis will ultimately find a resolution through democratic procedures and without bloodshed.

text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump formally rescinded a temporary freeze on most refugee arrivals late last October, a step anticipated to clear a path for individuals escaping violence and persecution to reach America. Instead, refugee admissions have experienced a dramatic decline. State Department figures examined by Reuters reveal that during the five-week window following the termination of the ban, entries dropped by 40 percent compared to the final five weeks the restriction remained active, a decrease that has largely flown under the radar.

Alongside the lifting of the ban, the Trump administration introduced stricter screening protocols and effectively paused entries from 11 nations classified as high-risk. This second measure played a major role in driving down the overall admission figures. In fact, the newly implemented restrictions have emerged as a significantly higher hurdle for refugees than the prior temporary suspension, which had seen its reach narrowed by the Supreme Court.

Shifts are also evident in the demographics of individuals being permitted entry, according to the State Department records. While Muslim refugees accounted for a quarter of the total during the ban, that share fell to just under 10 percent once the restrictions were lifted. 

Although a five-week timeframe represents a brief window for drawing broad inferences—and resettlement numbers typically accelerate later in the fiscal year, which commenced in October—the steep decline has sparked concern among advocates. Eric Schwartz, president of Refugees International, remarked that the administration is effectively winding down the refugee program without explicitly stating that intention, utilizing bureaucratic mechanisms and national security arguments to advance unjustifiable and nefarious goals.

Conversely, officials within the administration maintained that the initial temporary ban and subsequent security measures were designed to protect the American public from potential terrorist threats. Proponents of the policy also contended that the refugee system required an overhaul and that increased stringency would ultimately reinforce its integrity. Joshua Meservey, a senior policy analyst at the Heritage Foundation—a conservative research organization—and a former African refugee resettlement worker, voiced support for the changes, stating that the program needed tightening and that enhanced vetting and fraud reduction help protect the system in the long run.

A representative for the State Department attributed the downturn to intensified background checks, evaluations intended to flag potential security risks, and a reduced annual quota of 45,000 for the current year, marking the lowest ceiling in decades. Speaking anonymously, the official noted that refugee arrivals rarely follow a steady trajectory, often starting slowly at the beginning of the year before scaling up, and argued that evaluating the pace of the 2018 fiscal year at this stage is premature.

Immigration control has remained a cornerstone of Trump’s presidency, driven by stated commitments to national security and American employment. On the 2016 campaign trail, he asserted that Syrian refugees could potentially harbor ties to Islamist militants and pledged extreme vetting for all candidates. The White House declined to provide a comment when approached.

Following the expiration of the ban, the newly instated mandates included a 10-year biographical history requirement—up from five years—a suspension of the family reunification pathway, and an in-depth threat assessment for individuals originating from the 11 designated nations. A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security confirmed that this 90-day review commenced on October 25, the day after the previous ban was lifted. While officials indicated that refugees from Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Libya, Mali, North Korea, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, Syria, and Yemen would be evaluated individually on a case-by-case basis throughout the review, priority would be directed toward other applicants.

Historically, over the preceding three years, individuals from these 11 countries accounted for more than 40 percent of total U.S. refugee admissions. Although nine of these nations feature Muslim majorities, the individuals seeking asylum in the United States are frequently members of religious minorities, such as Christians and Jews. In practical terms, however, only Iran, Iraq, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, and Syria consistently produce significant numbers of refugees who ultimately resettle in the U.S.

Administration representatives asserted that the 90-day review does not equate to a blanket prohibition on travelers from the 11 targeted nations. Yet, concurrent with the launch of the review, arrivals from those specific countries nearly halted altogether. State Department records indicate that in the five weeks prior to the ban's removal, 587 refugees from those 11 countries gained entry despite strict eligibility criteria, whereas only 15 were admitted during the subsequent five-week period.

Across all nations, the State Department logged 1,469 refugee admissions between October 25 and November 28, representing a 41 percent reduction from the nearly 2,500 individuals who entered during the final five weeks of the formal ban. Demographically, Muslims comprised 9 percent and Christians 63 percent of those admitted between October 25 and November 28, compared to 26 percent Muslim and 55 percent Christian during the preceding five-week span. 

Higher admission numbers during the temporary ban occurred because the Supreme Court, when greenlighting the restriction in June, mandated exemptions for individuals possessing bona fide connections to the United States. Although legal challenges have been filed against the new directives, courts have yet to issue rulings.

Each shift in American refugee policy has left 34-year-old Alireza—a gay Iranian refugee residing in Turkey—struggling with confusion, a lack of information, and dwindling confidence that he will ever reach the United States. Alireza had already completed interviews with U.S. authorities and was progressing toward resettlement when the initial ban took effect in January. He withheld his family name because his relatives remain unaware of his sexual orientation, but he provided Reuters with documentation verifying his identity and refugee status. 

When federal courts initially blocked the Trump administration's ban, Alireza resumed the vetting process and neared final resettlement, only for the Supreme Court to reinstate the ban, which was subsequently succeeded by the current restrictions. Categorized as a refugee from one of the 11 nations subjected to enhanced scrutiny, he finds himself once again trapped in uncertainty. 

Alireza questions the security rationale behind the new assessments. Following harassment, physical assaults, and extortion in Iran, he and his partner of 13 years fled to Turkey in 2014. Human rights organizations note that Iranian laws targeting sexual minorities expose them to severe violence and discrimination. In Turkey, he explained, they survive on precarious part-time labor while growing increasingly uneasy over what they perceive as rising anti-gay sentiment in the local population. Speaking by phone from the northwestern Turkish city of Eskisehir, he asked why individuals who suffered under Iran’s Islamist system would spend three years enduring hardship in Turkey simply to travel to America and engage in terrorism.

Plans are reportedly under consideration by the Trump administration to skip submitting a presidential budget to Congress next year, marking a departure from tradition. The rationale behind this potential decision is to sidestep potential criticism. Legal experts point out that while the Congressional Budget Act mandates that the president deliver the fiscal 2018 budget between January 2 and February 6, bypassing this rule is technically possible without breaking the law. According to Forbes, citing an insider within the GOP congressional leadership, Trump could argue that the legal obligation to fulfill this requirement fell to the outgoing Obama administration prior to the January 20 inauguration. 

While never done before, this possibility sparked the trending hashtag #TrumpFirsts on Twitter, drawing commentary on presidential norms. Since the implementation of the Congressional Budget Act during the mid-1970s, every incoming president has put forth a budget. Although these initial submissions or updates to late outgoing budgets frequently arrived past the early February deadline in a shortened format rather than the standard multi-volume set, a financial blueprint outlining the new administration's agenda has always emerged over the past four decades.

Usually, a newly inaugurated president looks forward to presenting a budget as a primary vehicle to showcase upcoming plans and outline specific priorities. However, releasing such a proposal inevitably opens the administration up to scrutiny from critics. Avoiding the formal proposal entirely effectively removes that specific avenue for pushback. 

Opting out of this process would also allow the administration to bypass the release of data tables reflecting the ambitious GDP growth targets touted during the campaign, anticipated high interest rates predicted by numerous economists, and forecasts regarding employment and job creation that critics view as unrealistic. 

This approach echoes the campaign decision to withhold personal tax returns, another departure from traditional presidential behavior. Meanwhile, the current unemployment rate stands at 4.6 percent.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — An appeal brought by Texas to reinstate its stringent voter-identification rules was turned away by the U.S. Supreme Court on Monday. A lower court had previously determined that these Republican-supported regulations disproportionately impacted Hispanic and Black voters. By leaving in place the July 2016 lower court ruling, the justices allowed to stand the conclusion that the 2011 statute violated federal legislation prohibiting racial discrimination during elections, while also instructing a lower tribunal to develop a remedy for the measure's discriminatory impact on minority populations.

None of the eight justices recorded a dissent regarding the decision to pass on the case. However, Chief Justice John Roberts offered a rare explanatory statement on the refusal, pointing out that proceedings regarding the issue remain active in the lower courts. Roberts mentioned that while no obstacles prevented the high court from reviewing the matter, every legal question could still be brought up on appeal later on.

The legislation—which originated in a Republican-controlled legislature and received the signature of a Republican governor—stood as one of the nation's most rigorous measures of its kind. Legal challenges against it came from individual voters, civil rights organizations, and the U.S. Justice Department during the presidency of Barack Obama. Opponents, including the Obama administration, argued that this statute and comparable measures in other Republican-led states were intentionally crafted to create voting barriers for minority groups, such as Hispanic and Black citizens, who typically lean toward the Democratic Party. Conversely, proponents defended the rules as essential safeguards against voter fraud, notwithstanding a scarcity of proof regarding such offenses.

Under the statute, exactly seven forms of official identification were deemed acceptable for proving identity, encompassing items like a driver’s license, a U.S. passport, a military identification card, and a concealed handgun license, while excluding state university identification cards and credentials given out for welfare assistance. 

A larger, 15-judge configuration of the New Orleans-based 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals determined by a 9-6 vote that the Texas statute breached the U.S. Voting Rights Act due to its discriminatory impact, though the bench split along different lines on other aspects of the verdict. The appellate court instructed a federal district judge to review arguments from plaintiffs asserting that the measure was designed with discriminatory intent rather than merely resulting in a discriminatory outcome. A district court hearing concerning that specific issue had been slated for Tuesday, though it was postponed following a motion by the administration of President Donald Trump. While the preceding Obama administration supported the lawsuit against the Texas mandates, a shift in position by the Trump administration remained a possibility.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican whose office spearheaded the appeal, expressed frustration over the court's outcome via a statement. Paxton asserted that Texas implemented a sensible voter ID measure to protect election integrity and pledged to continue defending the statute before the district court, the Fifth Circuit, and potentially the Supreme Court once more.

Opponents of the measure estimated that as many as 600,000 individuals could be disenfranchised if the rules were fully enforced, given the substantial population of voters lacking the narrow selection of accepted identification documents. Following the circuit court's decision, the state and the plaintiffs negotiated an agreement for a temporary fix implemented during the November 2016 election. 

The Texas statute represents just one of several enacted by Republican-led statehouses following the year 2010. A comparable measure in North Carolina was invalidated by a federal appellate court in July 2016.

GENEVA (Reuters) — According to a United Nations human rights committee statement issued on Monday, women in North Korea face widespread sexual assault in workplaces, domestic abuse, and systemic barriers to employment and education. Following a routine examination of Pyongyang's human rights practices, the U.N. Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women highlighted worries regarding the abuse and rape of female detainees, particularly those who are sent back to the country after escaping across borders. 

The independent expert group noted that females in North Korea experience disadvantages and low representation in higher education, law enforcement, the judicial system, security agencies, and managerial roles across all unconventional employment sectors. Nicole Ameline, a member of the committee, explained to Reuters that gathering accurate data remains a primary obstacle, noting a general absence of details regarding national policies, legal frameworks, and information systems despite numerous inquiries.

During a session on November 8, North Korean representatives informed the panel that the state actively promotes gender equality and women's rights. However, Pyongyang argued that international sanctions related to its missile and nuclear activities are placing a heavy burden on vulnerable children and mothers. 

The committee pointed out that domestic abuse is widespread, accompanied by minimal societal awareness, insufficient legal assistance, and a scarcity of shelters and psychological support services for survivors. Furthermore, the panel indicated that economic penalties heavily affect women disproportionately. 

Malnutrition rates among North Korean women are notably severe, impacting 28 percent of nursing and pregnant mothers, the report stated. Ameline emphasized that the committee urged the administration to prioritize food security and nutritional needs, viewing them as fundamental requirements that demand government investment and accountability, though she expressed pessimism regarding how fast conditions might get better.

The assessment also revealed that punishments for rape are frequently inadequate for the gravity of the offenses and that perpetrators often evade justice entirely. Amendments made to the legal code in 2012 actually decreased sentences for specific categories of sexual assault, such as crimes involving children, repeat offenses, and assaults committed by employment supervisors. Consequently, the mandated prison term for coercing a female subordinate into sexual relations dropped from four years down to three, based on the findings.

Additionally, the document indicated that women who are trafficked to other countries and subsequently repatriated frequently face imprisonment or assignment to labor training facilities on charges of unauthorized border crossing. Once detained, these individuals frequently encounter additional human rights abuses, which include forced abortions and sexual violence perpetrated by security personnel.

On Tuesday, a federal judge signed off on a settlement negotiated by the U.S. Justice Department and the municipality of Ferguson, Missouri, aimed at overhauling the local police force. This arrangement stems from the 2014 fatal shooting of an unarmed Black teenager, an incident that ignited days of intense demonstrations. 

The 129-page document, endorsed by U.S. District Judge Catherine Perry of the Eastern District of Missouri, also calls for a complete overhaul of the municipal legal codes in this St. Louis suburb. The text of the consent decree emphasizes a shared understanding between federal authorities and the city that effective public safety relies entirely on the trust and bond between law enforcement and the residents they protect.

Under the newly approved terms, personnel within the Ferguson Police Department are mandated to complete training focused on bias awareness, alongside the establishment of a robust oversight framework. Furthermore, the municipality committed to ensuring that all enforcement actions—including stops, searches, and detentions—are free from discrimination regarding race or other legally protected characteristics. 

Civil unrest had gripped the predominantly Black community following a grand jury's decision not to bring charges against Darren Wilson, a white officer involved in the death of 18-year-old Michael Brown. Prior to the judicial sign-off, the Ferguson City Council voted in favor of the package back in March, following federal guarantees that the financial burden of compliance would not devastate the municipal budget. 

Ferguson joins a growing roster of American municipalities that have adopted similar federally monitored reform pacts, a group that includes Albuquerque, New Mexico, and Seattle, Washington. 

The court's decision coincided with a separate incident roughly 10 miles southeast of Ferguson, where a white officer from the St. Louis police department shot and killed a Black suspect tied to a carjacking. According to statements provided to the press by St. Louis Metropolitan Police Chief Sam Dotson, the individual aimed a firearm at law enforcement before an officer discharged his weapon. Authorities confirmed that none of the officers sustained injuries and that the patrol vehicle was not equipped with a dashboard camera.

AUSTIN, Texas — Texas Governor Greg Abbott approved legislation on Tuesday curbing insurance coverage for abortions, mandating that women purchase an additional, separate policy if they wish to have the procedure covered. The GOP governor argued that House Bill 214 shields those morally opposed to abortion from having to financially support it. Meanwhile, Democratic opponents condemned the legislation, labeling it a mandate for "rape insurance."

As the largest state governed by Republicans, Texas consistently leads the nation in implementing limitations on abortion, often setting a trend that other socially conservative states subsequently adopt. Upon taking effect on December 1, HB 214 will make Texas the eleventh state to limit abortion coverage within privately issued state insurance policies. 

In an official statement, Abbott remarked that as a dedicated supporter of Texas values, he felt honored to enact a law guaranteeing that no resident is forced to fund a procedure terminating a fetus. State Senator Brandon Creighton, the Republican author behind the companion legislation regarding abortion insurance, previously informed regional journalists that the extra policies would run between $12 and $80 annually. 

Having cleared both legislative chambers this month largely along party lines, House Bill 214 contains no exemptions for situations involving incest or rape. Reproductive rights organizations have indicated intentions to challenge the measure in court to block its implementation. 

State Representative Chris Turner, a Democrat who voted against the measure, argued on Tuesday that by approving HB 214, the governor essentially informed women and families that they must shell out extra funds for what amounts to "rape insurance." 

Data from the Guttmacher Institute, an organization monitoring reproductive legislation, indicates that 25 states already limit abortion coverage within health plans established via state exchanges under the Affordable Care Act, which was enacted by former President Barack Obama, a Democrat. 

Furthermore, Abbott approved a separate bill on Tuesday that broadens the mandates for reporting medical complications stemming from abortions.

Monday evening brought the resignation of Michael Flynn from his role as President Donald Trump's national security adviser, following mounting controversy surrounding his communications with Russian authorities. The White House made the departure public following a period of ambiguity regarding Flynn's future, which stemmed from reports that he had provided unclear accounts of his Russian contacts to Vice President Mike Pence and other administration personnel. 

Last month, key figures within the Trump administration, such as White House counsel Don McGahn, received briefings regarding Flynn's apparent discrepancies concerning his talks with Russian representatives. Although Yates was removed from her position a few days subsequent to declining to implement the executive order on the travel ban, an insider indicated that the briefing on Flynn was seemingly unrelated to her termination. The initial disclosure of this briefing came from The Washington Post on Monday, with the White House confirming Flynn's exit soon after.

In his letter of resignation, Flynn stated that during his capacity as the incoming National Security Advisor, he participated in numerous telephone conversations with international counterparts, ministers, and ambassadors aimed at ensuring a seamless transition and establishing foundational connections between the incoming president, his advisors, and foreign leaders, noting that such discussions represent standard procedure during transitions of this scale. He acknowledged that he unintentionally provided the Vice President Elect and others with partial details regarding his interactions with the Russian Ambassador, adding that he offered a sincere apology to both the President and the Vice President, which they accepted.

Stepping in as the interim national security adviser and leader of the National Security Council is Keith Kellogg, who currently serves as the chief of staff for the National Security Council. Retired Army Gen. Barry McCaffrey, a decades-long acquaintance of Kellogg, described him on Tuesday as a capable individual who stood out as an early supporter of Trump.

Flynn had long remained a contentious figure within national security circles and faced strong disapproval from mainstream aides under Trump, who argued that he promoted the president's conspiracy theories and skepticism toward intelligence agencies. Nonetheless, he retained the backing of the president, who valued his perceived loyalty and perspective on military matters. Additionally, Flynn shared a close bond with Stephen Bannon, the chief strategist to the president, who held significant influence over the administration both philosophically and strategically.

According to a White House insider, Bannon pulled Flynn aside for a discussion over the weekend. This official noted that Gannon, who had previously backed Flynn through various difficulties, advised him to take the honorable path and step down.

Search efforts for a permanent successor have already commenced within the White House. Sources with knowledge of the schedule indicated that retired Gen. David Petraeus is set to hold a meeting with Trump at the White House on Tuesday. During the transition period, Petraeus was briefly evaluated for the position of secretary of state, though he was ultimately bypassed, partially due to his 2015 conviction related to the mishandling of classified information. 

Trump has historically held Petraeus in high regard and sought his advice. An individual close to the president remarked that Trump appreciates and holds respect for him. Requests for comment sent via email to Petraeus went unanswered.

MANILA (Reuters) — Monday saw the Philippine government voice apprehension regarding Beijing's trials of a giant dredging vessel, emphasizing that authorities intend to monitor its movements carefully, notwithstanding Chinese guarantees that the vessel will stay away from disputed territories. Beijing has invested massive sums into constructing artificial landmasses to reinforce its territorial assertions throughout the majority of the South China Sea, and it has now commenced trials for a vessel engineered to enhance its capacity for land creation. 

Delfin Lorenzana, the country's defense chief, remarked to journalists that the vessel's mere existence causes a degree of worry, adding that its destination remains uncertain. According to defense personnel, the craft—named Tian Kun—features a surface area comparable to nine basketball courts and stands to become the biggest vessel of its kind in Asia. 

Beijing asserts sovereignty over virtually the entire South China Sea, an essential waterway carrying upwards of $3 trillion in annual maritime commerce. Competing territorial claims in these waters are also maintained by Brunei, Malaysia, Taiwan, Vietnam, and the Philippines. 

Lorenzana mentioned that personnel stationed across nine Philippine-held outposts within the South China Sea have received directives to keep a close watch on Chinese naval vessels, maritime law enforcement ships, and fishing vessels operating within the Spratly archipelago. Regular air patrols, alongside ongoing tracking efforts, ensure that the movements of the exceptionally large dredging ship will be kept under observation, he noted. 

Trials for the dredger coincide with the approach of two significant regional summits taking place in Vietnam and the Philippines over the current and following weeks, which are expected to draw leaders from both Beijing and Washington. 

During August, Chinese authorities and the foreign ministers of Southeast Asian nations endorsed a preliminary framework intended to guide negotiations for a South China Sea code of conduct. While participants celebrated this development as a positive step, skeptics viewed it as a maneuver allowing Beijing additional time to solidify its maritime dominance. Although all involved governments describe the framework merely as an initial guide for drafting the code, detractors point out that the document omits any primary goal for a legally binding and enforceable agreement, nor does it include a mechanism for resolving disputes, thereby casting doubt on its ultimate efficacy. 

In the Chinese capital, Assistant Foreign Minister Chen Xiaodong told the press that discussions concerning the framework had made substantial headway and anticipated tangible outcomes during the upcoming Southeast Asian leaders' summit in Manila, which is set to feature Chinese Premier Li Keqiang. 

Chen explained that the final characteristics of the code, including whether and how it might carry legal weight, will emerge from the ongoing negotiations between Beijing and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, noting that such matters cannot be determined unilaterally by any single participant. Meanwhile, Chinese President Xi Jinping is scheduled to participate in the separate gathering of Asia-Pacific leaders hosted in Vietnam.

BRUSSELS (Reuters) — According to Amnesty International, European nations share responsibility for severe human rights abuses in Libya, pointing to European backing for local forces that frequently collaborate with traffickers and subject refugees and migrants to torture. 

In a statement released on Tuesday, Amnesty reported that an estimated 20,000 individuals are currently confined within Libyan migrant detention facilities, facing systematic torture, extortion, forced labor, and extrajudicial killings—findings that echo concerns raised by other human rights groups over the past several months.

This European backing for the Libyan administration forms a core component of a broader strategy designed to stem the flow of African migration through the Mediterranean. The initiative is intended to reduce migrant drownings at sea and alleviate the political pressures that high arrival rates create for EU leadership. Italy has taken the lead in executing this strategy, notably by providing equipment and training to the Libyan coastguard and allocating millions of euros to support relief operations managed by United Nations agencies inside Libya.

John Dalhuisen, who directs Amnesty’s European program, asserted that EU capitals are fully cognizant of these violations, arguing that their active assistance in blocking maritime departures and trapping people inside Libya makes them complicit in the resulting crimes.

During an address to parliament on Tuesday ahead of an upcoming summit of the bloc's leaders in Brussels, Italian Prime Minister Paolo Gentiloni defended the current European approach, noting that maritime arrivals have fallen by two-thirds since the previous July. Pointing to the millions contributed by Italy and the EU to upgrade conditions for those stranded in the country, Gentiloni maintained that Italy's efforts have brought much-needed visibility to human rights issues in Libya.

Meanwhile, a spokesperson for the European Commission acknowledged the severe and inhumane circumstances confronting many individuals, emphasizing that the EU's primary goal aligns with Amnesty's: saving lives. The spokesperson added that European funding has enabled the International Organization for Migration (IOM) to facilitate the repatriation of more than 15,000 people from Libya back to their countries of origin in Africa, while the bloc continues the gradual process of accepting individuals identified as genuine refugees.

Serving as the primary transit point for migrants attempting maritime journeys to Europe, Libya has seen a sharp decline in departures since July, as local factions and authorities began halting boats under pressure from Italy, the principal destination for arrivals. Over the preceding four years, more than 600,000 people have crossed via this route.

Amnesty contends that while the EU assists the Libyan coastguard in intercepting travelers bound for Europe, these same local forces maintain close ties with traffickers who extort money through torture. Dalhuisen argued that by enabling the containment of people within Libya, European leaders have demonstrated that their primary objective is sealing off the central Mediterranean corridor, regardless of the human suffering involved.

Although certain diplomats and EU officials remain uneasy about the bloc's dependence on armed militias that rose to power following the 2011 overthrow of Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, the bloc's leaders are set to reaffirm their commitment to the strategy during their Brussels meeting on Dec. 14-15, citing the tangible reduction in sea crossings as proof of the policy's success. 

Previously, the leadership of Libya's U.N.-supported administration asserted last month that the nation suffers as a victim of unauthorized migration rather than acting as its source, calling on international partners to assist in halting migration flows directly at the countries of origin.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Democratic vice-presidential hopeful Tim Kaine stepped up to defend Hillary Clinton on Sunday regarding the controversy surrounding her management of sensitive government secrets while leading the State Department. According to Kaine, Clinton failed to recognize the confidential nature of certain email communications because the messages lacked proper markers. 

Back in July, the FBI criticized the Democratic presidential contender for relying on a home-brew email server during her 2009-to-2013 tenure as America's top diplomat, characterizing her actions regarding classified data as "extremely careless." Furthermore, documentation published by the bureau on a recent Friday revealed that during a July conversation with investigators, Clinton stated she had no recollection of receiving instructions regarding classified protocols or federal record-keeping regulations. 

Appearing on ABC’s "This Week," Kaine—a Virginia senator who serves on both the Senate Foreign Relations and Armed Services panels—explained that public servants process such massive quantities of data that identifying designated secrets is frequently challenging. 

“There were emails that contained classified information that had been improperly marked. So when she received the email, the material that was classified - which is supposed to be flagged and identified as classified - in many instances was improperly labeled,” Kaine stated during the broadcast. He further noted, “We look at so much material, unless it is specifically pulled out and identified, it is difficult to know sometimes whether a statement or a paragraph is classified or not.”

During the same television appearance, Kaine drew a parallel between Republican opponent Donald Trump’s recent appeal for Russia to locate 30,000 deleted messages from Clinton's server and the infamous 1972 Watergate break-in at the Democratic headquarters in Washington, an event that ultimately brought down Richard Nixon's administration. 

“He has openly encouraged Russia to engage in cyber hacking to try to find more e-mails or materials, and we know that this cyber attack on the DNC was likely done by Russia,” Kaine remarked to the Sunday audience, adding, “This is serious business.”

Trump’s remarks were directed at roughly 30,000 messages that Clinton’s legal team classified as personal and opted "not to keep," whereas thousands of other work-related messages were handed back to federal authorities in 2014. While this move is broadly understood to mean the personal records were erased, aides have consistently avoided verifying whether that actually occurred. 

Vying against Trump for the presidency in the upcoming November 8 election, Clinton has spent over a year dealing with the negative consequences of setting up an unapproved private server based in her Chappaqua, New York residence. She has maintained adamantly that she never transmitted or received secret intelligence through that channel, despite federal regulations strictly prohibiting the management of such material outside of secure networks. 

Contradicting Clinton's assertions that no sensitive information crossed her private server, the FBI reported that a minimum of 81 email threads held data that was classified at the moment of transmission, with the agency suggesting the ultimate tally could surpass 2,000. Even though the bureau reprimanded Clinton over her security practices, officials ultimately advised against pursuing criminal charges against her. Clinton has since acknowledged that looking back, utilizing a personal network as secretary of state was a mistake. 

Public opinion surveys indicate that doubts regarding Clinton's integrity and reliability remain her primary political liabilities. Recent polling data indicates a narrowing contest over the preceding several weeks. Specifically, a Reuters/Ipsos survey conducted between August 26 and September 1 showed Trump drawing 40 percent among likely voters compared to Clinton's 39 percent. Clinton's numbers in that weekly tracking poll have experienced a continuous decline since August 25, completely erasing a prior eight-point advantage.

In an op-ed published by Vice, Krang remarked that the post was obviously satirical, yet the internet proved to have plenty of gullible individuals who reported the tweet out of existence. The suspension extended so far that the work account was also blocked due to a shared phone number, while inquiries to Twitter for comment remained unanswered prior to publication. It is also worth pointing out that Donald Trump has never faced a suspension on the platform.

This kind of reaction tends to be routine among certain segments of the population. People have genuinely believed that Hillary Clinton operated a child sex ring from the basement of a pizzeria that lacks a basement, that anti-fascist groups intend to murder white women, or that Malia Obama was arrested for purchasing six pounds of marijuana stored inside a Prada handbag. WASHINGTON (Reuters) — A fresh legal battle over immigration policy began Thursday as advocates launched an uphill campaign to salvage a portion of President Barack Obama’s directive designed to protect millions of undocumented immigrants from removal. The strategy involves a newly filed lawsuit aimed at contesting the nationwide reach of the judicial injunction that previously stalled the initiative. According to the attorneys behind the complaint, successful outcomes could eventually help dismantle the rulings that halted the November 2014 presidential program across the country. 

Had the administration's initiative gone into effect fully, it might have granted work permits to as many as four million individuals lacking legal status. The legal action was lodged in a federal tribunal in New York, naming 25-year-old Mexican immigrant Martin Batalla Vidal as a plaintiff. Vidal, who arrived in the U.S. at age seven, had previously gained advantages from the policy before a Texas judge's February 2015 decision to block the program led to the revocation of his initial three-year work permit. That earlier injunction stemmed from a challenge brought by Texas alongside 25 additional states. Despite this setback, Vidal remains qualified for a two-year employment authorization through a separate, unchallenged previous program that remained untouched by the court order. 

Representatives from the National Immigration Law Center, who are representing Vidal, argue that a victory could carry significant weight by potentially reviving the Obama initiative for roughly 60 percent of prospective applicants located in regions outside the scope of the Texas decision. The initial ruling by the Texas jurist survived an appellate review, and the Supreme Court subsequently split 4-4 on June 23, maintaining the lower court's outcome. Because Justice Antonin Scalia passed away in February, the high court currently operates with a vacancy while it weighs whether to take up the matter again once all nine seats are filled.
