BOGOTA (Reuters) - Public officials in Colombia expressed outrage on Thursday over an inventory of property submitted by the FARC rebel movement for victim compensation, which featured items like shoes and citrus squeezers, prompting the administration to form a dedicated verification body. 

Under the terms of the 2016 peace accord with the state, the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia committed to surrendering all financial resources and real estate to compensate those impacted by land mines, forced displacement, kidnapping, rape, and forced disappearances. For generations, the organization generated income through extortion of business owners and landowners, ransom payments from kidnapping victims, and the sale of coca—the primary component of cocaine—to narcotics traffickers.

According to officials, the inventory—initially submitted to the United Nations and kept out of the public eye—contained numerous goods lacking any meaningful financial worth, which critics argued insulted the victims. 

"Pots, orange juicers, lemon juicers, plates, boots, which will be depreciated and don't have a commercial value and which above all will not be a source of reparation for victims," Attorney General Nestor Humberto Martinez stated to reporters, while also calling for the complete inventory to be made public.

Later on Thursday, the administration announced that a specialized commission would examine the catalog to track down unlisted assets, confirm their sources, and determine how to handle them.

Justice Minister Enrique Gil warned that any property left off the inventory that is uncovered later will mandate penalties and standard judicial proceedings for FARC members. Interior Minister Guillermo Rivera added that every asset will go exclusively toward repairing victims rather than funding reintegration initiatives for former combatants.

Colombian authorities have previously alleged that the FARC holds substantial amounts of liquid cash, alongside commercial properties, cattle ranches, and high-end residences, some situated outside the country. 

Meanwhile, Enrique Santiago, an attorney acting for the FARC, informed a domestic radio station that the insurgents had stopped generating revenue years prior and were forced to spend heavily on sustaining a force of over 7,000 combatants after abandoning extortion and hostage-taking during negotiations. 

Earlier this month, the guerrillas concluded the surrender of upwards of 8,000 firearms to the U.N., which managed their disarmament process. The movement is scheduled to begin a gathering on Sunday anticipated to formalize its shift into a political entity.

LONDON (Reuters) - Turkish EU Minister Omer Celik stated in a Thursday interview that Ankara experiences a sense of betrayal due to certain European Union figures advocating for the termination of membership negotiations, though the country maintains its long-term aspiration of entering the union. Criticism of Turkey's bid has intensified across the bloc following President Tayyip Erdogan's widespread crackdown against academics, journalists, and other critics in the wake of the unsuccessful 2016 military coup attempt. Back in March, Erdogan compared German actions to "Nazi-like" methods after authorities in Germany blocked Turkish government ministers from addressing rallies of expatriates. Furthermore, German Chancellor Angela Merkel stated during a televised election debate that it had become evident Turkey ought not to become a member and that negotiations should be halted, notwithstanding Ankara's status as a vital ally within NATO.

During his interview with Reuters, Celik criticized the rhetoric employed by various EU leaders regarding Turkey's candidacy, arguing that figures like Merkel leverage anti-Turkey sentiment to distract voters from the bloc's internal crises, including migration challenges, Brexit, and institutional reforms. Through a translator, Celik asserted that these leaders sideline critical matters and cultivate hostility toward Turkey to mask their own pressing domestic difficulties, expressing explicit disappointment in Merkel and other European partners who left Turkey isolated during one of the most perilous moments in its modern history. When specifically queried on whether this amounted to a feeling of betrayal, he answered affirmatively.

The failed putsch, which resulted in over 260 fatalities as rebellious troops utilized tanks, attack helicopters, and fighter jets in an effort to overthrow the government, has widened the divide separating Ankara from Western governments. Officials in Turkey argued that numerous Western partners displayed a sluggish response in expressing solidarity with the administration following the uprising, which the government viewed as a calculated assault on Turkish democracy. In the aftermath, approximately 50,000 individuals—encompassing civil servants, dissidents, journalists, and others—have been arrested, sparking deep concern among international human rights organizations and Western capitals.

Celik noted that European leaders, including Merkel, have fallen short of honoring commitments made regarding Turkey's candidacy, which officially commenced with an application to the European Economic Community in 1987, followed by the formal opening of accession talks in 2005. Contending that the EU has failed to fulfill its pledges while Turkey has upheld its end, Celik also addressed remarks made by European Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker, who stated on Wednesday that he anticipates no possibility of Turkish membership in the near future. Challenging Juncker's approach, Celik questioned what significant actions the Commission president has undertaken to bridge the gap between Europe and Ankara. 

He further warned that if Berlin continues dictating directives to European institutions, such as pushing for the severance of talks with Turkey, such a dynamic would ultimately empower racist factions throughout Europe. While formally concluding the negotiation process demands unanimous agreement among all member states—a consensus that currently does not exist—a majority vote would suffice to suspend the talks. As a potential path forward, Celik proposed convening a joint summit between European Union and Turkish leaders to repair bilateral ties, emphasizing that Ankara remains fully committed to achieving full membership and eager to negotiate constructive solutions for progress. 

European leaders are scheduled to deliberate on the status of Turkey during an upcoming summit in Brussels, though any definitive resolution regarding the relationship's future may be delayed until the following spring. Addressing separate concerns, Celik dismissed notions that Turkey's acquisition of the S-400 missile defense system from Russia signals a geopolitical shift away from Western alliances. Asserting that Turkey's geopolitical alignment is clear and that the nation has significantly bolstered European security and economic well-being, he maintained that maintaining a firm role within NATO and cultivating friendly ties with Moscow are mutually compatible rather than mutually exclusive objectives.

MADRID (Reuters) — According to official survey data released on Tuesday, the secessionist movement in Catalonia has rapidly climbed to become the second most significant anxiety for people across Spain, trailing only joblessness and jumping significantly from its position as the ninth major worry back in September. The severe political standoff involving the northeastern territory and the central administration peaked on the first of October. This occurred after regional president Carles Puigdemont proceeded with an independence referendum that Madrid deemed unlawful, subsequently making a declaration of separation prior to his dismissal and replacement by authorities. 

Based on the research conducted between October 2 and October 11, roughly 29 percent of participants pointed to the Catalan separation effort as the nation's primary issue. This represented a sharp rise from only 7.8 percent recorded in the prior survey conducted at the start of September. Meanwhile, joblessness—representing the second highest rate across the European continent—remained the top issue for 66.2 percent of the populace. 

The same study indicated that if a general election were to take place immediately, the governing People's Party would maintain its minority administration by capturing 28 percent of ballots, marking a slight decline from the 28.8 percent recorded during the previous survey in July. Conversely, the pro-market Ciudadanos party, which originated in Catalonia, experienced an increase in backing, moving from 14.5 percent in July to 17.5 percent in October. Meanwhile, the Socialists would keep their standing as the second-biggest faction within parliament, though their numbers shifted slightly to 24.2 percent from the prior 24.9 percent. The polling sample comprised a total of 2,487 respondents.

SHANGHAI (Reuters) — The ruling Communist Party in China formally integrated President Xi Jinping’s massive "Belt and Road" trade and infrastructure initiative into its constitution on Tuesday, a surprising move that elevates the policy's importance and raises the stakes for its implementation. 

The update to the party charter, which was formally adopted as the twice-a-decade congress drew to a close, includes a commitment to "pursue the Belt and Road initiative." Observers noted that this development highlights Xi's growing authority and suggests the grand, Silk Road-inspired project will outlast his time in office. Analysts also pointed out that the decision demonstrates a heightened focus on foreign affairs by the Communist Party and points to Xi's ambition for China to step into a prominent global leadership position.

"Everyone knows that the Belt and Road is very important to Xi, it has his personal stamp and authority," remarked Peter Cai, a non-resident fellow at the Lowy Institute, a think tank based in Sydney. "But to have major policy, especially an external engagement policy, to be written into a party constitution, at least in recent memory, it is something quite significant," he added.

Originally introduced by Xi during a 2013 address to students at a university in Kazakhstan, the strategy serves as a mechanism for Beijing to expand its international influence by financing and constructing trade and transport networks across more than 60 nations. Xi has been a tireless advocate for the scheme, hosting global leaders in Beijing for a landmark summit in May where he committed $124 billion (94 billion) toward the project. In response, private corporations, state-owned enterprises, and regional Chinese administrations have scrambled to back the effort through overseas loans and investments.

Detractors have suggested that the campaign is merely a way for Beijing to offload surplus industrial capacity while extending its geopolitical reach. They argue that the project—which has saddled several emerging nations with substantial debt burdens—demands better governance and greater openness.

"China has made commitments and pledges to many developing countries and it will take that length of time, 10 years or more, to complete the initiative," observed Rajiv Biswas, the chief economist for the Asia Pacific region at IHS Markit. "This has also strengthened China s soft power globally, so it wouldn t make sense for China s point of view to suddenly pull away from all of this," he noted.

Conversely, some experts cautioned that elevating the initiative could prove to be a double-edged sword, increasing the pressure to deliver results for a program that remains loosely defined and subject to wide interpretation.

"The danger of having given it greater visibility is that actually there are going to be more of those efforts to play to the policy in a political way rather than considering carefully the costs and benefits of each portion of what one is doing," explained Dali Yang, a political science professor at the University of Chicago.

Already, numerous regional governments have unveiled customized Belt and Road strategies, while commercial investors have rushed to rebrand their ventures under the initiative's umbrella. Throughout the week-long political gathering, executives from major Chinese corporations—including China Aerospace Science and Industry Corporation [SASAAI.UL] and China Communications Construction Co—told Reuters that they intend to prioritize the expansion of their international operations to back the Belt and Road project. 

The party congress concluded with Xi solidifying his political dominance ahead of his upcoming second five-year term. By having his personal political philosophy written directly into the nation's charter, Xi was elevated to a status alongside Mao Zedong, the founder of modern China.

DES MOINES (Reuters) — Just one week before the kickoff of the 2016 election cycle in Iowa, Democratic front-runner Hillary Clinton leaned heavily on her governing background on Monday to counter criticism regarding her decision-making from challenger Bernie Sanders. During a CNN town hall event held at Drake University, Sanders maintained that the next commander-in-chief needs strong judgment above all else, rather than Clinton's extensive resume. In her defense, Clinton pointed to President Barack Obama, noting that his decision to appoint her secretary of state served as a testament to her sound judgment. Emphasizing the need for a battle-tested contender, Clinton told the audience that a proven fighter is essential.

Seeking to fend off the challenge from the democratic socialist, Clinton aimed to persuade Democratic voters to look past Sanders' populist appeal and maintain their support despite widespread enthusiasm for anti-establishment figures. Unlike a traditional debate, the Drake University gathering featured individual segments where Sanders, former Maryland Governor Martin O’Malley, and Clinton each answered questions from the crowd. 

While the atmosphere remained courteous—a departure from the contentious fourth debate the previous week—Clinton appeared more energetic than usual as she raised her voice to emphasize her points, and Sanders amused the crowd with humor. Sanders pointed to Clinton's 2002 vote in the Senate approving the Iraq war, alongside her past backing of the Keystone Pipeline stretching from Canada to Texas, as proof that her longevity in politics was accompanied by flawed choices. Pointing out that Sanders had opposed both measures from the beginning, he acknowledged that experience matters, but stressed that judgment is equally critical, noting that Clinton has since changed her stance on those matters.

The Vermont senator also stood by his proposals to increase taxes in order to finance universal healthcare, infrastructure projects, and free college tuition. Admitting candidly that taxes would indeed go up, Sanders argued that families would ultimately come out ahead financially because they would no longer have to shoulder private health insurance costs.

Throughout her campaign, Clinton has highlighted her years as a New York senator and secretary of state as proof of her readiness. On the town hall stage, she deflected Sanders' jabs about her judgment by invoking President Obama, who continues to enjoy high favorability among Democrats despite having used her Iraq war vote against her during their 2008 primary battle. Recalling that Obama ultimately tapped her to lead the State Department, Clinton stated that the appointment stemmed from his trust in her judgment through their four years of working closely together.

Although Clinton held a commanding lead for months following her 2008 primary defeat, recent polling has revealed a notable rise in momentum for Sanders. Clinton has argued that while Sanders' aspirations regarding social inequality are admirable, some are unrealistic and he lacks the breadth of experience needed to handle an array of unpredictable challenges. Speaking earlier on Monday at the Jewish Federation of Greater Des Moines, Clinton remarked that life in the White House requires readiness for every unforeseen issue rather than picking and choosing topics.

Additionally, Clinton used the town hall platform to take aim at Republican front-runner Donald Trump, specifically condemning his rhetoric targeting minority groups. Pointing out his trajectory, she noted that he began by attacking Mexicans and later turned his focus to Muslims.

Meanwhile, on the same day exactly one week prior to the state's inaugural nominating contest leading up to the November 8 election, Clinton received a timely boost from President Obama in a Politico interview. Without directly taking aim at Sanders—whose platform centers on tackling income inequality and reining in Wall Street—Obama lauded Clinton's vast experience and described her approach as rooted in pragmatism. Characterizing her as exceptionally knowledgeable and wicked smart on policy, Obama observed that her extensive background can sometimes make her cautious, leading to a campaign defined more by prose than poetry.

WASHINGTON — Following the collapse of their healthcare initiative, White House officials sent a clear message to rebellious conservatives: fall in line with President Donald Trump’s legislative priorities, or face the possibility of being sidelined during upcoming battles, particularly over tax reform. 

Reince Priebus, the White House chief of staff, raised the prospect of forging a broad bipartisan alliance—potentially incorporating moderate Democrats—for the tax overhaul. This warning coincided with an announcement from the Republican leader of the House tax-writing committee, who stated his intention to advance a tax measure through his panel this spring. 

Kevin Brady, chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, mentioned during an appearance on Fox News that his team continued drafting tax legislation concurrently with the unsuccessful healthcare push. According to Brady, the committee never halted its efforts and will keep making refinements, aiming to bring the bill forward in the spring. He emphasized his preference for the House framework to serve as the foundation for the president's tax plan, rather than seeing competing proposals emerge from the Treasury Department and the White House.

Wall Street investors have expressed concern that the defeat of the healthcare bill signals trouble for tax reform. Equity markets had surged following the election largely due to anticipation of tax reductions. Without the boost from fiscal stimulus, economic growth is expected to slow, and U.S. equity index futures dropped to a six-week low.

Both the president and his chief of staff took aim at hardline conservatives who voted down the administration's replacement for the Affordable Care Act. During an interview on "Fox News Sunday," Priebus left the door open to collaborating with moderate Democrats and Republicans alike on other major components of the presidential agenda, such as the upcoming budget, the restructuring of the tax code, and a renewed push for healthcare reform.

While Priebus noted that passing a bill with Republican votes alone remains the preferred path if the president's objectives can be met, he described the overture to other lawmakers as a warning shot demonstrating a willingness to negotiate more broadly than ever before.

Friday’s withdrawal of the healthcare bill from the House floor marked a significant setback for a president who campaigned heavily on his reputation as a master negotiator. The measure had to be pulled after failing to secure sufficient backing within the Republican caucus, while Democrats remained entirely opposed. Despite intensive lobbying efforts by the administration, members of the conservative House Freedom Caucus and several moderate Republicans withheld their votes, leaving leadership short of the threshold needed for passage. 

External conservative organizations—such as Heritage Action for America and the Club for Growth, both closely tied to the Freedom Caucus—lobbied aggressively against the Republican healthcare proposal and urged lawmakers to vote against it. On Sunday morning, Trump took to Twitter to criticize both the caucus and these allied groups, writing that their actions left Democrats smiling in Washington.

Priebus lamented the decision by conservative lawmakers to withhold their support, adding that the president felt let down by individuals he previously believed were loyal to him.

Following the healthcare defeat, tax reform has jumped to the forefront of the administration's legislative schedule. Priebus confirmed that the president remains committed to including a border tax in the legislation, alongside a middle-class tax cut that could potentially draw support from moderate Democrats.

Demonstrating that the Freedom Caucus is not entirely monolithic, U.S. Representative Ted Poe of Texas announced his resignation from the group, offering a glimmer of encouragement for the administration's tax efforts. In a short statement, Poe stressed the need for unity to fulfill the conservative promises made to voters over the past eight years, noting that leadership requires solutions rather than mere obstruction.

Meanwhile, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer criticized the administration's handling of the healthcare debate and predicted that Republicans would continue to encounter resistance from their own conservative flank on subsequent issues. Suggesting that the party risks repeating its healthcare missteps during the tax debate, Schumer encouraged the president to distance himself from the Freedom Caucus and engage with Democrats instead. He indicated that while Democrats would review the president's proposals, any cooperation would be shaped by their own core principles.

Rep. Mark Meadows, a Republican from North Carolina who chairs the Freedom Caucus, expressed optimism on Sunday regarding tax reform, suggesting his faction could back a proposal that lacks complete revenue neutrality. Arguing that lower taxes generate increased economic activity, Meadows stated that his personal view is that full offsets are not strictly necessary.

Another member of the caucus, Representative Jim Jordan, urged a move away from mutual recriminations in the wake of the healthcare defeat, calling instead for a renewed focus on the work ahead.

FORMER NPR CEO DITCHES AND SWITCHES: How A Liberal Learned to Love the ‘Right’ [Video]

Ken Stern, the former chief executive officer of NPR, has made a notable shift after breaking out of his previous liberal environment. In a recent discussion with Tucker Carlson, he talked about leaving behind the liberal bubble. Observers are praising his move away from the left and toward the conservative side. 

STERN RECENTLY SPOKE WITH BREITBART’S ALEX MARLOW:

Describing his background, Stern noted that he was a lifelong Democrat who previously worked in Democratic politics, led NPR, and lived within a heavily Democratic household inside an overwhelmingly Democratic ward. Driven by worries regarding the nation's growing political divide, he decided to travel into red-state America to gain a firsthand perspective of the political opposition. 

His defining "a-ha!" moment stemmed from a local neighborhood tradition in Washington, D.C., where children annually recited a pledge at a block party. The pledge welcomed everyone on Hobart Street—regardless of gender, sexual orientation, or race—with the sole exception of Republicans. Although framed as a joke, it carried a serious undertone, signaling how people were beginning to treat the opposing side. For Stern, it served as a catalyst, making him realize he needed to escape his Democratic bubble, interact with the rest of the country, and discover whether the other half of America consisted of "deplorables" or everyday citizens just like him. That realization shaped his year of exploration.

Discussing media structures, Stern pointed out that NPR differs from other organizations because its staff is spread nationwide rather than being centralized solely in political and media hubs. Pointing to outlets like The New York Times, where the vast majority of personnel are based in New York, he noted that NPR functions as a membership organization with local stations across the country, giving it unusual geographic representation. However, as he recently pointed out in the New York Post, the challenge remains that despite being geographically dispersed, mainstream journalistic entities largely draw from a liberal talent pool. This dynamic fosters groupthink and increases the likelihood that chosen stories fail to represent the broader country.

Stern argued that ideological bubbling affects both sides of the political spectrum. Because the nation has become politically fragmented, with Democrats and Republicans primarily associating only with their own, it is simple to embrace cartoonish and harsh caricatures of the opposition. He referenced a Washington Post poll from the previous year asking voters from both parties to summarize the other side in a single word, yielding extreme terms like "bigot" for Republicans and "traitor" for Democrats—exaggerated stereotypes of political opponents. 

According to Stern, Hillary Clinton’s remarks—and subsequent apology—referring to a segment of Trump supporters as a "basket of deplorables" accurately mirrors how many individuals view conservatives, though he emphasized that this tendency exists on both sides of the aisle, hindering true understanding.

His journey across the political divide involved various unconventional experiences, such as participating in a pig hunt in Texas and visiting small Assembly of God churches to engage with individuals holding different viewpoints. His travels also took him to declining coal mining communities in Pikeville, Kentucky, and to Youngstown, Ohio, among other places. The subtitle of his book, "How I Left the Liberal Bubble and Learned to Love the Right," reflects these encounters. While he did not agree with everyone he met, he encountered hundreds of individuals who were admirable, contributed positively to their communities, and completely defied stereotypical depictions of Middle America.

To test convictions he once viewed as absolute—such as guns, poverty programs, and climate change—Stern engaged directly with opposing perspectives, consulting gun-control skeptic John Lott Jr., attending gun shows, conducting his own research, and even going hunting. By intentionally viewing issues through the eyes of others, his own perspective naturally shifted.

Recounting a particularly striking experience for someone coming from an urban, gun-control background, he described hunting in Georgia. There, he received gun safety instructions from an eight-year-old and hunted alongside a diverse group that bore no resemblance to coastal stereotypes of rural white men. 

As an agnostic Jew from Washington, D.C., Stern's prior exposure to evangelicals was limited to pop culture references like the movie *Footloose* and figures like Jerry Falwell, who had passed away a decade prior to his project. This unfamiliarity changed when he attended the Urbana Conference alongside roughly 15,000 evangelical youths. Expecting cinematic caricatures, he instead found young people discussing ways to welcome and aid refugees, promote campus diversity, and dedicate their lives to feeding the poor and housing the homeless. Witnessing this group firsthand demonstrated to him that with 50 million evangelicals in existence, there are 50 million distinct stories, making broad generalizations impossible.

Stern also observed that media professionals often cluster together, reinforcing their own confirmation biases, stereotypes, and groupthink. He views this as a profound and difficult hurdle for networks like CNN and others to recognize and overcome. Furthermore, he noted that in the era of Trump, conflict has proven financially advantageous for the media. President Trump's criticisms of outlets like the "failing New York Times" are met with responses from the publication, creating a self-reinforcing cycle that ultimately benefits the bottom line of both parties involved, which he considers a significant issue.

TORONTO (Reuters) - Wednesday afternoon departures headed to the United States from Toronto's primary international airport faced delays following an event that forced certain travelers to undergo customs screening all over again, according to a representative. 

Beverly MacDonald, a spokesperson for Toronto Pearson International Airport, stated via email that a security breach took place in Terminal 3 not long after 3:30 p.m. (2030 GMT). 

She noted that while authorities looked into the matter, boarding procedures were paused and specific travelers were directed back through U.S. Customs for reprocessing, noting further that the situation was cleared up near 5 p.m. (2200 GMT). 

The security lapse happened when individuals getting off an incoming flight from Calgary mistakenly gained entry to a bypass route leading directly into the U.S. departure zone, explained Lauren Stewart, a representative for WestJet Airlines Ltd (WJA.TO), in an email message to Reuters. 

Based on details provided by the airport's official website, Terminal 3 handles U.S.-bound services operated by Delta Air Lines Inc (DAL.N), American Airlines Group Inc (AAL.O), WestJet, and Alaska Air Group Inc (ALK.N).

Yet, despite their fierce competition, the two candidates share a distinct aversion to gambling. When *Bild*, a widely read newspaper, questioned Merkel about how she might handle a multimillion-euro lottery jackpot, the incumbent leader replied that she simply does not participate in the game. Coming from an upbringing in the former communist East as the daughter of a pastor, and having trained as a physicist, the conservative head of government also noted that any financial awards or prize money she receives are traditionally passed on to charitable organizations.

Similarly, Schulz—who bypassed university and formerly led the European Parliament—disavowed any history with games of chance. He informed the publication that he had never bought a lottery ticket throughout his entire life, explaining that he preferred not to leave his achievements up to probability or a drawing machine. Beyond their mutual avoidance of gambling, the pair expressed comparable perspectives on the role of prayer. Upon being asked if she directed prayers toward securing an electoral victory, Merkel stated that she avoids invoking divine intervention for specific political outcomes, emphasizing that prayer remains deeply private. Schulz, whose political faction currently lags behind Merkel's conservative bloc by a margin of double digits, aligned with that sentiment, remarking that political figures must always recognize the existence of forces greater than their personal achievements.

A participant on President Trump’s Diversity Council has indicated a willingness to resign over the administration's decision to scrap DACA. 

During an appearance on CNN Newsroom on September 4, 2017, the council member discussed the potential departure with reporter Jim Acosta, tweeting the exchange online. The member emphasized the business and economic rationale for keeping the program, noting that these individuals do not receive government benefits and contribute over $2 billion in taxes.

This claim contrasts sharply with the financial burden DACA and broader immigration policies place on the public and government systems. On average, individuals holding college degrees contribute more in taxes than they take in through public assistance, whereas those lacking a degree consume more in tax revenue than they contribute across federal, state, and local levels. 

Research published by the Heritage Foundation in 2013 projected that granting amnesty to 11 million undocumented immigrants would increase federal expenditures by $6,300 billion over a span of 50 years. This amounts to about $550,000 per person, or roughly $10,000 annually per individual, largely driven by future eligibility for Medicare and Social Security. Furthermore, these figures exclude additional expenses that could arise if newly legalized citizens sponsor additional low-skilled family members. 

Applying the Heritage Foundation's methodology, if the 3 million DACA recipients and their parents attain legal status or citizenship, the program is projected to cost Americans approximately $1,700 billion over the next half-century. 

Beyond direct fiscal impacts, DACA participants contribute to an influx of undocumented labor that suppresses wages for working-class Americans, such as urban youth and prior immigrants. According to an academies report, the influx of low-cost labor results in American workers losing an estimated $500 billion annually in wages due to this immigration tax.

WARSAW (Reuters) — Prime Minister Beata Szydlo announced on Tuesday that she will unveil a government shake-up in the near future, though she chose not to address rumors suggesting her own position could be in jeopardy. There has been widespread chatter in financial markets and media outlets regarding a potential overhaul, as the ruling Law and Justice (PiS) party reportedly considers removing certain ministers who are dragging down its generally favorable polling numbers ahead of the 2018 regional contests. 

The weekly publication Sieci Prawdy reported on Monday that the 54-year-old Szydlo might step down in favor of Jaroslaw Kaczynski, the leader of the conservative PiS party to which they both belong. Meanwhile, the tabloid Fakt published a report on Tuesday indicating that while Szydlo is expected to retain her post, officials like Foreign Minister Witold Waszczykowski and Environment Minister Jan Szyszko—who struggle with low public approval—could be ousted. 

Kaczynski, aged 68 and widely recognized as a polarizing figure who ranks among the least trusted political figures in the country, wields immense power from behind the scenes. Press reports have suggested he might be eyeing Szydlo's premier role with an eye on the 2019 national elections. 

Speaking to the private television network TVN 24, Szydlo stated that she wished to put an end to ongoing rumors about cabinet modifications, noting that her choices would be revealed shortly. She emphasized that the determination has been made to alter the cabinet composition, and mentioned that she consulted with Kaczynski, describing that step as completely normal. When questioned regarding the potential of her own exit, Szydlo declined to engage in guesswork and asserted that she neither feels exhausted nor burned out. Public surveys consistently place her as the second-most trusted political figure in the nation, trailing only President Andrzej Duda.

Jaroslaw Flis, a sociologist affiliated with Jagiellonian University in Krakow, noted that a more restricted shake-up targeting only a handful of ministers would likely stem from a natural impulse to clear out the administration's weakest performers. 

The current PiS administration has polarized public opinion, steering Warsaw toward friction with the European Union over initiatives like expanding oversight of the judicial system and public broadcasting, which opponents argue threaten democratic norms. Nevertheless, the party maintains robust public support. According to findings from state polling agency CBOS, 44 percent of participants identified as backers of the administration, marking the highest level of support seen in six years.

ANKARA (Reuters) - State television reported that numerous Iranians participated in demonstrations nationwide on Friday to protest U.S. President Donald Trump's recent choice to acknowledge Jerusalem as the capital of Israel. 

Ever since the 1979 Islamic revolution, hostility toward Israel and backing for Palestinians has remained a core pillar of Iranian foreign policy. Iranian leadership has strongly criticized Trump's declaration, which also encompasses shifting the American embassy to Jerusalem. Footage broadcast on state television showed demonstrators carrying Palestinian banners and flags, displaying signs that declared "Quds belongs to Muslims"—employing the Arabic term for the city—while shouting slogans such as "Death to America" and "Death to Israel." Local media outlets noted that effigies of Trump were set on fire in multiple municipalities. 

Iran does not acknowledge the existence of the Jewish state, viewing the entirety of the holy land as Palestinian territory. The country routinely advocates for Israel's elimination and provides support to various militant Islamic organizations opposing it. 

Labeling both the United States and Israel as oppressors, Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei stated earlier on Wednesday that Trump's announcement demonstrated failure and incompetence. 

The backlash against the U.S. policy has brought together Iran's pragmatist and hardline political groups. Both hardline Revolutionary Guards commanders and pragmatist President Hassan Rouhani called upon citizens to participate in countrywide "Day of Rage" demonstrations. 

Amid chants of "Death to the Devil," demonstrators destroyed photographs of both Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu by fire. 

Rouhani characterized the U.S. policy shift as highly dangerous, provocative, wrong, and illegitimate. Meanwhile, state TV coverage showed senior cleric Ayatollah Ahmad Khatami telling the congregation during Friday prayers at Tehran University that the global Muslim community must band together against Israel. 

During those same Friday services in the capital, attendees chanted, "We will not leave Palestinians alone," according to television broadcasts. Additionally, IRNA, Iran's official news agency, quoted army chief Major General Mohammad Bagheri, who termed the Jerusalem decision unwise and warned it could heighten instability throughout the volatile Middle East.

A group of nine former United States permanent representatives to the United Nations submitted a letter to lawmakers on Tuesday, cautioning that severe budget cuts to the international organization would undermine American standing abroad and hand over leadership opportunities to adversarial nations. 

The bipartisan group of signatories—consisting of Andrew Young, Donald McHenry, Thomas Pickering, Edward Perkins, Madeleine Albright, Bill Richardson, John Negroponte, Susan Rice, and Samantha Power—represented administrations from both major political parties. 

Speaking to the press, Albright stressed that reducing financial support for the organization harms national security and global standing, noting that countries like Russia and China are eager to step into any vacuum left behind. 

Lawmakers were pressed in the correspondence to steer clear of deep budgetary reductions and instead allow the current U.S. envoy, Nikki Haley, alongside U.N. leader Antonio Guterres, adequate time to pursue organizational reforms aimed at improving efficiency and responsiveness. 

As the organization's primary financial backer, the United States currently covers 22 percent of the $5.4 billion core operating expenses and provides 28.5 percent of the $7.9 billion dedicated to peacekeeping missions, with all member states agreeing upon these assessments through the General Assembly. 

Characterizing the American financial burden as inequitable, President Trump has advocated for unspecified cuts to U.N. operations and agencies, alongside the implementation of a strict 25 percent ceiling on peacekeeping contributions. 

Anonymous concerns have also been raised within diplomatic circles regarding the potential fallout of a withdrawal of American financial backing. One high-ranking diplomat remarked that pulling back could inadvertently result in a "China first" outcome rather than an "America first" approach by surrendering influence. 

During a White House luncheon on Monday with envoys from the Security Council, Trump indicated that financial contributions could be justified if the institution successfully implements operational overhauls. Remarking to the fifteen diplomats present, he stated that effective performance makes the budget secondary, describing the costs as minimal relative to the significance of their mission. 

Earlier in the week on Friday, Guterres held his inaugural meeting with Trump at the White House following the recent transition of power for both officials. 

Meanwhile, the State Department announced earlier this month that financial support for the United Nations Population Fund—an agency operating across more than 150 nations to support maternal health, child welfare, and family planning—would be terminated, prompting Guterres to caution that the decision carries the potential for severe consequences.

The sentiment expressed is that while single individuals can be pressured into compliance, collective bodies cannot easily be silenced. The stated goal is to halt what they describe as an ongoing push by a coalition—including Obama, Holder, Sharpton, Soros, BlackLivesMatter, the Black Panthers, Louis Farrakhan, Black Liberation Theology, CAIR, liberal academia, the Socialist Party, the Democrat Party, Anarchists, and the Communist Party—to keep race at the forefront. Such student unions are currently emerging at tertiary institutions across both Australia and the United States.

Recently, upwards of 30 "White Student Union" pages have surfaced on Facebook over the course of several days, aligning themselves with various campuses nationwide. National attention was first drawn by the creation of an "Illini White Student Union" Facebook page launched on November 18 following a "Black Student Solidarity Rally" at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, though this appears to represent only a small fraction of the trend. Research conducted on Sunday by The College Fix revealed that at least 33 additional pages bearing this name have materialized on Facebook within the past week. Notably, these profiles have been established for Stanford, Penn State, UCLA, UC Berkeley, the University of Missouri, and NYU, among others.

At present, these online spaces exist purely as social media constructs, leaving it ambiguous whether they were actually established by students of the respective schools or whether they intend to transition into official campus organizations. An exception is a page for a North Carolina university stating an intention to organize group meetings, info sessions, rallies, and protests directly on the UNC campus. Proponents maintain they are safeguarding the interests of white students whom they believe are becoming marginalized within campus life and political discourse. A specific video is cited as exposing the perceived hypocrisy of the Left. 

The Illinois page asserts that at least seven unofficial unions have rapidly materialized over the preceding week, claiming to speak for students of European heritage at the University of Queensland, the University of Southern Queensland, the University of Technology Sydney, Macquarie University, Western Sydney University, the University of NSW, and the University of Western Australia. Conversely, allegations persist that the entire phenomenon is an elaborate trolling campaign directed at universities and media outlets by participants on online forums such as 4chan and 8chan.

Should the movement prove to be a hoax, observers note it is a sophisticated one, given that members have actively contacted news.com.au to articulate their desire to advocate for the interests of white students. This proliferation mirrors developments in the United States, where similar entities have garnered substantial social media support and planned physical presences for the upcoming year, despite also facing dismissal as hoaxes. Australian universities have publicly distanced themselves from these unofficial bodies, which face heavy backlash online from peers and others labeling them as racist and aligned with white supremacy. Online reactions span from expressions of heritage pride to explicit rejections, alongside sheer disbelief regarding the authenticity of the pages.

Despite accusations, the creators deny any equivalence between white pride and racism, asserting an equal right to representation in university life. The Western Sydney University White Student Union, formed over the weekend with membership already reaching the double digits, insists it has no intention of antagonizing anyone, according to a representative. This spokesperson, identifying as a 24-year-old journalism student, approached news.com.au with his name withheld due to unverified identity. 

The representative explained that the group, which plans to seek formal university registration in 2016 and currently maintains a six-person committee, aims to advance white student interests and establish a supportive community space. Describing the group as genuine rather than a trolling effort, the spokesperson compared their initiative to existing safe spaces for other demographics, framing it as a matter of following prevailing politically correct standards in pursuit of equality. Anticipating negative reactions, the goal is to test administrative boundaries. Furthermore, the representative claimed anecdotal backing from ethnic students, noting that primary opposition originates from older white academics whom they accuse of manufacturing a narrative of universal disapproval.

Universities are nevertheless treating the emergence with seriousness. A spokesperson for Western Sydney University emphasized that the group lacks official recognition, reiterating the institution's commitment to diversity and its condemnation of actions undermining it. A counter-question is raised regarding whether colleges apply similar scrutiny to Black Lives Matter organizations or protests, pointing to an alleged double standard. Both the University of Technology Sydney and Macquarie University clarified that the respective white student groups are unauthorized and do not represent institutional or majority student views. 

The "About" section for the UTS page states an objective to advance rights for people of European descent while opening membership to all backgrounds. Macquarie University administrators reached out to page managers to request the removal of campus imagery and the cessation of claims representing the institution, viewing the profile as a potential North American-rooted hoax while continuing investigations. The University of Queensland went further, explicitly denouncing its local counterpart group as a racist web hoax.

A November 24 post complains of overstretched facilities, difficulties with non-English-speaking international peers during group assignments, and anti-social behavior from students treating study spaces as social areas. Anonymity was requested by the founders to protect their voices from being stifled by political correctness. They maintain that collective organization for mutual interests is a legitimate right for white people, explicitly rejecting notions of inherent superiority or dominance over others. They argue that contemporary Western political correctness promotes damaging concepts regarding white privilege, portraying white individuals—particularly men—as inherently privileged and deserving of hardship.

When asked for proof of enrollment, the UWS spokesman cited safety concerns and death threats as reasons to maintain anonymity. Meanwhile, Michael, a third-year student at the University of Western Australia, acknowledged founding the UWA White Student Association over the weekend. His group's platform includes lobbying for fluent English proficiency among staff and students, the celebration of European holidays, the formal recognition of racist attacks against white students, and the reinstatement of a recently canceled European studies major. Michael described the mission as representing white student interests and countering the perceived decline of Western civilization driven by mass immigration and shifting family values. 

A UWA spokesperson stated that the institution rejects racially or culturally offensive behavior while upholding a commitment to diversity and preparing students to navigate differences comfortably. Responding to racism allegations, Michael maintained that supporting white students does not equate to hatred toward other demographics and expressed willingness to collaborate with ethnic minority clubs toward shared objectives. He reiterated that white students increasingly struggle to express their identity without facing immediate backlash and labels of racism, arguing they are treated more poorly than minorities when deviating from multicultural orthodoxy. 

Similar US university groups, including those at Berkeley and Harvard, have been interpreted as reactions to recent anti-racism demonstrations, such as the Illinois chapter appearing shortly after a black solidarity gathering. While Mast failed to respond to phone inquiries, she returned to Facebook soon after to offer an explanation regarding her promotion of the Third Reich leader's words. Insisting she "was not in any way agreeing with Hitler's words," Mast maintained that her intention was to draw a comparison between the dictator and Planned Parenthood. 

Approximately an hour later, she updated her page by sharing a link to a Christian blog written by JulieRoys.com. The linked material featured footage of anti-abortion activist Gianna Jessen delivering congressional testimony that targeted Planned Parenthood. During that testimony, Jessen had referenced Hitler to argue that the women's health organization employed identical propaganda methods. The specific Hitler quote mentioned was: "The receptivity of the masses is very limited, their intelligence is small, but their power of forgetting is enormous. In consequence of these facts, all effective propaganda must be limited to a very few points and must harp on these in slogans until the last member of the public understands what you want him to understand by your slogan."

The social media activity drew sharp criticism from community leaders, including Rabbi Moti Rieber, the executive director of Kansas Interfaith Action, an organization dedicated to combating racism. Expressing clear disapproval, Rieber stated that "There's nothing profound, and there's no room in American politics for the words or thought of Adolph Hitler."

Addressing the backlash in one of her follow-up Facebook updates, Mast attempted to clear up the confusion: "To clarify the intent of my previous post: Planned Parenthood has learned well the same tactics and deception used by Hitler regarding innocent lives. I was making a connection between the ideology he used and the arguments made by Planned Parenthood."

Laura McQuade, president of Planned Parenthood Great Plains Votes, issued a statement via email condemning the representative's statements, emphasizing that the organization "is a trusted health care provider for thousands of Kansans and we reject and condemn Representative Peggy Mast's offensive remarks." Fortunately, Mast is not currently seeking re-election.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Following President Donald Trump’s decision to withhold certification of the Iran nuclear accord, newly drafted Senate legislation proposes stringent conditions for the agreement. Should it become law, the bill would bring back sanctions if Tehran blocks inspectors from accessing any facilities or tests a ballistic missile capable of delivering a warhead. 

Authored by Republican Senators Tom Cotton and Bob Corker with backing from the Trump administration, the proposal faces pushback from critics who warn its passage could cause the United States to breach the international pact. Reuters reviewed the legislative draft on Tuesday, which began taking shape around the time Trump made his October 13 announcement rejecting formal certification of Iranian compliance and urging lawmakers to strengthen the accord. 

To secure the necessary votes for passage, Corker has been holding discussions with Senate Democrats, who maintain that the U.S. must collaborate with the deal's European co-signatories prior to implementing alterations. Alongside Russia and China, European nations including the United Kingdom, France, Germany, and the EU itself were signatories to the agreement. They have cautioned that Trump's approach threatens U.S. standing internationally and could fracture relations with Washington. 

As head of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, Corker emphasized to Reuters last week that the administration needs to maintain close cooperation with European partners while formulating its updated Iran strategy. 

The proposed legislation takes the form of an amendment to the 2015 Iran Nuclear Agreement Review Act. It expands the mandatory government evaluations regarding Iranian compliance to encompass additional criteria, ranging from trade activities to determining whether U.S.-licensed commercial airplanes are being utilized for non-civilian tasks. 

Furthermore, the measure would immediately reinstate the sanctions that were previously removed under the accord—a process known as a "snap back"—if Iran's timeline for potentially producing a nuclear weapon shrinks to under a year. 

Complicating the legislative path is an ongoing feud between Trump and Corker, which intensified when the president criticized the senator for the creation of the accord during the administration of former President Barack Obama. While global leaders have pressed Trump to preserve the pact, it faced unanimous opposition from congressional Republicans at the time, including Corker. In response, Corker criticized the president's handling of the office and accused him of damaging vital global partnerships. A spokesperson for Corker did not immediately provide a statement regarding whether this political fallout would impact the future of the Iran bill.

SAN FRANCISCO (Reuters) — Documents reviewed by Reuters reveal that roughly twenty major corporations, hailing from the tech sector and beyond, are getting ready to form a coalition pushing for laws that would grant young undocumented immigrants a route to permanent legal status. The newly formed Coalition for the American Dream plans to press Capitol Hill to enact bipartisan measures this year to secure the right for these individuals—widely known as “Dreamers”—to stay and work in the country. Among the participants named in the paperwork are prominent American enterprises such as Alphabet’s Google, Microsoft, Amazon, Facebook, Intel, Uber, IBM, and Marriott International, with Reuters breaking the story. While Amazon, Intel, Uber, and Univision Communications acknowledged their involvement, the remaining firms did not issue immediate responses, and organizers noted that the rollout plans remain subject to change.

Intel representative Will Moss expressed support in an official statement, noting the company is glad to partner with others to press lawmakers for protections for Dreamers. Similarly, Uber spokesperson Matthew Wing highlighted the company's backing for the initiative, pointing out that they stand with Dreamers and have previously hosted town hall meetings, offered legal aid, and set up an online resource hub specifically for drivers who are Dreamers. 

This legislative push follows President Donald Trump’s announcement in September winding down the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, or DACA, program by March. Put in place in 2012 by the Obama administration, the initiative has granted work authorization to roughly 900,000 undocumented individuals. Following the Trump administration's decision, an earlier plea urging congressional action to safeguard Dreamers drew signatures from about 800 businesses, an effort organized by FWD.us, a pro-reform advocacy group co-established by Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg in 2013. A significant portion of the corporations backing that prior appeal are now listed as participants in this latest alliance.

An internal email reviewed by Reuters indicated that the coalition has explored placing advertisements in media outlets, though those strategies could still shift. Recruitment materials being circulated to bring other businesses on board describe Dreamers as integral members of the community who contribute to the economy and national defense, while a registration document for the initiative notes that DACA recipients are employed by 72 percent of the top 25 Fortune 500 corporations.

During his presidential campaign, Trump made strict border enforcement and the construction of a southern border wall central pillars of his platform, and he has ultimately placed the responsibility of determining DACA's future onto lawmakers. A legislative window could open as soon as December, when lawmakers are required to approve federal funding legislation to avert a government shutdown, leading Democrats to weigh making protections for Dreamers a mandatory condition for supplying the votes needed to keep federal operations running. Todd Schulte, the head of FWD.us, noted during a Thursday interview—where he chose not to speak about the new coalition directly—that no lawmaker wants to face headlines over the holidays about DACA recipients spending their final season in the United States, adding that this pressure campaign will only intensify as the year draws to a close.

The arrest follows an anti-corruption investigation that linked him to suitcases and boxes containing over 51 million reais, equivalent to $16.52 million, after investigators discovered his fingerprints on the hidden money. When Vieira Lima stepped down from his ministerial position in November, he represented the fifth cabinet departure from the administration stemming from corruption accusations. President Temer subsequently faced corruption charges brought by the nation's chief prosecutor, though he successfully survived the vote in the lower house of Congress in August.

Meanwhile, Gamil Foppel, the legal representative for Vieira Lima, argued that his client had been denied access to judicial records concerning the police evidence, which he described as a blatant breach of legal norms. ($1 = 3.0875 reais)

ZURICH (Reuters) - On Wednesday, the man expected to become Switzerland's new foreign minister advocated for a reset in the difficult negotiations regarding relations with the European Union, which stands as the neutral nation's primary economic partner. 

Ignazio Cassis, aged 56, was chosen by parliament, marking the first time in nearly two years—specifically 18 years—that a minister has hailed from the Italian-speaking Ticino canton. Once the four-party coalition cabinet distributes departments on Friday, Cassis is widely anticipated to take over as the country's leading diplomat. The physician, who speaks multiple languages and represents the business-friendly Liberal Democrats, is stepping into the role previously held by Didier Burkhalter, whose resignation was made public in June.

Assuming Cassis assumes control of the foreign portfolio—as cabinet assignments are determined by seniority—he will take charge of managing various unresolved economic and political matters concerning the EU. The bloc in Brussels is pushing for an overarching framework agreement to substitute the existing web of over 100 bilateral agreements that currently regulate the relationship. Nevertheless, major Swiss political factions have grown hesitant about this prospect, particularly with the approach of the United Kingdom's departure negotiations with Brussels.

During his acceptance speech, Cassis drew attention by referencing Marxist thinker Rosa Luxemburg on the importance of valuing differing viewpoints. Speaking to the press afterward, he argued that the conversation surrounding EU relations needs to move away from what he described as a poisoned lexicon. He emphasized the necessity of having the bravery to initiate a fresh chapter, pointing out that the precise contents of a framework treaty remain unclear as both sides attempt to restructure their connections. According to Cassis, language forms our environment, and when the discourse becomes tainted by words, those words must be altered.

Leaders such as European Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker and German Chancellor Angela Merkel have maintained that agreeing to a new treaty is a prerequisite for any future trade agreements involving Switzerland. Previously, the Alpine nation narrowly averted a diplomatic collision with the EU following a 2014 public vote favoring immigration caps, as lawmakers ultimately implemented a framework prioritizing domestic job seekers already listed with local employment agencies. 

Any hesitation by the Swiss to advance a new agreement before the UK's talks with the EU gain full momentum risks plunging ties into a severe freeze, potentially halting advancements on pending commercial matters. Meanwhile, the nationalist Swiss People's Party, which holds the position of the nation's biggest political force, remains firmly against any agreement that would grant the European Court of Justice jurisdiction over arbitrating conflicts.

BRUSSELS (Reuters) - Nearly two decades ago, the European Union reacted with extreme hostility when an Austrian chancellor integrated the far-right into the nation's government, with certain EU figures even suggesting a boycott of Tyrolean ski slopes as a form of protest. This Monday, however, the strong possibility that Sebastian Kurz’s center-right might bring the Freedom Party back into a Vienna administration elicited little more than a whisper in Brussels. This muted response highlights both the evolution of the FPO away from its neo-Nazi origins and a broader rightward drift across Europe, particularly regarding immigration. A senior EU official noted that an Austrian government steered by an advocate of strict border controls and including the FPO would have triggered "an earthquake" across the continent just a couple of years ago. 

However, in the wake of the 2015-16 crisis that saw over a million refugees and migrants arriving by sea in Greece and Italy—frequently traveling onward to Germany through Austria—opponents of open borders have successfully steered European politics in their direction. Another Brussels insider remarked, "They’ve built setItems the theater that we are all playing in now." A pragmatic agreement with Turkey to stem the flow of Syrian refugees, more aggressive detention and deportation measures for unsuccessful asylum applicants, the reduction of rescue vessel operations, and partnerships with Libyan authorities have all driven a significant drop in new arrivals. In Germany, where ideological allies of the FPO weakened Chancellor Angela Merkel during the previous month's election, her famous 2015 refugee welcome has been replaced by backing for strengthened border security.

European Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker extended his congratulations to the 31-year-old Kurz following Sunday's election win, touching upon anxieties regarding a eurosceptic administration in Vienna. The head of the Brussels executive branch expressed hope that Kurz would successfully build a "stable, pro-European government." Meanwhile, Juncker’s spokesperson declined to confirm whether the Commission was urging Kurz to exclude the FPO—unlike the approach taken by EU leaders when Chancellor Wolfgang Schuessel partnered with the party, then headed by Joerg Haider, back in 2000. 

Nearly 18 years ago, in February 2000, Juncker served as Luxembourg's prime minister and joined 13 other EU leaders in virtually ignoring Schuessel and his ministers for a half-year, subsequently amending EU treaties to establish mechanisms for penalizing wayward member states. Strong rhetoric abounded at the time. The Belgian foreign minister—father to current premier Charles Michel—even urged travelers to avoid winter vacations in Austria. 

By contrast, current Belgian Foreign Minister Didier Reynders joined numerous peers at an EU gathering in offering polite congratulations to their absent young Austrian counterpart, expressing anticipation of cooperating with his upcoming administration. Not a single official brought up the punitive suspension powers the EU adopted after failing to sway Schuessel. Instead, fellow ministers uniformly praised Kurz’s pro-EU stance. Johannes Hahn, a party colleague of Kurz who represents Austria on Juncker’s Commission, stated that whatever coalition Kurz assembled would maintain "a very pro-European agenda because all the major political parties are very much committed to the European Union."

This shift mirrors the transformation of the FPO under Heinz-Christian Strache, who has softened his anti-EU rhetoric and distanced the party from anti-Semitism while maintaining critiques of Islam. The sole strong condemnation outside of mild reactions came from the far-left leader within the European Parliament. Gabi Zimmer asserted that the election results ought to "strike fear into everyone" and charged Kurz with utilizing "bigotry and prejudices" to triumph over a faction led by a "neo-Nazi."

Nevertheless, Kurz confronts a vastly different Europe than the one that previously isolated Schuessel. The political landscape has tilted toward conservatives, a stark contrast to 2000 when left-leaning administrations governed countries like Germany, France, Britain, and Italy. Furthermore, the EU's expansion into the former communist east has integrated numerous leaders, notably in Poland and Hungary, who openly oppose immigration, particularly from Muslim populations. Kurz received a notably enthusiastic commendation from his Hungarian counterpart. Additionally, a growing number of governments—in France, the Netherlands, Nordic nations, and now Germany—grapple with the same challenge Schuessel faced regarding a popular far-right movement. 

This reality has fostered a reluctance to reprimand EU counterparts over tactics used to manage such political insurgencies, although leaders will expect Kurz to keep the FPO in check, mirroring past efforts to justify readmitting Schuessel into their diplomatic circle. That historical lesson—learned after rushing to rhetorical opposition without a viable exit strategy and failing to move Schuessel—explains the current hesitation to suspend Hungary or Poland over democratic shortcomings. As one EU official summarized, "Austria in 2000 showed us how not to go in without an exit strategy."

A federal judge sitting in Texas handed down an order on Saturday putting the brakes on an Obama administration initiative that aimed to broaden anti-bias protections under the Affordable Care Act to cover abortion services and transgender healthcare. The ruling comes in favor of a coalition consisting of Texas, seven additional states, and three faith-based healthcare organizations that contested the directive. According to the judge, the contested rule categorized sex discrimination as encompassing both "termination of pregnancy" and "discrimination on the basis of gender identity." 

Just 24 hours prior to the scheduled implementation of the regulation, U.S. District Judge Reed O'Connor granted the injunction, concluding that the measure runs afoul of the Administrative Procedure Act, which regulates federal rule-making procedures. Furthermore, the judge determined that the challengers stood a strong chance of succeeding on their argument that the policy breaches the Religious Freedom Restoration Act by infringing upon the rights of private medical providers. 

In his 46-page written opinion, O'Connor noted the plaintiffs' contentions that the mandate would compel them to offer medical coverage and perform procedures related to abortions and gender transitions, despite any medical judgment or religious objections to the contrary. O'Connor previously issued a comparable injunction back in August against a different federal policy that would have mandated public schools to permit transgender students access to the restrooms corresponding with their gender identity, a directive opposed by 13 states. 

Questions remained regarding whether the outgoing administration, facing only 20 days remaining in its term, would pursue an appeal against this newest judicial block. Katie Hill, speaking as a White House spokeswoman, criticized the outcome. She described the ruling as a disappointing hurdle, though expressing hope that it would prove short-lived, maintaining that every individual deserves access to affordable, high-end healthcare free from bias, regardless of sexual orientation, sex, or gender identity.

Enacted in 2010, the Affordable Care Act—frequently referred to as Obamacare—contains provisions prohibiting insurers from denying coverage or levying higher costs based on factors such as race, age, disability, sex, or national origin. The specific regulation at the center of Saturday's dispute was formulated by the Department of Health and Human Services to carry out those statutory anti-discrimination measures, explicitly integrating transgender care and abortion services into the definition of sex bias. 

The court document outlined that the regulation defined gender identity as a person's internal understanding of their gender—which could align with male, female, a blend of both, or neither—and which might differ from the sex they were assigned at birth. Under the leadership of Texas, various Republican-governed states have spearheaded numerous legal challenges against social initiatives championed by President Barack Obama, most prominently his 2014 executive order providing deportation relief and work authorization to millions of undocumented immigrants, a program that was ultimately blocked by the courts. Nevertheless, the Supreme Court upheld the broader Affordable Care Act—the signature legislative achievement of the administration—through decisions handed down in 2012 and 2015.

UNITED NATIONS (Reuters) - The United States faced deeper isolation on Monday after single-handedly blocking a United Nations Security Council resolution demanding the reversal of President Donald Trump's designation of Jerusalem as Israel's capital. While the other 14 members of the council backed the measure brought forward by Egypt—which avoided explicitly naming Trump or the U.S. while voicing "deep regret at recent decisions concerning the status of Jerusalem"—Washington exercised its veto.

U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley reacted to the outcome by calling it an insult that would not be forgotten, noting it was the first time in over six years that the U.S. had used its veto power. Defending the move, Haley stated that protecting American sovereignty and the nation's position in the Middle East peace process was not embarrassing for the U.S., but rather should embarrass the rest of the Security Council.

The proposed text asserted that any actions or decisions aimed at altering the demographic makeup, status, or character of Jerusalem hold no legal standing, are considered null and void, and must be canceled in line with prior Security Council resolutions. This came on the heels of Trump’s sudden departure from decades of American foreign policy earlier in the month, which sparked widespread anger among Palestinians and across the Arab world, alongside apprehension from Western partners of Washington.

Prior to the vote, U.N. Middle East peace envoy Nickolay Mladenov briefed the Security Council, warning that tensions had escalated since the American announcement, marked by a rise in confrontations between Palestinians and Israeli security forces as well as rocket fire originating from Gaza. Alongside the capital recognition, Trump has announced intentions to relocate the American embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem, prompting the U.N. draft resolution to urge all nations against setting up diplomatic missions in the city.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu shared a video message on his Facebook account expressing gratitude to both Trump and Haley for the veto. Israel views Jerusalem as its undivided and eternal capital and pushes for all embassies to be located there, whereas Palestinians claim the eastern portion of the city—seized by Israel in a 1967 conflict and subsequently annexed in an action lacking international recognition—as the capital for a future independent state.

In the wake of the veto, the Egyptian Foreign Ministry announced that Arab nations, which previously agreed earlier in the month to pursue the Security Council measure, would convene to assess developments and decide on subsequent actions. Meanwhile, Palestinian Foreign Minister Riyad al-Maliki stated that Palestinians intend to push for an uncommon emergency special session of the 193-member U.N. General Assembly regarding the Jerusalem announcement. 

Based on a resolution from 1950, such an emergency session allows the General Assembly to review an issue and provide members with recommendations for collective action if the Security Council is unable to reach a decision. This mechanism has only been utilized 10 times previously, with the most recent occurrence taking place in 2009 to address Israeli military actions in occupied Palestinian territories. Although any decisions resulting from such a session lack legal binding, they carry significant political influence.

During a Tuesday broadcast, Morning Joe co-host Joe Scarborough made a striking on-air statement, conceding that the economic theory of trickle-down economics is a falsehood that has exclusively served to enrich the wealthy. While attempting to account for the massive conservative support behind Republican primary leader Donald Trump, Scarborough pointed out that for three decades, Republican politicians have misled their base by promising that tax cuts for the rich would eventually benefit everyone else. 

This reality is starkly illustrated by the expanding wealth gap over the past thirty years, which has left the richest one percent possessing a larger share of the nation's wealth than the lower fifty percent combined. As the wealthy accumulate more money and the impoverished grow poorer, the once-strong American middle class is steadily vanishing. Scarborough acknowledged the shortcomings of his former party, noting that for thirty years, Republicans have failed to offer an economic message that resonates with working-class Americans in the way Donald Trump's platform does. 

He pointed out that the GOP continually pushes for capital gains tax cuts that will never apply to the thousands of people cheering at Trump rallies, nor will the elimination of the death tax impact them. Furthermore, he noted that the praised free trade agreements never actually benefit the individuals attending these rallies. The former GOP congressman explicitly stated that trickle-down economics has failed, pointing out that wealth simply never reaches the working class. 

According to Scarborough, the people in Trump's audiences are the very ones who lost their jobs when employment was relocated to Mexico and other foreign countries, while the Republican donor class profited immensely as their capital shifted overseas to generate higher returns. He observed that voters this election cycle are even willing to support a candidate who defends Planned Parenthood if they believe that candidate offers an economic strategy with a better chance of helping them in the future. 

The decades-long GOP promise that cutting taxes on the elite would resolve the economic worries of everyday Americans has proven entirely false. Instead, trickle-down policies have only led to overseas job losses, leaving citizens empty-handed and far from the prosperity the party guaranteed. This dynamic is comparable to waiting for apples to fall from a tree, only to find the fruit rotten and worthless—assuming the tree doesn't hoard the apples entirely, much like the wealthy hoarding their money today. Ultimately, trickle-down economics stands as an unsuccessful policy that must be abandoned in favor of measures that genuinely support the population, requiring the rich to contribute their proper share so the middle class can reclaim the wealth taken by Republicans and their wealthy backers.

Following Ted Cruz's controversial address at the Republican National Convention on Wednesday evening, where he chose not to offer a clear endorsement of Donald Trump and instead advised conservatives to vote their conscience, New Jersey Governor Chris Christie was quick to voice his strong disapproval. Speaking out against the speech, Christie labeled it selfish and terrible, arguing that Cruz failed to honor a signed pledge and disappointed an audience that had anticipated a different conclusion.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — Wednesday marked the release of a recommendation from a congressional commission urging the establishment of a national museum celebrating women’s history, ideally situated on or close to the National Mall in Washington. Supporters pointed out that while the nation's capital boasts institutions dedicated to numerous subjects ranging from espionage and aviation to postal history and African American culture, it currently lacks a space entirely devoted to women. According to the findings released by the all-female, seven-member panel established by Congress two years prior, the country requires and has earned a physical national institution highlighting the historical contributions and experiences of American women. 

Bringing the museum to fruition would require roughly ten years dedicated to securing financial backing, building community support, and constructing the facility. The document estimates that a structure spanning between 75,000 square feet (6,900 square meters) and 90,000 square feet (8,400 square meters) would carry a price tag ranging from $150 million to $180 million, financed through private donations. Additionally, the commission suggested that lawmakers contribute land at no cost or make an existing structure available for the project. 

Under the proposal, the institution would integrate into the Smithsonian Institution—recognized as the largest museum network globally—and would be supervised by a congressional-appointed board. While private funds would cover construction, the operational and maintenance expenses would be handled by the federal government. 

Three specific locations on or adjacent to the National Mall—the two-mile (3.2 km) stretch often dubbed "America's front lawn" running from the Lincoln Memorial eastward to the U.S. Capitol—were put forward by the panel. The first option sits directly across from the recently opened National Museum of African American History and Culture. The second choice points to the historic, 19th-century Arts and Industries Building situated on the Mall, while the final option designates a location within the U.S. Capitol grounds. 

Although a legislative declaration in 2003 barred new construction on the Mall, an exception was previously granted for the African American museum. Given that the area is already densely packed with memorials and exhibition spaces, urban planners in Washington are actively exploring alternative ways to honor significant American figures and milestones outside of this central zone.

The BfV, Germany's domestic intelligence agency, emphasized in the advisory that transactions involving specific technologies continue to be prohibited, notwithstanding the lifting of sanctions resulting from the 2015 Iran nuclear agreement.
