While the advisory mentioned that recent occurrences prompted the reminder, no specifics were provided. On Monday, German Foreign Minister Sigmar Gabriel informed the press that Berlin maintains its apprehension regarding Iranian actions in the Middle East and its missile advancements, while simultaneously affirming that Tehran continues to adhere to the nuclear accord.

The BfV filing indicated that German security services are maintaining active and deep investigations into whether Iranian entities are attempting to bypass current laws to obtain technology and expertise within Germany. A previous report released by the agency in June noted a sharp decrease in Iranian procurement efforts targeting the nuclear program, while procurement attempts aimed at missile development stayed steady. The report omitted specific figures regarding the volume of these acquisition efforts.

Separately, North Rhine-Westphalia—Germany's industrial center and most heavily populated region—published its 2016 intelligence findings on Tuesday. The regional report documented 32 procurement efforts linked probably or certainly to proliferation during 2016, marking a significant drop from the record-setting 141 attempts recorded the previous year. The vast majority of these procurement activities targeted Iran's missile efforts, alongside a small number connected to Pakistan, according to the document.

State authorities successfully blocked the vast majority of these transactions from being fulfilled, as regional intelligence personnel alerted businesses promptly or the targeted companies themselves identified suspicious purchase orders. The report detailed that Tehran frequently employs front corporations for these acquisitions, routinely routing shipments through nations such as Turkey, China, and the United Arab Emirates.

CHICAGO (Reuters) — Amid falling crop prices that are heavily pressuring sector profits, American agricultural organizations are actively seeking ongoing dialogues with the presumptive major-party presidential candidates to shape their respective farm policies. 

On Friday, delegates from roughly twelve trade groups—such as the National Farmers Union and the American Farm Bureau Federation—traveled to New York for a briefing at Hillary Clinton’s campaign headquarters. THE ULTIMATE COMMUNITY ORGANIZER: IS YOUR NEIGHBORHOOD TOO WHITE? IS IT TOO RICH? Obama Plans To ‘Fix’ Them Using Government to Force Diversity

According to the administration, housing choices remain restricted in far too many areas due to discrimination, market operations, and investment decisions made by capital holders—a phrase pulled directly from an official HUD document. To address this, the president has directed the Department of Housing and Urban Development to introduce a directive named Affirmatively Furthering Fair Housing, aimed at compelling local neighborhoods to become more diverse.

Naturally, this initiative means the government will need to tackle the broader issue of income inequality, given that underprivileged Americans and illegal aliens might lack the financial resources required to settle into wealthier suburbs and communities. Socialism has arrived, and unless a member of Congress steps up to challenge the president, the fruits of hard-working Americans' labor risk being seized by government coercion. This is the outcome of placing a community organizer in the White House, as he attempts to restructure neighborhoods straight from Washington.

Under this new policy, federal authorities will gather extensive data concerning the racial, ethnic, and socioeconomic characteristics of numerous local municipalities, searching for any disparities related to race, color, religion, sex, familial status, national origin, or disability regarding access to community assets. Communities producing unfavorable outcomes will then be targeted, utilizing billions in federal grants to pressure or compel them into altering their housing and zoning regulations.

Housing discrimination has already been outlawed since 1968, making this initiative distinct from simply preventing such practices. It remains illegal to refuse a loan or block a home purchase based on race, creed, or color. However, socioeconomic status is and should remain a separate issue; purchasing an upscale suburban home requires the financial means to do so, though the administration apparently views this as unfair discrimination by capital holders. Granting federal bureaucrats control over local community management undermines freedom, as local autonomy remains vital to liberty. As Milton Friedman observed in *Capitalism and Freedom*: “If I don’t like what my local community does, be it in sewage disposal, zoning or schools, I can move to another local community. . . . If I don’t like what my state does, I can move to another. If I do not like what Washington imposes, I have few alternatives in this world of jealous nations.” Washington lacks any authority to dictate zoning and housing rules to countless local municipalities.

This policy could surface as a factor in the presidential campaign, particularly since HUD Secretary Julian Castro—tasked with rolling out the initiative—frequently appears on shortlists for Hillary Clinton's running mate. Furthermore, as Stanley Kurtz of the National Review notes, gathering the necessary data will require time, meaning decisions regarding its application will ultimately fall to the incoming president.

Communities nationwide will understandably react with outrage to this regulation. The federal government has no business dictating whether a neighborhood has too many Caucasian residents, too many Jewish residents, or an excess of married couples. Even so, Republicans must proceed cautiously, as Democrats hope the GOP will oppose the rule, allowing them to frame Republicans as defenders of wealthy, white suburbs who seek to exclude impoverished people of color.

Conservatives must emphasize a clear message: every American, regardless of race, color, or creed, should enjoy the freedom to reside wherever they choose. Achieving this requires fostering economic opportunities at the lower end of the spectrum, enabling individuals to secure better jobs and education so they can eventually afford superior neighborhoods.

Throughout the current administration, such opportunities have dwindled for those at the bottom of the economic ladder. Despite rhetoric surrounding inequality, the poor have grown poorer while the wealthy have enriched themselves. Data from the recovery period shows that households in the top 5 percent—those averaging incomes above $320,000—were the sole group to experience income growth between 2009 and 2013. Conversely, the bottom 20 percent suffered the most, enduring an average 7 percent drop in real income. As Arthur C. Brooks, president of the American Enterprise Institute, points out: “Our putatively progressive president has inadvertently executed a plutocratic tour de force.” Allowing Washington to oversee the housing and zoning decisions of local municipalities will not resolve this dynamic. Instead of compelling local governments to construct affordable housing within affluent areas, the real solution lies in reviving upward mobility so a greater number of people can naturally afford to live in those neighborhoods.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — President Donald Trump’s plan to achieve a balanced federal budget within ten years relies heavily on hitting a consistent 3 percent yearly economic expansion—a target from his campaign—alongside an undefined “feedback” mechanism projected to slash yearly government deficits by massive sums. Economists and the Federal Reserve view these forecasts as an ambitious gamble, pointing out challenges like an aging population and sluggish productivity growth. Furthermore, the strategy depends on maintaining low inflation, minimal interest rates, and full employment, essentially banking on a ten-year stretch entirely devoid of severe economic disruptions or even the typical mild recessions associated with standard market cycles.

Administration data made public on Monday evening indicate that gross domestic product growth is projected to climb to 3 percent per year by the conclusion of Trump's initial term and maintain that pace through at least 2027. This optimistic outlook comes despite an annualized first-quarter growth rate of just 0.7 percent, whereas the Federal Reserve projects overall growth for the year closer to 2.1 percent. The administration contends that this robust expansion will drive roughly 5 percent annual increases in tax revenue, notwithstanding the president's pledges that forthcoming tax reductions will stimulate investment and employment.

Additional assumptions built into the budget include inflation meeting the Federal Reserve's 2 percent target and remaining steady, contrasting with current Fed projections sitting slightly below 2 percent. The administration also estimates that the unemployment rate will tick up slightly from its 4.4 percent level, ultimately settling at a long-term average of 4.8 percent. Government figures indicate that without the projected acceleration in growth and an entirely stable macroeconomic backdrop, annual deficits would swell by as much as $500 billion, hovering near their current levels. This calculation factors in a so-called economic feedback effect that is anticipated to shrink the federal shortfall by up to $496 billion annually by 2027, though the initial release provided no specific explanation regarding how this feedback functions.

By comparison, the final budget proposal under President Barack Obama projected annual growth of 2.6 percent, a figure that professional economists and central bank officials already viewed as overly optimistic. Federal Reserve policymakers currently estimate the long-term trend for U.S. growth to be near 1.8 percent. Meanwhile, a quarterly survey conducted by the Philadelphia Fed shows that Wall Street analysts factoring in potential tax-cutting measures anticipate growth reaching 2.3 percent by 2020. 

In a client note published on Sunday, UniCredit chief economist Erik Nielsen remarked that the comprehensive fiscal scenario pushed by the administration was never grounded in realistic expectations. Historical data shows that U.S. economic growth has averaged 1.9 percent annually since the year 2000. Over a ten-year period, compounding the gap between that historical average and the administration's 3 percent target accounts for an additional $2 trillion each year in economic activity that would otherwise bypass spending, investment, and taxation.

The fiscal blueprint also banks on prolonged low interest rates, projecting that the yield on the 10-year Treasury note will rise to 3.8 percent and stay level—a crucial variable for estimating government borrowing expenses. Although the 10-year yield has averaged close to that threshold over the course of the century and currently sits well below it, periods of accelerated economic expansion typically trigger higher interest rates driven by tighter monetary policy and shifts in demand for U.S. debt securities.

The Last Time This Happened, It Signaled The Global Financial Crash Of 2008. Now, It’s Happening Again.

A sharp collapse in this specific trade metric previously foreshadowed the onset of the worldwide financial crash of 2007 and 2008. At present, the exact same phenomenon is recurring, though the gauge has now plunged to an all-time low. 

The Baltic Dry Index measures the expenses associated with transporting dry commodities globally. Traditionally, the index functions as an indicator for worldwide economic health because declining prices indicate shrinking trade volume, which subsequently signals an impending economic downturn. 

Late in 2013, the Baltic Dry Index reached a strong level of 2,330, and even as recently as last August, it maintained a solid figure of 1,222. However, it recently plummeted to a mere 354.

Image via Business Insider

This dramatic drop warrants serious concern because the previous instance preceded the 2008 global financial crisis—an event from which numerous economies still struggle to recover—and at that time, the index remained above 600. 

As Business Insider points out, multiple other instances exist where the index has signaled major corrections in the world economy. Operating in its modern form since 1985, the Baltic Dry Index experienced an initial substantial drop in mid-1986, roughly a year ahead of the 1987 Black Monday market crash. Later, in 1999, the index dropped to 12-year lows shortly before the dot-com bubble ruptured, and it fell to another significant low in 2001, coinciding with a United States economic recession that persisted until 2003.

Does this guarantee a crash matching the magnitude of 2008? Not necessarily, as it would be unwise to claim this indicator is entirely foolproof. Even so, combined with other economic warning signs, it demands careful consideration.

William White, the former chief economist at the Bank for International Settlements located in Switzerland, has cautioned that a massive wave of debt is approaching the global economy, stating that current conditions are worse than those of 2007. He noted that policy makers have effectively depleted their macroeconomic ammunition to combat economic downturns, leaving only the question of whether society will confront reality in an orderly manner or face a disorderly outcome.

White is far from alone in his assessment, as major financial institutions such as Goldman Sachs and the Royal Bank of Scotland have also delivered grim warnings regarding an approaching financial crisis. Furthermore, Baltic Exchange CEO Jeremy Penn remarked to The Telegraph that conditions have reached a point where individuals struggle to recall any period matching this level of difficulty, surpassing the 1990s, 1980s, and 1970s, to the extent that terms like living memory become applicable. Ultimately, disregarding these signals comes with significant risk.

Bernie Sanders Could End Up Winning Iowa

21st Century Wire reports that the Democratic primary in Iowa went down as one of the tightest contests ever, with mainstream outlets claiming Hillary Clinton triumphed by a razor-thin margin of just 0.3%. Yet, questions remain regarding whether Clinton truly emerged victorious. 

The National Review suggests the outcome is far from settled. Beltway journalist Quinn Hillyer points out that when looking at the ultimate tally of state convention delegates—excluding the seven secured by Martin O’Malley—Clinton ended up with 699 while Sanders held 695. However, based strictly on direct voter choices, Sanders actually led with 695 to Clinton's 693, alongside six ties. While Clinton currently heads to the state convention holding four more committed delegates than her rival, her lead came not from ballots cast by voters, but rather through a strange sequence of coin tosses. 

History shows precedent for such shifts; four years prior in 2012, major news networks initially declared Mitt Romney the winner of the GOP Iowa primary, only to issue a retraction later after realizing Rick Santorum had actually captured the caucus majority. Even then, neither Romney nor Santorum secured the bulk of Iowa's delegates heading into the national gathering. That distinction belonged to party outsider Ron Paul—a reality that mainstream American television networks largely swept under the rug. Paul pulled off this feat because his team grasped the true nature of the Iowa Caucuses as a massive statewide straw poll, executing a remarkably fierce delegate approach. The fallout within the Republican party was severe enough that the Republican National Convention subsequently created new rules to address the "Ron Paul Problem," ensuring outsider candidates could no longer establish a state-level presence without establishment backing.

Similarly, should Bernie Sanders manage to execute effective grassroots work focused on a robust county-level delegate plan, followed by capturing at least five of the seven uncommitted delegates left behind by the departed Martin O’Malley during the upcoming Iowa State Convention, Sanders might still turn out to be the true delegate victor in Iowa. 

Patrick Henningsen of 21WIRE discussed these topics with RT International, addressing the Sanders campaign's push for a recount alongside other debated elements of the 2016 race for the White House, such as the controversy involving Donald Trump and Ted Cruz.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — Defying the stance of top party leaders in the Senate, moderate Republican Senator Susan Collins of Maine voiced strong admiration for President Barack Obama's Supreme Court choice on Tuesday, though her appeal for confirmation proceedings was swiftly rejected. Collins marked just the second Republican in the chamber to sit down with Merrick Garland since the moderate appeals court judge was put forward last month to succeed the late Justice Antonin Scalia, who died on February 13. 

The sixty-minute discussion unfolded while GOP senators deal with heavy demands from conservative groups to support Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell's strategy of obstructing any selection put forth by Obama. Following the talk, Collins expressed to journalists that the encounter strengthened her belief that the procedure ought to move forward, adding that public sessions in front of the Judiciary Committee should be the upcoming phase. 

Roughly two hours afterward, McConnell countered by telling the press that it is certain neither proceedings nor votes will take place regarding Garland. Both McConnell and Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley maintain that the open seat left by Scalia ought to be filled by whoever succeeds Obama in the presidency, with the election scheduled for November 8 and the inauguration set for January 20. With an even 4-4 ideological split currently dividing the bench between conservatives and liberals, the next justice could shape the court's balance for a long time. 

Describing Garland as highly knowledgeable, reflective, remarkable, exceptionally intelligent, and deeply aware of the constitutional boundaries separating the executive, legislative, and judicial branches, Collins offered high praise. Meanwhile, the administration announced that Garland is scheduled to sit down next week for courtesy discussions with GOP Senators Kelly Ayotte, Rob Portman, Lisa Murkowski, and Jeff Flake. 

Garland previously held talks last week with Illinois Senator Mark Kirk, who criticized members of his own party as close-minded for declining to evaluate the pick. Additionally, a spokesperson for Grassley stated on Monday that the committee chairman invited Garland to a breakfast gathering so he can personally articulate the rationale behind withholding hearings. 

Democrats continued criticizing the GOP blockade, with Senate Democratic whip Dick Durbin pointing out that if McConnell maintains his position, Garland will become the initial high court nominee in American history to be refused a hearing. Conversely, Flake suggested that if a Democrat secures the presidency, the Senate ought to approve Garland swiftly during a legislative session following the election, as certain conservatives worry that Democratic front-runner Hillary Clinton might put forward someone far more liberal than Garland. 

However, Senator Lindsey Graham, a fellow Republican on the Judiciary Committee, brushed aside the notion of a post-election lame-duck approval for Garland, asserting that confirmation is out of the question and questioning the point of holding a hearing solely to berate the nominee.

Factbox: What do the new U.S. sanctions on Russia target?

WASHINGTON (Reuters) - This week, U.S. President Donald Trump gave his signature—albeit reluctantly—to a comprehensive sanctions package directed at Russia, North Korea, and Iran. Ahead of a weekend meeting in Manila between U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson and Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov at a regional gathering, the following outlines the key components of the new measures against Moscow:

* Lawmakers instituted a legislative review mechanism empowering Congress to halt any attempt by President Trump to roll back or terminate the restrictions on Russia. The legislation was advanced by members of Congress to penalize Moscow for its purported meddling in the 2016 American presidential election, the seizure and annexation of Crimea from Ukraine, and its participation in the civil conflict in Syria.

* Under the new rules, the sitting president is required to deliver a detailed report to the relevant congressional committee outlining the justification for any proposed relaxation of penalties, alongside an assessment of how such a move would impact American national security. Legislators are granted a minimum of thirty days to conduct hearings and subsequently cast votes regarding the adjustment. Should Congress pass a joint resolution of disapproval, the executive branch is legally blocked from altering the penalties.

* Fresh economic penalties are directed at organizations engaging in commerce with the military or intelligence sectors of Russia, firms participating in offshore oil ventures connected to Russia, and entities taking part in the building of Russian gas or oil pipelines located within the country. This broad reach across multiple Russian industrial sectors threatens to inflict additional damage on an economy that was previously battered by penalties enacted in 2014 following the annexation of Crimea.

* Additional penalties are applied to any group or individual participating in cyber attacks on behalf of Moscow, as well as organizations owned by or operating for such entities. While the president retains the authority to grant waivers for these specific measures if deemed vital to national security, such actions remain subject to congressional oversight.

* Six distinct executive orders previously issued by President Barack Obama have now been formally codified into law, ensuring that Trump cannot unilaterally undo them through executive action. Enacted between 2014 and 2016, these earlier actions focused on Russian defense, financial services, energy, and additional sectors as a response to the Ukraine incursion, the seizure of Crimea, and election meddling and cyber operations directed at the United States.

* Furthermore, the legislation mandates a coordinated government report detailing prominent Russian oligarchs and senior political figures, which must include estimates of their fortunes, revenue sources, potential links to corruption, and their ties to Russian leader Vladimir Putin.

Jean-Marie Simon, who works as an attorney and private school teacher and is 63 years old, used 140,000 miles on December 3 to buy first-class tickets for a trip taking her from Washington D.C. to Guatemala and returning home. On December 18, during the final leg of her journey home originating from George Bush Intercontinental Airport, a weather delay of approximately an hour occurred. When boarding time arrived, Simon stated that the gate attendant scanned her paper ticket only to be told it was missing from the system. The attendant asked her if she had canceled her flight, to which Simon responded that she only wanted to go home. She was informed that her seat, 1A, was occupied, and she was moved to row 11 in Economy Plus after receiving a $500 voucher.

Simon subsequently discovered that U.S. Rep. Sheila Jackson Lee, a Democrat from Houston, was occupying the seat she had pre-purchased. Simon accused the congresswoman of receiving preferential treatment, an allegation denied by United Airlines. Following a mechanical issue that delayed the flight's takeoff for about 50 minutes, passengers had been invited to speak with a gate agent regarding alternative flights. Simon went to the front area, took a photo of Jackson Lee, and informed a flight attendant of her reason for being bumped. A fellow congressman on the same flight claimed that Jackson Lee engages in this behavior repeatedly. 

Jackson Lee stated that she observed Simon talking with an African-American flight attendant and taking the photograph. In her official statement, Jackson Lee suggested race played a role, noting that the individual's continued actions seemed, upon reflection, to stem from the fact that Jackson Lee is an African-American woman and an easy target alongside the very nice African-American flight attendant. Jackson Lee expressed sadness over this during the holiday season given ongoing efforts to help people, yet stated that out of sincerity and the holiday spirit, if anyone perceived her as having anything to do with the situation, she would simply say sorry. 

Simon responded that Jackson Lee's statement accused her of racism, pointing out that she had no knowledge of who was in her seat when complaining at the gate about it being given away, as terminal views into seated areas are impossible. Approximately five minutes after capturing the photo onboard, Simon reported that another flight attendant sat beside her to ask if she intended to be a problem, prompting Simon to reply that she merely wished to return home.

When Simon requested the identical free meal and beverage privileges associated with her first-class ticket alongside the $500 voucher, she asserted that the gate agent mocked her by stating, "And I want a Mercedes Benz, but I'm not going to get it." The gate agent initially offered $300—amounts Simon noted people typically receive in greater sums for voluntarily surrendering seats on overbooked flights—and eventually presented an ultimatum to accept the $500 or have the plane depart without her.

A law professor raised the question of whether the House Ethics Committee ought to investigate whether the Texas Democrat pressured the airline to secure her first-class seat, suggesting the committee examine what pressure Jackson Lee may have applied and how United accommodated her, while placing United under oath because claims that Simon canceled her own reservation are unbelievable.

Although multiple major news outlets relying on an Associated Press source reported that United Airlines issued an apology for their mistake, Simon publicly challenged these reports and demanded corrections, stating that United had not apologized to her. She clarified that on December 23, a low-level call center employee expressed a verbal apology over the phone, while the voucher served as compensation for her canceled flight and the reassignment of her seat to Jackson Lee. Simon insisted that media outlets correct their coverage to show that corporate United never apologized, and that the $500 voucher originated from an exasperated gate agent rather than serving as an apology.

In an emailed statement provided on the condition of anonymity, the defense official mentioned that the agency recognizes the report's existence and is collaborating closely with various interagency departments to fulfill this legal obligation under the NDAA, anticipating the delivery of the final document to Capitol Hill shortly.

Prior to that statement, House Speaker Paul Ryan, a Republican, released a public statement demanding that the Democratic president present a genuine and comprehensive plan to eliminate Islamic State by Monday. 

Currently, the U.S. spearheads an ongoing military offensive targeting the extremist faction, which has taken control of extensive regions across Iraq and Syria. Congressional Republicans have repeatedly found fault with Obama's handling of Islamic State, arguing that his initial underestimation of the danger allowed the militant network to expand its influence and power. 

Meanwhile, U.S. Defense Secretary Ash Carter kicked off discussions in Brussels on Thursday involving over twenty defense ministers, where he urged international partners to step up their contributions to the coalition's mission.

MANILA (Reuters) - Disaster authorities and the coastguard reported that a Philippine ferry carrying 251 people overturned in severe weather on Thursday close to Manila, leaving four dead and seven unaccounted for. Maritime incidents frequently occur in the Philippines due to the heavy reliance on inter-island boat travel. Although these vessels frequently exceed passenger limits, the coastguard confirmed that the ferry was not overcrowded and possessed a maximum capacity of 286 passengers. Several hours after the vessel capsized and sank roughly eight miles away from Real town located in Quezon province, rescue boats dispatched by the coastguard alongside local fishermen managed to pull 240 individuals from the water. 

Coastguard spokesman Captain Armand Balilo stated that search and rescue efforts will persist until every passenger and crew member is located. The majority of the survivors were transported to Dinahican port, while the fatalities consisted of two men and two women who drowned. Having departed from a port in Real around daybreak, survivors recounted to reporters that weather conditions deteriorated three hours into the journey, bringing powerful winds and massive waves. The vessel quickly started filling with water before overturning and sinking within minutes. 

Emergency management officials noted that the ongoing search operations faced significant obstacles due to torrential rain and towering waves whipped up by a tropical storm impacting the southern region of the country. The tropical storm was anticipated to hit the southern island of Mindanao either late Thursday night or early Friday morning. In advance of the storm, which featured central winds reaching 65 kph (40 mph), the weather bureau issued warnings regarding widespread flooding and landslides across the archipelago.

text:
WASHINGTON — Rex Tillerson, the nominee for secretary of state, took stances during his Wednesday confirmation proceedings that conflicted with several core foreign policy positions held by President-elect Donald Trump, touching on topics such as climate change, trade agreements, nuclear proliferation, and ties with Mexico. Appearing before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee for a marathon nine-hour session, the former Exxon Mobil chief executive stated that current U.S. sanctions against Russia ought to be maintained for the time being, and agreed that NATO members had valid reasons to feel threatened by Moscow's escalating aggression. 

Russia remained a central focus throughout the proceedings, driven by bipartisan anxiety over the 2014 annexation of Crimea, involvement in the Syrian civil war, and meddling in the American presidential election. Lawmakers also pressed the nominee on the Islamic State threat, human rights issues, Beijing's actions in the South China Sea, and whether he could successfully separate himself from his extensive background at the oil giant to lead the State Department. 

Addressing his divergent views from the incoming president, Tillerson maintained that these differences would not necessarily create friction with the White House. He characterized himself as transparent and open, explaining that Cabinet members would have opportunities to debate matters before a final presidential determination is made. 

In clear contrast to Trump's past statements, Tillerson asserted that allowing additional U.S. allies to acquire nuclear weapons would be unacceptable. When Democratic Senator Edward Markey inquired about Trump’s previous interview remarks suggesting he would not oppose nations like Japan pursuing nuclear arms, Tillerson answered directly that he disagreed. Furthermore, he stated he did not support the creation of a Muslim registry, noting he opposed targeting specific groups, and clarified that he did not oppose the Trans-Pacific Partnership trade agreement—which Trump has heavily criticized—though he conceded the negotiated pact might not fully serve American interests. 

At the same time, Tillerson aligned with Trump by leaving the door open for significant revisions to Obama-era initiatives, including trade policies concerning Cuba and the Iran nuclear agreement, which he argued should be subjected to a comprehensive review. 

Amid occasional interruptions by demonstrators, the 64-year-old nominee is widely anticipated to secure confirmation within the Republican-led Senate. However, senators repeatedly voiced unease regarding his past connections to Russia through Exxon Mobil, particularly given Trump’s stated objective to foster closer ties with Moscow. Tillerson declined to label Russian leader Vladimir Putin a war criminal and kept options open regarding potential adjustments to sanctions, mentioning he had not yet reviewed classified intelligence on election interference. “I would leave things in the status quo so we are able to convey this can go either way,” Tillerson remarked, advocating for candid discussions with Moscow to clarify its motivations. 

He attributed Russian hostility toward Ukraine dating back to 2014 to a lack of American leadership, arguing that stronger deterrent measures should have been deployed. “I’m advocating for responses that will deter and prevent further expansion of a bad actor’s behavior,” he stated. While acknowledging it was a fair assumption that Putin knew about efforts to disrupt the U.S. election, Tillerson admitted he had not conferred with Trump on Russia policy, a fact Democratic Senator Robert Menendez termed remarkable. 

During a sharp exchange, Republican Senator Marco Rubio challenged Tillerson on whether Putin bore responsibility for war crimes stemming from military campaigns supporting the Syrian government in Aleppo. Tillerson responded that the label involved extremely serious charges requiring substantially more information before drawing a conclusion. Rubio, a former rival for the Republican presidential nomination, pushed back, asserting that ample evidence was already publicly available regarding military actions in Syria, and expressed disappointment at the nominee's reluctance to acknowledge what he deemed globally accepted facts. 

Tillerson similarly avoided taking firm stances on human rights abuses in nations like the Philippines and Saudi Arabia, stating he preferred to examine the facts first. Following the hearing, Rubio told reporters he remained undecided on whether to support the nomination. As one of 11 Republicans on the 21-seat panel, Rubio's vote is vital for securing the committee's approval.

Regarding the 2015 Iran nuclear agreement—in which Tehran curbed its nuclear program in exchange for the lifting of economic sanctions—Tillerson recommended a complete review rather than an immediate outright rejection, despite Trump's conflicting statements and threats to dismantle the pact. On Asian affairs, Tillerson maintained that China should be barred from utilizing artificial islands constructed in contested areas of the South China Sea. Regarding North Korea, which recently claimed proximity to testing an intercontinental ballistic missile, he outlined an approach centered on sanctions and strict enforcement as part of a long-term strategy. 

When questioned about potential conflicts of interest stemming from his tenure at the world’s largest publicly traded oil company, Tillerson pledged to prioritize American interests. He also navigated queries concerning human-induced climate change by stating that risks and serious consequences do exist and warrant action, though he noted that predictive capabilities regarding greenhouse gas impacts remain very limited. This contrasted with Trump's past characterization of global warming as a Chinese hoax and threats to withdraw from the Paris climate accord. 

Describing Mexico as a long-standing neighbor and friend, Tillerson offered a view distinct from Trump's campaign rhetoric, which included plans for a border wall and controversial characterizations of Mexican migrants. 

Throughout the proceedings, Tillerson maintained a calm and measured demeanor, rarely relying on notes. Addressing past actions, he recalled opposing the 2014 sanctions against Russia over Crimea because he believed they would prove ineffective. While he maintained he never personally lobbied against the measures and was unaware of Exxon Mobil doing so directly, he later conceded that he had spoken with U.S. Treasury Secretary Jack Lew regarding discrepancies between American and European sanctions policies. Democratic Senator Chris Murphy confronted Tillerson over the matter, arguing that contacting a U.S. senator to voice concerns about the measures effectively constituted lobbying, which regulatory filings show the company did engage in regarding energy-related matters following the annexation of Crimea.

Law enforcement officers in Kiev placed Mikheil Saakashvili, the ex-president of Georgia, back into custody on Friday. The move quickly sparked fresh demonstrations in the heart of the Ukrainian capital by followers who had previously helped him escape from police custody earlier in the week. This event marks the latest chapter in an ongoing political conflict between the Ukrainian government and Saakashvili, who shifted from an ally of President Petro Poroshenko to a vocal opponent demanding his ouster and alleging official corruption. 

Yuriy Lutsenko, the General Prosecutor, announced via a Facebook update that the opposition figure was being held at a temporary facility, noting he faces suspicions of aiding a criminal organization. Lutsenko emphasized that law enforcement had taken care to prevent bloodshed and extreme violence during the operation. 

The renewed detention comes on the heels of bizarre events earlier in the week, which featured Saakashvili climbing onto a rooftop to evade authorities and later being liberated from a police van by demonstrators following violent confrontations with large numbers of riot police on Tuesday. 

Davit Sakvarelidze, an ally and fellow Georgian who previously lost his job as a high-ranking Ukrainian prosecutor in March, urged capital residents to mobilize and protest the arrest. Speaking to NewsOne near the central detention facility, Sakvarelidze accused Poroshenko of surpassing all previous limits and sealing his legacy as a dictator targeting political rivals. 

By 2200 GMT, several hundred demonstrators had congregated close to the detention center, located near the parliament building. Surrounded by a heavy presence of riot police, the crowd chanted slogans such as "Shame!" and "Kiev, get up!" 

Saakashvili initially arrived in Ukraine to serve as a regional governor in 2015 at the personal request of Poroshenko, though the relationship eventually deteriorated. The politician has consistently rejected all accusations against him. 

This ongoing standoff risks bringing international embarrassment to Ukraine's pro-Western leadership, particularly as they already face mounting pressure from international backers and domestic reformers regarding perceived stagnation on reforms and pressure on anti-corruption agencies. Addressing the situation on Friday, President Poroshenko insisted that the legal proceedings against Saakashvili are entirely valid and urged him to cooperate fully with investigators, warning that running away would destroy his credibility. 

Following his initial escape from custody, Saakashvili had urged supporters to attend an anti-Poroshenko rally in Kiev scheduled for Sunday. However, he maintained a low profile over the preceding days, reportedly falling ill after staying in a makeshift protest encampment outside the parliament building. 

Prior to Friday's action, police attempted a raid on the camp on Wednesday to retake the former Georgian leader, which similarly resulted in violent skirmishes with his supporters. Despite having a dedicated group of followers, Saakashvili commands modest backing throughout the wider country. Findings from an October poll conducted by the Razumkov Centre, a think-tank based in Kiev, indicated that only 1.7 percent of the electorate would back his Movement of New Forces party at the ballot box. While his supporters view him as a courageous fighter against graft, detractors argue that his public speeches lack substance.

Sarah Palin And Other Conservatives Fly Into A Panic After Seeing UN Vehicles On The Road (SCREENSHOTS)

Right-wing circles frequently view everyday occurrences through the lens of conspiracy, with a prevailing delusion focused on the notion that the United Nations intends to seize control of the United States and strip citizens of their firearms. Consequently, when a motorist belonging to this political persuasion spotted a shipment of UN vehicles being hauled from a domestic manufacturer toward an overseas shipping point, they panicked and rushed to social media with warnings of an impending UN takeover. 

"Can't begin to tell you how many of these I passed today on 81 near Lexington VA," posted conservative Jeff Stern, accompanied by pictures of the trucks riding on trailers. 

This post sparked widespread hysteria among right-wing commentators, echoing the kind of frantic bunker-building and weapon-stockpiling seen among Texas conservatives during the Jade Helm military training exercise. Stern observed the transport on Interstate 81 close to Lexington, Virginia—a detail that some individuals mistakenly associated with Lexington, Kentucky, thereby fueling rumors of sightings across both states. Matters escalated further when the Daily Mail sensationalized the situation by questioning whether the UN had arrived in anticipation of an economic collapse, inadvertently driving even more anxiety among anxious conservatives.

The panic extended to standard vehicle specifications, such as bullet-resistant windows and poison gas seals. Given the global deployment zones of UN personnel, these protective measures are standard and entirely practical; comparable American military equipment features identical defenses for identical reasons. 

Snopes reached out to the creator of these specific units and obtained a logical rationale regarding the transit. In contrast to the Daily Mail's approach, inquiries directed to Alpine Armoring—the company identified in the report—clarified the situation. A representative from Alpine explained that these specific units were bought by the United Nations for deployment outside American borders. Because various defense contractors maintain operations in the Washington, D.C. area, which encompasses Virginia, for straightforward logistical purposes, the spokesperson verified that the trucks were bound for international service.

Following production, these UN units must be moved to domestic ports for export. Driving them directly to departure points would accumulate thousands of miles prior to loading onto cargo vessels or aircraft, making flatbed transport a logical choice. It follows that these same vehicles could plausibly appear in other Southern states along transit routes toward shipping terminals in the South.

Naturally, reason failed to prevail among conservatives, who shared Stern's update upwards of 120,000 times alongside reactionary commentary. Sarah Palin herself amplified the widespread hysteria by endorsing the notion that the UN had arrived to confiscate domestic firearms. The sheer scale of the absurdity remains striking.

WASHINGTON AND GREEN BAY, WIS. — Amid declining poll numbers against his Democratic rival, Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump argued during a campaign stop on Monday that the upcoming November 8 contest is “rigged,” pointing to studies he contends demonstrate widespread voter irregularities. Despite the businessman's claims, Republican legal experts have labeled his assertions completely unfounded. 

Speaking to supporters at a Wisconsin rally in Green Bay, the GOP nominee warned that efforts to manipulate the outcome might occur directly at polling locations, asserting that numerous municipalities suffer from widespread corruption and frequent voter fraud. To back up his claims, Trump referenced a 2012 analysis by the Pew Charitable Trusts that advocated for voter registration updates due to millions of inaccurate entries. He also pointed to a 2014 Washington Post piece co-authored by two political scientists, which suggested non-citizen voting could have swung a small number of close 2008 races, though the researchers admitted their sample size was quite limited.

Conversely, multiple investigations have demonstrated that electoral fraud in the United States remains exceedingly uncommon. Chris Ashby, a Republican campaign attorney, characterized Trump's warnings as dangerous and capable of inciting civil disturbance. During an interview, Ashby explained that declaring an election fixed essentially tells supporters that their ballots hold no value, noting that such rhetoric could provoke unrest at voting sites. These warnings have prompted some party members to urge the candidate to drop the rhetoric, particularly as mail-in and early voting are already underway across numerous jurisdictions.

Mark Braden, a former chief counsel for the Republican National Committee and partner at Baker and Hostetler, argued that nationwide election manipulation is practically impossible given the complex network of safeguards currently in place. In an interview, Braden emphasized that the American framework relies heavily on bipartisan oversight and local volunteers, a system he credits with functioning exceptionally well over the years due to grassroots involvement.

Additionally, Trump seized upon FBI documents released on Monday, describing them as proof of severe corruption. The records included statements from an FBI official alleging that a high-ranking State Department representative attempted to pressure the bureau in 2015 to remove classified markings from an email originating on Hillary Clinton’s private server. Clinton’s reliance on that private setup throughout her tenure as secretary of state between 2009 and 2013 has consistently drawn accusations of poor national security judgment. Denouncing the situation as worse than the Watergate scandal, Trump also unveiled an ethics platform promising a five-year lobbying ban for departing administration officials if he wins the presidency.

Meanwhile, Clinton campaign manager Robby Mook dismissed Trump's attacks on the electoral process as a sign of desperation from a candidate who recognizes he is behind. Citing current RealClearPolitics polling averages, Clinton holds a 7.1 percentage point advantage nationally, standing at 46 percent compared to Trump's 38.9 percent.

Efforts to push back against the nominee's fraud allegations also came from within his own party. AshLee Strong, a spokeswoman for House Speaker Paul Ryan—the nation's highest-ranking elected Republican—stated that Ryan maintains absolute trust in the states' ability to execute a secure election. In Ohio, a key battleground, the state's Republican chief election officer likewise rejected claims of widespread problems. Ohio Secretary of State Jon Husted assured CNN that he personally oversees the state's voting procedures and guarantees they will not be compromised.

Research consistently underscores the extreme rarity of such issues. A New York University School of Law Brennan Center report titled “The Truth About Voter Fraud” estimated incident rates between 0.00004% and 0.0009%. Similarly, an August investigation by the Washington Post identified only 31 credible instances of voter impersonation out of more than a billion ballots cast between 2000 and 2014, with Arizona State University publishing comparable findings in 2012 and 2016. While several conservative-led states have enacted stricter identification mandates aimed at stopping fraud, courts have struck down multiple provisions over rulings that they intentionally suppressed minority turnout.

Trump’s presidential bid has faced intense turbulence following the publication ten days prior of a 2005 video featuring the candidate making crude remarks about non-consensual kissing and touching of women. Although multiple women have subsequently stepped forward with complaints regarding similar conduct, Trump has denied all accusations, accusing the press of attempting to manipulate voter perceptions with sensationalized headlines about fabricated incidents.

The controversy returned to the forefront on Monday as Melania Trump addressed the "Access Hollywood" tape publicly for the first time. The former model, who has largely remained away from the campaign trail, told CNN she was taken aback by her husband's language, suggesting he was nudged into making crude remarks that she described as typical “boy talk.” She further claimed that the accusations of unwanted physical contact were coordinated by political opponents and criticized the media for failing to vet the accusers. In a separate discussion with the Fox News Channel, she confirmed she had accepted his apology for the recorded comments, stating that the remarks were offensive and inappropriate, but emphasized that they have forgiven him and are moving forward.

BEIJING (Reuters) - Military exercises by China's air force recently involved sending bombers and additional warplanes across a pair of vital passages close to Taiwan, as well as traversing the disputed waters of the South China Sea, according to state media reports released on Thursday. 

Xinhua, the official news agency, reported that various jets alongside multiple H-6K bombers executed a "combat patrol," passing through the Miyako Strait located in Japan's southern region and the Bashi Channel situated between the Philippines and Taiwan, in addition to flying over the South China Sea. 

Shen Jinke, an Air Force spokesman cited by Xinhua, did not specify the exact start date of the exercises, though he confirmed that all participating aircraft concluded their patrols on Thursday. These maneuvers were designed to sharpen actual combat capabilities at sea and develop the military's strategic battle tactics, according to Shen. 

Beijing has grown more assertive regarding territorial claims in both the East and South China Seas. Furthermore, concerns persist regarding Taiwan, which is governed by an administration Beijing suspects of pursuing formal independence. 

The Chinese leadership has consistently refused to renounce the potential use of military force to place the democratic island under its governance, cautioning that steps toward formal independence could trigger an armed intervention. 

Presently, China is undertaking a sweeping military modernization effort encompassing the development of stealth fighters and the construction of aircraft carriers, aiming to project military might at significant distances from its coastline. Although Taiwan maintains a well-equipped military relying primarily on American arms, Taipei continues to urge Washington to provide additional advanced technology to strengthen its deterrence against Beijing.

An Iranian nuclear scientist, who provided crucial details to the enemy, was put to death on Sunday by Iran. Shahram Amiri went missing back in 2009 while visiting Mecca in Saudi Arabia. Following a year-long disappearance, he reappeared in the United States in June 2010. Amiri maintained that the CIA abducted him and subjected him to severe psychological pressure to extract sensitive data, asserting that he resisted U.S. attempts to break him. Conversely, the U.S. Government maintained at the time that Amiri defected of his own accord and received millions of dollars in exchange for valuable insights concerning the nation's nuclear program.

The following month, he showed up at the Pakistani embassy's Iranian interests section in Washington DC, expressing a desire to go back to Iran. He secured safe passage home a few days later, initially receiving a hero's welcome upon arrival. However, authorities arrested and prosecuted him for treason in May 2011. Although his relatives thought he received a ten-year prison sentence—which would have allowed for his release in 2022—he actually faced capital punishment. Ultimately, the execution took place on August 7, 2016. 

Gholamhosein Mohseni-Ejei, a spokesman for the Islamic Republic of Iran, stated during his weekly press conference that Amiri possessed confidential military secrets and maintained ties to the Great Satan, which they consider public enemy number one. Mohseni-Ejei noted that a primary court handed down the death sentence, and the Supreme Court upheld it following Amiri's appeal. He added that the CIA believed their activities remained hidden from the Iranian Intelligence Ministry when they brought Amiri to Saudi Arabia.

To most observers, the sequence of events appears quite standard: he published a video stating he shared national secrets with the CIA, the United States verified his actions, and he somehow believed it was safe to head back home. This represents the established historical record, unless the perspective belongs to Tom Cotton.

As it turns out, Amiri's name appeared within recently made-public Clinton emails. Cotton asserted that these messages, which only recently entered the public sphere, triggered Amiri's 2011 arrest and subsequent death sentence. Nine days prior to Amiri's return to Iran, Richard Morningstar, who formerly served as the State Department special envoy for Eurasian energy, wrote that they faced a diplomatic and psychological challenge rather than a legal one, adding that their friend needed a way out and that their person could not accomplish anything anyway, so if he had to leave, it should happen.

During an appearance on "Face the Nation," Cotton strongly criticized Clinton, stating that while he would not comment on potential work done for the United States government, conversations among her top advisors regarding this individual existed within the emails stored on Hillary Clinton's private server. Cotton claimed this demonstrated the reckless and careless nature of her choice to store such highly classified details on a private server, arguing that her judgment disqualified her from keeping the nation safe—apparently overlooking the fact that these events transpired years prior to the email release.

In reality, the timeline appears irrelevant to conservative commentators. Jim Hoft of the Gateway Pundit claimed that Clinton's unprotected emails led to the execution of an Iranian nuclear scientist. Hoft wrote that they discovered the individual's work for the US via Hillary Clinton's emails, concluding with a sarcastic remark. He also incorporated a specific tweet into his commentary.

BERLIN (Reuters) — German Chancellor Angela Merkel emphasized that any deployment of United Nations peacekeepers to eastern Ukraine needs to operate across all areas controlled by Russian-backed separatists. During a telephone conversation on Monday, Russian President Vladimir Putin brought up the concept of sending U.N. personnel to the region with Merkel, proposing that these forces could safeguard monitors from the international OSCE observer mission.

As pressure mounts within Germany to ease European Union sanctions imposed on Russia because of the crisis in Ukraine, Moscow has shown interest in initiatives aimed at easing trade restrictions that have negatively impacted living standards for Russians. 

Speaking to the FUNKE media group on Friday, Merkel remarked that Putin's suggestion to use U.N. forces for the protection of OSCE monitors was noteworthy, adding that she had spoken with him a few days prior about ensuring these troops receive authorization to travel wherever the OSCE maintains a presence across the entirety of the Donetsk and Luhansk areas.

Since the fighting began in 2014, the clashes between Ukrainian troops and Moscow-supported separatists have resulted in a death toll exceeding 10,000. While Western nations maintain that Moscow engineered the hostilities and supplied weapons and personnel, Russia rejects these claims. 

The monitoring personnel are tasked with overseeing compliance with a 2015 peace agreement negotiated in Minsk, though the pact has largely failed to resolve the hostilities despite persistent appeals from Berlin and Paris. 

Certain German political figures have argued that punitive measures against Moscow could be removed if the Minsk accord is put into practice. Christian Lindner, who heads the Free Democrats and could potentially join Merkel's governing coalition following the September 24 elections, went so far as to propose that Berlin acknowledge Russia's annexation of the Crimean peninsula.

Calling Putin's ideas "tender shoots" of advancement, Merkel noted they do not currently provide a justification for relaxing sanctions. She also dismissed Lindner's stance, stating that the annexation violates international law and cannot be condoned.

Speculation abounds regarding what President Obama's professional path will look like come January, once his tenure as Commander-in-Chief concludes. While the Obama family plans to remain based in Washington, D.C., for the near future, his post-presidential endeavors will not necessarily be confined to the nation's capital. Setting his sights westward rather than toward Wall Street, Obama expressed in an interview with Bloomberg that if his life had taken a different path away from politics, launching a business would likely be his true calling. He noted that the competencies utilized in organizing presidential campaigns, assembling cohesive teams, and promoting concepts align closely with the private sector tasks he would find fulfilling.

Regarding his potential corporate ambitions, Obama expressed a desire to make a global impact, focusing his interests on medicine and science. Drawing a parallel to figures like Bill Gates, he discussed leveraging capitalism for positive change through localized initiatives, mentioning goals like bringing electricity to a village or conserving water in arid regions. He emphasized that the distinctiveness of the U.S. economy rests not only on capitalism and markets, but also on a commitment to science, reason, pragmatism, and ongoing discovery. He frequently advises interns and youth not to romanticize a return to past eras, noting that he has lived long enough to remember those times firsthand.

While talking to journalists during the Oracle Open World event, Hurd questioned the logic of educating individuals from abroad in domestic institutions, granting them degrees, and subsequently preventing them from utilizing their newly acquired skills domestically, launching businesses, contributing to tax revenues, and raising families.

DUBAI (Reuters) - According to an announcement made by the Bahraini Public Prosecution on Tuesday, a court in Bahrain handed down life sentences to 10 individuals and stripped them of their citizenship after finding them guilty of setting up a terror cell and planning assaults. The prosecutor's office stated that the defendants had traveled to Iran and Iraq to undergo military training at camps, learning how to handle weapons and explosives intended for attacks within Bahrain. 

Connecting to Saudi Arabia via a 25-kilometer (15-mile) causeway, the compact island nation of Bahrain holds significant strategic value for Western powers, notably serving as the base for the United States Fifth Fleet. While the ruling Sunni royal family governs the country, its population is predominantly Shiite Muslim. Citing a history of lethal bombings and shootings targeting security personnel, authorities maintain that the state deals with militant aggression supported by Iran, its primary adversary. Additionally, the Public Prosecution announced on Monday that 19 other individuals, whose names were not released, received prison sentences for communicating with an illegal political group that the state claims is linked to Iran and connected to extremist violence. Meanwhile, human rights advocates contend that the Bahraini administration suppresses peaceful opposition, though officials consistently deny these allegations.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — Testifying before Congress on Thursday, Donald Trump’s nominee for secretary of defense placed Moscow at the very top of his concerns regarding American security. Retired Marine General James Mattis stated that the nation must be prepared to push back against Russia when necessary, though he simultaneously supported the president-elect's desire for improved diplomatic ties. 

Mattis's statements represented yet another instance where a Cabinet choice appointed by Trump distanced himself from the campaign trail rhetoric of the incoming president, who had previously lauded Russian President Vladimir Putin and promised better relations. A day earlier, Rex Tillerson, nominated to head the State Department, also voiced perspectives that diverged from Trump on several major foreign policy matters, including trade pacts, climate change, nuclear proliferation, and ties with Mexico. 

According to Mattis, the American-led global order faces its most severe threats since the Second World War from Russia, China, and militant Islamist groups. He additionally urged lawmakers to eliminate budget caps that he argued were harming military preparedness. 

While expressing openness to diplomatic engagement, Mattis emphasized the necessity of acknowledging the reality of Russian actions, noting a shrinking number of opportunities for bilateral cooperation with Moscow. When lawmakers inquired about primary threats to national interests, he stated that Russia takes precedence. 

Addressing the prospect of new American penalties, Mattis indicated a desire to collaborate with Trump’s national security team in formulating a strategy to hold Moscow accountable for its past behavior. With just eight days remaining before taking office, Trump acknowledged on Wednesday that Russian actors likely carried out cyberattacks against the Democratic National Committee and the email accounts of prominent Democrats during the 2016 election race—a conclusion previously established by U.S. intelligence agencies. 

Alongside cyber warfare and hacking operations, Mattis pointed to treaty breaches, destabilizing foreign operations, and concerning rhetoric emanating from Moscow concerning atomic weaponry as key challenges. He also accused the Russian government of seeking to weaken the NATO alliance. In contrast to Trump, who expressed skepticism toward the alliance on the campaign trail, Mattis offered a robust endorsement, describing NATO as foundational to American defense and asserting that Putin aims to fracture the North Atlantic partnership. 

Republican Senator John McCain, who chairs the committee, declared himself extremely pleased with the nomination, while issuing a sharp warning against overly optimistic approaches to Putin, stating that the Russian leader actively requires the U.S. as an adversary and will never function as an ally. 

Furthermore, Mattis drew attention to Beijing's maneuvers in the South China Sea, where artificial islands outfitted with anti-missile and anti-aircraft defenses have been constructed. He categorized Chinese behavior, alongside Russian actions and extremist threats, as part of a broader challenge to international stability, insisting that relations with Beijing demand careful management. In his view, the global architecture is enduring its heaviest assault since WWII due to Russia, terrorist organizations, and Chinese activities in the region. 

Criticizing the legislative spending restrictions currently in place, Mattis asserted that the U.S. armed forces currently lack the strength required to adequately deter potential foes. Having retired in 2013, Mattis technically falls short of the seven-year civilian requirement for the Pentagon post, necessitating a congressional waiver—an exemption not granted since 1950, though lawmakers appeared ready to approve it. 

Following his testimony, the waiver successfully passed its initial legislative test as the Senate Armed Services Committee voted in favor. The broader Senate subsequently endorsed the waiver by a decisive 81 to 17 margin, underscoring the deep backing Mattis commands among lawmakers. 

Mark Cancian, a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, noted that bipartisan backing would likely help Mattis bypass minimal resistance. Cancian added that Mattis is also viewed by some as a potential check against certain extreme tendencies of Trump. 

At age 66, Mattis has reportedly advised Trump behind closed doors to avoid waterboarding, a simulated drowning method used for interrogation that has been widely condemned as torture by human rights organizations, lawmakers, and senior officials. A similar stance was taken on Thursday by Trump's nominee for the CIA, who testified that he would resist the incoming administration if pressured to adopt such enhanced interrogation methods. 

Turning to the Middle East, Mattis delivered harsh criticism of Iran, warning that Tehran was expanding its harmful regional footprint. In written testimony submitted to the panel, he called Iran the primary destabilizing force in the region with policies running counter to U.S. objectives. Nevertheless, Mattis refrained from repeating Trump's campaign threats to scrap the international nuclear agreement under which Iran restricted its atomic program in exchange for sanctions relief. Characterizing the accord as flawed, Mattis maintained that Washington should still adhere to it, asserting that the United States must honor its commitments.

Chaffetz Says Screw Congress, Might Leave Before His Term Is Up (DETAILS)

Jason Chaffetz, the Republican representative from Utah and Chairman of the House Oversight Committee, is apparently reconsidering his future as a federal lawmaker. After already shocking observers by revealing he will not seek another congressional campaign, he has now hinted that he could step down well before his current term concludes.

During a Thursday interview with Doug Wright on KSL News Radio, Chaffetz mentioned that his next steps remain undecided and acknowledged the possibility of an early departure. He noted that he is actively evaluating how Utah would manage a vacancy if he decides to vacate his post prematurely. "I will continue to weigh the options, but I might depart early," he explained to the host, emphasizing that a final choice has not yet been reached.

This followed his Wednesday declaration that he will skip any run for the House or Senate in the upcoming 2018 elections. Even so, he has consistently left the door open for a potential bid for a different position down the road, specifically pointing to the governorship of Utah.

Thus far, his congressional office has not provided an official statement or responded to inquiries seeking comment. Currently in his fifth term, Chaffetz would be eligible under current House GOP guidelines to retain his leadership of the Oversight Committee through 2020, as those rules permit committee leaders to serve up to three terms.

According to Chaffetz, his motivation for potentially walking away from Capitol Hill stems from a desire to be with his family and a readiness to transition back into the private sector. Should he opt for an early exit, a contest to succeed him as the head of the Oversight Committee would immediately begin. At this time, no members of the influential panel have stepped forward publicly to state whether they would pursue the chairmanship.

Characterized by numerous observers as a hate group or a domestic terrorist organization, Black Lives Matter has previously motivated several professional athletes to disrespect the American flag by kneeling during the national anthem. In a surprising turn of events, this organization—frequently accused of fostering animosity toward law enforcement—has apparently gained support from police officers in Cleveland, Ohio. 

The controversy surrounding the anthem protests gained widespread attention when former San Francisco quarterback Colin Kaepernick chose to remain seated during the pre-game performances. Kaepernick's refusal to stand was widely interpreted as an expression of disrespect toward both the flag and the police. Following his departure from San Francisco without receiving a new contract offer to play in the NFL, the quarterback became the focal point of a major dispute. Subsequently, the NAACP partnered with Black Lives Matter to pressure an NFL owner into signing the controversial and struggling player.

Cleveland Browns players have a prior history of exhibiting hostility toward law enforcement. Following the racially charged 2016 Super Bowl halftime performance by Beyoncé, Browns running back Isaiah Crowell shared an inflammatory image on Instagram depicting a police officer being decapitated, though he later issued an apology and the matter was dropped. 

Escalating the protests, multiple Cleveland Browns players have chosen to kneel during the anthem while the remaining attendees and players stand to respect the nation and its flag. This behavior has drawn frustration from local veterans, who never sacrificed for the country to watch it disrespected by these individuals. To express their discontent, these veterans placed a sign outside their facility directed at the protesting players.

Furthering the controversy regarding political correctness, local law enforcement personnel in Cleveland have reportedly aligned with the anti-police movement's method of flag disrespect. As documented by a September 1, 2017, post from Fox & Friends, Cleveland police officers and emergency medical services withdrew from a planned deployment to hold the American flag on the field at a Browns game after 12 players declined to stand for the anthem.

Reports indicate that James Comey, while serving as FBI director, sought to inform the public regarding Russian interference in the 2016 election months prior to the vote, though the Obama administration ultimately prevented him from doing so. 

Information provided to Newsweek suggests that Comey shared a draft opinion piece with senior administration figures during a White House gathering that took place in either June or July. An insider noted that he brought a draft or an outline, holding up a paper during the discussion to ask for opinions on moving forward. Present at this meeting were individuals such as former Secretary of State John Kerry, former Attorney General Loretta Lynch, and former national security adviser Susan Rice.

The proposal was turned down because officials at the White House felt a collective statement involving multiple agencies would carry greater weight than a single perspective. The source explained that an opinion piece lacks the same level of authority since it originates from just one individual.

Another source indicated to Newsweek that the proposed text—which Comey likely intended for publication in the New York Times—featured the identical details that eventually appeared in the January 6 intelligence report regarding Russian President Vladimir Putin's efforts to sway the presidential contest.

This rejection of Comey's draft occurred around the same period he made public statements concerning the investigation into Hillary Clinton's emails. During a House Intelligence Committee hearing, the FBI director confirmed that the agency was actively probing Russian meddling in the 2016 election. 

Describing the hacking of U.S. Democratic party computers to the Intelligence Committee, he remarked that the Russians acted very loudly and unusually conspicuously, adding that it felt as though they remained indifferent to whether their actions were discovered.

He told the anchor that his team simply wanted the network to perform actual journalism, arguing that CNN had abandoned the news business in favor of attacking the president.

She pointed out that Gorka’s team had reached out to request his appearance on the show. He claimed that CNN's obsession with specific topics had caused its viewership ranking to drop to 13th place nationwide, asserting that Nick-at-Nite cartoons draw a larger audience. 

Camerota defended the network's numbers, insisting their ratings were performing adequately. In response, Gorka delivered a final jab, noting that Nick-at-Nite held the 11th position and concluding that viewers had a greater interest in cartoons.

Authorities and a close associate revealed on Tuesday that a Pakistani peace activist vanished in the eastern city of Lahore over the weekend. Raza Mehmood Khan, aged 40, is affiliated with Aghaz-i-Dosti—which translates to Start of Friendship—an organization dedicated to fostering peace between the bitter adversaries Pakistan and India. Rahim-ul-Haq, a friend and colleague, stated that Khan has been unreachable since departing from his residence on Sunday, noting that the organization maintains operations in both nations. According to police official Shehzad Raza, relatives filed a report indicating Khan has been missing since Saturday, though the filing does not point the finger at any specific suspect. Raza confirmed that an investigation is currently underway.

Over the past few months, multiple social media commentators known for speaking out against the military, as well as local extremists and militant factions, have disappeared within Pakistan. Earlier this year, four such individuals reappeared roughly a month following their initial disappearance. Two of these men, namely Ahmad Waqas Goraya and Asim Saeed, subsequently claimed through social media statements and interviews with the BBC that they were seized and subjected to torture by Pakistani intelligence while detained. The Pakistani military has consistently rejected these allegations.

Haq mentioned that Khan participated in a panel discussion on Saturday centered around the issue of extremism. According to Haq, attendees shared their perspectives, and Khan naturally expressed strong criticism during the event. Haq added that Khan's recent social media activity on Facebook featured criticisms directed at the Pakistani military, particularly in the aftermath of a prolonged sit-in demonstration by hard-line groups that brought Islamabad to a standstill for upwards of two weeks. That standoff concluded through a military-brokered pact in which the extremists achieved nearly all their objectives, forcing the resignation of a government minister they targeted with blasphemy accusations.

December 19th might mark the moment 38 courageous electors step forward to rescue the country from Donald Trump's presidency. Typically treated as an afterthought by the general public, that date brings all 538 electors from every state together in Washington D.C. to officially cast their presidential ballots. While electors generally just rubber-stamp the outcomes determined on Election Day, the nation's founders designed the Electoral College specifically to block unqualified demagogues from the Oval Office. Essentially, it serves as the ultimate safeguard should uninformed voters accidentally choose a dangerous candidate for the highest office.

For the very first time in American history, electors possess the opportunity to utilize this exact mechanism. To support and urge the 38 necessary electors to block Trump, a coalition of prominent figures—featuring West Wing star Martin Sheen, M.A.S.H. cast members Loretta Swit and Mike Farrell, and Will & Grace actress Debra Messing, alongside numerous others—has joined forces.

In a newly released video, Sheen and his peers point out that Alexander Hamilton noted in the Federalist Papers that the Electoral College's purpose is ensuring the presidency goes to an individual possessing the requisite qualifications for the job to an eminent degree. Urging these 38 individuals to act heroically and make the proper choice, the video highlights that since Donald Trump fails to meet that standard, the Electoral College must fulfill its original design by selecting an alternative candidate. 

Running since the previous month, an online petition urges electors to follow their consciences instead of permitting Trump to assume office and ruin the nation, having already accumulated nearly five million signatures. Distinct from the petition, however, Sheen and the participating entertainers are not pushing for a vote for Hillary Clinton; rather, they want to prevent Trump from taking power. This objective can be achieved if 38 electors cast their ballots for any alternative, including a different Republican—preferably a reasonable one who will not demolish the government and the nation.

This urgency has intensified following conclusions from the CIA and 17 additional intelligence agencies stating that Russia interfered in the American political system to assist Trump's victory. The Electoral College remains in place precisely as a protection against such scenarios, making it the patriotic duty of the electors to rectify the error of Election Day.
