LOS ANGELES (Reuters) — McDonald’s Corp issued a prompt retraction and removal of a Thursday post from its corporate Twitter feed that heavily criticized President Donald Trump, explaining that hackers had taken over the profile. 

The offending message circulated extensively across the platform via screenshots prior to its removal. The incident occurred just one day after a wave of similar compromises hit verified profiles belonging to prominent news outlets, government bodies, and corporate chief executives. 

Terri Hickey, a spokesperson for McDonald's, released a statement addressing the situation: “Based on our investigation, we have determined that our Twitter account was hacked by an external source. We took swift action to secure it, and we apologize this tweet was sent through our corporate McDonald’s account.”

Because of their massive audiences and the immediate press coverage that mistakes generate, corporate handles frequently draw the attention of malicious actors. Twitter Inc provides two-factor authentication as an optional security layer capable of blocking many unauthorized access attempts. When contacted on Thursday, Twitter declined to provide a statement, pointing to security and privacy policies.

The unauthorized post, published via @McDonaldsCorp during morning hours on Thursday, stated: “@realdonaldtrump You are actually a disgusting excuse of a President and we would love to have @BarackObama back, also you have tiny hands.” The president did not issue any public response to the post through his own feed.

Just a day prior, numerous prominent accounts fell victim to a series of Turkish-language anti-Nazi posts amid rising diplomatic tensions between Turkey, Germany, and the Netherlands. Twitter reported that a third-party application served as the vector for that breach, prompting the company to revoke the app's access permissions.

President Trump, widely known for his affinity for fast food, previously shared images of himself consuming meals from McDonald's and competing chains during his presidential run. Furthermore, a 2002 television advertisement featured Trump alongside the company's Grimace character to promote a budget-friendly price point for the now-retired Big N’ Tasty sandwich. 

This security breach arrives as the six-decade-old fast-food corporation invests in technological upgrades, introducing kiosk and mobile ordering platforms to update its operations. 

Industry analysts noted that while the hack cast doubt on Twitter's platform security, the fallout for the restaurant chain itself is expected to remain minimal. 

Mike Froggatt, intelligence director at the brand tracking firm L2, observed: “As long as Trump doesn’t tweet at them directly, which could be pretty disastrous, this will be a short-term thing for them.” He added, “Twitter trending topics last for maybe 6 hours, a backlash for 10 to 12 hours and then it goes and the herd moves on.”

The provocative statement from the globe's biggest restaurant brand quickly went viral, generating widespread amusement, commentary, and archived screenshots among users. 

Some commentators, including Vanessa Veasley, pointed out potential reactions from the president's base, drawing comparisons to a previous boycott threat directed at Starbucks Corp after its CEO promised to employ a large number of refugees following a presidential executive order restricting refugee entry. 

“McDonald’s already deleted the tweet? lol Well at least Trump supporters can finally boycott something they can actually afford,” Veasley posted under the handle @VanessaVeasley. 

Conversely, other consumers voiced support for the company, which has recently worked to counteract consecutive years of declining visitor numbers. “Suddenly I want a Big Mac, well done @McDonalds,” wrote Shay Steward Bouley via @blackgirlinmain. 

Meanwhile, various supporters of the president argued that the apology fell short and called for economic retaliation against the brand. “Hey @McDonaldsCorp YOU can’t just undo a tweet!!! Since you don’t support America, Americans will not support YOU!!! #BoycottMcDonalds,” posted user Deborah Brewer under the handle @Debbie92083.

McDonald's is far from the first major enterprise to experience an unauthorized corporate profile takeover; previous victims of similar incidents include Sony Music, Jeep, and Burger King.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — In a report released Friday that accompanied its funding legislation for the State Department, a key Senate panel strongly criticized the Trump administration's foreign policy strategy, arguing that the approach diminishes America's global influence. 

The unanimous 31-0 vote by the Senate Appropriations Committee on Thursday advanced a spending bill providing over $51 billion for foreign operations and the State Department—an amount falling nearly $11 billion higher than the total requested by President Donald Trump's administration. The accompanying report published Friday took aim at the administration's proposal to slash funding for these areas by 30 percent compared to the fiscal year concluding on September 30, 2017.

The document emphasized that insights gained following September 11, 2001, demonstrate that military might alone cannot sustain U.S. power and determination internationally, noting that firepower and combat technology cannot substitute for developmental efforts and diplomacy. Furthermore, the report asserted that the administration's apparent philosophy of withdrawal—which features a distancing of the U.S. from multilateral and collective mechanisms for resolving disputes—serves exclusively to diminish the nation's international standing.

Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, who chairs the subcommittee on State and Foreign Operations responsible for drafting the measure, mentioned on Thursday that he had requested additional specifics from the White House regarding its budget proposals, adding that they received no response. Meanwhile, Senator Patrick Leahy, the senior Democrat on the subcommittee, described the diplomatic and developmental functions of the State Department as entirely indispensable.

Ever since its publication earlier in the year, the administration's budget proposal has faced fierce criticism from both Democratic lawmakers and numerous members of Trump's own party, particularly given that Congress holds the constitutional authority over federal spending rather than the executive branch. Conversely, the administration maintains that the State Department would achieve greater effectiveness through streamlined management, contending that reductions in other sectors are necessary to support a substantial expansion of military expenditure.

Enactment of the committee's bill remains far from guaranteed, as it still requires approval by the full Senate, harmonization with a corresponding measure from the House of Representatives, and either a presidential signature from Trump or the accumulation of sufficient votes to overcome a veto. 

Additionally, the Senate panel's legislation diverged from the administration's agenda in other aspects, such as endorsing financial support for the United Nations climate organization and declining to impose bans on funding for international entities that offer abortion services or counseling. Nevertheless, these provisions face a difficult path in the House. While the Republican party holds majorities in both legislative chambers, conservative members who hold deep skepticism toward climate change and strong opposition to abortion wield greater influence in the House than in the Senate.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — Hours before delivering the final State of the Union speech of his tenure, President Barack Obama remarked during a television appearance that he could picture Donald Trump delivering such an address, though only within the context of a comedy routine. 

Appearing alongside Vice President Joe Biden in interviews broadcast Tuesday on NBC's "Today" program, the Democratic president was questioned about whether he could visualize the real-estate mogul and Republican contender eventually standing at the podium as commander-in-chief. 

"Well, I can imagine it - in a 'Saturday Night' skit," Obama remarked, alluding to NBC's staple late-night sketch program, "Saturday Night Live." He added, "Look, anything’s possible. And I think, you know, we shouldn’t be complacent."

Biden adopted a more cautious tone, declining to dismiss the possibility of a Trump win in the upcoming November presidential race. "Yes, I think it’s possible," Biden stated, expressing a wish that a President Trump would subsequently become "a lot more serious about the issues."

"He is divisive – I think he’d have to acknowledge that he’s very divisive – and that’s not healthy," according to Biden, who also noted, "We always do best when we act as one America. We always do poorly when we appeal to our fears and our differences."

During the conversation, which was recorded on Monday, Obama admitted disappointment over falling short of his objective to bring Americans together, particularly within the nation's capital. Nevertheless, he expressed doubt that the electorate would ultimately embrace Trump's polarized tactics.

"I’m pretty confident that the overwhelming majority of Americans are looking for the kind of politics that does feed our hopes and not our fears, that does work together and doesn’t try to divide is that isn’t looking for simplistic solutions and scapegoating," Obama said.

Trump, known for frequently employing racially charged language, has proposed the deportation of every undocumented immigrant and advocated for a complete prohibition on Muslims entering the United States back in December. Additional coverage of the 2016 presidential contest can be found on the Reuters blog, “Tales from the Trail.”

The nation's highest court has declined to support what critics describe as extreme GOP voter suppression and racism. Specifically, the Supreme Court recently let stand a lower court decision finding that a pair of North Carolina congressional maps from the 2011 redistricting cycle were unconstitutional racial gerrymanders, ordering that the boundaries be redrawn within a fortnight. 

According to Raw Story, the federal judicial panel prohibited holding elections in the predominantly Black 1st and 12th districts until fresh maps receive approval. These developments arrive just ahead of the state's congressional primaries, which are scheduled for March 15.

Political analysts suggest this could be the beginning of a larger trend for the Republican Party. Following their 2010 electoral gains, the GOP swiftly enacted strict voter identification requirements, closed down polling locations, shortened voting windows, and aggressively altered district lines. Facing a declining demographic among their older base, these measures were implemented to maintain electoral viability through map manipulation.

These strategies depended heavily on a Supreme Court largely disinclined to intervene in voter suppression cases unless they were flagrant. However, following the passing of Antonin Scalia, the ideological balance of the bench is expected to shift leftward, potentially paving the way for additional challenges to Republican-drawn maps. Legal precedents of this nature could compel the creation of fairer districts, potentially jeopardizing the party's majority in the House of Representatives.

This prospect explains the intense anxiety among conservatives regarding the vacancy on the high court. As the judiciary begins to dismantle these voting restrictions, observers anticipate increasingly frantic reactions from the political right.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — According to an individual familiar with the plan, the White House is seeking to reduce the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s funding by a quarter, zeroing in on initiatives aimed at combating climate change and tackling hazards like lead in air and water. While Donald Trump has frequently expressed his desire to dismantle Barack Obama's climate policies, the Republican commander-in-chief has maintained that his rollbacks of environmental rules would preserve clean air and water. 

The draft 2018 budget document spans 23 pages and seeks to lower the agency's total funding to $6.1 billion—a 25 percent reduction—while decreasing personnel by 20 percent down to 12,400 positions. These reductions, intended to help finance a boost in military spending, would significantly impact enforcement, environmental justice, and climate defense initiatives. While other media organizations such as Politico had previously broken the news regarding the overall funding and staffing cuts, the source provided specifics concerning the effects on state grants and particular programs. 

The proposed reductions drew immediate criticism from environmental advocates, though any changes require the backing of a Congress controlled by Republicans. Neither the EPA nor the White House provided immediate statements when asked for comment regarding the budget plan. 

The document, delivered to the agency during the week, details a 30 percent reduction to state grants for lead remediation, bringing them down to $9.8 million, the source revealed to Reuters after reviewing the paperwork. Similarly, grants assisting Native American tribes with pollution reduction would drop by 30 percent to $45.8 million. A climate initiative focused on lowering greenhouse gas emissions, including methane, would face a 70 percent reduction, leaving it with $29 million. 

Furthermore, the brownfields program dedicated to cleaning up industrial properties would see its budget shrink by 42 percent to $14.7 million. Funding dedicated to policing pollution regulations would decrease by 11 percent to $153 million. However, the spending plan left state revolving funds untouched—the same funding sources Congress utilized previously to assist Flint, Michigan, during its lead water emergency. 

Every employee attached to the Global Change Research initiative, alongside 35 other programs, would be eliminated under the blueprint. Certain elements of the plan are viewed as improbable to clear the Republican-dominated legislature due to bipartisan support. For instance, lawmakers are not expected to support terminating the entire staff of a diesel emissions reduction initiative. 

Newly installed EPA Administrator Scott Pruitt addressed mayors on Thursday, stating that upgrading water infrastructure and remediating hazardous waste sites would remain central focuses for him, despite the steep reductions suggested by the administration. Pruitt acknowledged ongoing discussions with lawmakers over historical grant initiatives, noting that he is actively conveying to both the White House and Capitol Hill the critical importance of the Superfund, brownfields, water grants, and state revolving funds. 

Travis Nichols, representing Greenpeace, criticized the discrepancy, noting that Trump frequently highlighted the agency's shortcomings in Flint during his campaign, yet the current proposal slashes lead remediation funds by nearly a third, calling it a hollow commitment to the public. 

Meanwhile, representatives from the Environmental Council of the States—representing state-level regulators—expressed apprehension to the administration regarding a budget formulation they felt excluded input from the states directly impacted. Council leaders planned discussions with the Office of Management and Budget's environmental team on Friday, alongside a scheduled call with Pruitt in March. Alexandra Dapolito Dunn, who leads ECOS, noted that state officials had felt optimistic following Pruitt's confirmation hearings regarding receiving adequate operating resources, but now felt deeply exposed.

BEREA, Ohio (Reuters) - Following a crucial triumph on home turf, Ohio Governor John Kasich is launching the next phase of his long-shot presidential bid. His campaign team hopes this momentum will carry him past Republican front-runner Donald Trump by forcing an uncommon contested convention. Tuesday's primary win in Ohio, coupled with U.S. Senator Marco Rubio's exit from the race, leaves Kasich as the party establishment's final hope to block the New York billionaire from securing the Republican presidential nomination for the November 8 general election. Both Trump and his closest competitor, Texas U.S. Senator Ted Cruz, face deep unpopularity among mainstream Republican figures.

Addressing supporters at a rally near Cleveland, the 63-year-old Kasich declared, "I want you to know, the campaign goes on." Taking aim at Trump's aggressive campaign style, he added, "I will not take the low road to the highest office in the land." 

Trump, aged 69, secured victories in Florida, Illinois, and North Carolina on Tuesday, and MSNBC projected him as the winner of a tight contest against Cruz in Missouri. However, dropping the winner-take-all contest in Ohio—which offered 66 delegates—makes it harder for Trump to reach the 1,237 delegates required to lock up the nomination ahead of the July convention in Cleveland. Because most remaining contests award delegates proportionally, Kasich’s strategists believe he can prevail at a convention where no single candidate holds a majority. 

"The plan is to win Ohio, and some other states, and if that happens, nobody is going to have enough delegates to win the nomination on the first ballot," explained John Weaver, Kasich’s chief campaign strategist, whose past experience includes managing the unsuccessful presidential bids of Republican Senator John McCain in 2000 and 2008.

According to his campaign staff, Kasich intends to use this momentum to secure additional endorsements from party establishment figures and major Republican donors. Riding this wave, he aims for further triumphs in upcoming primary contests across states like Pennsylvania, Maryland, Wisconsin, Connecticut, and California, where campaign advisers feel the electorate is more receptive to his brand of moderate conservatism. 

To secure the nomination and face Democratic hopefuls Hillary Clinton or Bernie Sanders in November, a Republican contender must capture a majority of the 2,472 total delegates. Following Tuesday's races—excluding the Missouri results—Trump leads the pack with 619 delegates, followed by Cruz at 394 and Kasich with 136. If no contender hits the required threshold before the final primary on June 7, the convention will almost certainly be contested, a rare occurrence in modern history that would highlight deep divisions within the party. No major party convention has gone past the first ballot since 1952.

While Kasich holds virtually no chance of gathering enough delegates to win outright—Ohio remains his sole primary victory—he aims to block Trump from achieving a majority. He could then present himself to convention delegates as a more electable alternative to both Trump and Cruz, a 45-year-old conservative evangelical who currently stands as Trump's most formidable Republican challenger.

Evidence of the party establishment rallying behind Kasich emerged this week. Mitt Romney, the 2002 Republican presidential nominee who recently denounced Trump as a "fraud" in a sharp speech, joined Kasich on the campaign trail in Ohio on Monday. 

"He has the kind of record that you want in Washington," Romney stated in North Canton, Ohio, standing alongside Kasich, whose resume includes 18 years as a U.S. congressman and six years as governor. "You look at this guy, and unlike the other people running, he has a real track record."

Kasich's schedule on Wednesday brings him to a campaign event in Pennsylvania, followed by three stops on Friday in Utah, where the former Massachusetts governor enjoys strong backing among local Republicans. Utah, holding 40 delegates, is set to vote on March 27, while Pennsylvania participates in a five-state primary on April 26.

Ford O’Connell, an unaligned Republican strategist, noted that Kasich's home-state victory should attract more backing from party insiders. "There are really just two options left: Either Trump gets enough delegates, or nobody does," O’Connell observed. "Kasich’s win in Ohio means Trump must now win roughly 60 percent of the remaining delegates before the convention. I would say we now have a 50-50 chance of a brokered convention." 

O’Connell also pointed out that under Republican regulations, a contender needs a clear overall majority of primary votes to secure the nomination. Republican primary history features numerous examples of candidates who managed a plurality of votes rather than a majority and ultimately missed out on the nomination. 

Kasich's campaign advisers are drawing inspiration from past primary battles, specifically pointing to Wendell Willkie’s road to the 1940 Republican nomination. In that contest, three front-runners—Robert Taft, Thomas Dewey, and Arthur Vandenberg—all arrived at the convention short of the delegates needed to win. Willkie, a businessman and former Democrat who had never previously sought public office, opposed the party's isolationist wing and backed Britain's war efforts. His campaign gathered significant momentum following the Nazi blitzkrieg across Europe in May 1940. By the sixth ballot, delegates from Pennsylvania, New York, and Michigan abandoned other candidates to back Willkie, handing him the nomination. 

Trump, Cruz, and Kasich could encounter a parallel scenario this year, which would compel them to lobby delegates directly on the convention floor until one secures a majority. 

"A lot of people who do not want Trump have been sitting back to see how Kasich and Rubio do in their home states on Tuesday," remarked Republican strategist Charlie Black, who signed on as a Kasich adviser on Tuesday night.

An Air France journey traveling from Paris to Los Angeles was forced to touch down in eastern Canada on Saturday following a major malfunction affecting one of its four engines while flying over the Atlantic Ocean, according to the carrier. Air France confirmed that Flight 66, which departed from Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport, touched down safely at Goose Bay in Labrador at 1542 GMT, adding that all passengers and crew members emerged uninjured. 

In an official statement, the airline praised the flight deck and cabin personnel, stating they managed the severe situation with flawless execution. Data from the aircraft tracking site airfleets.net indicated that the plane was an Airbus 380 with an age of approximately seven years. Propulsion for the aircraft was provided by an Engine Alliance powerplant, which is a collaborative enterprise involving General Electric Co and the Pratt & Whitney division of United Technologies Corp.

This unscheduled landing in Canada's easternmost province bears similarities to an event from seven years prior, when a Qantas A380 experienced mid-air engine failure following a departure from Singapore due to issues with a Rolls Royce powerplant. That previous occurrence in November 2010 resulted in a temporary suspension of operations for the entire Qantas A380 fleet—consisting of six aircraft at that point—which lasted for more than three weeks. 

Shortly after the plane came to a halt, pictures captured by individuals traveling on the Air France service began spreading across the web. The photographs seemed to display the front inlet section of the powerplant completely detached, though the core of the engine appeared to remain in place. 

Passenger Rick Engebretsen shared details via a post on Twitter, reporting that he experienced a significant vibration accompanied by a loud bang during the flight. The exact cause of the engine trouble has not yet been determined. Representatives for Airbus were not reachable for immediate comment regarding the situation. Meanwhile, Engine Alliance released a statement noting that they are currently examining the reported problems associated with one of their powerplants. 

Authorities with the Transportation Safety Board of Canada were similarly unavailable for remarks on Saturday. The carrier indicated that plans are underway to transport the stranded passengers onward to their final destination in Los Angeles. Goose Bay Airport, located in the province of Newfoundland and Labrador, is frequently utilized by aircraft performing trans-Atlantic crossings when emergency refueling is required.

Additional reporting from The Independent indicates that kill-or-capture missions managed from the Balad base, located 50 miles (80 km) north of Baghdad, formed a lesser-known component of Britain's shadow war. Despite capturing or killing up to 3,500 insurgents, these operations under General Stanley McChrystal—which marked a pivot from searching for weapons of mass destruction to intensive man-hunting—generated significant friction. A senior commander with a background in the SAS questioned why British forces were participating with what he termed Latin American-style death squads. Disagreements over these tactics resulted in UK personnel being excluded from certain missions, formal complaints lodged by a British SAS commander against US authorities, and the eventual ostracization of an SAS colonel who served under McChrystal.

The Chilcot Report touches upon these growing strategic divergences, noting that US and UK approaches separated after Britain concentrated its efforts on Multi-National Division South East (MND-SE) in the British-run zone starting in 2003. According to the 2.6-million-word document, this led to differing priorities, leaving the UK only marginally engaged in stabilizing Baghdad and managing sectarian divisions, while prioritizing calm conditions in Basra to facilitate an eventual withdrawal. Consequently, American leadership grew increasingly worried that the UK was primarily seeking a quick exit from an unpopular war.

In 2006, former SAS soldier Ben Griffin spoke out about tactics used around Baghdad before being silenced by UK court injunctions. He told the Telegraph that American forces employed a sweeping approach to detaining suspects through draconian and ineffective methods, which included sending local farmers to Abu Ghraib or transferring them to Iraqi authorities despite the known risk of torture. Observers have also pointed out that the SAS commander's invocation of Latin American-style death squads coincided with the UK stepping up its own training programs for Colombian paramilitary forces in July 2003. At that time, Amnesty International criticized these actions, warning that the absence of implemented UN human rights recommendations by the Colombian government meant military assistance effectively condoned ongoing army abuses.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — Returning to the Senate floor on Tuesday, Democratic presidential candidate Bernie Sanders launched a sharp attack against a White House-supported measure addressing Puerto Rico’s economic emergency, describing the legislation as the height of "colonialism." 

The Vermont independent, whose grassroots White House campaign focused heavily on fighting economic disparity, cautioned lawmakers that the bill facing a vital vote on Wednesday would impose GOP trickle-down policies on the territory while benefiting predatory investors over vulnerable, struggling residents. According to a staff member, this marked Sanders's initial Senate address since the month of December.

During an eight-minute speech backing a prolonged address by New Jersey Democratic Senator Robert Menendez against the measure, Sanders expressed outrage, asking whether such principles belonged in the U.S. Senate. The democratic socialist targeted specific provisions of the bill, which establishes a seven-member control board to oversee Puerto Rico and mandates that the territory cover $370 million in administrative expenses over five years, all while reducing budgets for pensions, healthcare, and schools.

During a discussion with Menendez, Sanders expressed disbelief over the price tag of the board's administration, remarking that the figure seemed so ridiculous people might suspect he was exaggerating, before asking his colleague if he agreed the situation represented extreme colonialism. Menendez answered in the affirmative.

The legislation had already cleared the Republican-led House and encountered resistance from senators across both political parties. Even so, the White House and GOP congressional leaders pushed for approval ahead of a July 1 deadline, at which point the territory faces a $1.9 billion debt payment as part of its total $70 billion liability. Sanders had stated the previous week that he would support presumptive Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton in the upcoming November election against Donald Trump.

During a Friday evening broadcast on CNN, a campaign surrogate for Donald Trump found himself the target of open mockery from the anchor and fellow guests after defending the candidate's claims regarding Hillary Clinton and firearms. 

Earlier in the day, the Republican hopeful addressed members of the National Rifle Association in an effort to secure their endorsement, during which he criticized Clinton's stance on the Second Amendment. Later, campaign adviser Stephen Miller appeared on the network to reiterate those talking points, leading to a tense and chaotic segment.

Anchor Don Lemon directly challenged the assertion that the Democratic contender intended to dismantle the Second Amendment, noting that numerous fact-checkers, along with the campaign itself, had thoroughly debunked the claim. Lemon pressed the adviser on why the campaign persisted in repeating the statement.

Before Miller could fully assert that the claim was factual, the entire panel—including the host—burst into open laughter. 

Regaining his composure, Miller attempted to justify the argument by pointing to the landmark Supreme Court case *District of Columbia v. Heller*, which struck down local bans on handgun registration and carrying unregistered firearms. He argued that reversing this ruling would effectively nullify the Second Amendment entirely.

Panelist Sally Kohn quickly pushed back against that logic, pointing out that various firearm regulations existed long before the *Heller* ruling. Kohn also reminded viewers that even the late conservative Justice Antonin Scalia acknowledged that the Constitution permits certain reasonable limitations and controls on firearms.

Texas Senator John Cornyn faced severe backlash online after directing criticism toward Special Counsel Robert Mueller amid the ongoing investigation into Russia. As pressure mounts from the probe, GOP lawmakers have increasingly targeted both Mueller and the FBI. 

The friction began Friday when former Attorney General Eric Holder issued a stern warning on Twitter, declaring that any effort by congressional Republicans to oust Bob Mueller would face fierce opposition from the overwhelming majority of citizens. Cornyn quickly responded by quote-tweeting Holder with the brief rebuke, "You don't. You don't."

When Bloomberg journalist Steven Dennis suggested on Saturday that Cornyn's primary grievance seemed directed at Holder rather than Mueller himself, the Texas Republican clarified his stance. Cornyn posted that the Special Counsel still needed to remove partisan actors from his team.

Greg Sargent of The Washington Post then pressed the senator on whether he would ultimately recognize the conclusions of the Mueller investigation. Cornyn replied that it would be wise to review the findings before passing judgment.

Meanwhile, social media users swiftly condemned Cornyn's remarks and broader GOP efforts to undermine the investigation. Numerous accounts threatened to mobilize against him and fellow Texas Senator Ted Cruz in upcoming elections. Commenters accused Cornyn of shielding the administration, with one user warning that attempting to dismiss Mueller would guarantee a swift end to his political career. Others echoed Holder's sentiment, emphasizing that the public expects accountability and warning that history would judge uncooperative lawmakers harshly.

During a Sunday appearance on CNN, GOP Senator Tom Cotton conceded that the newly proposed Republican healthcare overhaul will fail to reduce insurance costs for working-class citizens. The legislation, designed to dismantle the Affordable Care Act, has faced severe criticism from lawmakers across the political spectrum. Although President Donald Trump has praised the measure, the public has expressed widespread anger over projections that tens of millions could lose coverage and face drastically higher medical expenses, particularly seniors and low-income families.

During the broadcast, CNN anchor Jake Tapper pressed Cotton on the future of the Medicaid expansion, noting that Arkansas—Cotton's home state—ranks among the poorest in the country. In response, Cotton advocated for a complete restructuring of Medicaid to exclude healthy adults, suggesting they secure employment to cover their medical needs. Critics have pointed out, however, that a significant portion of Medicaid recipients are indeed employed, yet earn wages too low to purchase private coverage. 

Later in the discussion, Cotton acknowledged the shortcomings of the Republican package regarding the private market. He stated that the legislation falls short of lowering monthly premiums for Americans, describing the House proposal as only a partial fix and admitting that it fails to solve the primary issue of affordability in the private insurance sector.
